Abstract.
Continuing our previous work on the integral Arnold conjecture [14], we establish the foundation of Hamiltonian Floer theory over integer coefficients on any compact symplectic manifold. This package produces a well-defined chain homotopy class of Floer complexes, chain-level continuation maps, the Piunikhin–Salamon–Schwarz (PSS) isomorphism, and an associative pair-of-pants product. When the Hamiltonian is the 𝗉{\sf p}-th iteration for a prime number 𝗉{\sf p}, we also establish the ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant Floer theory in characteristic 𝗉{\sf p}, including the equivariant Floer complex and the ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant pair-of-pants product. Moreover, we define quantum Steenrod operations for any compact symplectic manifold and compare them with the equivariant pair-of-pants products via the ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant PSS map. We also obtain chain-level invariants such as spectral numbers and barcodes and prove quantitative properties of the equivariant pair-of-pants product.
The counting theory is based on Fukaya–Ono’s normally polynomial perturbation scheme [29] and its realization by the authors in [13], termed FOP perturbations, adapted in the abstract setting of flow categories, flow multimodules, and homotopies of flow bimodules. Along the way, we construct global Kuranishi charts for the relevant moduli spaces following Abouzaid–McLean–Smith’s framework and its adaptation to the Hamiltonian Floer setting due to the authors, which may be of independent interest.

1. Introduction
Floer theory is one of the most influential discoveries in geometry and topology. In symplectic topology, the Hamiltonian Floer homology [24] provides a powerful framework for studying Hamiltonian dynamics. Most notably, it leads to proofs of various versions of the famous Arnold conjecture [6]. Several variations, such as quantitative Floer theory and local Floer theory, played important roles in many other applications in Hamiltonian dynamics.
The development of Floer homology was accompanied by the advancement of the understanding of pseudoholomorphic curves [32] and regularizations of their moduli spaces. In earlier works [24][35][50] where certain vanishing or positivity conditions were assumed, when defining the Floer complexes, one only needs to consider moduli spaces of virtual dimensions at most one; one can achieve transversality of such moduli spaces by perturbing geometrically and can obtain Floer complexes with coefficients in ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}. When the semipositivity condition was removed, there is no known way to achieve transversality via geometric perturbations without imposing further conditions (cf. [20]). The abstract perturbation methods used in [43][30][36][53] require one to regularize the moduli spaces via Kuranishi models or polyfolds and to apply virtual perturbations or integrations. One then has to deal with moduli spaces of negative virtual dimensions and to organize all the constructions in a compatible way which can be formalized using Cohen–Jones–Segal’s notion of flow categories [22]. The lack of geometric transversality is closely intertwined with the orbispace structure of the moduli spaces, which naturally leads to fractional counts of curves and chain-level structures only defined over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}.
The main purpose of the current work is to extend Floer theory from rational to integer coefficients for general closed symplectic manifolds. In [14] we have already established a portion of the integral Floer theory which provides a proof of the Arnold conjecture over ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}. The motivation to go beyond the scope of [14], besides a complete package of the integral Hamiltonian Floer theory, resides in the potential applications in Hamiltonian dynamics. For this purpose, we will construct quantum Steenrod operations for general symplectic manifolds (see [72][59][61][62] under semipositivity or stronger assumptions). In an upcoming joint work with Shelukhin and Wilkins [12], we will extend many dynamical applications (see [63][64][65][21][7]) of quantum Steenrod operations to greater generality.
The integral extension is possible due to the recent developments in the virtual technique. The most crucial idea was given by Fukaya–Ono [29]. Roughly speaking, the moduli spaces carry natural stable complex structures, which allow a specific type of single-valued perturbations (normally polynomial perturbations) resulting in well-defined integer counts. Fukaya–Ono discussed the original idea for a local Kuranishi model, while B. Parker [54] further explored strategies to globalize. In [13] we provide a rigorous treatment of Fukaya–Ono’s proposal and define the so-called “FOP transversality condition” for normally polynomial perturbations.
Another crucial concurrent development is the Abouzaid–McLean–Smith construction of global Kuranishi charts (see [3, 34, 4]). This new technique helps avoid the complicated inductive arguments involving multiple charts (such as having good coordinate systems [25]). Meanwhile, the smoothing argument of [3] replaces the hard analytic approach [28] by a soft topological approach. These novel ideas helped significantly in the case of Hamiltonian Floer theory. One of the main challenges in Floer theory is to carry out AMS construction for infinitely many moduli spaces compatibly.
We hope that the foundational work laid in this paper can serve as a useful package for applications of Floer theory to Hamiltonian dynamics on general compact symplectic manifolds. Our joint paper with Shelukhin and Wilkins [12] showcases how the technical work done here can efficiently lead to interesting statements for Hamiltonian maps on general compact symplectic manifolds. Meanwhile, we hope the technical procedures can serve as a model to be adopted in other situations such as in Lagrangian Floer theory or contact topology.
Our main results fall into three parts:
(1)
Integral Hamiltonian Floer theory at the chain level (Theorems A—G).
(2)
Equivariant Floer theory and quantum Steenrod operations (Theorems H—J).
(3)
Quantitative refinements, including spectral invariants and barcodes (Theorems K—M) as well as results about Floer complexes of homologically nontrivial orbits (Theorem 1.11 and Theorem 1.12).
Below we state these main results in a way that readers can directly cite.
1.1. Main results on Floer complexes
1.1.1. Floer complexes and Floer homology
First and foremost, by applying the FOP perturbation scheme to the moduli spaces of Floer trajectories, we construct a Floer complex with integer coefficients, which is well-defined up to chain homotopy equivalence. Under certain restrictions of the Hamiltonian, such a complex was constructed by the authors [14] without proving the homotopy equivalence between different choices.
We start by recalling the basic setup. Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a compact symplectic manifold. Let
Π:=π2​(X)ker⁡(ω)∩ker⁡(c1),\Pi:=\frac{\pi_{2}(X)}{{\rm ker}(\omega)\cap{\rm ker}(c_{1})},
(1.1)
which is a finitely generated free abelian group. Let ΛΠ\Lambda^{\Pi} be the Novikov ring with integer coefficients:
ΛΠ={∑i=1∞aiTAi|ai∈ℤ,Ai∈Π,limi→∞ω(Ai)=+∞}.\Lambda^{\Pi}=\Big\{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}a_{i}T^{A_{i}}\ |\ a_{i}\in{\mathbb{Z}},\ A_{i}\in\Pi,\ \lim_{i\to\infty}\omega(A_{i})=+\infty\Big\}.
(1.2)
If HH is a nondegenerate 1-periodic Hamiltonian generating a 1-periodic family of Hamiltonian vector fields XHtX_{H_{t}}, a 1-periodic orbit is a map x:S1→Xx:S^{1}\to X solving
x′​(t)=XHt​(x⁡(t)).x^{\prime}(t)=X_{H_{t}}(x(t)).

|p|:=12​dimℝ​X−CZ⁡(p).|p|:=\frac{1}{2}{\rm dim}_{\mathbb{R}}X-{\rm CZ}(p).
Let 𝒪⁡(H){\mathcal{O}}(H) be the set of all contractible 1-periodic orbits and 𝒪~​(H)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(H) be the set of all capped 1-periodic orbits.
Theorem A (Floer chain complex).
Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a compact symplectic manifold. Let HH be a nondegenerate 1-periodic Hamiltonian. Then for each 11-periodic family of ω\omega-compatible almost complex structures JJ and a certain choice Ξ\Xi, there is a ΛℤΠ\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\Pi}-linear differential on the chain group
CF∗(H):={∑i=1∞aipi|ai∈ℤ,pi∈𝒪~(H),limi→∞𝒜H(pi)=−∞}CF_{*}(H):=\Big\{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}a_{i}p_{i}\ |\ a_{i}\in{\mathbb{Z}},\ p_{i}\in\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(H),\ \lim_{i\to\infty}{\mathcal{A}}_{H}(p_{i})=-\infty\Big\}
(which has the structure of a module over ΛΠ\Lambda^{\Pi}), making it a chain complex of finitely generated free ΛΠ\Lambda^{\Pi}-modules
C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ,ΛΠ)CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi;\Lambda^{\Pi})
with a ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-grading defined by the Conley–Zehnder index. Moreover, the chain homotopy type of C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ,ΛΠ)CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi;\Lambda^{\Pi}) does not depend on the choice Ξ\Xi.
Next we establish the continuation map with expected properties.
Theorem B (Continuation Map).
Let (H1,J1,Ξ1)(H_{1},J_{1},\Xi_{1}) and (H2,J2,Ξ2)(H_{2},J_{2},\Xi_{2}) be two triples such that the Floer chain complexes
C​F∗​(H1,J1,Ξ1,ΛΠ),\displaystyle\ CF_{*}(H_{1},J_{1},\Xi_{1};\Lambda^{\Pi}),\
C​F∗​(H2,J2,Ξ2,ΛΠ)\displaystyle\ CF_{*}(H_{2},J_{2},\Xi_{2};\Lambda^{\Pi})
are defined.
(1)
There exists a ΛΠ\Lambda^{\Pi}-linear chain homotopy equivalence, called the continuation map
Φ12​(Θ):C​F∗​(H1,J1,Ξ1,ΛΠ)→C​F∗​(H2,J2,Ξ2,ΛΠ)\Phi^{12}(\Theta):CF_{*}(H_{1},J_{1},\Xi_{1};\Lambda^{\Pi})\to CF_{*}(H_{2},J_{2},\Xi_{2};\Lambda^{\Pi})
whose definition further depends on a system of choices Θ\Theta.
(2)
The chain homotopy class of the continuation map does not depend on the system of choices Θ\Theta.
(3)
For (H1,J1,Ξ1)=(H2,J2,Ξ2)(H_{1},J_{1},\Xi_{1})=(H_{2},J_{2},\Xi_{2}), any continuation map is homotopic to the identity map of C​F∗​(H1,J1,Ξ1,ΛΠ)CF_{*}(H_{1},J_{1},\Xi_{1};\Lambda^{\Pi}).11
1
However we do not know if the identity map on the Floer chain complex can be realized as a continuation map.
(4)
If (H3,J3,Ξ3)(H_{3},J_{3},\Xi_{3}) is another triple for which the complex C​F∗​(H3,J3,Ξ3,ΛΠ)CF_{*}(H_{3},J_{3},\Xi_{3};\Lambda^{\Pi}) is defined, and
Φ23​(Θ′):C​F∗​(H2,J2,Ξ2,ΛΠ)→C​F∗​(H3,J3,Ξ3,ΛΠ)\Phi^{23}(\Theta^{\prime}):CF_{*}(H_{2},J_{2},\Xi_{2};\Lambda^{\Pi})\to CF_{*}(H_{3},J_{3},\Xi_{3};\Lambda^{\Pi})
is a continuation map. Then the composition Φ23​(Θ′)∘Φ12​(Θ)\Phi^{23}(\Theta^{\prime})\circ\Phi^{12}(\Theta) is homotopic to a continuation map from C​F∗​(H1,J1,Ξ1,ΛΠ)CF_{*}(H_{1},J_{1},\Xi_{1};\Lambda^{\Pi}) to C​F∗​(H3,J3,Ξ3,ΛΠ)CF_{*}(H_{3},J_{3},\Xi_{3};\Lambda^{\Pi}).
Theorem A and Theorem B lead to the definition of a canonical object
H​F∗​(X,ω,ΛΠ)HF_{*}(X,\omega;\Lambda^{\Pi})
which we call the integral Floer homology of (X,ω)(X,\omega).
1.1.2. Pair-of-pants product
Next we consider the pair-of-pants product.
Theorem C (Pair-of-pants product).
Let (Hi,Ji,Ξi)(H_{i},J_{i},\Xi_{i}), i=1,2,3i=1,2,3 be triples for which the Floer chain complexes are defined as stated in Theorem A. Then there is a ΛΠ\Lambda^{\Pi}-linear chain map
C​F∗​(H1,J1,Ξ1,ΛΠ)​⊗ΛΠ​C​F∗​(H2,J2,Ξ2,ΛΠ)→C​F∗​(H3,J3,Ξ3,ΛΠ)CF_{*}(H_{1},J_{1},\Xi_{1};\Lambda^{\Pi})\underset{\Lambda^{\Pi}}{\otimes}CF_{*}(H_{2},J_{2},\Xi_{2};\Lambda^{\Pi})\to CF_{*}(H_{3},J_{3},\Xi_{3};\Lambda^{\Pi})
(1.4)
of degree −12​dim​X-\frac{1}{2}{\rm dim}X whose definition depends on a system of choices. Moreover, the chain map satisfies the following properties.
(1)
The homotopy class of (1.4) is independent of the choices.
(2)
This chain map is compatible with continuation maps. Hence it induces a canonical linear map
H​F∗​(X,ω,ΛΠ)​⊗ΛΠ​H​F∗​(X,ω,ΛΠ)→H​F∗​(X,ω,ΛΠ)HF_{*}(X,\omega;\Lambda^{\Pi})\underset{\Lambda^{\Pi}}{\otimes}HF_{*}(X,\omega;\Lambda^{\Pi})\to HF_{*}(X,\omega;\Lambda^{\Pi})
called the pair-of-pants product.
(3)
The map (1.4) is associative up to homotopy. Hence H​F∗​(X,ω,ΛΠ)HF_{*}(X,\omega;\Lambda^{\Pi}) is a graded ring.
(4)
There exists a multiplicative identity
𝟏∈H​F∗​(X,ω,ΛΠ),{\bf 1}\in HF_{*}(X,\omega;\Lambda^{\Pi}),
of cohomological degree zero called the Floer fundamental class.33
3
We do not know if it coincides with the image of the classical fundamental class under the PSS map.
1.1.3. Poincaré duality
We then discuss Poincaré-type pairings on Hamiltonian Floer homology.
Theorem D (Poincaré duality).
Let C​F∗​(H1,J1,Ξ1)CF_{*}(H_{1},J_{1},\Xi_{1}) and C​F∗​(H2,J2,Ξ2)CF_{*}(H_{2},J_{2},\Xi_{2}) be Floer chain complexes provided by Theorem A. Then up to a choice Θ\Theta, there is a ΛΠ\Lambda^{\Pi}-bilinear pairing
ΦPD​(Θ):C​F∗​(H1,J1,Ξ1)​⊗ΛΠ​C​F∗​(H2,J2,Ξ2)→ΛΠ\Phi^{\rm PD}(\Theta):CF_{*}(H_{1},J_{1},\Xi_{1}){\underset{\Lambda^{\Pi}}{\otimes}}CF_{*}(H_{2},J_{2},\Xi_{2})\to\Lambda^{\Pi}
(1.5)
called the chain-level Poincaré pairing which satisfies the following conditions.
(1)
The homotopy type of the pairing is well-defined.
(2)
The pairing is compatible with continuation maps. Namely, suppose C​F∗​(H3,J3,Ξ3)CF_{*}(H_{3},J_{3},\Xi_{3}) is another Floer chain complex and Φ31:C​F∗​(H3,J3,Ξ3)→C​F∗​(H1,J1,Ξ1)\Phi^{31}:CF_{*}(H_{3},J_{3},\Xi_{3})\to CF_{*}(H_{1},J_{1},\Xi_{1}) is a chain-level continuation map. Then the pairing
ΦPD​(Φ31​(⋅),⋅):C​F∗​(H3,J3,Ξ3)​⊗ΛΠ​C​F∗​(H2,J2,Ξ2)→ΛΠ\Phi^{\rm PD}(\Phi^{31}(\cdot),\cdot):CF_{*}(H_{3},J_{3},\Xi_{3}){\underset{\Lambda^{\Pi}}{\otimes}}CF_{*}(H_{2},J_{2},\Xi_{2})\to\Lambda^{\Pi}
is homotopic to a chain-level Poincaré pairing.
(3)
In field coefficients, the induced Poincaré pairing on homology is nondegenerate. More precisely, let 𝐊{\bf K} be a field and Λ𝐊Π\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi} be the Novikov field. Then the induced bilinear pairing
ΦPD:(H​F∗​(X)​⊗ΛℤΠ^​H​F∗​(X))​⊗ΛℤΠ​Λ𝐊Π→Λ𝐊Π\Phi^{\rm PD}:\left(HF_{*}(X)\widehat{\underset{\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\Pi}}{\otimes}}HF_{*}(X)\right)\underset{\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\Pi}}{\otimes}\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi}\to\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi}
is nondegenerate.
(4)
The Poincaré duality is compatible with the pair-of-pants product. More precisely, the following diagram commutes.
H​F∗​(X,ω)​⊗ΛΠ^​H​F∗​(X,ω)​⊗ΛΠ^​H​F∗​(X,ω)\textstyle{HF_{*}(X,\omega)\widehat{\underset{\Lambda^{\Pi}}{\otimes}}HF_{*}(X,\omega)\widehat{\underset{\Lambda^{\Pi}}{\otimes}}HF_{*}(X,\omega)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}Φpants⊗Id\scriptstyle{\Phi^{\rm pants}\otimes{\rm Id}}Id⊗Φpants\scriptstyle{{\rm Id}\otimes\Phi^{\rm pants}}H​F∗​(X,ω)​⊗ΛΠ^​H​F∗​(X,ω)\textstyle{HF_{*}(X,\omega)\widehat{\underset{\Lambda^{\Pi}}{\otimes}}HF_{*}(X,\omega)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}ΦPD\scriptstyle{\Phi^{\rm PD}}H​F∗​(X,ω)​⊗ΛΠ^​H​F∗​(X,ω)\textstyle{HF_{*}(X,\omega)\widehat{\underset{\Lambda^{\Pi}}{\otimes}}HF_{*}(X,\omega)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}ΦPD\scriptstyle{\Phi^{\rm PD}}ΛΠ\textstyle{\Lambda^{\Pi}}
1.1.4. PSS map and isomorphism
Second, we consider the Piunikhin–Salamon–Schwarz (PSS) map (cf. [55]) from the Morse complex to the Floer complex and a map in the reversed direction called the SSP map.
Theorem E (PSS and SSP maps).
Let (f,g)(f,g) be a Morse–Smale pair on XX with the associated Morse–Smale–Witten complex C​M∗​(f,g)CM_{*}(f,g).
(1)
Let C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ,ΛΠ)CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi;\Lambda^{\Pi}) be a Floer chain complex provided by Theorem A. Then there exists a ΛΠ\Lambda^{\Pi}-linear chain map
ΦPSS:C​M∗​(f,g)​⊗ℤ​ΛΠ→C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ,ΛΠ)\Phi^{\rm PSS}:CM_{*}(f,g)\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}\Lambda^{\Pi}\to CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi;\Lambda^{\Pi})
of degree −n:=−12​dim​X-n:=-\frac{1}{2}{\rm dim}X
and a ΛΠ\Lambda^{\Pi}-linear chain map
ΦSSP:C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ,ΛΠ)→C​M∗​(f,g)​⊗ℤ​ΛΠ\Phi^{\rm SSP}:CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi;\Lambda^{\Pi})\to CM_{*}(f,g)\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}\Lambda^{\Pi}
of degree nn whose definitions depend on various choices.
(2)
The chain homotopy classes of ΦPSS\Phi^{\rm PSS} and ΦSSP\Phi^{\rm SSP} are independent of these choices.
(3)
The PSS and SSP maps are compatible with continuation maps, hence induce well-defined maps
ΦPSS:H∗​(X,ΛΠ)→H​F∗−n​(X,ω,ΛΠ)\Phi^{\rm PSS}:H_{*}(X;\Lambda^{\Pi})\to HF_{*-n}(X,\omega;\Lambda^{\Pi})
ΦSSP:H​F∗​(X,ω,ΛΠ)→H∗+n​(X,ΛΠ).\Phi^{\rm SSP}:HF_{*}(X,\omega;\Lambda^{\Pi})\to H_{*+n}(X;\Lambda^{\Pi}).
Theorem F.
The PSS map on homology is an isomorphism of graded ΛΠ\Lambda^{\Pi}-modules.
Remark 1.1.
We point out that we do not know if the PSS and the SSP maps are inverses to each other up to homotopy. In particular, the proof of Theorem F involves new moduli spaces beyond those appearing in the constructions of Theorem E.
Of course, the Arnold conjecture over integer coefficients now follows from Theorem F as a corollary, although in [14] we proved it by only considering the Floer chain complex for special HH and proving only the injectivity part of Theorem F.
Corollary 1.2 (Integral Arnold conjecture, cf. [14]).
Let ϕ:X→X\phi:X\to X be a nondegenerate Hamiltonian diffeomorphism. Let NN be the minimal Chern number of (X,ω)(X,\omega). Then the number of fixed points of ϕ\phi is no less than the minimal number of generators of a ℤ/2​N{\mathbb{Z}}/2N-graded complex of free abelian groups whose homology is isomorphic to H∗​(X,ℤ)H_{*}(X;{\mathbb{Z}}) viewed as a ℤ/2​N{\mathbb{Z}}/2N-graded abelian group.
If we compose the Floer-theoretic Poincaré pairing with the PSS map, then it induces a nondegenerate bilinear pairing on the homology H∗​(X,ΛΠ)H_{*}(X;\Lambda^{\Pi}).
Definition 1.3.
The FOP Poincaré pairing on H⁡(X,ΛΠ)H(X;\Lambda^{\Pi}) is the bilinear pairing
⟨ΦPSS​(⋅),ΦPSS​(⋅)⟩:H⁡(X,ΛΠ)​⊗ΛΠ​H​(X,ΛΠ)→ΛΠ.\langle\Phi^{\rm PSS}(\cdot),\Phi^{\rm PSS}(\cdot)\rangle:H(X;\Lambda^{\Pi}){\underset{\Lambda^{\Pi}}{\otimes}}H(X;\Lambda^{\Pi})\to\Lambda^{\Pi}.
If we use the PSS map defined using the technology of [30][43][53], then over rational coefficients, such a pairing coincides with the classical Poincaré pairing on homology. This is because the orbifold Euler classes satisfy properties needed for S1S^{1}-localization, so there is no contribution from moduli spaces of curves with nonzero energy. However, the FOP Euler characteristic classes arising in our perturbation scheme do not necessarily satisfy these properties and we do not know if the pairing is classical or not. This phenomenon is similar to the case of quantum KK-theory (see [41]) or quantum generalized cohomology developed by Abouzaid–McLean–Smith [4]. The point of introducing the quantum-corrected Poincaré pairing is to define an associative product analogous to the quantum product on H∗​(X,ΛΠ)H_{*}(X;\Lambda^{\Pi}) in our context, where we use the pairing to turn three-pointed Gromov–Witten type counts into a bilinear operation on H∗​(X,ΛΠ)H_{*}(X;\Lambda^{\Pi}) to dualize a marked point into an output marked point.
Another corollary is the invertibility of the Seidel map with integer coefficients defined in [11]. Recall that for each loop of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms ϕ:S1→Ham⁡(X)\phi:S^{1}\to{\rm Ham}(X), one has a Hamiltonian fibration M~ϕ→S2\widetilde{M}_{\phi}\to S^{2} with fibres being MM. By counting holomorphic sections u:S2→M~ϕu:S^{2}\to\widetilde{M}_{\phi} (via FOP perturbation), one can define a map
S⁡(ϕ):H⁡(X,ΛΠ)→H⁡(X,ΛΠ)S(\phi):H(X;\Lambda^{\Pi})\to H(X;\Lambda^{\Pi})
which only depends on the homotopy class [ϕ]∈π1​(Ham⁡(X))[\phi]\in\pi_{1}({\rm Ham}(X)).44
4
One uses the classical Poincaré duality in the definition. Hence we do not expect that S⁡(ϕ)​S​(ψ)=S⁡(ϕ​ψ)S(\phi)S(\psi)=S(\phi\psi). However, the main use in [11] of the Seidel map is its invertibility. In the semipositive case, using classical perturbation method, one can prove that S⁡(ϕ)S(\phi) is invertible by showing S⁡(ϕ​ψ)=S⁡(ϕ)​S​(ψ)S(\phi\psi)=S(\phi)S(\psi) and S⁡(1)=IdS(1)={\rm Id}. However, the invertibility of the Seidel maps can only be shown using the Hamiltonian model for the quantum cohomology.
Corollary 1.4 (Seidel representation).
The Seidel map S⁡(ϕ)S(\phi) is invertible.
Proof.
Fix an almost complex structure JJ. Choose a nondegenerate Hamiltonian HtH_{t}. Let Ht′H_{t}^{\prime} be the pullback by the loop ϕt\phi_{t}. On S2=ℝ∪S1∪{±∞}S^{2}={\mathbb{R}}\cup S^{1}\cup\{\pm\infty\} one can turn on a family of Hamiltonian connections parametrized by S∈[0,∞)S\in[0,\infty) which is Ht​d​tH_{t}dt on [−S,S]×S1[-S,S]\times S^{1} and which vanishes near ±∞\pm\infty. We regard this as a family of Hamiltonian connections σS\sigma_{S} on M~ϕ→S2\widetilde{M}_{\phi}\to S^{2} written with respect to the negative trivialization ψ−\psi_{-}. Then with respect to the positive trivialization, the connection reads H′​d​tH^{\prime}dt. Then consider the family of moduli spaces of holomorphic sections with respect to this family of Hamiltonian connections. When S=0S=0, one obtains a bimodule defining the Seidel map S⁡(ϕ)S(\phi), given as a chain map
S~​(ϕ):C​M​(f)→C​M​(f).\tilde{S}(\phi):CM(f)\to CM(f).
The induced map on homology is the Seidel map S⁡(ϕ)S(\phi). When S=+∞S=+\infty, one obtains a triple concatenation of a bimodule for PSS map, a bimodule for continuation map, and a bimodule for SSP map. Therefore, S~​(ϕ)\tilde{S}(\phi) is chain homotopic to the composition of these three maps. By Theorem B and Theorem E, on cohomology level S⁡(ϕ)S(\phi) is invertible.
∎
1.1.5. Comparison with known construction
When (X,ω)(X,\omega) is weakly monotone (also called semi-positive), then by perturbing either the almost complex structure JJ or the Hamiltonian HH, Hofer–Salamon [35] and Ono [50] defined the Floer chain complex over integers. Such constructions can also be carried out to define continuation maps, pair-of-pants products, and Künneth isomorphisms with integer coefficients for weakly monotone (X,ω)(X,\omega). It is natural to wonder if our constructions agree with the classical definitions in the weakly monotone setting. As a proof of principle, we demonstrate that this is the case for the Floer homology.
Theorem G.
When (X,ω)(X,\omega) is weakly monotone, our Floer chain complex C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ)CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi) is chain homotopy equivalent to the one defined using the classical method.
We expect that the proof methods can be generalized to establish the identification between our Floer-theoretic invariants and the classical versions.
Remark 1.5.
On the other hand, for a general compact (X,ω)(X,\omega), Floer chain complex C​F∗ℚ​(H,J)CF_{*}^{\mathbb{Q}}(H,J) over rational coefficients is constructed using the classical virtual technique (see [43][30][53]). Using the setup similar to here, C​F∗ℚ​(H,J)CF_{*}^{\mathbb{Q}}(H,J) is a module over the rational Novikov field ΛℚΠ\Lambda_{\mathbb{Q}}^{\Pi}. Although there is an isomorphism
H​F∗​(X,ω,ΛΠ)​⊗ΛΠ​ΛℚΠ≅H​F∗ℚ​(X,ω)HF_{*}(X,\omega;\Lambda^{\Pi})\underset{\Lambda^{\Pi}}{\otimes}\Lambda_{\mathbb{Q}}^{\Pi}\cong HF_{*}^{\mathbb{Q}}(X,\omega)
via the PSS maps in the two setups and the universal coefficient theorem for ordinary homology, one does not have an obvious relation on the chain level, between
C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ,ΛΠ)​⊗ΛΠ​ΛℚΠandC​F∗ℚ​(H,J)CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi;\Lambda^{\Pi})\underset{\Lambda^{\Pi}}{\otimes}\Lambda_{\mathbb{Q}}^{\Pi}\ \ \ {\rm and}\ \ \ CF_{*}^{\mathbb{Q}}(H,J)
without going through Morse theory.
1.2. Main results on equivariant Floer theory and Steenrod operations
To discuss Steenrod operations and other aspects of equivariant Floer theory, we switch to the cohomological convention, partially to match with the fact that classical Steenrod operations are cohomological operations. In this way, by considering ascending flows rather than descending flows, one obtains the Floer cochain complex C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ)CF^{*}(H,J,\Xi) associated to a Floer flow category whose cochains are formal infinite linear combinations of capped 1-periodic orbits of HH whose actions go to +∞+\infty.
Let 𝗉{\sf p} be a prime number. Abbreviate ℤ𝗉:=ℤ/𝗉​ℤ{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}:={\mathbb{Z}}/{\sf p}{\mathbb{Z}}. When we view it as a field serving as the coefficient field of cohomology, we use 𝐅𝗉{\bf F}_{\sf p} instead. In characteristic 𝗉{\sf p}, on any topological space, there are the Steenrod power operations which can be organized as a single nonlinear map.
We will primarily use the “Tate” version of equivariant theory. Recall that the more familiar “Borel” version of the ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant cohomology of a point is
Hℤ𝗉Borel​(pt,𝐅𝗉)=𝐅𝗉​[𝚄]​⟨θ⟩H^{\rm Borel}_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}({\rm pt};{\bf F}_{\sf p})={\bf F}_{\sf p}[\mathtt{U}]\langle\uptheta\rangle
over 𝐅𝗉{\bf F}_{\sf p} generated by a degree 22 variable 𝚄\mathtt{U} and a degree 11 variable θ\uptheta satisfying
𝚄​θ=θ​𝚄,\displaystyle\ \mathtt{U}\uptheta=\uptheta\mathtt{U},\
θ2={𝚄,𝗉=2,0,𝗉>2.\displaystyle\ \uptheta^{2}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}\mathtt{U},&{\sf p}=2,\\
0,&{\sf p}>2.\end{array}\right.
It is defined as the ordinary cohomology of the classifying space B​ℤ𝗉B{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}} and admits a nice Morse model. We often need to take the completion by allowing formal power series.
The Tate version of the equivariant cohomology of a point differs from the Borel one by inverting the variable θ\uptheta (in characteristic 22) resp. 𝚄\mathtt{U} (in odd characteristics), i.e. (after completion)
Hℤ𝗉Tate​(pt,𝐅𝗉)={𝐅2​((θ)),𝗉=2,𝐅𝗉​((𝚄))​⟨θ⟩,𝗉>2.H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}^{\rm Tate}({\rm pt};{\bf F}_{\sf p})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}{\bf F}_{2}{(\!(\uptheta)\!)},&\ {\sf p}=2,\\
{\bf F}_{\sf p}{(\!(\mathtt{U})\!)}\langle\uptheta\rangle,&\ {\sf p}>2.\end{array}\right.
Remark 1.6.
There are two main reasons why we prefer the Tate version. First, all the nice properties of the equivariant Floer theory hold for the Tate version but not the Borel one, for example, localization. Second, the inversion of the variable 𝚄\mathtt{U} follows more naturally from our geometric construction. The Borel version, instead, is regarded as a truncation of the Tate version. From now on, all equivariant cochain complexes or cohomology, without further declaration, will be the Tate version.
We introduce the following notions. Let
𝐊𝗉:={𝐅2​((θ)),𝗉=2,𝐅𝗉​((𝚄)),𝗉>2{\bf K}_{\sf p}:=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}{\bf F}_{2}{(\!(\uptheta)\!)},&\ {\sf p}=2,\\
{\bf F}_{\sf p}{(\!(\mathtt{U})\!)},&\ {\sf p}>2\end{array}\right.
The chain-level construction we use will always produce algebraic structures linear over 𝐊𝗉{\bf K}_{\sf p}. On the other hand, denote
𝐊~𝗉:={𝐊𝗉,𝗉=2,𝐊𝗉​⟨θ⟩,𝗉>2.\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}:=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}{\bf K}_{\sf p},&\ {\sf p}=2,\\
{\bf K}_{\sf p}\langle\uptheta\rangle,&\ {\sf p}>2\end{array}\right..
The resulting cohomology groups (not complexes) will be modules over 𝐊~𝗉\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}. However, such module structure is not an algebraic consequence, but needs to be constructed geometrically.
1.2.1. The quantum Steenrod operations
The classical Steenrod square resp. power operations are cohomological operations which can be formulated as a single map (for 𝗉=2{\sf p}=2)
S​t2:H∗​(X,𝐅2)→H∗​(X,𝐅2​[θ])⊆H∗​(X,𝐊~𝗉)St_{2}:H^{*}(X;{\bf F}_{2})\to H^{*}(X;{\bf F}_{2}[\uptheta])\subseteq H^{*}(X;\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p})
resp. (𝗉>2{\sf p}>2)
S​t𝗉:H∗​(X,𝐅𝗉)→H∗​(X,𝐅𝗉​[𝚄]​⟨θ⟩)⊆H∗​(X,𝐊~𝗉).St_{\sf p}:H^{*}(X;{\bf F}_{\sf p})\to H^{*}(X;{\bf F}_{\sf p}[\mathtt{U}]\langle\uptheta\rangle)\subseteq H^{*}(X;\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}).
The map S​t𝗉St_{\sf p} is additive and linear over 𝐅𝗉{\bf F}_{\sf p}. Moreover, if we regard 𝚄\mathtt{U} of degree 22 and θ\uptheta of degree 11, then S​t𝗉St_{\sf p} multiplies the grading by 𝗉{\sf p}. Fukaya proposed the idea of defining quantum Steenrod operation [31]. It has been adapted in the Floer setting by Seidel [61] and Shelukhin–Zhao [62] and in the quantum cohomology setting by Wilkins [72] and Seidel–Wilkins [59]. A key point in the construction is the integrality of curve counts, which then admit well-defined mod 𝗉{\sf p} reduction. Hence the existing constructions are all restricted to monotone or semipositive settings. The FOP perturbation method developed in [13] allows one to extend to the general setting.
Theorem H (Quantum Steenrod operation on general symplectic manifold).
For any compact symplectic manifold (X,ω)(X,\omega), for each prime 𝗉{\sf p}, there are well-defined additive maps
Q​S​t2:Hk​(X,𝐅2)→H2​k​(X,Λ𝐅2​[[θ]]Π)⊆H2​k​(X,Λ𝐊~2Π),(𝗉=2)Q​S​t𝗉:Hk​(X,𝐅𝗉)→H𝗉​k​(X,Λ𝐅𝗉​[[𝚄]]Π​⟨θ⟩)⊆H𝗉​k​(X,Λ𝐊~𝗉Π)​(𝗉>2)\begin{split}QSt_{2}:&\ H^{k}(X;{\bf F}_{2})\to H^{2k}(X;\Lambda_{{\bf F}_{2}{[\![\uptheta]\!]}}^{\Pi})\subseteq H^{2k}(X;\Lambda_{\tilde{\bf K}_{2}}^{\Pi}),\ ({\sf p}=2)\\
QSt_{\sf p}:&\ H^{k}(X;{\bf F}_{\sf p})\to H^{{\sf p}k}(X;\Lambda_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}{[\![\mathtt{U}]\!]}}^{\Pi}\langle\uptheta\rangle)\subseteq H^{{\sf p}k}(X;\Lambda_{\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi})\ ({\sf p}>2)\end{split}
satisfying the following conditions.
(1)
The classical part (i.e., setting the Novikov parameter to be zero) of Q​S​t𝗉QSt_{\sf p} coincides with the classical Steenrod operation.
(2)
When (X,ω)(X,\omega) is semipositive, Q​S​t𝗉QSt_{\sf p} coincides with the quantum Steenrod operation defined by Seidel–Wilkins [59] (which, in 𝗉=2{\sf p}=2 and monotone case, agrees with Wilkins’ definition of quantum Steenrod square in [72]).
1.2.2. Equivariant Floer cohomology
The Floer-theoretic version of the Steenrod operation has played important roles in many recent dynamical applications of Floer theory, see [61] [63, 64, 65] [21] etc. In this paper, we also generalize the construction of the Floer-theoretic Steenrod operation to general compact symplectic manifolds. Let C​F∗​(H)CF^{*}(H) be a Floer chain complex associated to a nondegenerate Hamiltonian HH, a compatible almost complex structure JJ, and a system of choices Ξ\Xi; to simplify notation, we suppress JJ and Ξ\Xi from the notation.
Theorem I (Equivariant Floer cohomology).
Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a compact symplectic manifold and 𝗉{\sf p} be a prime.
(1)
Let HH be a 1-periodic Hamiltonian such that its 𝗉{\sf p}-th iteration H♮​𝗉H^{\natural{\sf p}} is nondegenerate. Then there exists a cochain complex (the Tate ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant Floer complex)
C​Fℤ𝗉​(H♮​𝗉,Ξℤ𝗉)CF_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(H^{\natural{\sf p}},\Xi^{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}})
of finitely generated Λ𝐊𝗉Π\Lambda_{{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}-modules whose definition depends on a choice Ξℤ𝗉\Xi^{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}.
(2)
For Hamiltonians H1,H2H_{1},H_{2} with both H1♮​𝗉H_{1}^{\natural{\sf p}} and H2♮​𝗉H_{2}^{\natural{\sf p}} nondegenerate and choices Ξ1ℤ𝗉\Xi_{1}^{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}} and Ξ2ℤ𝗉\Xi_{2}^{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}} to define their equivariant Floer cochain complex, there is a chain homotopy equivalence
C​Fℤ𝗉​(H1♮​𝗉,Ξ1ℤ𝗉)→C​Fℤ𝗉​(H2♮​𝗉,Ξ2ℤ𝗉)CF_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}(H_{1}^{\natural{\sf p}},\Xi_{1}^{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}})\to CF_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(H_{2}^{\natural{\sf p}},\Xi_{2}^{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}})
called the equivariant continuation map.
(3)
The equivariant continuation maps are well-defined up to chain homotopy. Moreover, the composition of two equivariant continuation maps is homotopic to an equivariant continuation map. Hence there is a well-defined symplectic invariant of (X,ω)(X,\omega), denoted by
H​Fℤ𝗉​(X)HF_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}(X)
called the (Tate) ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant Hamiltonian Floer cohomology.
(4)
There is a natural equivariant PSS map
Φℤ𝗉𝕄​𝔽:H∗​(X,Λ𝐊~𝗉Π)→H​Fℤ𝗉∗​(X)\Phi_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}^{\mathbb{MF}}:H^{*}(X;\Lambda_{\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi})\to HF_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}^{*}(X)
and an equivariant SSP map
Φℤ𝗉𝔽​𝕄:H​Fℤ𝗉∗​(X)→H∗​(X,Λ𝐊~𝗉Π)\Phi_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}^{\mathbb{FM}}:HF_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}^{*}(X)\to H^{*}(X;\Lambda_{\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi})
which are isomorphisms of Λ𝐊𝗉Π\Lambda_{{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}-modules.
Remark 1.7.
The equivariant cohomology H​Fℤ𝗉​(X)HF_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(X) is naturally a module over the field Λ𝐊𝗉Π\Lambda_{{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}. When 𝗉=2{\sf p}=2, this is the same as the ring Λ𝐊~𝗉Π\Lambda_{\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}. When 𝗉>2{\sf p}>2, there is no Λ𝐊~𝗉Π\Lambda_{\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}-module structure on the complex C​Fℤ𝗉​(H♮​𝗉)CF_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(H^{\natural{\sf p}}) as “multiplying by θ\uptheta” is not a chain map. However, one could define a Λ𝐊~𝗉Π\Lambda_{\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}-module structure on the cohomology H​Fℤ𝗉​(H♮​𝗉)HF_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(H^{\natural{\sf p}}). However, we do not consider this additional structure in the current paper.
There is an algebraically defined ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant chain complex
Cℤ𝗉​(C​F​(H)⊗𝗉)C_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(CF(H)^{\otimes{\sf p}})
whose underlying cochain group is a suitable completion of
(CF(H)⊗Λ𝐅𝗉Π⋯⊗Λ𝐅𝗉ΠCF(H))⊗Λ𝐊~𝗉Π.\Big(CF(H)\underset{\Lambda_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}}{\otimes}\cdots\underset{\Lambda_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}}{\otimes}CF(H)\Big)\otimes\Lambda_{\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}.
The differential is linear over Λ𝐊𝗉Π\Lambda_{{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}. The quasi-Frobenius map is an 𝐅𝗉{\bf F}_{\sf p}-linear map
q​F:H​F​(H,Λ𝐅𝗉Π)→Hℤ𝗉​(C​F​(H)⊗𝗉)qF:HF(H;\Lambda_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi})\to H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(CF(H)^{\otimes{\sf p}})
which is, roughly speaking, induced by the chain-level map x↦x⊗⋯⊗xx\mapsto x\otimes\cdots\otimes x.
1.2.3. Floer-theoretic Steenrod operation
Theorem J (Floer-theoretic Steenrod operation).
Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a compact symplectic manifold and JJ be an ω\omega-compatible almost complex structure.
(1)
For any pair of Hamiltonians H−H_{-} and H+H_{+} with H−H_{-} nondegenerate and H+♮​𝗉H_{+}^{\natural{\sf p}} nondegenerate, there exists a cochain map called the equivariant pair-of-pants product
P~:Cℤ𝗉​(C​F​(H−)⊗𝗉)→C​Fℤ𝗉​(H+♮​𝗉)\widetilde{P}:C_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(CF(H_{-})^{\otimes{\sf p}})\to CF_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}(H_{+}^{\natural{\sf p}})
It is well-defined up to chain homotopy.
(2)
The map on cohomology, denoted by
P:Hℤ𝗉​(C​F​(H−)⊗𝗉)→H​Fℤ𝗉​(H+♮​𝗉)P:H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(CF(H_{-})^{\otimes{\sf p}})\to HF_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(H_{+}^{\natural{\sf p}})
is an isomorphism of Λ𝐊𝗉Π\Lambda_{{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}-modules.
(3)
The composition defining the Floer-theoretic Steenrod operation is given by
H​F​(X,Λ𝐅𝗉Π)\textstyle{HF(X;\Lambda_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}H⁡(C​F​(H−)⊗Λ𝐅𝗉Π)\textstyle{H(CF(H_{-})\otimes\Lambda_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}q​F\scriptstyle{qF}Hℤ𝗉​(C​F​(H−)⊗𝗉)\textstyle{H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(CF(H_{-})^{\otimes{\sf p}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}P\scriptstyle{P}H​Fℤ𝗉​(H+♮​𝗉)\textstyle{HF_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(H_{+}^{\natural{\sf p}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}H​Fℤ𝗉​(X)\textstyle{HF_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(X)}
denoted by
𝐹𝑆𝑡𝗉:H​F​(X,Λ𝐅𝗉Π)→H​Fℤ𝗉​(X){\it FSt}_{{\sf p}}:HF(X;\Lambda_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi})\to HF_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(X)
is independent of choices.
(4)
The following diagram commutes: when 𝗉=2{\sf p}=2;

1.3. Main results on quantitative Floer theory
Many successful applications of Hamiltonian Floer theory have a quantitative flavor. We also have the quantitative package under our framework. As many applications take advantage of using different coefficients, we phrase the statements using a general Novikov ring/field.
1.3.1. Action filtration and spectral invariants
We state the following theorem for the convenience for readers to cite. The proof has no difference from cases proved using other approaches is hence omitted.
Theorem K (Filtered Floer complex and continuation map).
Let RR be a commutative ring with unit and let C​F​(H,ΛRΠ)CF(H;\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi}) be a Floer complex provided by Theorem A tensored with ΛRΠ\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi}.
(1)
The differential of the Floer complex preserves the energy filtration. More precisely, for each τ∈ℝ\tau\in{\mathbb{R}}, the differential preserves the subgroups
C​F​(H,ΛRΠ)≤τ:={∑i=1∞ai​pi∈C​F​(H,ΛRΠ)|𝒜H​(pi)≤τ}CF(H;\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi})^{\leq\tau}:=\Big\{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}a_{i}p_{i}\in CF(H;\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi})\ |\ {\mathcal{A}}_{H}(p_{i})\leq\tau\Big\}
and
C​F​(H,ΛRΠ)<τ:={∑i=1∞ai​pi∈C​F​(H,ΛRΠ)|𝒜H​(pi)<τ}.CF(H;\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi})^{<\tau}:=\Big\{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}a_{i}p_{i}\in CF(H;\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi})\ |\ {\mathcal{A}}_{H}(p_{i})<\tau\Big\}.
(2)
Let C​F​(H1,ΛRΠ)CF(H_{1};\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi}) and C​F​(H2,ΛRΠ)CF(H_{2};\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi}) be two Floer complexes. Denote
c:=∫S1supX(H1,t−H2,t)​𝑑t.c:=\int_{S^{1}}\sup_{X}(H_{1,t}-H_{2,t})dt.
Then there exists a continuation map Φ12​(Θ)\Phi^{12}(\Theta) such that for all τ∈ℝ\tau\in{\mathbb{R}},
Φ12​(Θ)​(C​F​(H1,ΛRΠ)≤τ)⊆C​F​(H2,ΛRΠ)≤τ+c,\displaystyle\ \Phi^{12}(\Theta)(CF(H_{1};\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi})^{\leq\tau})\subseteq CF(H_{2};\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi})^{\leq\tau+c},\
Φ12​(Θ)​(C​F​(H1,ΛRΠ)<τ)⊆C​F​(H2,ΛRΠ)<τ+c.\displaystyle\ \Phi^{12}(\Theta)(CF(H_{1};\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi})^{<\tau})\subseteq CF(H_{2};\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi})^{<\tau+c}.
The filtered version of continuation map implies that for any nondegenerate Hamiltonian HH, the filtered homology groups
H​F​(H,ΛRΠ)≤τ,\displaystyle\ HF(H;\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi})^{\leq\tau},\
H​F​(H,ΛRΠ)<τ\displaystyle\ HF(H;\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi})^{<\tau}
only depend on HH. When RR is fixed in the local context, we omit the coefficient from the notations. Moreover, there are well-defined maps
H​F​(H)<τ→H​F​(X)HF(H)^{<\tau}\to HF(X)
compatible with maps (for τ1≤τ2\tau_{1}\leq\tau_{2})
H​F​(H)<τ1→H​F​(H)<τ2.HF(H)^{<\tau_{1}}\to HF(H)^{<\tau_{2}}.
This allows us to define the spectral invariants of Floer homology classes.
Definition 1.8.
Given a Hamiltonian HH, the spectral invariant of x∈H​F​(X,ΛRΠ)x\in HF(X;\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi}) is
cH​(x):=limi→∞{τ∈ℝ|x∈Im⁡(H​F​(Hi)<τ→H​F​(X))}∈ℝ∪{−∞}.c_{H}(x):=\lim_{i\to\infty}\Big\{\tau\in{\mathbb{R}}\ |\ x\in{\rm Im}\big(HF(H_{i})^{<\tau}\to HF(X)\big)\Big\}\in{\mathbb{R}}\cup\{-\infty\}.
Here the limit is taken for a sequence of nondegenerate Hamiltonians HiH_{i} converging to HH in C0C^{0}-norm.
Theorem L (Spectral invariants).
Fix a Noetherian ring RR. The spectral numbers cH​(x)c_{H}(x) for x∈H​F​(X,ΛRΠ)x\in HF(X;\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi}) satisfy the following properties.
(1)
(Spectrality) For any x∈H​F​(X,ΛRΠ)x\in HF(X;\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi}), the number
cH​(x)=−∞⟹x=0c_{H}(x)=-\infty\Longrightarrow x=0
and for x≠0x\neq 0, there exists a cycle 𝔵{\mathfrak{x}} representing xx such that
𝒜H​(𝔵)=cH​(x).{\mathcal{A}}_{H}({\mathfrak{x}})=c_{H}(x).
(2)
(Shifting Property) For x∈H​F​(X,ΛRΠ)x\in HF(X;\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi}) and a∈ΛRΠa\in\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi}, one has
cH​(a​x)=cH​(x)−𝔳⁡(a).c_{H}(ax)=c_{H}(x)-{\mathfrak{v}}(a).
(3)
(Lipschitz Continuity) cH​(x)c_{H}(x) is Lipschitz continuous with respect to the Hofer metric on the space of 1-periodic Hamiltonians.
(4)
(Isotopy Invariance) cH​(x)c_{H}(x) only depends on the element ϕ~\tilde{\phi} in H​am~​(X,ω){\rm H}\widetilde{\rm am}(X,\omega), the Hamiltonian isotopy induced from HH as an element of the universal cover of the Hamiltonian diffeomorphism group. Hence we can denote cH​(x)c_{H}(x) by cϕ~​(x)c_{\tilde{\phi}}(x).
(5)
(Symplectic Invariance) For any symplectomorphism ρ:X→X\rho:X\to X, one has cH∘ρ​(x)=cH​(ρ∗​(x))c_{H\circ\rho}(x)=c_{H}(\rho_{*}(x)) where ρ∗\rho_{*} is the automorphism
ρ∗:H​F​(X)→H​F​(X)\rho_{*}:HF(X)\to HF(X)
induced by ρ\rho.
(6)
(Triangle Inequality) For any x,y∈H​F​(X)x,y\in HF(X), ϕ~,ψ~∈H​am~​(X,ω)\tilde{\phi},\tilde{\psi}\in{\rm H}\widetilde{\rm am}(X,\omega), one has
cϕ~​ψ~​(x⋆y)≤cϕ~​(x)+cψ~​(y).c_{\tilde{\phi}\tilde{\psi}}(x\star y)\leq c_{\tilde{\phi}}(x)+c_{\tilde{\psi}}(y).
Here ⋆\star is the pair-of-pants product on Floer homology defined by Theorem C.
(7)
(Poincaré Duality) Let R=𝐊R={\bf K} be a field. Let Φ0PD\Phi_{0}^{\rm PD} be the composition
H​F​(X,Λ𝐊Π)⊗H​F​(X,Λ𝐊Π) ΦPD Λ𝐊Π 𝐊 .\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 61.81519pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-61.81519pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{HF(X;\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi})\otimes HF(X;\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 62.95053pt\raise 6.20831pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-3.20831pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\Phi^{\rm PD}}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 85.81519pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 85.81519pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 130.28323pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 130.28323pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.55554pt\hbox{$\textstyle{{\bf K}}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces.
Let H¯\overline{H} be the reversal of the Hamiltonian HH. Then one has
cH(x)=−inf{cH¯(y)|y∈HF(X;Λ𝐊Π),Φ0PD(x,y)≠0}.c_{H}(x)=-\inf\Big\{c_{\overline{H}}(y)\ |\ y\in HF(X;\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi}),\ \Phi_{0}^{\rm PD}(x,y)\neq 0\Big\}.
1.3.2. Barcodes
Another quantitative structure widely used in applications is the barcode. We follow the approach of Usher–Zhang [69] which requires slightly modified setup.
For a symplectic manifold XX with the abelian group Π\Pi defined by (1.1), a (concise) barcode (see [69]) is a finite multiset of elements of (ℝ/ω(Π))×(0,+∞]({\mathbb{R}}/\omega(\Pi))\times(0,+\infty].
It is most useful when considering Floer barcodes with field coefficients. Then the complex
C​F​(H,Λ𝐊Π):=C​F​(H,ΛℤΠ)⊗Λ𝐊ΠCF(H;\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi}):=CF(H;\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\Pi})\otimes\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi}
is a (slight generalization of) Floer-type complex in the sense of [69, Definition 4.1]. It follows from [69, Definition 6.3, Theorem 7.1] that there is a barcode canonically associated to the complex C​F​(H,Λ𝐊Π)CF(H;\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi}).
Corollary 1.9 (Floer barcodes).
The barcode associated to the Floer complex C​F​(H,Λ𝐊Π)CF(H;\Lambda_{{\bf K}}^{\Pi}) only depends on the Hamiltonian HH. Moreover, the dependence on HH is Lipschitz with respect to the bottleneck distance on barcodes and the Hofer metric on the space of 11-periodic Hamiltonians.
Proof.
It follows from applying Proposition 7.38 and Theorem 7.40 to the filtered Floer complex constructed in Theorem K.
∎
1.3.3. Quantitative features of equivariant Floer theory
The equivariant Floer cochain complex also has an energy filtration. Notice that the equivariant cochain complex C​Fℤ𝗉​(H♮​𝗉)CF_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(H^{\natural{\sf p}}) is a module over Λ𝐊𝗉Π\Lambda_{{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}. We can prove that it is a Floer-type complex. On the other hand, the ordinary Floer complex C​F​(H,Λ𝐅𝗉Π)CF(H;\Lambda_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}) also induces an equivariant complex coming from its own 𝗉{\sf p}-fold tensor power, denoted by
Cℤ𝗉​(C​F​(H)⊗𝗉)C_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(CF(H)^{\otimes{\sf p}})
which is also a Floer-type complex.
Theorem M (Barcode stretching under prime iteration).
Let XX be a compact symplectic manifold, 𝗉{\sf p} be a prime, and HH be a Hamiltonian on XX such that the 𝗉{\sf p}-th iteration H♮​𝗉H^{\natural{\sf p}} is nondegenerate.
(1)
The equivariant Floer cochain complex C​Fℤ𝗉​(H♮​𝗉)CF_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(H^{\natural{\sf p}}) is a Floer-type complex over the Novikov field Λ𝐊𝗉Π\Lambda_{{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}.
(2)
The equivariant pair-of-pants product has a chain-level realization
P:Cℤ𝗉​(C​F​(H)⊗𝗉)→C​Fℤ𝗉​(H♮​𝗉)P:C_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(CF(H)^{\otimes{\sf p}})\to CF_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(H^{\natural{\sf p}})
which is a filtered chain homotopy equivalence for Floer-type complexes.
(3)
Suppose the bar-length spectrum of C​F​(H)CF(H) is 0<β1​(H)≤⋯≤βm​(H)0<\beta_{1}(H)\leq\cdots\leq\beta_{m}(H). Then the bar-length spectrum of C​Fℤ𝗉​(H♮​𝗉)CF_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(H^{\natural{\sf p}}) is
βi,ℤ2(H♮​2)=2βi(H),i=1,…,m\beta_{i,{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}}(H^{\natural 2})=2\beta_{i}(H),\ i=1,\ldots,m
when 𝗉=2{\sf p}=2 and
β2​i−1,ℤ𝗉(H♮​𝗉)=β2​i,ℤ𝗉(H♮​𝗉)=𝗉βi(H),i=1,…,m\beta_{2i-1,{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(H^{\natural{\sf p}})=\beta_{2i,{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(H^{\natural{\sf p}})={\sf p}\beta_{i}(H),\ i=1,\ldots,m
when 𝗉>2{\sf p}>2.
1.3.4. Quantitative Hamiltonian Floer theory for noncontractible orbits
We state the main quantitative results about Floer theory for noncontractible orbits. We follow very much the treatment of Sugimoto [67]. Since the resulting homology group always vanishes, there are no spectral invariants; hence the barcodes are the main quantitative aspects here.
Choose a possibly noncontractible loop γ:S1→X\gamma:S^{1}\to X which represents a nonzero class
[γ]≠0∈H1​(X,ℤ)free.[\gamma]\neq 0\in H_{1}(X;{\mathbb{Z}})_{\rm free}.
One can consider noncontractible periodic orbits of a Hamiltonian HH which are homologous (over ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}) to γ\gamma.
Definition 1.10.
Let HH be a 1-periodic Hamiltonian on (X,ω)(X,\omega).
(1)
Let x:S1→Xx:S^{1}\to X be a 1-periodic orbit of HH. A γ\gamma-capping of xx is an oriented cobordism u:Σ→Xu:\Sigma\to X from γ\gamma to xx (where Σ\Sigma could be a higher genus surface).
(2)
Two γ\gamma-cappings are equivalent if their difference, which is a class in H2​(X,ℤ)H_{2}(X;{\mathbb{Z}}), has zero symplectic area. A γ\gamma-capped orbit of HH is a 1-periodic orbit together with an equivalence class of γ\gamma-cappings.
(3)
Let
𝒪~γ​(H)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_{\gamma}(H)
denote the set of γ\gamma-capped orbits of HH, on which there is a free action by the group
Γ:=H2​(X,ℤ)/ker⁡(ω).\Gamma:=H_{2}(X;{\mathbb{Z}})/{\rm ker}(\omega).
In our setup we do not keep the ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-grading but only consider the ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}-grading on γ\gamma-capped orbits. Each γ\gamma-capped orbit pp has a well-defined symplectic action 𝒜H,γ​(p)∈ℝ{\mathcal{A}}_{H,\gamma}(p)\in{\mathbb{R}}. The construction of the filtered Floer complex is summarized below and will be proved in Section 28.
Theorem 1.11 (Filtered Floer chain complex for noncontractible periodic orbits).
Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a compact symplectic manifold and let γ:S1→X\gamma:S^{1}\to X be a smooth loop with [γ]≠0∈H1​(X,ℤ)free[\gamma]\neq 0\in H_{1}(X;{\mathbb{Z}})_{\rm free}. Let HH be a nondegenerate 11-periodic Hamiltonian. Then for each 11-periodic family of ω\omega-compatible almost complex structures JJ, there is a differential on the ℤ/2{\mathbb{Z}}/2-graded abelian group
CFγ(H):={∑i=1∞aipi|ai∈ℤ,pi∈𝒪~γ(H),limi→∞𝒜H,γ(pi)=−∞}CF_{\gamma}(H):=\Big\{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}a_{i}p_{i}\ |\ a_{i}\in{\mathbb{Z}},\ p_{i}\in\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_{\gamma}(H),\ \lim_{i\to\infty}{\mathcal{A}}_{H,\gamma}(p_{i})=-\infty\Big\}
leading to a ℤ/2{\mathbb{Z}}/2-graded complex of abelian groups
C​Fγ​(H,J,Ξ).CF_{\gamma}(H,J,\Xi).
Moreover, for each field 𝐊{\bf K}, the tensor product
C​Fγ​(H)⊗Λ𝐊ΓCF_{\gamma}(H)\otimes\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Gamma}
is a Floer-type complex over Λ𝐊Γ\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Gamma} whose filtered isomorphism class only depends on HH.
Under the assumption that [γ]≠0∈H1​(X)[\gamma]\neq 0\in H_{1}(X), we expect that a continuation map argument can prove the vanishing of the resulting homology group. The main use of the noncontractible Floer chain complex is on the quantitative side. The main purpose of developing this theory is to generalize the work of Sugimoto [67], which uses the equivariant pair-of-pants product as a primary tool. We state the main result regarding the quantitative implications, which is also proved in Section 28.
Theorem 1.12.
Under the assumption of Theorem 1.11, let 𝗉{\sf p} be a prime and suppose H♮​𝗉H^{\natural{\sf p}} is nondegenerate.
(1)
There exists a Floer-type complex
C​Fℤ𝗉​(H♮​𝗉,γ)CF_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(H^{\natural{\sf p}},\gamma)
over Λ𝐊𝗉Γ\Lambda_{{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Gamma} which is freely generated by 𝗉{\sf p}-periodic orbits homologous to γ\gamma. Its filtered isomorphism class only depends on HH.
(2)
There exists a filtered homotopy equivalence
Pγ:Cℤ𝗉​(C​Fγ​(H)⊗𝗉)→C​Fℤ𝗉​(H♮​𝗉,γ(𝗉))P_{\gamma}:C_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(CF_{\gamma}(H)^{\otimes{\sf p}})\to CF_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(H^{\natural{\sf p}},\gamma^{({\sf p})})
of Floer-type complexes over Λ𝐊𝗉Γ\Lambda_{{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Gamma}.
(3)
Let
β1γ​(H)≤⋯≤βNγ​(H)\beta_{1}^{\gamma}(H)\leq\cdots\leq\beta_{N}^{\gamma}(H)
be the bar-length spectrum of C​Fγ​(H)⊗Λ𝐅𝗉ΓCF_{\gamma}(H)\otimes\Lambda_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}^{\Gamma}. Then it only depends on HH and the homology class of γ\gamma. Moreover, the bar-length spectrum of C​Fℤ𝗉,γ(𝗉)​(H♮​𝗉)CF_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}},\gamma^{({\sf p})}}(H^{\natural{\sf p}}) is
2​β1γ​(H),…,2​βNγ​(H)2\beta_{1}^{\gamma}(H),\ldots,2\beta_{N}^{\gamma}(H)
when 𝗉=2{\sf p}=2 (with the same number of finite bars) and is
𝗉​β1γ​(H),𝗉​β1γ​(H),…,𝗉​βNγ​(H),𝗉​βNγ​(H){\sf p}\beta_{1}^{\gamma}(H),{\sf p}\beta_{1}^{\gamma}(H),\ldots,{\sf p}\beta_{N}^{\gamma}(H),{\sf p}\beta_{N}^{\gamma}(H)
when 𝗉>2{\sf p}>2 (with twice the number of finite bars).
1.4. What we do “virtually”
We would like to explain the general principle of our construction (on the virtual side) along with some historical remarks.
In a very general sense, the Floer complexes and other chain-level structures are constructed via counting solutions to the Floer equation. To count beyond the cases where transversality can be achieved by geometric perturbations ([24][35][50]), the so-called virtual technique was invented (see [42][30][27][36][53] etc.). Such constructions, depending on the extent of applications, usually require building a complete package of abstract theory (such as Kuranishi theory and polyfold theory); the application of these abstract theories can typically be broken down into two main components: (virtual) regularization and (virtual) perturbation/integration.
From now on we only discuss under the finite-dimensional/Kuranishi approach, the one upon which the current paper is based, rather than the infinite-dimensional/polyfold approach. The issues and challenges we will address in the finite-dimensional approach may not be manifested in the infinite-dimensional situation.
A central issue in the finite-dimensional construction is the choice-dependence. Unlike the algebro-geometric situation, one rarely obtains canonical objects such as a perfect obstruction theory ([15]). To obtain choice-independent results, one needs to include various kinds of equivalence relations in the abstract package, or perhaps higher categorical structures. The choice-independence is not yet a significant challenge in cases where one deals with a single or finitely many moduli spaces, such as Gromov–Witten theory. But it causes much more serious difficulties in Floer-type theories. In Floer theory, essentially one obtains virtual fundamental chains rather than cycles; the virtual fundamental chains satisfy expected properties (such as d2=0d^{2}=0) only if we make the constructions for infinitely many moduli spaces compatibly. It could be a delicate issue when developing the abstract package incorporating such compatibility conditions and when fulfilling these conditions in the concrete regularization procedure.55
5
The work of Abouzaid [5] takes a different approach where the choices are made universally in his notion of “theories of virtual counts.”
We would like to emphasize two important developments which precede the current piece of work. The first one, regarding the perturbation component, starts from [29] which proposed the principle leading to integer-valued curve counts even when the orbifold locus of a moduli space is obstructed. After technical exploration by Parker [54], the authors rigorously established this new perturbation method in [13], which we call the FOP perturbation scheme. The second one, regarding the regularization component, is the construction of global Kuranishi charts starting from [3]. It provides a powerful method producing global Kuranishi models regularizing any single moduli space and greatly reduces the technicality when discussing the compatibility among local Kuranishi charts. In [14] we produced the global Kuranishi chart construction for Floer complexes and PSS maps, which is being extended to other chain-level structures in the current paper (with certain upgrades coming from [4] and [34]).
Now we summarize the technical framework underlying our implementation of the virtual technique. Compared to the regularization component, the perturbation component is to simply apply a blackbox theorem (Theorem N) which was already established in [13]. However, the delicate prerequisite for the blackbox theorem, along with other requirements, demands careful fine-tunings of the regularization component. Since each stage produces different kinds of objects whose compatibility conditions all look similar to flow category structure, each stage-wise construction is phrased as producing a flow category enriched in a particular “regular stratification category.” The objects of such a category are stratified in a way similar to manifolds with corners, with a monoidal structure corresponding to (direct) product and disjoint union.
To be more concrete, the whole procedure we are describing can be summarized in the following zig-zag of functors
⏞regularization​𝐓𝐨𝐩¯←𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯NC→𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯NC←𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯FOP→𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯⏟perturbation.\hbox to0.0pt{$\overbrace{\phantom{\underline{\smash{\bf Top}}\leftarrow\underline{\smash{\bf Kur}}_{\rm finite}^{\rm NC}\rightarrow\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{\rm NC}}}^{{\rm regularization}}$\hss}\underline{\smash{\bf Top}}\leftarrow\underline{\smash{\bf SKur}}^{\rm NC}\rightarrow\underbrace{\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{\rm NC}\leftarrow\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{\rm FOP}\rightarrow\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}}_{\rm perturbation}.
The items are all regular stratification categories where
•
𝐓𝐨𝐩¯\underline{\smash{\bf Top}} is the category of stratified topological spaces;
•
𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯NC\underline{\smash{\bf SKur}}^{\rm NC} is the category of normally complex smooth Kuranishi charts;
•
𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯NC\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{{\rm NC}} is the category of normally complex derived orbifolds;
•
𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}} is the category of pseudomanifolds.
In the case of Floer complex, the geometric data of Floer theory (the Hamiltonian and the almost complex structure) provides a flow category enriched in 𝐓𝐨𝐩¯\underline{\smash{\bf Top}}. The regularization component can be summarized as constructing a “lift” of this flow category to 𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯NC\underline{\smash{\bf SKur}}^{\rm NC}. This step is basically accomplished by repackaging the AMS construction [3, 4] (where the construction of the normal complex structure also borrows ideas from [2]), which contains several delicate steps. Once this lift is constructed, it automatically descends to a flow category enriched in 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯NC\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{\rm NC}, where the blackbox theorem on FOP perturbations can be directly applied. After the FOP perturbation, the flow category becomes enriched in 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}, which automatically produces a chain complex over integers.
To obtain chain-level structures such as continuation maps, pair-of-pants products etc., we also consider two “higher” analogues of flow categories, i.e., flow multimodules and flow homotopies. Typically, flow categories induce chain complexes, multimodules induce chain maps, and flow homotopies induce chain homotopies. These chain-level structures are also obtained from compatibly implementing the AMS+FOP procedure, namely, producing multimodules and homotopies enriched in categories appearing in the above zig-zag diagram. The differences from the flow category cases only lie in various sub-technical levels.
1.4.1. Other AMS-type regularization schemes
There have been several related works which carry out AMS-type constructions in Floer theory, which aim at constructing not only a single global chart construction, but a compatible system for all involved moduli spaces. These works include [57], [33], [17], [44], and [56], as well as our previous work [14].
One distinct feature of our work is the formal description of the compatibility condition using the notion of “lifts” of flow categories to various “regular stratification categories.” Having realized that each step of the AMS construction requires a certain compatibility for the choices made for individual moduli spaces (such as the thickening data, stable smoothing, normal complex structure etc.), the formal notions of regular stratification categories and lifts are more convenient and rigorous, although one needs to carefully define each regular stratification category.
The compatibility condition we require here is also most refined since we need to construct genuine perturbations (essentially the same level of refinedness should be established in [57] and [56], both of which use the FOP perturbation method developed by us). The specific requirement is contained in the definition of various regular stratification categories, most notably ⌊𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯rigNC{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf SKur}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm NC}, the category of collared rigidified normally complex smooth Kuranishi spaces. Here the collaredness and rigidifiedness are what make the inductive perturbation possible, from low-energy moduli spaces to high-energy ones. Some other works such as [33] and [17] where genuine perturbations are not needed, the requirement of compatibility can be relaxed. On the other hand, the work [44], which also relies on constructing compatible (multi-valued) perturbations, uses a different strategy to interpolate not-so-compatible choices over the collar regions.
1.5. Structure of the paper
This paper is divided into four main parts. In Part 1, we introduce a series of formal notions, including various categories such as those of pseudomanifolds with corners, Kuranishi spaces, derived orbifolds, and their variants; the notions of flow categories, multimodules, and homotopies; the abstract construction of chain-level objects; and the blackbox of FOP perturbation method. In Part 2, we introduce flow categories, multimodules, and homotopies appearing in (non-equivariant) Floer theory, state the main technical theorems about AMS regularization, and prove most of the main results stated in the introduction. In Part 3, we provide the details of the AMS construction asserted in Part 2. In Part 4, we modify all the previous constructions in the equivariant setting and establish results related to the quantum Steenrod operations.
