We thank Egor Shelukhin and Nicolas Wilkins for related discussions involving our collaboration [12]. We thank Zihong Chen, Helmut Hofer, Rohil Prasad, Sobhan Seyfaddini for their interest in our work and encouragement.
Part I FORMAL NOTIONS
Outline of Part 1
We introduce the abstract framework underlying the formulation of Floer theory in various levels. Several concepts related to Floer theory and the virtual construction are described in more abstract ways, including the abstract notion of flow categories/multimodules/homotopies/concatenations enriched in so-called regular stratification categories and their lifts to different categories. Concrete examples of such regular stratification categories will appear in the geometric construction, including Kuranishi spaces, derived orbifolds, pseudomanifolds, etc. We also formulate the abstract mechanism for deriving chain-level structures from flow categories/multimodules/homotopies. Lastly, we provide the FOP perturbation method as a blackbox theorem which can be directly applied.
2. Regular Stratification Categories
2.1. Regular posets
The purpose of this subsection is to introduce notions associated with partially ordered sets which will be used to define the index sets of stratifications of various moduli spaces coming from geometric constructions.
2.1.1. Partially ordered sets
The term “partially ordered set” is abbreviated as poset, which is always assumed to be countable. The partial order relations are denoted by ≤\leq, ⪯\preceq, etc. A poset map is a map of the underlying sets which respects the partial orders.
For a poset AA, let Amax=Atop⊆AA^{\max}=A^{\rm top}\subseteq A be the subset of maximal elements. A poset AA has a canonical Alexandrov topology: a subset U⊆AU\subseteq A is Alexandrov open if α∈U\alpha\in U and α≤β\alpha\leq\beta imply that β∈U\beta\in U. By definition, poset maps are continuous under the Alexandrov topology. A special class of closed subset indexed by α∈A\alpha\in A
∂αA={β∈A|β≤α}\partial^{\alpha}A=\{\beta\in A\ |\ \beta\leq\alpha\}
is used frequently in this paper.
Remark 2.1.
Our convention is opposite from that of Abouzaid [5], where he regards top strata as minimal elements of the labelling poset.
The product of finitely many posets carries a canonically induced partial order from the lexicographic order. Indeed, if A1,…,AkA_{1},\ldots,A_{k} are posets, then the relation
(α1,…,αk)≤(β1,…,βk)​if and only if​αi≤βi​∀i=1,…,k,(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k})\leq(\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{k})\ \text{if and only if}\ \alpha_{i}\leq\beta_{i}\ \forall i=1,\ldots,k,
is a partial order on A1×⋯×AkA_{1}\times\cdots\times A_{k}.
Notation 2.2.
Let SS be a countable subset. Let A(S)A^{(S)} denote the set of all finite subsets of SS whose partial order is α≤β⟹β⊆α\alpha\leq\beta\Longrightarrow\beta\subseteq\alpha. So its maximal element is the empty set.
Now we introduce the kind of posets which can model manifolds with corners.
Definition 2.3.
(Homogeneous posets)
(1)
A poset AA is called homogeneous if for each α∈A\alpha\in A, the length of a maximal sequence of elements α=α0<α1<⋯<αk\alpha=\alpha_{0}<\alpha_{1}<\cdots<\alpha_{k} with αk∈Amax\alpha_{k}\in A^{\max}, is finite and only depends on α\alpha (but not the maximal string and αk\alpha_{k}). This length is called the depth or codimension of α\alpha, denoted by depth⁡(α){\rm depth}(\alpha). In particular,
α∈Amax⟺depth⁡(α)=0.\alpha\in A^{\max}\Longleftrightarrow{\rm depth}(\alpha)=0.
(2)
A poset map between homogeneous posets is called homogeneous of degree kk if the map increases the depth function by k≥0k\geq 0.
(3)
Given a homogeneous poset AA, define
𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖γ:={β<γ|depth⁡(β)=depth⁡(γ)+1}\mathbb{Face}^{\gamma}:=\{\beta<\gamma\ |\ {\rm depth}(\beta)={\rm depth}(\gamma)+1\}
and
𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ:={β∈𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖γ|α≤β<γ}.\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}:=\{\beta\in\mathbb{Face}^{\gamma}\ |\ \alpha\leq\beta<\gamma\}.
Definition 2.4.
A homogeneous poset AA is called regular if every γ∈A\gamma\in A satisfies the following conditions.
(1)
For any α≤γ\alpha\leq\gamma, 𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma} is always a finite set (but not necessarily 𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖γ\mathbb{Face}^{\gamma}).
(2)
The natural map to the set of subsets of 𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖γ\mathbb{Face}^{\gamma}
fγ:∂γA→A(𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖γ),α↦𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγf_{\gamma}:\partial^{\gamma}A\to A^{(\mathbb{Face}^{\gamma})},\ \alpha\mapsto\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}
is injective.
(3)
For any finite subset S⊆𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖γS\subseteq\mathbb{Face}^{\gamma}
⋂β∈S∂βA={∅,S∉Im​fγ,∂αA,S=fγ​(α)\bigcap_{\beta\in S}\partial^{\beta}A=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}\emptyset,&S\notin{\rm Im}f_{\gamma},\\
\partial^{\alpha}A,&S=f_{\gamma}(\alpha)\end{array}\right.
We often need to identify the faces that are only adjacent to one top stratum.
Definition 2.5.
Let AA be a regular poset.
(1)
A true boundary stratum of AA is an element β∈A\beta\in A of depth 11 which has only one top stratum above. The true boundary of AA is the Alexandrov closure of the set of true boundary strata.
(2)
A regular poset is called normal if each depth-one element is either adjacent to one top stratum (true boundary) or adjacent to two top strata (fake boundary).
Remark 2.6.
The poset A(S)A^{(S)} in Notation 2.2 is regular with depth function given by depth⁡(α)=#​α{\rm depth}(\alpha)=\#\alpha. On the other hand, the poset of three elements α<β<γ\alpha<\beta<\gamma is homogeneous but not regular.
We prove several important properties of regular posets.
Lemma 2.7 (Properties of regular posets).
Let AA be a regular poset. Then the following is true.
(1)
Any Alexandrov closed subset or Alexandrov open subset is also regular.
(2)
For α≤γ\alpha\leq\gamma, the natural map
fγ​α:{β∈A|α≤β≤γ}→A(𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ),β↦𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖βγf_{\gamma\alpha}:\{\beta\in A\ |\alpha\leq\beta\leq\gamma\}\to A^{(\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma})},\ \beta\mapsto\mathbb{Face}_{\beta}^{\gamma}
(2.1)
is a homogeneous bijection.
(3)
For any α≤γ\alpha\leq\gamma,
depth⁡(α)=depth⁡(γ)+#​𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ.{\rm depth}(\alpha)={\rm depth}(\gamma)+\#\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}.
(4)
When α≤β≤γ\alpha\leq\beta\leq\gamma, there is a canonical bijection
𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ∖𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖βγ≅𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αβ.\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}\setminus\mathbb{Face}_{\beta}^{\gamma}\cong\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\beta}.
Moreover, when α≤β≤γ≤δ\alpha\leq\beta\leq\gamma\leq\delta, the composition 𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αβ→𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ→𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αδ\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\beta}\to\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}\to\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\delta} coincides with the inclusion 𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αβ→𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αδ\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\beta}\to\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\delta} defined from the above bijection.
(5)
If i:A→A′i:A\to A^{\prime} is a homogeneous poset injection to another regular poset A′A^{\prime}, then for any α≤γ\alpha\leq\gamma in AA, the induced map 𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ→𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖i⁡(α)i⁡(γ)\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}\to\mathbb{Face}_{i(\alpha)}^{i(\gamma)} is a bijection.
Proof.
(1) follows from the definition of the Alexandrov topology and the definition of regular posets. For (2), we show that the fγ​αf_{\gamma\alpha} is bijective. By the definition of regular posets, this is an injection. For surjectivity, assume on the contrary that S⊆𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγS\subseteq\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma} is not in the range of fγ​αf_{\gamma\alpha}. Then it is not in the range of fγf_{\gamma} either. By the definition of regular posets, we must have
⋂β∈S∂βA=∅.\bigcap_{\beta\in S}\partial^{\beta}A=\emptyset.
However, the above intersection at least contains α\alpha, a contradiction. Hence fγ​αf_{\gamma\alpha} is surjective. Moreover, it is clear that fγ​αf_{\gamma\alpha} is a poset map. One can verify that fγ​αf_{\gamma\alpha} is homogeneous by an easy inductive argument. Then (3) follows from the homogeneity condition.
For (4), for any λ∈𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ∖𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖βγ\lambda\in\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}\setminus\mathbb{Face}_{\beta}^{\gamma}, consider
∂λA∩∂βA=∂λA∩⋂τ∈𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖βγ∂τA.\partial^{\lambda}A\cap\partial^{\beta}A=\partial^{\lambda}A\cap\bigcap_{\tau\in\mathbb{Face}_{\beta}^{\gamma}}\partial^{\tau}A.
Then the subset {λ}∪𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖βγ⊆𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ\{\lambda\}\cup\mathbb{Face}_{\beta}^{\gamma}\subseteq\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}, under the inverse of fγ​αf_{\gamma\alpha}, gives an element κ\kappa between α\alpha and β\beta whose depth is one bigger than that of β\beta, hence defines a map from 𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ∖𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖βγ\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}\setminus\mathbb{Face}_{\beta}^{\gamma} to 𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αβ\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\beta}. One can verify that this is a bijection.
For (5), the homogeneity condition implies that ii induces an injection from 𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma} to 𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖i⁡(α)i⁡(γ)\mathbb{Face}_{i(\alpha)}^{i(\gamma)}. Then by (3), we have
#​𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ=depth⁡(γ)−depth⁡(α)=depth⁡(i⁡(γ))−depth⁡(i⁡(α))=#​𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖i⁡(α)i⁡(γ),\#\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}={\rm depth}(\gamma)-{\rm depth}(\alpha)={\rm depth}(i(\gamma))-{\rm depth}(i(\alpha))=\#\mathbb{Face}_{i(\alpha)}^{i(\gamma)},
which shows that the induced map is a bijection.
∎
It is straightforward to check that regular posets admit finite products (Cartesian product) and finite coproducts (disjoint union).
Definition 2.8.
The category of regular posets, denoted by 𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐏𝐨𝐬¯\underline{\smash{\bf RegPos}}, has objects being countable regular posets and morphisms being injective homogeneous poset maps.
Proposition 2.9.
𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐏𝐨𝐬¯\underline{\smash{\bf RegPos}} is a distributive monoidal category with respect to the direct product and disjoint union, whose units are posets with a single element.
Proof.
This is straightforward from checking the definitions.
∎
2.2. Regular stratification categories and presentations
Definition 2.10.
A regular stratification category is a distributive monoidal category 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}} together with a distributive monoidal functor 𝐂¯→𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐏𝐨𝐬¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}\to\underline{\smash{\bf RegPos}}, called the forgetful functor, satisfying the following properties. In the following, we say an object KK of 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}} an AA-stratified object if the forgetful functor sends KK to AA.
(1)
There is an initial object which is ∅\emptyset-stratified.
(2)
For any morphism f:A→Bf:A\to B in 𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐏𝐨𝐬¯\underline{\smash{\bf RegPos}} and any BB-stratified object KK, there is a canonical “pullback,” which is an AA-stratified object f∗​Kf^{*}K, together with a canonical morphism f~:f∗​K→K\tilde{f}:f^{*}K\to K. The pullback needs to satisfy the functoriality condition. Namely, the composition of pullbacks is the pullback by the composition.
In particular, for any AA-stratified object KK and α∈A\alpha\in A there is a restriction ∂αK\partial^{\alpha}K for each α∈A\alpha\in A.
As we will see below, there are a few examples of regular stratification categories such as those of regularly stratified topological spaces (with morphisms being embeddings), regularly stratified topological/smooth manifolds, regularly stratified Kuranishi charts, and Kuranishi presentations. On the other hand, if 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}} is any category, then the product 𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐏𝐨𝐬¯×𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf RegPos}}\times\underline{\smash{\bf C}} is a regular stratification category with respect to the obvious forgetful functor.
2.3. Stratified spaces, manifolds, and pseudomanifolds
2.3.1. Regularly stratified spaces
Although we can define stratified spaces in general, in this paper all such spaces have strata indexed by regular posets. Therefore, we restrict to this situation. We will specify a regular stratification category 𝐓𝐨𝐩¯\underline{\smash{\bf Top}} of regularly stratified topological spaces.
Definition 2.11.
Let AA be a countable regular poset. An AA-stratified space (AA-space for short) is a locally compact, Hausdorff and second countable topological space XX endowed with a map
s:X→As:X\to A
which is continuous with respect to the Alexandrov topology on AA whose range is finite.
In particular, we can write
X=⨆α∈AXα,where​Xα:=s−1​(α),X=\bigsqcup_{\alpha\in A}X_{\alpha},\ {\rm where}\ X_{\alpha}:=s^{-1}(\alpha),
which satisfies the following conditions.
(1)
Each XαX_{\alpha} (called a stratum) is locally closed.
(2)
All but finitely many strata are empty.
(3)
For each α∈A\alpha\in A, the subset
∂αX:=⨆β≤αXβ\partial^{\alpha}X:=\bigsqcup_{\beta\leq\alpha}X_{\beta}
is a closed set (which may contain the closure of XαX_{\alpha} properly66
6
This condition is weaker than the “axiom of frontier:” Xα∩Xβ¯≠∅⟹Xα⊆Xβ¯X_{\alpha}\cap\overline{X_{\beta}}\neq\emptyset\Longrightarrow X_{\alpha}\subseteq\overline{X_{\beta}}, which is part of the usual definition of a stratification.). Note that this condition follows from the continuity of ss.
Remark 2.12.
An open subset of an AA-stratified space is still regarded as AA-stratified, although the subset may have more empty strata.
We introduce the following notions for stratified spaces.
Definition 2.13.
(Category of regularly stratified spaces)
(1)
A map from an A1A_{1}-space X1X_{1} to an A2A_{2}-space X2X_{2} is a commutative diagram
X1\textstyle{X_{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}f\scriptstyle{f}s1\scriptstyle{s_{1}}X2\textstyle{X_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}s2\scriptstyle{s_{2}}A1\textstyle{A_{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}i\scriptstyle{i}A2\textstyle{A_{2}}
where i:A1→A2i:A_{1}\to A_{2} is a morphism in 𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐏𝐨𝐬¯\underline{\smash{\bf RegPos}} and ff is a continuous map. We usually call such a map a stratified map to emphasize that it respects the stratifications.
(2)
A stratified map f:X1→X2f:X_{1}\to X_{2} as above is called an embedding if ff is a homeomorphism onto its image. ff is called an open embedding if it is an embedding with an open image; it is called a homeomorphism if ff is a homeomorphism of topological spaces and the underlying poset map is an isomorphism.
(3)
The category 𝐓𝐨𝐩¯\underline{\smash{\bf Top}} is the category of topological spaces stratified by regular posets whose morphisms are stratified embeddings.
(4)
Let GG be a topological group. A GG-action on an AA-space XX is a continuous GG-action on XX which preserves each stratum. In this case, the ∂αA\partial^{\alpha}A-space ∂αX\partial^{\alpha}X has an induced GG-action.
2.3.2. Notations for corners
In order to define stratified pseudomanifolds, we need to fix the notations for corners. Let ϵ>0\epsilon>0 be a positive real number. The model for collars is the space [0,ϵ)k[0,\epsilon)^{k} which is stratified by subsets of {1,…,k}\{1,\ldots,k\}. More generally, for any finite set SS, consider
[0,ϵ)S={(xa)a∈S|xa∈[0,ϵ)}[0,\epsilon)^{S}=\{(x_{a})_{a\in S}\ |\ x_{a}\in[0,\epsilon)\}
which is stratified by A(S)A^{(S)}.
Definition 2.14.
Let AA be a countable regular poset.
(1)
An AA-space XX is said to have corners if for each x∈Xαx\in X_{\alpha} and each maximal γ∈Amax\gamma\in A^{\max} with α≤γ\alpha\leq\gamma, there exists a corner chart, i.e., a stratified open embedding onto an open neighborhood of xx in XX
Ux,α×[0,ϵ)𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ\textstyle{U_{x,\alpha}\times[0,\epsilon)^{\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}φ\scriptstyle{\varphi}∂γX\textstyle{\partial^{\gamma}X\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}{α}×A(𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ)\textstyle{\{\alpha\}\times A^{(\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma})}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}∂γA\textstyle{\partial^{\gamma}A}
where Ux,αU_{x,\alpha} is an open neighborhood of xx in XαX_{\alpha} (which is stratified by {α}\{\alpha\}). Here the underlying poset map, whose image is {β∈A|α≤β≤γ}⊆∂γA\{\beta\in A\ |\ \alpha\leq\beta\leq\gamma\}\subseteq\partial^{\gamma}A, is the inverse of the isomorphism (2.1).
(2)
An AA-stratified manifold is an AA-stratified space XX which has corners such that each XαX_{\alpha} (the “interior” of ∂αX\partial^{\alpha}X) is a topological manifold.77
7
It follows from this condition that each ∂αX\partial^{\alpha}X is a topological manifold with boundary whose interior is XαX_{\alpha}. A smooth structure on an AA-stratified manifold XX consists of smooth structures on all XαX_{\alpha} and a maximal atlas of corner charts which are smoothly compatible.
Then we can define the notion of smooth functions, tensors, vector bundles, Lie group actions, on smooth AA-manifolds. We omit the details. Moreover, we obtain a regular stratification category 𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{\bf Man}} of topological manifolds and a regular stratification category 𝐒𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{\bf SMan}} of smooth manifolds.
2.3.3. Stratified pseudomanifolds
Definition 2.15.
An nn-dimensional pseudomanifold is a topological space MM with a partition M=Int​M⊔δ​MM={\rm Int}M\sqcup\delta M satisfying
(1)
Int​M{\rm Int}M is open, dense, and itself an nn-dimensional topological manifold.
(2)
δ​M\delta M admits a partition into topological manifolds of dimensions at most n−2n-2.
Definition 2.16.
Let AA be a countable regular poset. An AA-stratified nn-dimensional pseudomanifold is an AA-stratified space XX together with partitions Xα=Int​Xα⊔δ​XαX_{\alpha}={\rm Int}X_{\alpha}\sqcup\delta X_{\alpha} such that
(1)
For each α∈A\alpha\in A, Xα=Int​Xα⊔δ​XαX_{\alpha}={\rm Int}X_{\alpha}\sqcup\delta X_{\alpha} is a pseudomanifold of dimension n−depth⁡(α)n-{\rm depth}(\alpha).
(2)
For x∈Xαx\in X_{\alpha} and each maximal γ∈Amax\gamma\in A^{\rm max} with α≤γ\alpha\leq\gamma, there exists a corner chart
Ux,α×[0,ϵ)𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ→∂γXU_{x,\alpha}\times[0,\epsilon)^{\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}}\to\partial^{\gamma}X
which sends IntUx,α×[0,ϵ)𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ{\rm Int}U_{x,\alpha}\times[0,\epsilon)^{\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}} resp. δUx,α×[0,ϵ)𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ\delta U_{x,\alpha}\times[0,\epsilon)^{\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}} into Int​∂γX{\rm Int}\partial^{\gamma}X resp. δ⁡(∂γX)\delta(\partial^{\gamma}X).
Notice that a stratified zero-dimensional pseudomanifold is a discrete collection of points and a stratified 1-dimensional pseudomanifold is a disjoint union of 1-manifolds (with boundary).
Definition 2.17.
An embedding of stratified pseudomanifolds from X1X_{1} to X2X_{2} is an embedding of stratified spaces f:X1→X2f:X_{1}\to X_{2} such that f⁡(Int​X1)⊆Int⁡(X2)f({\rm Int}X_{1})\subseteq{\rm Int}(X_{2}) and f⁡(δ​X1)⊆δ​X2f(\delta X_{1})\subseteq\delta X_{2}. The category of stratified pseudomanifolds, denoted by 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}, has objects being stratified pseudomanifolds and morphisms being embeddings.
One can check that 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}} is a regular stratification category (Definition 2.10).
3. Kuranishi Spaces
The Kuranishi theory for moduli spaces of pseudoholomorphic curves originated from the efforts of extending the definition of symplectic Gromov–Witten invariants and Hamiltonian Floer homology to full generality. It is based on the fundamental fact that the Cauchy–Riemann operator is elliptic. Fukaya–Ono [30] firstly introduced the package of Kuranishi structures, alongside another finite-dimensional reduction approach of Li–Tian [42] (see also [66] [58]). While the method of Kuranishi structures was further developed by Fukaya–Oh–Ohta–Ono (see the comprehensive treatment in [27]) together with closely related works by McDuff–Wehrheim [49, 47, 48], there are alternate approaches with considerable novelties, including the algebraic version of Pardon [53] as well as the more recent “global chart construction” of Abouzaid–McLean–Smith [3] (followed up by [34] and [4]).
The AMS construction was adopted by the authors in [13] in the Gromov–Witten setting and [14] in the Hamiltonian Floer setting.
We use 𝐊𝐮𝐫¯\underline{\smash{\bf Kur}}, 𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯\underline{\smash{\bf SKur}}, and 𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯NC\underline{\smash{\bf SKur}}^{\rm NC} to denote the category of Kuranishi charts in topological, smooth, or stably complex categories. When the discussion can be unified in the three cases, we simply use 𝐊𝐮𝐫¯\underline{\smash{\bf Kur}}. See below for the detailed definitions.
3.1. Kuranishi spaces
Definition 3.1.
Let AA be a countable regular poset.
(1)
An AA-stratified (topological) Kuranishi space (K-space for short) is a quadruple K=(G,V,E,S)K=(G,V,E,S) where GG is a compact Lie group, VV is an AA-manifold with a continuous GG-action, E→VE\to V is a GG-equivariant vector bundle, and S:V→ES:V\to E is a GG-equivariant section, such that the GG-action on VV has only finite stabilizers.
(2)
A Kuranishi space K=(G,V,E,S)K=(G,V,E,S) is said to be smooth if VV is a smooth AA-manifold, the GG-action is smooth, and E→VE\to V is a smooth equivariant vector bundle (we do not impose any smoothness condition on SS).
3.1.1. Morphisms of Kuranishi spaces
In order to define a regular stratification category (see Definition 2.10), we need to specify morphisms. We first define a general form of maps.
Definition 3.2.
A strict map of smooth/topological Kuranishi spaces from K1=(G1,V1,E1,S1)K_{1}=(G_{1},V_{1},E_{1},S_{1}) to K2=(G2,V2,E2,S2)K_{2}=(G_{2},V_{2},E_{2},S_{2}), denoted by ι21:K1→K2\iota_{21}:K_{1}\to K_{2}, consists of a Lie group homomorphism ι21G:G1→G2\iota_{21}^{G}:G_{1}\to G_{2} and a commutative diagram
E1\textstyle{E_{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}ι21E\scriptstyle{\iota_{21}^{E}}E2\textstyle{E_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}V1\textstyle{V_{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}S1\scriptstyle{S_{1}}ι21V\scriptstyle{\iota_{21}^{V}}V2\textstyle{V_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}S2\scriptstyle{S_{2}}
where ι21V\iota_{21}^{V} is an equivariant smooth/continuous map and ι21E\iota_{21}^{E} is an equivariant smooth/continuous bundle map.
Notice that strict maps can be composed.
We list a few special kinds of strict maps.
Definition 3.3 (Conjugation).
Let K=(G,V,E,S)K=(G,V,E,S) be a K-chart. The conjugation of KK by g∈Gg\in G is the strict map ιg:K→K\iota_{g}:K\to K where ιgG:G→G\iota_{g}^{G}:G\to G is the conjugation h↦g−1​h​gh\mapsto g^{-1}hg and ιgV\iota_{g}^{V} resp. ιgE\iota_{g}^{E} is the action of the form x↦g−1​xx\mapsto g^{-1}x. Two strict maps ι21,ι21′:K1→K2\iota_{21},\iota_{21}^{\prime}:K_{1}\to K_{2} are said to be conjugate if there exists g2∈G2g_{2}\in G_{2} such that ι21′=ιg2∘ι21\iota_{21}^{\prime}=\iota_{g_{2}}\circ\iota_{21}.
Definition 3.4 (Stabilization).
Let K=(G,V,E,S)K=(G,V,E,S) be an AA-stratified K-chart. Let πN:N→V\pi_{N}:N\to V be a GG-equivariant continuous resp. smooth vector bundle and let D⊆ND\subseteq N be a GG-invariant open (disk) subbundle.88
8
When we talk about disk bundles, we always assume that it is a subset of a certain vector bundle, although it may not appear so in notations. The stabilization of KK by DD, denoted by StabD​(K){\rm Stab}_{D}(K), is the AA-stratified K-chart
StabD​(K)=(G,D,πN∗​E⊕πN∗​N,πN∗​S⊕τN){\rm Stab}_{D}(K)=(G,D,\pi_{N}^{*}E\oplus\pi_{N}^{*}N,\pi_{N}^{*}S\oplus\tau_{N})
where τN:N→πN∗​N\tau_{N}:N\to\pi_{N}^{*}N is the tautological section. By abuse of language, we also call the morphism
ιD:K→StabD​(K)\iota_{D}:K\to{\rm Stab}_{D}(K)
induced by the zero section V→DV\to D and the obvious bundle embedding E→πN∗​E⊕πN∗​NE\to\pi_{N}^{*}E\oplus\pi_{N}^{*}N a stabilization morphism.
Definition 3.5 (Shrinking and open embedding).
(1)
Let K=(G,V,E,S)K=(G,V,E,S) be a K-chart. A shrinking of KK is a K-chart K′=(G,V′,E′,S′)K^{\prime}=(G,V^{\prime},E^{\prime},S^{\prime}) where V′⊆VV^{\prime}\subseteq V is a GG-invariant open neighborhood of S−1​(0)S^{-1}(0), E′=E|V′E^{\prime}=E|_{V^{\prime}}, and S′=S|V′S^{\prime}=S|_{V^{\prime}}.
(2)
A morphism ι21:K1→K2\iota_{21}:K_{1}\to K_{2} is called an open embedding if the underlying poset map is an isomorphism onto an Alexandrov open subset, the map V1→V2V_{1}\to V_{2} is an isomorphism onto an open subset, and the bundle map is an isomorphism of vector bundles when restricted to the open subset identified with V1V_{1}.
Definition 3.6 (Group enlargement).
Let K=(G,V,E,S)K=(G,V,E,S) be a K-chart. A group enlargement of KK by a Lie group embedding G↪G′G\hookrightarrow G^{\prime} is a K-chart
G′×GK=(G′,G′×GV,G′×GE,S′)G^{\prime}\times_{G}K=(G^{\prime},G^{\prime}\times_{G}V,G^{\prime}\times_{G}E,S^{\prime})
where S′:G′×GV→G′×GES^{\prime}:G^{\prime}\times_{G}V\to G^{\prime}\times_{G}E is the section naturally induced from SS. By abuse of language, the K-chart morphism
K→G′×GKK\to G^{\prime}\times_{G}K
induced from the natural maps V→G′×GVV\to G^{\prime}\times_{G}V and E→G′×GEE\to G^{\prime}\times_{G}E is also called a group enlargement.
Finally, the morphism which will be used most frequently in this paper is a combination of the above more elementary kinds.
Definition 3.7 (Morphisms of Kuranishi spaces).
A strict morphism or strict embedding of Kuranishi spaces from K1K_{1} to K2K_{2} is a strict map ι21:K1→K2\iota_{21}:K_{1}\to K_{2} such that there exists a commutative diagram of strict maps
K3\textstyle{K_{3}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}ιb\scriptstyle{\iota_{b}}K4\textstyle{K_{4}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}ιc\scriptstyle{\iota_{c}}K1\textstyle{K_{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}ιa\scriptstyle{\iota_{a}}ι21\scriptstyle{\iota_{21}}K2\textstyle{K_{2}}
(3.1)
where ιa\iota_{a} is a stabilization by a disk bundle, ιb\iota_{b} is a group enlargement, and ιc\iota_{c} is an open embedding. It implies in particular the group morphism ι21G\iota_{21}^{G}, the base map ι21V:V1→V2\iota_{21}^{V}:V_{1}\to V_{2}, and the bundle map ι21E:E1→E2\iota_{21}^{E}:E_{1}\to E_{2}, are all embeddings.
A conjugacy class of strict morphisms from K1K_{1} to K2K_{2} is called a morphism.
Remark 3.8.
The above definition basically says that a morphism ι21:K1→K2\iota_{21}:K_{1}\to K_{2} is an embedding if (up to group enlargement) the domain map is an embedding and the restriction of K2K_{2} to a neighborhood of the embedding image is isomorphic to a stabilization. One can also define a weaker “infinitesimal version” of K-chart embeddings. In the smooth category one can prove that the infinitesimal version is equivalent to the above definition. However, in the topological category it may not be so.
One can check that compositions of embeddings are still embeddings, which ultimately follows from the fact that every G′G^{\prime}-equivariant vector bundle over G′/GG^{\prime}/G for a group embedding G↪G′G\hookrightarrow G^{\prime} is induced from a GG-representation. Also notice that stabilization maps, open embeddings, and group enlargements are all special cases of embeddings.
Definition 3.9.
The categories of regularly stratified topological and smooth Kuranishi spaces, denoted by 𝐊𝐮𝐫¯\underline{\smash{\bf Kur}} and 𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯\underline{\smash{\bf SKur}}, are the categories whose objects are stratified Kuranishi charts in the topological and smooth categories and whose morphisms are embeddings.
Proposition 3.10.
𝐊𝐮𝐫¯\underline{\smash{\bf Kur}} and 𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯\underline{\smash{\bf SKur}} are regular stratification categories.
Proof.
Disjoint union and direct product make the category 𝐊𝐮𝐫¯\underline{\smash{\bf Kur}} distributive monoidal, with monoidal unit being the singleton K0=({0},pt,0,0)K_{0}=(\{0\},{\rm pt},0,0). On the other hand, one can obviously take pullbacks of any AA-stratified Kuranishi space with respect to homogeneous poset maps f:B→Af:B\to A.
∎
3.1.2. Free quotients
There is another relation among Kuranishi spaces which will appear in the construction. This notion first appeared as group enlargement in [3, Section 4] and then showed up as free quotient in [4, Lemma 3.5].
Definition 3.11.
Let K∼=(G∼,V∼,E∼,S∼)K^{\sim}=(G^{\sim},V^{\sim},E^{\sim},S^{\sim}) be a (topological or smooth) Kuranishi space where G∼=G×G′G^{\sim}=G\times G^{\prime} is the product of two compact Lie groups. Suppose the G′G^{\prime}-action on V∼V^{\sim} is free. Then the free quotient of K∼K^{\sim} by G′G^{\prime} is the Kuranishi space
K:=K/G′:=(G,V∼/G′,E∼/G′,S∼/G′).K:=K/G^{\prime}:=(G,V^{\sim}/G^{\prime},E^{\sim}/G^{\prime},S^{\sim}/G^{\prime}).
Notice that there is a natural strict morphism (which is not an embedding) from K∼K^{\sim} to KK. We also call the morphism a free quotient by G′G^{\prime}.
3.2. Rigidified embeddings
In our geometric construction we can obtain objects and morphisms living in a more rigid category of Kuranishi charts. In short, we only allow the stabilization to be a product bundle coming from a GG-representation.

A rigidified embedding from K1K_{1} to K2K_{2} is an embedding together with an equivalence class of rigidifications.

Then (D31⊆W31,θ31)(D_{31}\subseteq W_{31},\theta_{31}) is a rigidification of ι32∘ι21\iota_{32}\circ\iota_{21}, whose equivalence class only depends on the equivalence classes of the rigidifications of ι32\iota_{32} and ι21\iota_{21}.
Proof.
This lemma holds essentially because a trivial bundle over the total space of a trivial bundle is canonically trivial.
∎
Remark 3.14.
If in Definition 3.12 we do not require the bundle W21W_{21} to be trivial, then there is no well-defined composition for rigidified embeddings.
Remark 3.15.
One could criticize that rigidified embeddings are not anything natural. On the other hand, our geometric construction (the AMS construction) of Kuranishi flow categories allows us to obtain a topological Kuranishi flow category with rigidified embeddings as morphisms. This is very helpful in the smoothing procedure: once a stratum is smoothed, the total space of a trivial disk bundle is then canonically smoothed, giving a smooth tubular neighborhood in a higher stratum.
3.3. Stable complex structures and normal complex structures
Next, we discuss stable and normal complex structures on Kuranishi spaces. Geometrically, such structures arise from index-theoretic considerations of (virtual) tangent bundles of moduli spaces of pseudoholomorphic curves. Such structures are also instrumental for incorporating the FOP perturbation scheme to define integral invariants.
3.3.1. Stable morphisms of vector bundles
We start with a few basic definitions.
Definition 3.16.
Let GG be a Lie group, VV be a GG-space, and E→VE\to V be an equivariant vector bundle.
(1)
Let F→VF\to V be another GG-equivariant vector bundle. A GG-equivariant stable (iso)morphism from EE to FF is an equivalence class of triples (R−,R+,τ)(R^{-},R^{+},\tau) where R±R^{\pm} are a pair of real vector spaces (viewed as trivial representations of GG) and
τ:R¯−⊕E→R¯+⊕F\tau:\underline{\smash{R}}^{-}\oplus E\to\underline{\smash{R}}^{+}\oplus F
is a GG-equivariant (iso)morphism of vector bundles. The equivalence relation is induced by (R−,R+,τ)∼(R−⊕W,R+⊕W,τ⊕IdW¯)(R^{-},R^{+},\tau)\sim(R^{-}\oplus W,R^{+}\oplus W,\tau\oplus{\rm Id}_{\underline{\smash{W}}}) where WW is another real vector space. Denote a stable (iso)morphism by
τ:E​→𝑠​F.\tau:E\overset{s}{\to}F.
(2)
If E,FE,F are complex vector bundles, then a stable (iso)morphism τ:E​→𝑠​F\tau:E\overset{s}{\to}F is called complex if it is represented by a triple (R−,R+,τ)(R^{-},R^{+},\tau) where R±R^{\pm} are complex vector spaces and τ\tau is a complex vector bundle map.
One can verify that stable morphisms can be composed and stable isomorphisms admit inverses as stable isomorphisms.
3.3.2. Stable complex structures
Definition 3.17.
Let GG be a Lie group, VV be a GG-space, and E→VE\to V be a GG-equivariant vector bundle.
(1)
A GG-invariant stable complex structure on EE consists of an equivalence class of pairs (τ,F)(\tau,F) where F→VF\to V is a GG-equivariant complex vector bundle and τ:E​→𝑠​F\tau:E\overset{s}{\to}F is a GG-equivariant stable isomorphism. The equivalence relation is generated by the following relation: (τ1,F1)(\tau_{1},F_{1}) and (τ2,F2)(\tau_{2},F_{2}) are equivalent if there is a commutative diagram
E\textstyle{E\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}τ1\scriptstyle{\tau_{1}}IdE\scriptstyle{{\rm Id}_{E}}F1\textstyle{F_{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}E\textstyle{E\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}τ2\scriptstyle{\tau_{2}}F2\textstyle{F_{2}}
of stable isomorphisms where the right vertical arrow is a complex stable isomorphism.
(2)
Suppose E1E_{1} and E2E_{2} are GG-equivariant stably complex vector bundles over a GG-space VV. A GG-equivariant stable (iso)morphism f:E1​→𝑠​E2f:E_{1}\overset{s}{\to}E_{2} is said to be stably complex if there exist representatives (τ1,F1)(\tau_{1},F_{1}) and (τ2,F2)(\tau_{2},F_{2}) of their stable complex structures and a commutative diagram of stable (iso)morphisms
E1\textstyle{E_{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}τ1\scriptstyle{\tau_{1}}f\scriptstyle{f}F1\textstyle{F_{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}E2\textstyle{E_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}τ2\scriptstyle{\tau_{2}}F2\textstyle{F_{2}}
where the right vertical arrow is a GG-equivariant complex stable (iso)morphism.
(3)
Let VV be a smooth GG-manifold (with boundary and corners). A GG-equivariant stable complex structure on VV is a GG-equivariant stable complex structure on T​VTV. Notice that for each stratum ∂αV⊆V\partial^{\alpha}V\subseteq V, the stable complex structure on T​VTV induces a stable complex structure on T⁡(∂αV)T(\partial^{\alpha}V) because the normal direction is trivial.
Now we consider smooth Kuranishi space K=(G,V,E,S)K=(G,V,E,S) such that the GG-action on VV has only finite stabilizers. In this setting, T​VTV contains a trivial subbundle isomorphic to 𝔤¯\underline{\smash{\mathfrak{g}}}. On the other hand, in our construction, the obstruction bundle EE can always be made complex. This simplifies the definition of stable complex structures.
Definition 3.18.
A stably complex Kuranishi space is a smooth Kuranishi space K=(G,V,E,S)K=(G,V,E,S) equipped with a GG-invariant complex structure on EE and a GG-invariant stable complex structure on T​V/𝔤¯TV/\underline{\smash{\mathfrak{g}}}.
An open embedding of stably complex Kuranishi spaces from K1K_{1} to K2K_{2} is a smooth open embedding ι21:K1→K2\iota_{21}:K_{1}\to K_{2} such that 1) the vector bundle isomorphism
d​ι21V:T​V1/𝔤¯1→T​V2/𝔤¯2d\iota_{21}^{V}:TV_{1}/\underline{\smash{\mathfrak{g}}}_{1}\to TV_{2}/\underline{\smash{\mathfrak{g}}}_{2}
is stably complex and 2) the vector bundle isomorphism ι21E:E1→E2\iota_{21}^{E}:E_{1}\to E_{2} is complex linear.
We consider stabilizations of a stably complex Kuranishi space K=(G,V,E,S)K=(G,V,E,S) by a disk bundle πD:D→V\pi_{D}:D\to V contained in a GG-equivariant complex vector bundle N→VN\to V, which is
StabD​(K)=(G,D,πD∗​E⊕πD∗​N,πD∗​S⊕τN){\rm Stab}_{D}(K)=(G,D,\pi_{D}^{*}E\oplus\pi_{D}^{*}N,\pi_{D}^{*}S\oplus\tau_{N})
Then πD∗​E⊕πD∗​N\pi_{D}^{*}E\oplus\pi_{D}^{*}N carries a canonical complex structure. On the other hand, the bundle T​D/𝔤¯TD/\underline{\smash{\mathfrak{g}}} is non-canonically isomorphic to πD∗​T​V/𝔤¯⊕πD∗​N\pi_{D}^{*}TV/\underline{\smash{\mathfrak{g}}}\oplus\pi_{D}^{*}N. An isomorphism can be induced from a GG-invariant connection on the fiber bundle D→VD\to V.
Definition 3.19.
The stabilization of a stably complex Kuranishi space K=(G,V,E,S)K=(G,V,E,S) by a disk bundle DD contained in a GG-equivariant complex vector bundle N→VN\to V (equipped with a GG-invariant complex linear connection) is the smooth stabilization StabD​(K){\rm Stab}_{D}(K) with the induced stably complex structure on T​D/𝔤¯TD/\underline{\smash{\mathfrak{g}}} and the complex structure on πD∗​E⊕πD∗​N\pi_{D}^{*}E\oplus\pi_{D}^{*}N.
Definition 3.20.
A strict embedding of stably complex Kuranishi spaces from K1K_{1} to K2K_{2} consists of a smooth strict embedding ι21:K1→K2\iota_{21}:K_{1}\to K_{2} such that in the diagram (3.1), the stabilization ιa:K1→K3\iota_{a}:K_{1}\to K_{3} is provided by a disk bundle in a complex vector bundle and the open embedding ιc:K4→K2\iota_{c}:K_{4}\to K_{2} is an open embedding of stably complex Kuranishi spaces.
An embedding of stably complex Kuranishi spaces is a conjugacy class of strict embeddings.
Lemma 3.21.
(Strict) embeddings of stably complex Kuranishi spaces can be composed.
Proof.
Essentially one needs to consider disk bundles over disk bundles to ensure the compatibility of stable complex structures. Given Ehresmann connections on D21→V1D_{21}\to V_{1} and D32→V2D_{32}\to V_{2}, the horizontal distribution of D21D_{21} can then be lifted to D32D_{32}, giving a Ehresmann connection on the iterated bundle.
∎
Remark 3.22.
We could define the category
𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯ℂ\underline{\smash{\bf SKur}}^{\mathbb{C}}
whose objects are regularly stratified stably complex (in particular, smooth) Kuranishi spaces and whose morphisms are embeddings. It is easy to see that this is a regular stratification category, and there is a natural forgetful functor
𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯ℂ→𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯.\underline{\smash{\bf SKur}}^{\mathbb{C}}\to\underline{\smash{\bf SKur}}.
One can also consider the rigidified version. However, it is rather complicated to obtain stably complex Kuranishi spaces in our construction (although we could). Below we consider a more flexible one using normal complex structures, which suffices for our purpose.
3.3.3. Normally complex Kuranishi spaces
Moduli spaces of pseudoholomorphic curves admit stable complex structure because of the nature of the Cauchy–Riemann operator. In Section 16 we will follow the strategy of Abouzaid–Blumberg [1, 2] to do the explicit construction. However, it is a bit cumbersome to construct stable complex structures compatibly. Instead, we will only construct the normal complex structure which is sufficient for our applications and where the compatibility is easier to achieve.
Let VV be a GG-space. Notice that a stable morphism of GG-equivariant vector bundles E,F→VE,F\to V (Definition 3.16) induces the following well-defined linear maps. For each x∈Vx\in V, let Gx⊆GG_{x}\subseteq G be the stabilizer. Then the fibers ExE_{x} and FxF_{x} split as
Ex=E̊x⊕Eˇx,\displaystyle\ E_{x}=\mathring{E}_{x}\oplus\check{E}_{x},\
Fx=F̊x⊕Fˇx\displaystyle\ F_{x}=\mathring{F}_{x}\oplus\check{F}_{x}
where E̊x\mathring{E}_{x}, F̊x\mathring{F}_{x} are GxG_{x}-trivial summands and Eˇx\check{E}_{x}, Fˇx\check{F}_{x} are GxG_{x}-nontrivial pieces. Then an equivalence class of stable isomorphisms induces well-defined GxG_{x}-equivariant maps
τˇx:Eˇx→Fˇx.\check{\tau}_{x}:\check{E}_{x}\to\check{F}_{x}.
(In particular, if GG is trivial, the maps τˇx\check{\tau}_{x} are all trivial.)
Definition 3.23.
Let GG be a Lie group, VV be a GG-space, and E→VE\to V be a GG-equivariant vector bundle.
(1)
Two stable complex structures on EE, represented by (τ1,F1)(\tau_{1},F_{1}) and (τ2,F2)(\tau_{2},F_{2}), are normally equivalent, if there exists a diagram of stable isomorphisms
E\textstyle{E\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}τ1\scriptstyle{\tau_{1}}IdE\scriptstyle{{\rm Id}_{E}}F1\textstyle{F_{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}E\textstyle{E\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}τ2\scriptstyle{\tau_{2}}F2\textstyle{F_{2}}
where the right vertical arrow is complex, such that for all x∈Vx\in V, the following induced diagram of linear maps commutes.
Eˇx\textstyle{\check{E}_{x}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}τˇ1,x\scriptstyle{\check{\tau}_{1,x}}Fˇ1,x\textstyle{\check{F}_{1,x}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}Eˇx\textstyle{\check{E}_{x}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}τˇ2,x\scriptstyle{\check{\tau}_{2,x}}Fˇ2,x\textstyle{\check{F}_{2,x}}
(2)
A GG-invariant normal complex structure on EE is a normal equivalence class of stable complex structures. Notice that a normal complex structure on EE equips each Eˇx\check{E}_{x} with a GxG_{x}-invariant complex structure.
(3)
Suppose E1,E2→VE_{1},E_{2}\to V are equipped with GG-equivariant normal complex structures. A GG-equivariant stable morphism τ:E1​→𝑠​E2\tau:E_{1}\overset{s}{\to}E_{2} is called normally complex if for each x∈Vx\in V, the induced linear map Eˇ1,x→Eˇ2,x\check{E}_{1,x}\to\check{E}_{2,x} is complex linear.
Now we define the notion of normal complex Kuranishi spaces.
Definition 3.24.
A normally complex Kuranishi space (NC Kuranishi space for short) is a smooth Kuranishi space K=(G,V,E,S)K=(G,V,E,S) equipped with a GG-invariant complex structure on EE and a GG-invariant normal complex structure on T​V/𝔤TV/{\mathfrak{g}}. An open embedding of NC Kuranishi spaces from K1=(G1,V1,E1,S1)K_{1}=(G_{1},V_{1},E_{1},S_{1}) to K2=(G2,V2,E2,S2)K_{2}=(G_{2},V_{2},E_{2},S_{2}) is a smooth open embedding ι21:K1→K2\iota_{21}:K_{1}\to K_{2} such that 1) the vector bundle isomorphism
d​ι21:T​V1/𝔤1→T​V2/𝔤2d\iota_{21}:TV_{1}/{\mathfrak{g}}_{1}\to TV_{2}/{\mathfrak{g}}_{2}
is normally complex and 2) the vector bundle isomorphism ι21E:E1→E2\iota_{21}^{E}:E_{1}\to E_{2} is complex-linear.
One can again discuss stabilizations (by complex vector bundles), strict embeddings, conjugations, and embeddings of normally complex Kuranishi spaces. Then one obtains a regular stratification category called the category of normally complex Kuranishi spaces, denoted by
𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯NC\underline{\smash{\bf SKur}}^{\rm NC}
and the corresponding rigidified category 𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯rigNC\underline{\smash{\bf SKur}}^{\rm NC}_{\rm rig}.
4. Derived Orbifolds
In this section we describe another regular stratification category called the category of derived orbifolds. We will consider as general as the smooth category, but not the topological category.
4.1. Stratified orbifolds
All orbifolds, unless declared, are assumed to be smooth and effective. They are spaces which are locally modelled by U/ΓU/\Gamma where Γ\Gamma is a finite group and UU is an effective smooth Γ\Gamma-manifold. Orbifolds with boundary and corners are locally modelled on U/ΓU/\Gamma where UU is a Γ\Gamma-manifold with boundary and corners. If AA is a regular poset (Definition 2.4), then one can consider the notion of AA-orbifold. Without giving the detailed definition, we remind the reader that a smooth effective AA-orbifold contains charts of the form
Uα×[0,ϵ)(𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ),whereα≤γ∈Amax,U_{\alpha}\times[0,\epsilon)^{(\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma})},\ {\rm where\ }\alpha\leq\gamma\in A^{\max},
where UαU_{\alpha} is a Γ\Gamma-manifold without boundary. Here we always assume that the isotropy group acts trivially on the normal factors. For example, if XX is a smooth AA-manifold acted on by a compact Lie group GG with finite stabilizers, then the quotient X/GX/G is naturally a smooth effective AA-orbifold.
Definition 4.1 (Derived orbifolds).
Fix a regular poset AA. An AA-stratified derived orbifold is a triple 𝒟=(𝒰,ℰ,𝒮){\mathcal{D}}=({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}},{\mathcal{S}}) where 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} is an effective AA-orbifold, ℰ→𝒰{\mathcal{E}}\to{\mathcal{U}} is a smooth orbifold vector bundle, and 𝒮:𝒰→ℰ{\mathcal{S}}:{\mathcal{U}}\to{\mathcal{E}} is a continuous section. A derived orbifold 𝒟{\mathcal{D}} is called compact if the coarse space of 𝒮−1​(0){\mathcal{S}}^{-1}(0) is a compact topological space.
Similar to the case of Kuranishi spaces, we define embeddings of derived orbifolds as combinations of several more basic morphisms.
Definition 4.2.
Let 𝒟{\mathcal{D}} be an AA-stratified derived orbifold.
(1)
A morphism of derived orbifolds from an A1A_{1}-stratified derived orbifold 𝒟1=(𝒰1,ℰ1,𝒮1){\mathcal{D}}_{1}=({\mathcal{U}}_{1},{\mathcal{E}}_{1},{\mathcal{S}}_{1}) to an A2A_{2}-stratified derived orbifold 𝒟2=(𝒰2,ℰ2,𝒮2){\mathcal{D}}_{2}=({\mathcal{U}}_{2},{\mathcal{E}}_{2},{\mathcal{S}}_{2}) consists of a morphism i:A1→A2i:A_{1}\to A_{2} of 𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐏𝐨𝐬¯\underline{\smash{\bf RegPos}}, a smooth stratified orbifold map ϕ21:𝒰1→𝒰2\phi_{21}:{\mathcal{U}}_{1}\to{\mathcal{U}}_{2}, and a smooth orbibundle map ϕ^21:ℰ1→ℰ2\widehat{\phi}_{21}:{\mathcal{E}}_{1}\to{\mathcal{E}}_{2} covering ϕ21\phi_{21} such that the following diagram commutes.
ℰ1\textstyle{{\mathcal{E}}_{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}ϕ^21\scriptstyle{\widehat{\phi}_{21}}ℰ2\textstyle{{\mathcal{E}}_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}𝒰1\textstyle{{\mathcal{U}}_{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}ϕ21\scriptstyle{\phi_{21}}𝒮1\scriptstyle{{\mathcal{S}}_{1}}𝒰2\textstyle{{\mathcal{U}}_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}𝒮2\scriptstyle{{\mathcal{S}}_{2}}
Such a morphism induces an orbispace map 𝒮1−1​(0)→𝒮2−1​(0){\mathcal{S}}_{1}^{-1}(0)\to{\mathcal{S}}_{2}^{-1}(0).
(2)
An open embedding of derived orbifolds from 𝒟1{\mathcal{D}}_{1} to 𝒟2{\mathcal{D}}_{2} is a morphism such that the poset map i:A1→A2i:A_{1}\to A_{2} is an isomorphism onto an Alexandrov open subset, the orbifold map ϕ21\phi_{21} is an isomorphism onto an open subset, and the bundle map ϕ^21\widehat{\phi}_{21} is an isomorphism over the image of ϕ21\phi_{21}.
(3)
Given a derived orbifold 𝒟=(𝒰,ℰ,𝒮){\mathcal{D}}=({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}},{\mathcal{S}}), for any open subset 𝒰′⊆𝒰{\mathcal{U}}^{\prime}\subseteq{\mathcal{U}} with 𝒮−1​(0)⊆𝒰′{\mathcal{S}}^{-1}(0)\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}^{\prime}, the shrinking of 𝒟{\mathcal{D}} to 𝒰′{\mathcal{U}}^{\prime}, denoted by 𝒟|𝒰′{\mathcal{D}}|_{{\mathcal{U}}^{\prime}}, is the derived orbifold (𝒰′,ℰ|𝒰′,𝒮|𝒰′)({\mathcal{U}}^{\prime},{\mathcal{E}}|_{{\mathcal{U}}^{\prime}},{\mathcal{S}}|_{{\mathcal{U}}^{\prime}}). It admits a natural open embedding into 𝒟{\mathcal{D}}.
(4)
A disk bundle over an orbifold is an open neighborhood of the zero section of an orbifold vector bundle. A stabilization of a derived orbifold 𝒟=(𝒰,ℰ,𝒮){\mathcal{D}}=({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}},{\mathcal{S}}) by a disk bundle 𝒩→𝒰{\mathcal{N}}\to{\mathcal{U}} contained in a vector bundle πℱ:ℱ→𝒰\pi_{\mathcal{F}}:{\mathcal{F}}\to{\mathcal{U}} is the derived orbifold
Stab𝒩​𝒟=(𝒩,π𝒩∗​ℰ⊕π𝒩∗​ℱ,π𝒩∗​𝒮⊕τℱ){\rm Stab}_{\mathcal{N}}{\mathcal{D}}=({\mathcal{N}},\pi_{\mathcal{N}}^{*}{\mathcal{E}}\oplus\pi_{\mathcal{N}}^{*}{\mathcal{F}},\pi_{\mathcal{N}}^{*}{\mathcal{S}}\oplus\tau_{\mathcal{F}})
where τℱ\tau_{\mathcal{F}} is the tautological section. We call the natural morphism
𝒟→Stab𝒩​(𝒟){\mathcal{D}}\to{\rm Stab}_{\mathcal{N}}({\mathcal{D}})
the stabilization morphism by 𝒩{\mathcal{N}}.
(5)
An embedding of derived orbifolds from 𝒟1=(𝒰1,ℰ1,𝒮1){\mathcal{D}}_{1}=({\mathcal{U}}_{1},{\mathcal{E}}_{1},{\mathcal{S}}_{1}) to 𝒟2=(𝒰2,ℰ2,𝒮2){\mathcal{D}}_{2}=({\mathcal{U}}_{2},{\mathcal{E}}_{2},{\mathcal{S}}_{2}) is a morphism ϕ21:𝒟1→𝒟2{\bm{\phi}}_{21}:{\mathcal{D}}_{1}\to{\mathcal{D}}_{2} such that there exists a disk bundle 𝒩21→𝒰1{\mathcal{N}}_{21}\to{\mathcal{U}}_{1} and an open embedding θ21:Stab𝒩21​(𝒟1)→𝒟2\theta_{21}:{\rm Stab}_{{\mathcal{N}}_{21}}({\mathcal{D}}_{1})\to{\mathcal{D}}_{2} extending ϕ21\phi_{21}.
Definition 4.3.
The category of stratified derived orbifolds, denoted by 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}, has objects being stratified derived orbifolds and morphisms being embeddings of derived orbifolds.
The following is readily checked.
Proposition 4.4.
The category 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}} is a regular stratification category (Definition 2.10). ∎
One can see that there are functors
𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯→𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯→𝐓𝐨𝐩¯.\underline{\smash{\bf SKur}}\to\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}\to\underline{\smash{\bf Top}}.
The first arrow sends K=(G,V,E,S)K=(G,V,E,S) to the quotient 𝒟=(V/G,E/G,S/G){\mathcal{D}}=(V/G,E/G,S/G). Notice that a conjugacy class of Kuranishi space embeddings induces a well-defined embedding of derived orbifolds. The second arrow is induced by passing to the zero locus 𝒮−1​(0){\mathcal{S}}^{-1}(0) of a derived orbifold 𝒟=(𝒰,ℰ,𝒮){\mathcal{D}}=({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}},{\mathcal{S}}).
4.1.1. Rigidified embeddings
We would like to introduce an analogue of rigidified embeddings for orbifolds. We need to relax the triviality requirement. A flat orbifold vector bundle is an orbifold vector bundle together with a flat connection. A key property of flat vector bundles is, if ℰ→𝒰{\mathcal{E}}\to{\mathcal{U}} is flat and ℱ→ℰ{\mathcal{F}}\to{\mathcal{E}} is flat, then ℱ{\mathcal{F}} is canonically a flat bundle over 𝒰{\mathcal{U}}.
For example, if GG is a compact Lie group acting on a smooth manifold VV with only finite stabilizers and WW is a representation of GG, then the vector bundle (V×W)/G(V\times W)/G is flat. Notice that the pullback of rigid vector bundles is still rigid.
Definition 4.5.
Let ϕ21:𝒟1→𝒟2\phi_{21}:{\mathcal{D}}_{1}\to{\mathcal{D}}_{2} be an embedding of derived orbifolds.
(1)
A rigidification of ϕ21\phi_{21} consists of a disk bundle 𝒩21{\mathcal{N}}_{21} contained in a flat vector bundle ℱ21→𝒰1{\mathcal{F}}_{21}\to{\mathcal{U}}_{1} and an open embedding
ψ21:Stab𝒩21​(𝒟1)→𝒟2\psi_{21}:{\rm Stab}_{{\mathcal{N}}_{21}}({\mathcal{D}}_{1})\to{\mathcal{D}}_{2}
which extends ϕ21\phi_{21}.
(2)
Two rigidifications (𝒩21⊆ℱ21,ψ21)({\mathcal{N}}_{21}\subseteq{\mathcal{F}}_{21},\psi_{21}), (𝒩21′⊆ℱ21′,ψ21′)({\mathcal{N}}_{21}^{\prime}\subseteq{\mathcal{F}}_{21}^{\prime},\psi_{21}^{\prime}) are equivalent if there is a flat bundle isomorphism τ:ℱ21≅ℱ21′\tau:{\mathcal{F}}_{21}\cong{\mathcal{F}}_{21}^{\prime} which identifies 𝒩21{\mathcal{N}}_{21} with 𝒩21′{\mathcal{N}}_{21}^{\prime} after an appropriate shrinking such that
ψ21′=ψ21∘τ.\psi_{21}^{\prime}=\psi_{21}\circ\tau.
(3)
A rigidified embedding of derived orbifolds is an embedding together with an equivalence class of rigidifications.
One can see that rigid derived orbifold embeddings can be composed. Therefore we can define a category of derived orbifolds with rigid embeddings as morphisms. This category is denoted by
𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rig.\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}.
Notice that there is a quotient functor
𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯rig→𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rig.\underline{\smash{\bf SKur}}_{\rm rig}\to\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}.
4.2. Normal complex structures
Normal complex (NC for short) structures are essential for constructing FOP transverse perturbations. We recall the definitions here.
4.2.1. Basic notions
Suppose GG acts on a set AA. A subgroup H⊆GH\subseteq G is called an AA-essential subgroup, denoted by
H⊆AGH\subseteq_{A}G
if there exists a∈Aa\in A whose stabilizer is HH.
Given a real representation VV of a finite group Γ\Gamma, the basic decomposition of VV is the splitting
V=VΓ⊕VˇΓV=V_{\Gamma}\oplus\check{V}_{\Gamma}
where VΓV_{\Gamma} is the direct sum of trivial subrepresentations and VˇΓ\check{V}_{\Gamma} is the direct sum of nontrivial irreducible subrepresentations. An NC structure on VV is a Γ\Gamma-invariant complex structure on VˇΓ\check{V}_{\Gamma}.
4.2.2. NC structures
Definition 4.6.
Let UU be a Γ\Gamma-manifold and E→UE\to U be a Γ\Gamma-equivariant vector bundle. An NC structure on EE consists of, for each UU-essential subgroup H⊆UΓH\subseteq_{U}\Gamma, a HH-invariant complex structure IEˇHI^{\check{E}_{H}} on the subbundle
EˇH⊆E|UH\check{E}_{H}\subseteq E|_{U_{H}}
satisfying the following conditions.
(1)
For each g∈Γg\in\Gamma which conjugates HH to H′:=g​H​g−1H^{\prime}:=gHg^{-1}, the bundle isomorphism EˇH→Eˇg​H​g−1\check{E}_{H}\to\check{E}_{gHg^{-1}} sends IEˇHI^{\check{E}_{H}} to IEˇH′I^{\check{E}_{H^{\prime}}}.
(2)
For each pair of UU-essential subgroups K⊆H⊆ΓK\subseteq H\subseteq\Gamma, one has the KK-equivariant decomposition
EˇH≅EˇK⊕(EˇH∩EK|UH).\check{E}_{H}\cong\check{E}_{K}\oplus(\check{E}_{H}\cap E_{K}|_{U_{H}}).
We require that the restriction of IEˇHI^{\check{E}_{H}} to EˇK\check{E}_{K} coincides with IEˇKI^{\check{E}_{K}}.
Definition 4.7.
Let 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} be an effective orbifold and ℰ→𝒰{\mathcal{E}}\to{\mathcal{U}} be an orbifold vector bundle. An NC structure on ℰ{\mathcal{E}} consists of, for each bundle chart C^=(Γ,U,E)\hat{C}=(\Gamma,U,E) of ℰ{\mathcal{E}}, an NC structure 𝑰E{\bm{I}}^{E} on the vector bundle EE, such that chart embeddings respect those complex structures. An NC structure on 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} is by definition an NC structure on T​𝒰T{\mathcal{U}}.
A normally complex derived orbifold is a derived orbifold 𝒟=(𝒰,ℰ,𝒮){\mathcal{D}}=({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}},{\mathcal{S}}) together with NC structures on 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} and ℰ{\mathcal{E}}.
Definition 4.8 (Embeddings of NC derived orbifolds).
(1)
An open embedding of normally complex derived orbifolds from 𝒟1{\mathcal{D}}_{1} to 𝒟2{\mathcal{D}}_{2} is an open embedding of derived orbifolds which respects normal complex structures.
(2)
A stabilization of an NC derived orbifold is a stabilization by a disk bundle which is contained in a complex orbifold vector bundle.
(3)
An embedding of NC derived orbifolds ι21:𝒟1→𝒟2\iota_{21}:{\mathcal{D}}_{1}\to{\mathcal{D}}_{2} is an embedding such that there exists a stabilization of 𝒟1{\mathcal{D}}_{1} by a disk bundle 𝒩21→𝒰1{\mathcal{N}}_{21}\to{\mathcal{U}}_{1} and an open embedding from Stab𝒩21​(𝒟1)→𝒟2{\rm Stab}_{{\mathcal{N}}_{21}}({\mathcal{D}}_{1})\to{\mathcal{D}}_{2} which extends ι21\iota_{21}.
(4)
A rigidified embedding of NC derived orbifolds from 𝒟1{\mathcal{D}}_{1} to 𝒟2{\mathcal{D}}_{2} is a rigidified embedding whose rigidification can be represented by a disk bundle in a rigid complex vector bundle. Two rigidifications are equivalent if they (after appropriate shrinking to smaller disk bundles) differ by an isomorphism of rigid complex vector bundles.
Therefore we obtained the category 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯NC\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{\rm NC} of normally complex derived orbifolds with morphisms being embeddings and the category 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{{\rm NC}}_{\rm rig} with the same objects with morphisms being rigidified embeddings. One can see that they are both regular stratification categories.
Lemma 4.9.
There are natural functors of regular stratification categories
𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯NC→𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯NC,\displaystyle\ \underline{\smash{\bf SKur}}^{\rm NC}\to\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{{\rm NC}},\
𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯rigNC→𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC\displaystyle\ \underline{\smash{\bf SKur}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm NC}\to\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{{\rm NC}}_{\rm rig}
Proof.
Let K=(G,V,E,S)K=(G,V,E,S) be a stably complex Kuranishi space. Then by definition, EE has a GG-invariant complex structure and the vector bundle
T​V/𝔤¯TV/\underline{\smash{\mathfrak{g}}}
has a GG-invariant stable complex structure. This means there exists a real vector space RR and a complex structure on
T​V/𝔤¯⊕R¯.TV/\underline{\smash{\mathfrak{g}}}\oplus\underline{\smash{R}}.
Consider the quotient chart
K/G:=(𝒰,ℰ,𝒮)K/G:=({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}},{\mathcal{S}})
where 𝒰=V/G{\mathcal{U}}=V/G. Given any x∈Vx\in V with stabilizer Gx⊆GG_{x}\subseteq G, one has the GxG_{x}-invariant decomposition
Tx​V≅Tx​VGx⊕Nx​VGx.T_{x}V\cong T_{x}V_{G_{x}}\oplus N_{x}V_{G_{x}}.
The stable complex structure on T​V/𝔤¯TV/\underline{\smash{\mathfrak{g}}} induces a complex structure on Nx​VGxN_{x}V_{G_{x}}. The collection of these complex structures forms a normal complex structure on the quotient orbifold. One can easily check that the morphisms descend to morphisms in 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯NC\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{{\rm NC}} and 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{{\rm NC}}_{\rm rig}.
∎
5. Collars
Various inductive constructions require moduli spaces, which appear as, e.g., morphism spaces of flow categories, to have compatible collars. While one can possibly discuss collars in an abstract manner, we refrain from doing so. Instead, in this section we only consider the categories with geometric meanings. More precisely, in this section, the category 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}} belongs to the list 𝐓𝐨𝐩¯\underline{\smash{\bf Top}}, 𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{\bf Man}}, 𝐒𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{\bf SMan}}, 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}, 𝐊𝐮𝐫¯\underline{\smash{\bf Kur}}, 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}} etc. Following an idea of Fukaya, we explain how to equip the geometric objects of interest with collars “on the outside” which facilitates inductive constructions of various sorts.
5.1. The subcategory of collared objects
For the discussions in this section, let ϵ>0\epsilon>0 be a positive real number. The model for collars is the space [0,ϵ)k[0,\epsilon)^{k} which is stratified by subsets of {1,…,k}\{1,\ldots,k\}. More generally, for any finite set SS, we can form the collar [0,ϵ)S[0,\epsilon)^{S} stratified by the set A(S)A^{(S)} (Notation 2.2). These standard collars are objects of all the relevant regular stratification categories 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}} listed above.
Definition 5.1.
Let 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}} be either 𝐓𝐨𝐩¯\underline{\smash{\bf Top}}, 𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{\bf Man}}, 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}, 𝐒𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{\bf SMan}}, 𝐊𝐮𝐫¯\underline{\smash{\bf Kur}}, 𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯\underline{\smash{\bf SKur}}, or 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}.
For any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, an ϵ\epsilon-collaring of an AA-stratified object M∈Ob​𝐂¯M\in{\rm Ob}\underline{\smash{\bf C}} is a collection of open embeddings
∂αM×[0,ϵ)𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ→∂γM,α≤γ\partial^{\alpha}M\times[0,\epsilon)^{\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}}\to\partial^{\gamma}M,\ \alpha\leq\gamma
(called a collar embedding from α\alpha to γ\gamma)
such that 1) its restriction to ∂αM\partial^{\alpha}M is the inclusion of ∂αM\partial^{\alpha}M into MM and 2) whenever α≤β≤γ\alpha\leq\beta\leq\gamma, the following diagram commutes.
∂αM×[0,ϵ)𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ\textstyle{\partial^{\alpha}M\times[0,\epsilon)^{\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}∂γM\textstyle{\partial^{\gamma}M}∂αM×[0,ϵ)𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αβ×[0,ϵ)𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖βγ\textstyle{\partial^{\alpha}M\times[0,\epsilon)^{\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\beta}}\times[0,\epsilon)^{\mathbb{Face}_{\beta}^{\gamma}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}∂βM×[0,ϵ)𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖βγ\textstyle{\partial^{\beta}M\times[0,\epsilon)^{\mathbb{Face}_{\beta}^{\gamma}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
An ϵ\epsilon-collaring and an ϵ′\epsilon^{\prime}-collaring are germ-equivalent if for a certain ϵ′′≤ϵ,ϵ′\epsilon^{\prime\prime}\leq\epsilon,\epsilon^{\prime}, for all α≤γ\alpha\leq\gamma, the restrictions of the collar embeddings to ∂αM×[0,ϵ′′)𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ\partial^{\alpha}M\times[0,\epsilon^{\prime\prime})^{\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}} are identical. A collared object in 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}} is an object together with a germ-equivalence class of ϵ\epsilon-collarings.
Definition 5.2.
A morphism between two collared objects KK and K′K^{\prime} with underlying poset map i:A→A′i:A\to A^{\prime} is called collared if there exists a sufficiently small ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that for each α≤γ\alpha\leq\gamma in AA, the morphism over the strata γ↦i⁡(γ)\gamma\mapsto i(\gamma) in the collared neighborhoods of the strata α↦i⁡(α)\alpha\mapsto i(\alpha) is given by
∂αK×Collarϵ𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ\textstyle{\partial^{\alpha}K\times{\rm Collar}_{\epsilon}^{\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}∂i⁡(α)K′×Collarϵ𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖i⁡(α)i⁡(γ)\textstyle{\partial^{i(\alpha)}K^{\prime}\times{\rm Collar}_{\epsilon}^{\mathbb{Face}_{i(\alpha)}^{i(\gamma)}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}∂γK\textstyle{\partial^{\gamma}K\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}∂i⁡(γ)K′\textstyle{\partial^{i(\gamma)}K^{\prime}}
where the map along the collar direction is the identity map after identifying 𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ≅𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖i⁡(α)i⁡(γ)\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}\cong\mathbb{Face}_{i(\alpha)}^{i(\gamma)}.
In this way we obtain a subcategory
⌊𝐂¯{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf C}}
of collared objects, whose morphisms are collared morphisms. Notice that the empty set and singletons are always collared. Moreover, the collar structures respect products and disjoint unions. Therefore, the category ⌊𝐂¯{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf C}} is a regular stratification category (Definition 2.10).
5.2. Outercollaring construction
For manifolds with boundary, it is well-known that one can construct collars. However, it is not easy to find collars for more complicated objects, for example, smooth manifolds with corners. Here we would like to adopt the outercollaring construction from [27, Section 17] to avoid such discussions. Instead of finding collars in the given geometric object, we add collars outside. In general, for each category 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}} listed at the beginning of this section, we would like to construct monoidal functors called the ϵ\epsilon-outercollaring
{⋅}:𝐂¯→𝐂¯⌊.\{\cdot\}:\underline{\smash{\bf C}}\to{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf C}}.
Some care must be taken when we are in the smooth category.
5.2.1. Outercollaring of stratified spaces
We first discuss the outercollaring of objects in 𝐓𝐨𝐩¯\underline{\smash{\bf Top}}. Let AA be a regular poset and XX be an AA-space. Upon choosing a nonnegative number ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0, we would like to define a new AA-space denoted by ⌊X{}_{\lfloor}X called the outer collaring of XX of width ϵ\epsilon such that the association X↦⌊XX\mapsto{}_{\lfloor}X satisfies certain functorial properties (see Lemma 5.3).
We first assume that AA has a unique maximal element γ\gamma, i.e., XX has a single top stratum. Abbreviate 𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖α=𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖αγ\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}=\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}^{\gamma}. Define
X⌊=(⨆α∈A∂αX×[−ϵ,0]𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖α)/∼,{}_{\lfloor}X=\left(\bigsqcup_{\alpha\in A}\partial^{\alpha}X\times[-\epsilon,0]^{\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}}\right)/\sim,
where the equivalence relation ∼\sim is generated by the following relation: if α≤β\alpha\leq\beta (which implies 𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖β⊆𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖α\mathbb{Face}_{\beta}\subseteq\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}), we identify
(x,(ti)i∈𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖β)∈∂βX×[−ϵ,0]𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖β\big(x,(t_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{Face}_{\beta}}\big)\in\partial^{\beta}X\times[-\epsilon,0]^{\mathbb{Face}_{\beta}}
with
(y,(sj)j∈𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖α)∈∂αX×[−ϵ,0]𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖α\big(y,(s_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}}\big)\in\partial^{\alpha}X\times[-\epsilon,0]^{\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}}
if x=y∈∂αXx=y\in\partial^{\alpha}X, sj=0s_{j}=0 when j∉𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖βj\notin\mathbb{Face}_{\beta} and tj=sjt_{j}=s_{j} when j∈𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖βj\in\mathbb{Face}_{\beta}. We call ⌊X{}_{\lfloor}X the outer collaring of XX of width ϵ\epsilon (see Figure 1).

Now consider the general situation when the regular poset has arbitrarily many maximal elements. For each maximal γ∈Amax\gamma\in A^{\max}, one has the outer collaring
(∂γX)⌊.{}_{\lfloor}(\partial^{\gamma}X).
Notice that if α≤γ1,α≤γ2\alpha\leq\gamma_{1},\alpha\leq\gamma_{2}, then there is a natural isomorphism
(∂α(∂γ1X))⌊≅(∂α(∂γ2X))⌊.{}_{\lfloor}\big(\partial^{\alpha}(\partial^{\gamma_{1}}X)\big)\cong{}_{\lfloor}\big(\partial^{\alpha}(\partial^{\gamma_{2}}X)\big).
Then define
X⌊:=(⨆γ∈Amax(∂γX)⌊)/∼{}_{\lfloor}X:=\left(\bigsqcup_{\gamma\in A^{\max}}{}_{\lfloor}(\partial^{\gamma}X)\right)/\sim
where ∼\sim means we identify points in (∂γ1X)⌊{}_{\lfloor}(\partial^{\gamma_{1}}X) and points in (∂γ2X)⌊{}_{\lfloor}(\partial^{\gamma_{2}}X) with respect to the above natural isomorphisms. Figure 2 describes an example of the outer collaring of a space XX with two top strata.

The following statement is straightforward from the definition.
Lemma 5.3.
The ϵ\epsilon-outer collaring is a regular stratification functor
{⋅}⌊:𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐓𝐨𝐩¯→𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐓𝐨𝐩¯⌊.∎{}_{\lfloor}\{\cdot\}:\underline{\smash{\bf RegTop}}\to{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf RegTop}}.\qed
The outer collar construction is compatible with group actions. If GG acts on XX, then for each g∈Gg\in G and (x,(ti)i∈𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖α)∈∂αX×[−ϵ,0]𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖α(x,(t_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}})\in\partial^{\alpha}X\times[-\epsilon,0]^{\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}}, define
g⋅(x,(ti)i∈𝔽α)=(gx,(ti)i∈𝔽α)∈∂αX×[−ϵ,0]𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖α⊆X⌊.g\cdot(x,(t_{i})_{i\in{\mathbb{F}}_{\alpha}})=(gx,(t_{i})_{i\in{\mathbb{F}}_{\alpha}})\in\partial^{\alpha}X\times[-\epsilon,0]^{\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}}\subseteq{}_{\lfloor}X.
It is easy to check that this gives a GG-action on ⌊X{}_{\lfloor}X.
5.3. Category of admissible smooth manifolds and orbifolds
The outercollaring of stratified topological manifolds is completely identical to the case of stratified spaces. However, the case with smooth manifolds is tricky.
We recall the notion of admissible manifolds with corners introduced in [27, Chapter 25]. Let VV be a smooth manifold without boundary. For t=(t1,…,tk)∈[0,+∞)kt=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{k})\in[0,+\infty)^{k}, denote
Ti:=e1/ti.T_{i}:=e^{1/t_{i}}.
Consider smooth functions
f:V×[0,ϵ)k→ℝ.f:V\times[0,\epsilon)^{k}\to{\mathbb{R}}.
We consider the CmC^{m}-norm stratumwise using the above coordinates TiT_{i} instead of tit_{i}. Let
|f|Cm|f|_{C^{m}}
be the pointwise CmC^{m}-norm in the above sense.
Definition 5.4.
(cf. [27, Definition 25.3]) We say f:V×[0,ϵ)k→ℝf:V\times[0,\epsilon)^{k}\to{\mathbb{R}} is admissible if for each compact K⊆V×[0,ϵ)kK\subseteq V\times[0,\epsilon)^{k} and m>0m>0, there exist σ⁡(m,K)>0\sigma(m,K)>0 and C⁡(m,K)>0C(m,K)>0 such that
|∂f∂Ti|Cm≤C(m,K)e−σ⁡(m,K)​Ti,i=1,…,k.\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial T_{i}}\right|_{C^{m}}\leq C(m,K)e^{-\sigma(m,K)T_{i}},\ i=1,\ldots,k.
Admissible functions are smooth (see [27, Remark 25.5]). Using the ring of admissible functions (see [27, Lemma 25.13]), we can consider corner charts on a smooth manifold with corners with admissible coordinate changes. In this way, one obtains a subcategory
𝐒𝐌𝐚𝐧¯adm\underline{\smash{\bf SMan}}_{\rm adm}
of 𝐒𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{\bf SMan}}. Notice that the category ⌊𝐒𝐌𝐚𝐧¯{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf SMan}} of collared smooth manifolds is automatically a subcategory of 𝐒𝐌𝐚𝐧¯adm\underline{\smash{\bf SMan}}_{\rm adm}.
Similarly, one can consider the admissible versions of the categories 𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯\underline{\smash{\bf SKur}} and 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}. The key feature of the admissibility is that the outercollaring is well-defined (see [27, Section 17.3]). Indeed, for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exist functors
⌊ϵ:𝐂¯adm→⌊𝐂¯{}_{\lfloor}\epsilon:\underline{\smash{\bf C}}_{\rm adm}\to{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf C}}
where 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}} is either 𝐒𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{\bf SMan}}, or 𝐒𝐊𝐮𝐫¯\underline{\smash{\bf SKur}}, or 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}. For each admissible object MM, let the result be called the ϵ\epsilon-outercollaring of MM.
Finally, also notice that the standard collars are normally complex derived orbifolds. In fact manifolds are automatically normally complex orbifolds. Hence one has the collared versions
⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯NC,\displaystyle\ {}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{{\rm NC}},\
⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯NCrig.\displaystyle\ {}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{{\rm NC}}_{\rm rig}.
6. Flow Categories, Multimodules, and Homotopies
6.1. Flow categories
The concept of flow categories was introduced by Cohen–Jones–Segal [22]. We need a variant of the original construction similar to [52, Section 7] and [5, Section 7,8]. See also the formulations in [14].
Definition 6.1 (Flow categories).
Let 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}} be a regular stratification category (Definition 2.10). A 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}-enriched flow category 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} consists of the following elements.
(1)
The set of objects Ob​𝔽{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}, which is a countable poset (not assumed to be regular).
(2)
For any pair p≤qp\leq q of objects, a morphism space Mp​q𝔽M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}, which is an object of 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}} stratified by a normal poset Ap​q𝔽A_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}} (Definition 2.5).
(3)
For any triple p≤r≤qp\leq r\leq q of objects, the composition map is defined as follows. It consists of an injective poset map homogeneous of degree 11
Ap​r𝔽×Ar​q𝔽→Ap​q𝔽A_{pr}^{\mathbb{F}}\times A_{rq}^{\mathbb{F}}\to A_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}
with image
Ap​r​q𝔽⊆Ap​q𝔽,A_{prq}^{\mathbb{F}}\subseteq A_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}},
together with a morphism in 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}
ιp​r​q𝔽:Mp​r𝔽×Mr​q𝔽→Mp​q𝔽|Ap​r​q𝔽.\iota_{prq}^{\mathbb{F}}:M_{pr}^{\mathbb{F}}\times M_{rq}^{\mathbb{F}}\to M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}|_{A_{prq}^{\mathbb{F}}}.
Moreover, the following conditions must be satisfied.1010
10
The first four conditions are usually required for flow categories. The remaining conditions are imposed in order to obtain the correct chain level information.
(1)
Mp​q𝔽≠∅M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}\neq\emptyset if and only if p≤qp\leq q.
(2)
Mp​p𝔽M_{pp}^{\mathbb{F}} is a monoidal unit of 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}.
(3)
When p=rp=r resp. r=qr=q, the composition Mp​p𝔽×Mp​q𝔽→Mp​q𝔽M_{pp}^{\mathbb{F}}\times M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}\to M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}} resp. Mp​q𝔽×Mq​q𝔽→Mp​q𝔽M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}\times M_{qq}^{\mathbb{F}}\to M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}} is the natural isomorphism from the monoidal structure.
(4)
(Associativity) For any quadruple p≤r≤s≤qp\leq r\leq s\leq q of objects, the following diagram commutes, where the arrows are defined using composition maps:

(5)

Example 6.2.
A trivial flow category enriched in 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}, denoted by 𝕆{\mathbb{O}}, is the flow category whose object set has a single element ee with self-morphism space Me​e𝕆M_{ee}^{{\mathbb{O}}} being a monoidal unit of 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}.
6.2. Flow multimodules and homotopies
Flow bimodules are abstract packages of moduli spaces considered in situations such as continuation maps, PSS and SSP maps, etc. There is a more general notion of flow multimodules allowing multiple flow categories as inputs, which model situations such as the pair-of-pants product.
Definition 6.3.

Definition 6.4.
A multimodule over (𝔽;𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}) is called a bimodule, usually denoted by 𝔹{\mathbb{B}}.
6.2.1. Products of multimodules
In the above we only defined the situation with one output—this is the main scenario that will appear in this paper. On the other hand, there is no difficulty in extending the definition to multimodules with multiple output flow categories.
In general, let 𝔽1,…,𝔽m;𝔽1′,…,𝔽n′{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{n}^{\prime} be flow categories enriched over 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}. A multimodule over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽1′,…,𝔽n′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{n}^{\prime}), denoted by 𝕏{\mathbb{X}}, consists of objects
Mp1⋯pm;p1′⋯pn′𝕏∈Ob𝐂¯M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p_{1}^{\prime}\cdots p_{n}^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}}\in{\rm Ob}\underline{\smash{\bf C}}
together with structural maps
Mpi​qi𝔽i×Mp1⋯pi−1qipi+1⋯pm;p1′⋯pn′𝕏→Mp1⋯pm;p1′⋯pn′𝕏M_{p_{i}q_{i}}^{{\mathbb{F}}_{i}}\times M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1}q_{i}p_{i+1}\cdots p_{m};p_{1}^{\prime}\cdots p_{n}^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}}\to M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p_{1}^{\prime}\cdots p_{n}^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}}
and
Mp1⋯pm;p1′⋯pi−1′qi′pi+1′⋯pn′𝕏×Mqi′​pi′𝔽i′→Mp1⋯pm;p1′⋯pn′𝕏M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p_{1}^{\prime}\cdots p_{i-1}^{\prime}q_{i}^{\prime}p_{i+1}^{\prime}\cdots p_{n}^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}}\times M_{q_{i}^{\prime}p_{i}^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{F}}_{i}^{\prime}}\to M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p_{1}^{\prime}\cdots p_{n}^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}}
which satisfy conditions similar to those in Definition 6.3. We omit the details.
It is straightforward to define products of multimodules. Suppose 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} is a multimodule over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}) and 𝕐{\mathbb{Y}} is a multimodule over (𝔾1,…,𝔾n,𝔾′)({\mathbb{G}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{G}}_{n};{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}). Then for objects pi∈Ob​𝔽ip_{i}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{i}, qj∈Ob​𝔾jq_{j}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{G}}_{j}, p′∈Ob​𝔽′p^{\prime}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}, q′∈Ob​𝔾′q^{\prime}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}, the collection of objects
Mp1⋯pmq1⋯qn;p′q′𝕏×𝕐:=Mp1⋯pm;p′𝕏×Mq1⋯qn;q′𝕐M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m}q_{1}\cdots q_{n};p^{\prime}q^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}\times{\mathbb{Y}}}:=M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}}\times M_{q_{1}\cdots q_{n};q^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{Y}}
define a multimodule 𝕏×𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\times{\mathbb{Y}} over (𝔽1,⋯,𝔽m,𝔾1,…,𝔾n,𝔽′,𝔾′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\cdots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m},{\mathbb{G}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{G}}_{n};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime},{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}).
6.2.2. Homotopies of multimodules
For the following definition, denote by [0,1][0,1] the homogeneous poset with one unique maximal element, thought as the total space of the unit interval, and two codimension 11 element, which are the boundary points {0}\{0\} and {1}\{1\}.

6.3. Lifts of flow categories, multimodules, and homotopies
The key issue of constructing Floer chain complex (and various chain maps, homotopies) is to regularize certain moduli spaces. Using the terminologies we just introduced, the associated flow categories (and multimodules, homotopies), whose morphism spaces are certain moduli spaces, are enriched in 𝐓𝐨𝐩¯\underline{\smash{\bf Top}}. The regularization requires a lift to a better category which allows manipulations in differential topological or algebraic topological sense.
Let 𝐂¯^\underline{\smash{\hat{\bf C}}} and 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}} be two regular stratification categories (Definition 2.10). Let 𝐅:𝐂¯^→𝐂¯{\bf F}:\underline{\smash{\hat{\bf C}}}\to\underline{\smash{\bf C}} be a covariant functor satisfying the natural compatibility conditions.
(1)
𝐅{\bf F} respects the distributive monoidal structure.
(2)
The diagram 𝐂¯^\textstyle{\underline{\hat{\bf C}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}𝐅\scriptstyle{\bf F}𝐂¯\textstyle{\underline{\bf C}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐏𝐨𝐬¯\textstyle{\underline{\bf RegPos}} commutes.
(3)
𝐅{\bf F} respects the pullback. Namely, if M^\hat{M} is an AA-stratified object of 𝐂¯^\underline{\smash{\hat{\bf C}}} and B⊆AB\subseteq A, then one has the natural isomorphism
𝐅⁡(M^)|B≅𝐅⁡(M^|B).{\bf F}(\hat{M})|_{B}\cong{\bf F}(\hat{M}|_{B}).
Definition 6.6.
Suppose 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} is a 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}-enriched flow category. A lift of 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} with respect to 𝐅:𝐂¯^→𝐂¯{\bf F}:\underline{\smash{\hat{\bf C}}}\to\underline{\smash{\bf C}} is a 𝐂¯^\underline{\smash{\hat{\bf C}}}-enriched flow category 𝔽^\hat{\mathbb{F}} satisfying the following conditions.
(1)
The set of objects are identical Ob​𝔽^=Ob​𝔽{\rm Ob}\hat{\mathbb{F}}={\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}.
(2)
𝐅⁡(Mp​q𝔽^)=Mp​q𝔽{\bf F}(M_{pq}^{\hat{\mathbb{F}}})=M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}} and 𝐅∗​ιp​r​q𝔽^=ιp​r​q𝔽{\bf F}_{*}\iota_{prq}^{\hat{\mathbb{F}}}=\iota_{prq}^{\mathbb{F}}.
Definition 6.7.
Suppose 𝔽1,⋯,𝔽m,𝔽′{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\cdots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m},{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} are 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}-enriched flow categories and 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} is a multimodule over (𝔽1,⋯,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\cdots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}). Suppose 𝔽^1,…,𝔽^m,𝔽^′\hat{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\mathbb{F}}_{m},\hat{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} are lifts of 𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m},{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} in 𝐂¯^\underline{\smash{\hat{\bf C}}} respectively.
(1)
A lift of 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} which extends 𝔽^1,…,𝔽^m;𝔽^′\hat{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\mathbb{F}}_{m};\hat{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} is a multimodule 𝕏^\hat{\mathbb{X}} over (𝔽^1,…,𝔽^m,𝔽^′)(\hat{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\mathbb{F}}_{m};\hat{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}) such that for any tuple of objects p1,…,pm;p′p_{1},\ldots,p_{m};p^{\prime} of the involved flow categories and pi≤qip_{i}\leq q_{i}, q′≤p′q^{\prime}\leq p^{\prime}, one has
𝐅(Mp1⋯pm;p′𝕏^)=Mp1⋯pm;p′𝕏{\bf F}(M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\hat{\mathbb{X}}})=M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}}
and
𝐅∗ιp1⋯pi−1(piqi)pi+1⋯pm;p′𝕏^=ιp1⋯pi−1(piqi)pi+1⋯pm;p′𝕏,\displaystyle\ {\bf F}_{*}\iota_{p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1}(p_{i}q_{i})p_{i+1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\hat{\mathbb{X}}}=\iota_{p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1}(p_{i}q_{i})p_{i+1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}},\
𝐅∗ιp1⋯pm;q′p′𝕏^=ιp1⋯pm;q′p′𝕏.\displaystyle\ {\bf F}_{*}\iota_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};q^{\prime}p^{\prime}}^{\hat{\mathbb{X}}}=\iota_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};q^{\prime}p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}}.
(2)
Suppose 𝕏^0\hat{\mathbb{X}}_{0} and 𝕏^1\hat{\mathbb{X}}_{1} are two such lifts of multimodules 𝕏0{\mathbb{X}}_{0} and 𝕏1{\mathbb{X}}_{1} over (𝔽1,⋯,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\cdots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}) respectively. Let ℍ{\mathbb{H}} be a homotopy from 𝕏0{\mathbb{X}}_{0} to 𝕏1{\mathbb{X}}_{1}. A lift of ℍ{\mathbb{H}} to 𝐂¯^\underline{\smash{\hat{\bf C}}} which extends 𝔽^\hat{\mathbb{F}}, 𝔽^′\hat{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}, 𝕏^0\hat{\mathbb{X}}_{0}, and 𝕏^1\hat{\mathbb{X}}_{1} is a homotopy ℍ^\hat{\mathbb{H}} from 𝕏^0\hat{\mathbb{X}}_{0} to 𝕏^1\hat{\mathbb{X}}_{1} such that for any tuple of objects p1,⋯,pm;p′p_{1},\cdots,p_{m};p^{\prime}, q′,p′∈Ob​𝔽′q^{\prime},p^{\prime}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}, one has
𝐅(Mp1⋯pm;p′ℍ^)=Mp1⋯pm;p′ℍ,{\bf F}(M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\hat{\mathbb{H}}})=M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{H}},
𝐅∗ιp1⋯pi−1(piqi)pi+1⋯pm;p′ℍ^=ιp1⋯pi−1(piqi)pi+1⋯pm;p′ℍ,\displaystyle\ {\bf F}_{*}\iota_{p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1}(p_{i}q_{i})p_{i+1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\hat{\mathbb{H}}}=\iota_{p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1}(p_{i}q_{i})p_{i+1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{H}},\
