We can see that the previously discussed canonical construction of concatenations satisfies the above definition. On the other hand, in many situations, the construction of the concatenation 𝕏∘i𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}} is not canonical but involves choices one needs to make.
Remark 6.14.
We would like to reiterate that in Definition 6.13, 𝕏∘i𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}} is part of the data: we do not construct 𝕏∘i𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}} using 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} and 𝕐{\mathbb{Y}}. This is in contrast with the gluing construction in [2, Section 5], where the concatenation is carried out for bimodules enriched in 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}} by thickening up the boundary strata. In our applications, all 𝕏∘i𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}} arise from geometric context, and the notations in Definition 6.13 already ensure the desired chain-level statements.
6.6. Weak flow categories, bimodules, and homotopies
In certain cases it is convenient to use the notion of direct products of flow categories, which satisfy a weaker version of Definition 6.1. We make the following definitions in order to have a simple formulation of certain structures on multimodules involved in the equivariant pair-of-pants product.
Definition 6.15.
A weak flow category enriched in 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}, denoted by 𝔽{\mathbb{F}}, consists of a countable partially ordered set of objects Ob​𝔽{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}} and a morphism space Mp​q𝔽M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}} as an object of 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}} for each pair p≤qp\leq q, and composition maps ιp​r​q𝔽:Mp​r𝔽×Mr​q𝔽→Mp​q𝔽\iota_{prq}^{\mathbb{F}}:M_{pr}^{\mathbb{F}}\times M_{rq}^{\mathbb{F}}\to M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}} (whose underlying poset map is not necessarily homogeneous of degree 11) which satisfy (1)—(5) of Definition 6.1.
Example 6.16.
Let 𝔽1,…,𝔽m{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m} be (weak) flow categories. Define 𝔽1×⋯×𝔽m{\mathbb{F}}_{1}\times\cdots\times{\mathbb{F}}_{m} as a weak flow category with
Ob𝔽1×⋯×𝔽m=∏j=1mOb𝔽j,{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{1}\times\cdots\times{\mathbb{F}}_{m}=\prod_{j=1}^{m}{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{j},
morphism spaces
M(p1⋯pm)(q1⋯qm)𝔽1×⋯×𝔽m=∏j=1mMpj​qj𝔽j,M_{(p_{1}\cdots p_{m})(q_{1}\cdots q_{m})}^{{\mathbb{F}}_{1}\times\cdots\times{\mathbb{F}}_{m}}=\prod_{j=1}^{m}M_{p_{j}q_{j}}^{{\mathbb{F}}_{j}},
and product structural maps.
We can also define the similar notion of weak multimodules.
Definition 6.17.
Let 𝔽1,…,𝔽m;𝔽′{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} be weak flow categories enriched in 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}. A weak multimodule 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}) consists of the same type of objects Mp1⋯pm;p′𝕏M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}} and structural maps (whose underlying poset map is not necessarily homogeneous of degree 11) satisfying conditions (1)–(4) of Definition 6.3.
The following lemma is readily checked.
Lemma 6.18.
Let 𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m},{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} be flow categories enriched in 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}. Let 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} be a multimodule over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}). Then the objects Mp1⋯pm;p′𝕏M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}} and structural maps in 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} define a weak bimodule over (𝔽1×⋯×𝔽m;𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1}\times\cdots\times{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}).
The following notion is introduced merely to simplify the formulation of multimodule concatenations. It is not the same as the more geometric bimodule obtained via continuation maps.
Definition 6.19.
Let 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} be a (weak) flow category. The naive identity bimodule of 𝔽{\mathbb{F}}, denoted by 𝕀𝔽​𝔽{\mathbb{I}}^{\mathbb{FF}}, is the weak bimodule over (𝔽;𝔽)({\mathbb{F}};{\mathbb{F}}) with
Mp;q𝕀𝔽​𝔽=Mp​q𝔽M_{p;q}^{{\mathbb{I}}^{\mathbb{FF}}}=M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}
and structural maps induced from composition maps of 𝔽{\mathbb{F}}.
The case of homotopies is similar. We omit the definition and the corresponding lemma.
6.6.1. Multimodule concatenations as weak bimodule concatenations
Now we consider the situation of multimodule concatenations. Let 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} be a multimodule over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔾i)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{G}}_{i}) and 𝕐{\mathbb{Y}} be a multimodule over (𝔾1,…,𝔾n,𝔾′)({\mathbb{G}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{G}}_{n};{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}). The concatenation 𝕏∘i𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}} at 𝔾i{\mathbb{G}}_{i} is defined previously as a multimodule over (𝔾1,⋯,𝔾i−1,𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔾i+1,…,𝔾n,𝔾′)({\mathbb{G}}_{1},\cdots,{\mathbb{G}}_{i-1},{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m},{\mathbb{G}}_{i+1},\ldots,{\mathbb{G}}_{n};{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}) (together with other data). As multimodules can be treated as weak bimodules (Lemma 6.18), we can interpret the concatenation as a concatenation of a pair of weak multimodules.
First, notice that the notion of concatenations can be extended from multimodules to weak multimodules. Then we consider the product of weak bimodules
𝕀𝔾1​𝔾1×⋯×𝕀𝔾i−1​𝔾i−1×𝕏×𝕀𝔾i+1​𝔾i+1×⋯×𝕀𝔾n​𝔾n{\mathbb{I}}^{{\mathbb{G}}_{1}{\mathbb{G}}_{1}}\times\cdots\times{\mathbb{I}}^{{\mathbb{G}}_{i-1}{\mathbb{G}}_{i-1}}\times{\mathbb{X}}\times{\mathbb{I}}^{\mathbb{G}_{i+1}\mathbb{G}_{i+1}}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{I}^{\mathbb{G}_{n}\mathbb{G}_{n}}
as a weak bimodule over (𝔾1×⋯×𝔾i−1×𝔽1×⋯×𝔽m×𝔾i+1×⋯×𝔾n;𝔾1×⋯×𝔾n)({\mathbb{G}}_{1}\times\cdots\times{\mathbb{G}}_{i-1}\times{\mathbb{F}}_{1}\times\cdots\times{\mathbb{F}}_{m}\times{\mathbb{G}}_{i+1}\times\cdots\times{\mathbb{G}}_{n};{\mathbb{G}}_{1}\times\cdots\times{\mathbb{G}}_{n}). Then the multimodule concatenation 𝕏∘i𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}} is equivalent to the weak bimodule concatenation
(𝕀𝔾1​𝔾1×⋯×𝕀𝔾i−1​𝔾i−1×𝕏×𝕀𝔾i+1​𝔾i+1×⋯×𝕀𝔾n​𝔾n)∘𝕐.({\mathbb{I}}^{{\mathbb{G}}_{1}{\mathbb{G}}_{1}}\times\cdots\times{\mathbb{I}}^{{\mathbb{G}}_{i-1}{\mathbb{G}}_{i-1}}\times{\mathbb{X}}\times{\mathbb{I}}^{\mathbb{G}_{i+1}\mathbb{G}_{i+1}}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{I}^{\mathbb{G}_{n}\mathbb{G}_{n}})\circ{\mathbb{Y}}.
The purpose of introducing this formal notion is to simplify the definition of equivariance of multimodules when the symmetry group permutes the source flow categories.
7. Algebraic Structures
In this section we describe how to obtain algebraic structures such as chain complexes, chain maps, and chain homotopies from, respectively, flow categories, multimodules, and homotopies. When additional structures exist, these chain-level objects also carry corresponding structures such as equivariance and module structures over Novikov rings.
7.1. Unobstructedness, local finiteness, grading, and orientations
We start by considering the most basic properties of flow categories, multimodules, and homotopies that lead to chain-level structures. Notice that these structures will only produce chain complex etc. as abelian groups. To obtain objects as modules over various Novikov rings, one needs certain extra symmetries on the flow categories etc.
7.1.1. Unobstructedness
In geometric applications, the flow categories, multimodules, and homotopies always satisfy an additional property which does not have a general formulation. Here we specify this property.
Definition 7.1.
Let 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} be a flow category enriched in 𝐓𝐨𝐩¯\underline{\smash{\bf Top}}. It is said to be unobstructed1212
12
This terminology comes from Lagrangian Floer theory. If we formulate the Lagrangian Floer flow category, then in general the true boundary of moduli spaces contain configurations with disk bubbles, potentially causing obstruction to define a chain complex. if for any triple p<r<qp<r<q of objects, the structural morphism
ιp​r​q𝔽:Mp​r𝔽×Mr​q𝔽→Mp​q𝔽\iota_{prq}^{\mathbb{F}}:M_{pr}^{\mathbb{F}}\times M_{rq}^{\mathbb{F}}\to M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}
is a homeomorphism onto ∂p​r​qMp​q𝔽\partial^{prq}M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}. Hence the union of these strata is the true boundary of Mp​q𝔽M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}.
If 𝐂¯→𝐓𝐨𝐩¯\underline{\smash{{\bf C}}}\to\underline{\smash{\bf Top}} is a functor of regular stratification categories and 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} is a flow category enriched in 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}, 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} is called unobstructed if the induced flow category enriched in 𝐓𝐨𝐩¯\underline{\smash{\bf Top}} is unobstructed.
Similarly, we can define the notion of unobstructedness for multimodules and homotopies enriched in 𝐓𝐨𝐩¯\underline{\smash{\bf Top}}. We omit the details. In applications within this paper, all geometric flow categories and their lifts are unobstructed.
7.1.2. Convergence
We need certain properties guaranteeing the convergence of the chain-level objects in certain nonarchimedean completions. To incorporate the equivariant case, we allow a second functional which is bounded from one side to give a different completion.
Definition 7.2.
A filtration on a (weak) flow category 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} is a monotonic function
𝒜:Ob​𝔽→ℝk​(k≥1){\mathcal{A}}:{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{k}\ (k\geq 1)
where ℝk{\mathbb{R}}^{k} has the product partial order. The filtration is called locally finite if for each p∈Ob​𝔽p\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}} and any c>0c>0,
#{q∈Ob𝔽|p<q,𝒜α(p)−𝒜α(q)<c,α=1,…,k}<∞.\#\Big\{q\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}\ |\ p<q,\ {\mathcal{A}}_{\alpha}(p)-{\mathcal{A}}_{\alpha}(q)<c,\ \alpha=1,\ldots,k\Big\}<\infty.
A (weak) flow category equipped with a locally finite filtration is called a locally finite (weak) flow category.
Lemma 7.3.
If (𝔽i,𝒜i)({\mathbb{F}}_{i},{\mathcal{A}}_{i}), i=1,…,mi=1,\ldots,m are locally finite filtered flow categories, then the product (𝔽1×⋯×𝔽m,𝒜1⊕⋯⊕𝒜m)({\mathbb{F}}_{1}\times\cdots\times{\mathbb{F}}_{m},{\mathcal{A}}_{1}\oplus\cdots\oplus{\mathcal{A}}_{m}) is a locally finite weak flow category.
Proof.
Straightforward.
∎
Remark 7.4.
In a typical Floer theoretic setup, the action 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-valued. In the equivariant case considered in Part 4 of this paper, the action will have two components.
Now we consider the local finiteness condition for multimodules. The condition we need is not only to guarantee a well-defined convergent chain map, but also that multimodule concatenations preserve such conditions.
Definition 7.5.
Let (𝔽,𝒜)({\mathbb{F}},{\mathcal{A}}) and (𝔽′,𝒜′)({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime},{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}) be 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}-enriched locally finite (weak) flow categories. Suppose 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is ℝk{\mathbb{R}}^{k}-valued and 𝒜′{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime} is ℝk′{\mathbb{R}}^{k^{\prime}}-valued. A (weak) bimodule 𝔹{\mathbb{B}} over (𝔽;𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}) is called locally finite if the following conditions are satisfied.
(1)
For any p∈Ob​𝔽p\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}, c′∈ℝc^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{R}},
#{p′∈Ob𝔽′|Mp;p′𝔹≠∅,min1≤α≤k′𝒜α′(p′)≥c′}<∞.\#\Big\{p^{\prime}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}\ |\ M_{p;p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{B}}\neq\emptyset,\ \min_{1\leq\alpha\leq k^{\prime}}{\mathcal{A}}_{\alpha}^{\prime}(p^{\prime})\geq c^{\prime}\Big\}<\infty.
(2)
For all c∈ℝc\in{\mathbb{R}}
f𝔹​(c):=sup{max1≤α≤k′⁡𝒜α′​(p′)|max1≤α≤k⁡𝒜α​(p)≤c​and​Mp;p′𝔹≠∅}<+∞,f^{\mathbb{B}}(c):=\sup\Big\{\max_{1\leq\alpha\leq k^{\prime}}{\mathcal{A}}_{\alpha}^{\prime}(p^{\prime})\ |\ \max_{1\leq\alpha\leq k}{\mathcal{A}}_{\alpha}(p)\leq c\ {\rm and}\ M_{p;p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{B}}\neq\emptyset\Big\}<+\infty,
and
limρ→−∞h𝔹​(c,ρ):=limρ→−∞sup{min1≤α≤k′𝒜α′(p′)|max1≤α≤k𝒜α(p)≤c,min1≤α≤k𝒜α(p)≤ρ,andMp;p′𝔹≠∅}=−∞.\lim_{\rho\to-\infty}h^{\mathbb{B}}(c,\rho)\\
:=\lim_{\rho\to-\infty}\sup\Big\{\min_{1\leq\alpha\leq k^{\prime}}{\mathcal{A}}_{\alpha}^{\prime}(p^{\prime})\ |\ \max_{1\leq\alpha\leq k}{\mathcal{A}}_{\alpha}(p)\leq c,\ \min_{1\leq\alpha\leq k}{\mathcal{A}}_{\alpha}(p)\leq\rho,\ {\rm and}\ M_{p;p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{B}}\neq\emptyset\Big\}=-\infty.
The case of multimodules can be obtained as a special case of weak bimodules.
Definition 7.6.
Let (𝔽i,𝒜i)({\mathbb{F}}_{i},{\mathcal{A}}_{i}), i=1,…,mi=1,\ldots,m and (𝔽′,𝒜′)({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime},{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}) be locally finite flow categories enriched in 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}. A locally finite multimodule over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}) is a multimodule 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} which is a locally finite weak bimodule over (𝔽1×⋯×𝔽m;𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1}\times\cdots\times{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}).
We verify that concatenations of locally finite multimodules are locally finite.
Lemma 7.7.
Let 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}} be either 𝐓𝐨𝐩¯\underline{\smash{\bf Top}} or 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}. Let (𝔽i,𝒜i)({\mathbb{F}}_{i},{\mathcal{A}}_{i}), i=1,…,mi=1,\ldots,m, (𝔾j,ℬj)({\mathbb{G}}_{j},{\mathcal{B}}_{j}), j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n, (𝔾′,ℬ′)({\mathbb{G}}^{\prime},{\mathcal{B}}^{\prime}), be locally finite flow categories. Let 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} be a locally finite multimodule over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔾i)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{G}}_{i}) and 𝕐{\mathbb{Y}} be a locally finite multimodule over (𝔾1,…,𝔾n,𝔾′)({\mathbb{G}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{G}}_{n};{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}). Then the concatenation 𝕏∘i𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}} is a locally finite multimodule.
Proof.
We verify conditions of Definition 7.5 one by one. Suppose (1) of Definition 7.5 does not hold for the concatenation 𝕏∘i𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}}. Then there exist
p1∈Ob​𝔽1,…,pm∈Ob​𝔽m,r1∈Ob​𝔾1,…,ri−1∈Ob​𝔾i−1,ri+1∈Ob​𝔾i+1,…,rn∈Ob​𝔾n,p_{1}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,p_{m}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{m},r_{1}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{G}}_{1},\ldots,r_{i-1}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{G}}_{i-1},\ r_{i+1}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{G}}_{i+1},\ldots,r_{n}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{G}}_{n},
c′∈ℝc^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{R}} and infinitely many distinct rν′∈Ob​𝔾′r_{\nu}^{\prime}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime} such that
Mr1⋯ri−1p1⋯pmri+1⋯rn;r′𝕏∘𝕐≠∅,\displaystyle\ M_{r_{1}\cdots r_{i-1}p_{1}\cdots p_{m}r_{i+1}\cdots r_{n};r^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}\circ{\mathbb{Y}}}\neq\emptyset,\
min1≤β≤l′⁡ℬβ′​(rν′)≥c′\displaystyle\ \min_{1\leq\beta\leq l^{\prime}}{\mathcal{B}}_{\beta}^{\prime}(r_{\nu}^{\prime})\geq c^{\prime}
(7.1)
It follows that there exists a sequence ri,ν∈Ob​𝔾ir_{i,\nu}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{G}}_{i} such that
Mp1⋯pm;ri,ν𝕏≠∅,\displaystyle\ M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};r_{i,\nu}}^{\mathbb{X}}\neq\emptyset,\
Mr1⋯ri−1ri,νri+1⋯rn;rν′𝕐≠∅.\displaystyle\ M_{r_{1}\cdots r_{i-1}r_{i,\nu}r_{i+1}\cdots r_{n};r_{\nu}^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{Y}}\neq\emptyset.
By choosing a subsequence, we may assume the terms of the sequence ri,νr_{i,\nu} are either all identical, or all distinct. If all ri,νr_{i,\nu} are identical, then it contradicts the local finiteness of 𝕐{\mathbb{Y}}. Hence all ri,νr_{i,\nu} are distinct. Then by the local finiteness of 𝕏{\mathbb{X}}, for all α∈{1,…,li}\alpha\in\{1,\ldots,l_{i}\}, the sequence ℬi,α​(ri,ν){\mathcal{B}}_{i,\alpha}(r_{i,\nu}) is bounded from above; moreover, by choosing a subsequence, for some α\alpha the sequence ℬi,α​(ri,ν)→−∞{\mathcal{B}}_{i,\alpha}(r_{i,\nu})\to-\infty. Then by the local finiteness of 𝕐{\mathbb{Y}}, one has
limν→∞min1≤β≤l′⁡ℬβ′​(rν′)=−∞.\lim_{\nu\to\infty}\min_{1\leq\beta\leq l^{\prime}}{\mathcal{B}}_{\beta}^{\prime}(r_{\nu}^{\prime})=-\infty.
This contradicts (7.1). Therefore, (1) holds for the concatenation 𝕏∘i𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}}.
Now we verify (2) for the concatenation.
Choose c∈ℝc\in{\mathbb{R}}. We need to show that
f𝕏∘i𝕐​(c)<+∞f^{{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}}}(c)<+\infty
where f𝕏∘i𝕐f^{{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}}} is defined in Definition 7.5. Consider any collection of objects p1,…,pm,r1,…,ri−1,ri+1,…,rn,r′p_{1},\ldots,p_{m},r_{1},\ldots,r_{i-1},r_{i+1},\ldots,r_{n},r^{\prime} such that
max1≤α≤ki⁡𝒜i,α​(pi)≤c,max1≤β≤lj⁡ℬj,β​(rj)≤c\max_{1\leq\alpha\leq k_{i}}{\mathcal{A}}_{i,\alpha}(p_{i})\leq c,\ \max_{1\leq\beta\leq l_{j}}{\mathcal{B}}_{j,\beta}(r_{j})\leq c
and
Mr1⋯ri−1p1⋯pmri+1⋯rn;r′𝕏∘i𝕐≠∅.M_{r_{1}\cdots r_{i-1}p_{1}\cdots p_{m}r_{i+1}\cdots r_{n};r^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}}}\neq\emptyset.
Then by the definition of concatenation, there exists p′∈Ob​𝔽′p^{\prime}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} such that
Mp1⋯pm;ri𝕏≠∅,\displaystyle\ M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};r_{i}}^{{\mathbb{X}}}\neq\emptyset,\
Mr1⋯rn;r′𝕐≠∅.\displaystyle\ M_{r_{1}\cdots r_{n};r^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{Y}}}\neq\emptyset.
Then
max1≤β≤li⁡ℬi,β​(ri)≤f𝕏​(c).\max_{1\leq\beta\leq l_{i}}{\mathcal{B}}_{i,\beta}(r_{i})\leq f^{\mathbb{X}}(c).
Denote c′=max⁡{c,f𝕏​(c)}c^{\prime}=\max\{c,f^{\mathbb{X}}(c)\}. Then by the assumption, one has
max1≤β≤l′⁡ℬβ′​(r′)≤f𝕐​(c′).\max_{1\leq\beta\leq l^{\prime}}{\mathcal{B}}_{\beta}^{\prime}(r^{\prime})\leq f^{\mathbb{Y}}(c^{\prime}).
This proves that
f𝕏∘i𝕐​(c)≤f𝕐​(c′)<+∞.f^{{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}}}(c)\leq f^{{\mathbb{Y}}}(c^{\prime})<+\infty.
Moreover, suppose
ρ=min⁡{min1≤α≤kj⁡𝒜j,α​(pj)| 1≤j≤m}.\rho=\min\Big\{\min_{1\leq\alpha\leq k_{j}}{\mathcal{A}}_{j,\alpha}(p_{j})\ |\ 1\leq j\leq m\Big\}.
Then
min1≤β≤li⁡ℬi,β​(ri)≤h𝕏​(c,ρ)\min_{1\leq\beta\leq l_{i}}{\mathcal{B}}_{i,\beta}(r_{i})\leq h^{{\mathbb{X}}}(c,\rho)
Denote
ρ′:=min{h𝕏(c,ρ),min1≤β≤ljℬj,β(rj)|j≠i}.\rho^{\prime}:=\min\Big\{h^{{\mathbb{X}}}(c,\rho),\min_{1\leq\beta\leq l_{j}}{\mathcal{B}}_{j,\beta}(r_{j})\ |\ j\neq i\Big\}.
Then
min1≤β≤l′⁡ℬβ′​(r′)≤h𝕐​(c′,ρ′)\min_{1\leq\beta\leq l^{\prime}}{\mathcal{B}}_{\beta}^{\prime}(r^{\prime})\leq h^{\mathbb{Y}}(c^{\prime},\rho^{\prime})
which goes to −∞-\infty as ρ′→−∞\rho^{\prime}\to-\infty. Therefore (2) of Definition 7.5 holds for the concatenation 𝕏∘i𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}}.
∎
Lastly we state the local finiteness of multimodule homotopies.
Definition 7.8.
Let (𝔽,𝒜)({\mathbb{F}},{\mathcal{A}}) and (𝔽′,𝒜′)({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime},{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}) be two locally finite weak flow categories. Suppose 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is ℝk{\mathbb{R}}^{k}-valued and 𝒜′{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime} is ℝk′{\mathbb{R}}^{k^{\prime}}-valued. Suppose 𝔹0{\mathbb{B}}_{0} and 𝔹1{\mathbb{B}}_{1} are two locally finite weak bimodules over (𝔽;𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}) (Definition 7.5). Then a homotopy ℍ{\mathbb{H}} from 𝔹0{\mathbb{B}}_{0} to 𝔹1{\mathbb{B}}_{1} is called a locally finite homotopy if the following are satisfied.
(1)
For any p∈Ob​𝔽p\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}} and c′∈ℝc^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{R}},
#{p′∈Ob𝔽′|Mp;p′ℍ≠∅,min1≤α≤k′𝒜α′(p′)≥c′}<∞.\#\Big\{p^{\prime}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}\ |\ M_{p;p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{H}}\neq\emptyset,\ \min_{1\leq\alpha\leq k^{\prime}}{\mathcal{A}}_{\alpha}^{\prime}(p^{\prime})\geq c^{\prime}\Big\}<\infty.
(2)
For all c∈ℝc\in{\mathbb{R}}
sup{max1≤α≤k′⁡𝒜α′​(p′)|max1≤α≤k⁡𝒜α​(p)≤c​and​Mp;p′ℍ≠∅}<+∞,\sup\Big\{\max_{1\leq\alpha\leq k^{\prime}}{\mathcal{A}}_{\alpha}^{\prime}(p^{\prime})\ |\ \max_{1\leq\alpha\leq k}{\mathcal{A}}_{\alpha}(p)\leq c\ {\rm and}\ M_{p;p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{H}}\neq\emptyset\Big\}<+\infty,
and
limρ→−∞sup{min1≤α≤k′𝒜α′(p′)|max1≤α≤k𝒜α(p)≤c,min1≤α≤k𝒜α(p)≤ρ,andMp;p′ℍ≠∅}=−∞.\lim_{\rho\to-\infty}\sup\Big\{\min_{1\leq\alpha\leq k^{\prime}}{\mathcal{A}}_{\alpha}^{\prime}(p^{\prime})\ |\ \max_{1\leq\alpha\leq k}{\mathcal{A}}_{\alpha}(p)\leq c,\ \min_{1\leq\alpha\leq k}{\mathcal{A}}_{\alpha}(p)\leq\rho,\ {\rm and}\ M_{p;p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{H}}\neq\emptyset\Big\}=-\infty.
Definition 7.9.
Let (𝔽i,𝒜i)({\mathbb{F}}_{i},{\mathcal{A}}_{i}), i=1,…,mi=1,\ldots,m and (𝔽′,𝒜′)({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime},{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}) be locally finite flow categories enriched in 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}. Let 𝕏0{\mathbb{X}}_{0} and 𝕏1{\mathbb{X}}_{1} be locally finite multimodules over (𝔽1,⋯,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\cdots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}). A locally finite homotopy from 𝕏0{\mathbb{X}}_{0} to 𝕏1{\mathbb{X}}_{1} is a locally finite weak homotopy between the corresponding weak bimodules.
7.1.3. Grading
Now we consider gradings on the flow categories, multimodules, and homotopies. Let 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}} be a regular stratification category which is either 𝐊𝐮𝐫¯\underline{\smash{\bf Kur}}, 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}, or 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}. Define the notion of virtual dimension by
dimvir​C:={dim​U−dim​G−rank​E,C=(G,U,E,S)∈Ob​𝐊𝐮𝐫¯,dim​𝒰−rank​ℰ,C=(𝒰,ℰ,𝒮)∈Ob​𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯,dim​C,C∈Ob​𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯{\rm dim}^{\rm vir}C:=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}{\rm dim}U-{\rm dim}G-{\rm rank}E,&\ C=(G,U,E,S)\in{\rm Ob}\underline{\smash{\bf Kur}},\\
{\rm dim}{\mathcal{U}}-{\rm rank}{\mathcal{E}},&\ C=({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}},{\mathcal{S}})\in{\rm Ob}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}},\\
{\rm dim}C,&\ C\in{\rm Ob}\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}\end{array}\right.
We allow different components of CC to have different virtual dimensions.
Below we define gradings. In most of this paper, we will consider absolute, namely, ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-gradings; in certain situations we will reduce to cyclic gradings.
Definition 7.10.
Let NN be a nonnegative integer. All flow categories and multimodules are assumed to be enriched in either 𝐊𝐮𝐫¯\underline{\smash{\bf Kur}}, 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}, or 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}.
(1)
A (cohomological) ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-grading on a flow category 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} is a function p↦|p|∈ℤp\mapsto|p|\in{\mathbb{Z}} satisfying
dimvir​Mp​q𝔽=|q|−|p|−1,∀p,q∈Ob​𝔽.{\rm dim}^{\rm vir}M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}=|q|-|p|-1,\ \forall p,q\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}.
(2)
Let 𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m},{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} be flow categories equipped with ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-gradings. A multimodule 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}) is said to have cohomological degree rr if for all pi∈Ob​𝔽ip_{i}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{i} and p′∈Ob​𝔽′p^{\prime}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}
dimvirMp1⋯pm;p′𝕏=|p′|−|p1|−⋯−|pm|−r.{\rm dim}^{\rm vir}M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}}=|p^{\prime}|-|p_{1}|-\cdots-|p_{m}|-r.
7.1.4. Orientations
Defining chain complexes in characteristics other than 22 requires orientations. We do not include orientations as part of the structure on objects in the categories 𝐊𝐮𝐫¯\underline{\smash{\bf Kur}}, 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}, or 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}} as it is cumbersome to discuss orientations on the corners. Instead, we regard it as an extra structure on the flow category, multimodule, or homotopy.
Convention. Let MM be an oriented manifold with boundary. The induced boundary orientation is the one such that the
nout∧or∂M∈detT​M{\rm n}_{\rm out}\wedge{\rm or}_{\partial M}\in\det TM
coincides (up to positive scalar) with the orientation orM{\rm or}_{M} of MM.
Definition 7.11.
Let C=(𝒰,ℰ,𝒮)C=({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}},{\mathcal{S}}) be an AA-stratified derived orbifold with AA being a normal poset (Definition 2.5).
(1)
For each element α∈A\alpha\in A, an orientation on ∂αC\partial^{\alpha}C is an orientation of the virtual vector bundle T​∂α𝒰−ℰ|∂αVT\partial^{\alpha}{\mathcal{U}}-{\mathcal{E}}|_{\partial^{\alpha}V}, or equivalently an orientation on the determinant line
det(∂αC):=det(T​∂α𝒰)⊗det(ℰ∗|T​∂α𝒰).\det(\partial^{\alpha}C):=\det(T\partial^{\alpha}{\mathcal{U}})\otimes\det({\mathcal{E}}^{*}|_{T\partial^{\alpha}{\mathcal{U}}}).
Notice that for any face β∈𝔽​𝕒​𝕔​𝕖α\beta\in\mathbb{Face}_{\alpha}, an orientation on ∂αC\partial^{\alpha}C induces an orientation on ∂βC\partial^{\beta}C by regarding the collar coordinate to point “inward.”
(2)
An orientation on CC consists of orientations on all top strata ∂γC\partial^{\gamma}C such that for each fake boundary stratum β\beta, the orientation on ∂βC\partial^{\beta}C induced from the (exactly) two adjacent top strata are opposite.
(3)
Let C′=(𝒰′,ℰ′,𝒮′)C^{\prime}=({\mathcal{U}}^{\prime},{\mathcal{E}}^{\prime},{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}) be another A′A^{\prime}-stratified derived orbifold. An embedding ι:C→C′\iota:C\to C^{\prime} is said to be orientation-preserving if the underlying poset map has degree zero (i.e. maps top strata to top strata) and if for each top stratum γ∈A\gamma\in A (which is mapped to γ′∈A′\gamma^{\prime}\in A^{\prime}), the induced map of determinant lines
det(∂γC)→det(∂γ′C′)\det(\partial^{\gamma}C)\to\det(\partial^{\gamma^{\prime}}C^{\prime})
is orientation-preserving.
On the other hand, an orientation on a stratified pseudomanifold XX is defined to consist of orientations on all top strata γ∈Amax\gamma\in A^{\rm max} satisfying the similar compatibility condition on fake boundaries.
Definition 7.12.
Let 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} be a flow category enriched in 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}} (resp. 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}). A coherent orientation on 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} is a collection of orientations on the object Mp​q𝔽M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}} such that the singletons Mp​p𝔽M_{pp}^{\mathbb{F}} are positively oriented and such that whenever p<r<qp<r<q, the morphism
ιp​r​q𝔽:Mp​r𝔽×Mr​q𝔽→∂p​r​qMp​q𝔽\iota_{prq}^{\mathbb{F}}:M_{pr}^{\mathbb{F}}\times M_{rq}^{\mathbb{F}}\to\partial^{prq}M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}
is orientation-preserving up to factor
(−1)|p|−|r|.(-1)^{|p|-|r|}.
Here by the definition of flow categories (Definition 6.1), the top strata of ∂p​r​qMp​q𝔽\partial^{prq}M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}} are true boundaries of Mp​q𝔽M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}, hence have canonically induced orientations.
A flow category enriched in 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}} or 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}} equipped with a coherent orientation is called oriented.
Similarly we have the notion of orientation for multimodules. Notice the signs appearing in the definition, which are put in order to obtain the correct chain maps.
Definition 7.13.
Let 𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m},{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} be ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-graded oriented flow categories enriched in 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}} (resp. 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}). Let 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} be a degree zero multimodule over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}). Suppose all flow categories are equipped with coherent orientations. An coherent orientation on 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} consists of orientations on the charts Mp​q𝕏M_{pq}^{{\mathbb{X}}} such that
(1)
For each i=1,…,mi=1,\ldots,m, the morphism
Mpi​qi𝔽i×Mp1⋯pi−1qipi+1⋯pm;p′𝕏→∂Mp1⋯pm;p′𝕏M_{p_{i}q_{i}}^{{\mathbb{F}}_{i}}\times M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1}q_{i}p_{i+1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}}\to\partial M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}}
is orientation-preserving up to the sign
(−1)(∑j<i|pj|)​(|pi|−|qi|).(-1)^{(\sum_{j<i}|p_{j}|)(|p_{i}|-|q_{i}|)}.
In particular, for i=1i=1, the boundary orientation coincides with the product orientation.
(2)
The morphism
Mp1⋯pm;q′𝕏×Mq′​p′𝔽′→∂Mp1⋯pm;p′𝕏M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};q^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}}\times M_{q^{\prime}p^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}\to\partial M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}}
is orientation-preserving up to the sign
(−1)dimMp1⋯pm;q′𝕏+1.(-1)^{{\rm dim}M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};q^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}}+1}.
A multimodule over oriented flow categories equipped with coherent orientations is called an oriented multimodule.
We consider the orientation for concatenations. Let 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} be a multimodule over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔾i)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{G}}_{i}) and 𝕐{\mathbb{Y}} be a multimodule over (𝔾1,…,𝔾n,𝔾′)({\mathbb{G}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{G}}_{n};{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}). Recall that for each tuple pi∈Ob​𝔽ip_{i}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{i}, rj∈Ob​𝔾jr_{j}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{G}}_{j} and r′∈Ob​𝔾′r^{\prime}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}, the top strata of Mr1⋯ri−1p1⋯pmri⋯rn;r′𝕏∘i𝕐M_{r_{1}\cdots r_{i-1}p_{1}\cdots p_{m}r_{i}\cdots r_{n};r^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}}} is the disjoint union of the top strata of
⨆riMp1⋯pm;ri𝕏×Mr1⋯rn;r′𝕐.\bigsqcup_{r_{i}}M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};r_{i}}^{\mathbb{X}}\times M_{r_{1}\cdots r_{n};r^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{Y}}.
We define each of these products to be oriented by the product orientation times the sign
(−1)(∑j<i|rj|)dimMp1⋯pm;ri𝕏(-1)^{\left(\sum_{j<i}|r_{j}|\right){\rm dim}M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};r_{i}}^{\mathbb{X}}}
(if the concatenation happens at the i+1i+1-th input). The moduli spaces of the concatenation necessarily have fake boundaries and one can check easily that the above defined orientation on the interior induces an orientation on the orientations in the sense of Definition 7.11. We then need to check that these orientations on individual moduli spaces define a coherent orientation of the multimodule.
Lemma 7.14.
The orientation induced on 𝕏∘i𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}} is coherent.
Proof.
Fix a moduli space
Mr1⋯ri−1p1⋯pmri+1⋯rn;r′𝕏∘i𝕐.M_{r_{1}\cdots r_{i-1}p_{1}\cdots p_{m}r_{i+1}\cdots r_{n};r^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}}}.
We first need to verify that the orientations on two open strata of this moduli space induce opposite orientations on the shared fake boundary stratum. Choose objects ri<sir_{i}<s_{i} of 𝔽i{\mathbb{F}}_{i}. The two open strata are
Mp1⋯pm;ri𝕏×Mr1⋯rn;r′𝕐,\displaystyle\ M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};r_{i}}^{\mathbb{X}}\times M_{r_{1}\cdots r_{n};r^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{Y}},\
Mp1⋯pm;si𝕏×Mr1⋯ri−1siri+1⋯rn;r′𝕐.\displaystyle\ M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};s_{i}}^{\mathbb{X}}\times M_{r_{1}\cdots r_{i-1}s_{i}r_{i+1}\cdots r_{n};r^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{Y}}.
(7.2)
The shared fake boundary stratum is
Mp1⋯pm;ri𝕏×Mri​si𝔽i×Mr1⋯ri−1siri+1⋯rm;r′𝕐.M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};r_{i}}^{\mathbb{X}}\times M_{r_{i}s_{i}}^{{\mathbb{F}}_{i}}\times M_{r_{1}\cdots r_{i-1}s_{i}r_{i+1}\cdots r_{m};r^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{Y}}.
Use the product orientation as a reference. The orientation on this fake boundary induced from the first differs from the product orientation by
(∑j<i|rj|)dimMp1⋯pm;ri𝕏+dimMp1⋯pm;ri𝕏+(∑j<i|rj|)(|ri|−|si|).\left(\sum_{j<i}|r_{j}|\right){\rm dim}M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};r_{i}}^{\mathbb{X}}+{\rm dim}M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};r_{i}}^{\mathbb{X}}+\left(\sum_{j<i}|r_{j}|\right)(|r_{i}|-|s_{i}|).
The second orientation on the fake boundary differs by a sign
(∑j<i|rj|)dimMp1⋯pm;si𝕏+dimMp1⋯pm;ri𝕏+1.\left(\sum_{j<i}|r_{j}|\right){\rm dim}M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};s_{i}}^{\mathbb{X}}+{\rm dim}M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};r_{i}}^{\mathbb{X}}+1.
One can see that they are indeed opposite.
Then one has to verify conditions listed in Definition 7.13 for the concatenation. For breakings at some jj-th input sj∈Ob​𝔾js_{j}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{G}}_{j} for j<ij<i and breakings at some i+l−1i+l-1-th input ql∈Ob​𝔽lq_{l}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{l}, the verification is straightforward.
∎
Definition 7.15.
Let 𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m},{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} be ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-graded oriented flow categories enriched in 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}} (resp. 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}), 𝕏0,𝕏1{\mathbb{X}}_{0},{\mathbb{X}}_{1} be oriented flow multimodules over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}) of degree zero (see Definition 7.10). Let ℍ{\mathbb{H}} be a ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-graded homotopy from 𝕏0{\mathbb{X}}_{0} to 𝕏1{\mathbb{X}}_{1}. A coherent orientation on ℍ{\mathbb{H}} consists of orientations on the charts Mp​p′ℍM_{pp^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{H}}} such that
(1)
The embedding
(−Mp​p′𝔹0)⊔Mp​p′𝔹1→∂Mp​p′ℍ(-M_{pp^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}})\sqcup M_{pp^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{B}}_{1}}\to\partial M_{pp^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{H}}}
is orientation-preserving.
(2)
The embedding
Mpi​qi𝔽i×Mp1⋯pi−1qipi+1⋯pm;p′ℍ→∂Mp1⋯pm;p′ℍM_{p_{i}q_{i}}^{{\mathbb{F}}_{i}}\times M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1}q_{i}p_{i+1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{H}}}\to\partial M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{H}}}
is orientation-preserving up to the sign
(−1)(∑j<i|pj|)​(|pi|−|qi|).(-1)^{\left(\sum_{j<i}|p_{j}|\right)(|p_{i}|-|q_{i}|)}.
(3)
The embedding
Mp1⋯pm;q′ℍ×Mq′​p′𝔽′→∂Mp1⋯pm;p′ℍM_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};q^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{H}}}\times M_{q^{\prime}p^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}\to\partial M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{H}}}
is orientation-preserving up to the sign
(−1)dimMp1⋯pm;q′ℍ+1.(-1)^{{\rm dim}M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};q^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{H}}+1}.
7.2. Algebraic structures without symmetry
We define chain complexes, chain maps, and chain homotopies associated to flow categories, bimodules, and homotopies enriched in 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}. We only impose the Novikov convergence condition but not the symmetries. Hence the resulting objects are only modules over ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} but not the Novikov rings.
7.2.1. The chain group
We only state the construction for the ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-graded case. The cyclically graded case can be produced in a similar fashion.
To a ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-graded locally finite weak flow category (𝔽,𝒜)({\mathbb{F}},{\mathcal{A}}) enriched in 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}} (see Definition 7.2), one can associate a chain group
C∗(𝔽):={∑i=1∞aipi|ai∈ℤ,pi∈Ob𝔽,supi𝒜α(pi)<+∞∀α=1,…,m,∀c>0,#{i|𝒜α(pi)>−c∀α=1,…,k}<∞}.C_{*}({\mathbb{F}}):=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}a_{i}p_{i}\ \left|\ \begin{array}[]{l}a_{i}\in{\mathbb{Z}},\ p_{i}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}},\ \displaystyle\sup_{i}{\mathcal{A}}_{\alpha}(p_{i})<+\infty\ \forall\alpha=1,\ldots,m,\\
\forall c>0,\ \#\big\{i\ |\ {\mathcal{A}}_{\alpha}(p_{i})>-c\ \forall\alpha=1,\ldots,k\big\}<\infty\end{array}\right.\right\}.
It is not necessarily finitely generated over ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}. We call it the Floer chain group associated to (𝔽,𝒜)({\mathbb{F}},{\mathcal{A}}). It carries a natural valuation
𝔳=(𝔳1,…,𝔳k):C∗​(𝔽)∖{0}→ℝk,where​𝔳α​(∑i=1∞ai​pi)=supi𝒜α​(pi).{\mathfrak{v}}=({\mathfrak{v}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathfrak{v}}_{k}):C_{*}({\mathbb{F}})\setminus\{0\}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{k},\ {\rm where}\ {\mathfrak{v}}_{\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}a_{i}p_{i}\right)=\sup_{i}{\mathcal{A}}_{\alpha}(p_{i}).
For each k∈ℤk\in{\mathbb{Z}}, denote
Ck​(𝔽):={∑i=1∞ai​pi∈C∗​(𝔽)|deg⁡(pi)=k}.C_{k}({\mathbb{F}}):=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}a_{i}p_{i}\in C_{*}({\mathbb{F}})\ |\ {\rm deg}(p_{i})=k\right\}.
Suppose (𝔽′,𝒜′)({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime},{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}) and (𝔽′′,𝒜′′)({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime\prime},{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime\prime}) are two weak Novikov flow categories. The Floer chain group C∗​(𝔽′×𝔽′′)C_{*}({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}\times{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime\prime}) is a kind of completion of the tensor product chain groups of the factors. Indeed, on the algebraic (finite) tensor product
C∗​(𝔽′)​⊗ℤ​C∗​(𝔽′′)C_{*}({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime})\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}C_{*}({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime\prime})
there is the valuation 𝔳{\mathfrak{v}} induced by 𝔳′{\mathfrak{v}}^{\prime} and 𝔳′′{\mathfrak{v}}^{\prime\prime}. Then one can form the completion
C∗​(𝔽′)​⊗ℤ^​C∗​(𝔽′′).C_{*}({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime})\widehat{\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}}C_{*}({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime\prime}).
7.2.2. The differential
Now, we assume that the flow category 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} is enriched in 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}} and it is oriented. We define a linear map
d:Ck​(𝔽)→Ck−1​(𝔽),k∈ℤd:C_{k}({\mathbb{F}})\to C_{k-1}({\mathbb{F}}),\ k\in{\mathbb{Z}}
in the following way. Note that the morphism space Mp​q𝔽M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}} is an oriented and compact pseudomanifold of dimension
dim​Mp​q𝔽≡deg⁡(p)−deg⁡(q)−1.{\rm dim}M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}\equiv{\rm deg}(p)-{\rm deg}(q)-1.
When the dimension is zero, Mp​q𝔽M_{pq}^{{\mathbb{F}}} consists of finitely many oriented points, which defines a count np​q𝔽∈ℤn_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}\in{\mathbb{Z}}; in other cases, define np​q𝔽=0n_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}=0. Define
d⁡(∑i=1∞ai​pi)=∑i=1∞∑q∈Ob​𝔽ai​npi​q𝔽​q.d\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}a_{i}p_{i}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\sum_{q\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}}a_{i}n_{p_{i}q}^{\mathbb{F}}q.
The local finiteness property stated in Definition 7.2 implies that dd is well-defined.
Proposition 7.16.
If 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} is unobstructed, then d2=0d^{2}=0. Therefore, (C∗​(𝔽),d)(C_{*}({\mathbb{F}}),d) gives rise to a ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-graded chain complex of free abelian groups, called the complex associated to 𝔽{\mathbb{F}}.
Proof.
To show d2=0d^{2}=0, consider pairs p,qp,q with deg⁡(p)−deg⁡(q)=2{\rm deg}(p)-{\rm deg}(q)=2. By Definition 7.12, the coefficients of d2​(p)d^{2}(p) in qq is the oriented count of the union of products
⋃p<r<qMp​r𝔽×Mr​q𝔽.\bigcup_{p<r<q}M_{pr}^{\mathbb{F}}\times M_{rq}^{\mathbb{F}}.
Consider the 1-dimensional component of the pseudomanifold Mp​q𝔽M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}. The boundary points only appear on the true boundary strata of Mp​q𝔽M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}. By the definition of unobstructedness (Definition 7.1), the true boundary strata are all the top strata of the products Mp​r×Mr​qM_{pr}\times M_{rq}. By the coherence of the orientation (see Definition 7.12), these counts cancel. Hence d2=0d^{2}=0.
∎
If C⁡(𝔽′)C({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}) and C⁡(𝔽′′)C({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime\prime}) are complexes associated to flow categories 𝔽′{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} and 𝔽′′{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime\prime}, then the tensor product complex C⁡(𝔽′)​⊗ℤ​C​(𝔽′′)C({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime})\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}C({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime\prime}) is defined. The following can be checked readily.
Lemma 7.17.
The tensor product differential extends to the completion C⁡(𝔽′)​⊗ℤ^​C​(𝔽′′)\displaystyle C({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime})\widehat{\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}}C({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime\prime}).
7.2.3. Chain maps and homotopies
Now consider an oriented, unobstructed, ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-graded Novikov multimodule 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} enriched in 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}} over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}). Let
mp1⋯pm;p′𝕏∈ℤm_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}}\in{\mathbb{Z}}
be the count of Mp1⋯pm;p′𝕏M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}} when the dimension is zero and 00 otherwise. Define (formally) a linear map
Φ~𝕏:C(𝔽1)⊗ℤ⋯⊗ℤC(𝔽m)→C(𝔽′)\tilde{\Phi}^{\mathbb{X}}:C({\mathbb{F}}_{1}){\underset{{\mathbb{Z}}}{\otimes}}\cdots{\underset{{\mathbb{Z}}}{\otimes}}C({\mathbb{F}}_{m})\to C({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime})
by linearly extending (over ℤ{\mathbb{Z}})
Φ~𝕏(p1⊗⋯⊗pm):=∑p′∈Ob​𝔽′mp1⋯pm;p′𝕏p′.\tilde{\Phi}^{\mathbb{X}}(p_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes p_{m}):=\sum_{p^{\prime}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}m_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}}p^{\prime}.
(7.3)
The Novikov property (Definition 7.5) implies that Φ~𝕏\tilde{\Phi}^{\mathbb{X}} is well-defined and extends to the completion.
Proposition 7.18.
Φ~𝕏\tilde{\Phi}^{\mathbb{X}} extends to the completion C(𝔽1)⊗ℤ^⋯⊗ℤ^C(𝔽m)\displaystyle C({\mathbb{F}}_{1})\widehat{\underset{{\mathbb{Z}}}{\otimes}}\cdots\widehat{\underset{{\mathbb{Z}}}{\otimes}}C({\mathbb{F}}_{m}) and is a ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-linear chain map of degree index⁡(𝕏){\rm index}({\mathbb{X}}).
Proof.
The grading follows from the definition (see (2) of Definition 7.10). To prove that Φ~𝕏\tilde{\Phi}^{\mathbb{X}} is a chain map, one needs to look at the orientation. By definition, the differential of the tensor product is determined by
d(p1⊗⋯⊗pm)=∑i=1m(−1)∑j<i|pj|p1⊗⋯⊗pi−1⊗d𝔽i(pi)⊗pi+1⊗⋯⊗pm.d(p_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes p_{m})=\sum_{i=1}^{m}(-1)^{\sum_{j<i}|p_{j}|}p_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes p_{i-1}\otimes d^{{\mathbb{F}}_{i}}(p_{i})\otimes p_{i+1}\otimes\cdots\otimes p_{m}.
Look at one-dimensional components of the moduli space Mp1⋯pm;p′𝕏M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}} (see Definition 7.13), whose oriented boundary is
⨆i=1m((−1)(∑j<i|pj|)(|pi|−|qi)|Mpi​qi𝔽i×Mp1⋯pi−1qipi+1⋯pm;p′𝕏)⊔((−1)dimMp1⋯pm;q′𝕏+1Mp1⋯pm;q′𝕏×Mq′​p′𝔽′).\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{m}\Big((-1)^{(\sum_{j<i}|p_{j}|)(|p_{i}|-|q_{i})|}M_{p_{i}q_{i}}^{{\mathbb{F}}_{i}}\times M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1}q_{i}p_{i+1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}}\Big)\sqcup\Big((-1)^{{\rm dim}M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};q^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}}+1}M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};q^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}}\times M_{q^{\prime}p^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}\Big).
Moreover, each component above is nonempty only if both factors are zero-dimensional. It follows that (also using (7.3))
∑q′⟨Φ~𝕏(p1⊗⋯⊗pm),q′⟩⟨d𝔽′(q′),p′⟩=∑i=1m(−1)∑j<i|pj|∑qi∈Ob​𝔽i⟨d𝔽i(pi),qi⟩⟨Φ~𝕏(p1⊗⋯⊗pi−1⊗qi⊗pi+1⊗⋯⊗pm),p′⟩\sum_{q^{\prime}}\langle\tilde{\Phi}^{\mathbb{X}}(p_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes p_{m}),q^{\prime}\rangle\langle d^{{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}(q^{\prime}),p^{\prime}\rangle\\
=\sum_{i=1}^{m}(-1)^{\sum_{j<i}|p_{j}|}\sum_{q_{i}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{i}}\langle d^{{\mathbb{F}}_{i}}(p_{i}),q_{i}\rangle\langle\tilde{\Phi}^{{\mathbb{X}}}(p_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes p_{i-1}\otimes q_{i}\otimes p_{i+1}\otimes\cdots\otimes p_{m}),p^{\prime}\rangle
which means exactly that Φ~𝕏\tilde{\Phi}^{{\mathbb{X}}} is a chain map.
∎
Now we consider the situation of multimodule concatenations (see Subsection 6.5). Let
𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔾1,…,𝔾n,𝔾′{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m},{\mathbb{G}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{G}}_{n},{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}
be flow categories enriched in 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}} which are oriented, graded, and Novikov. Let 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} be a multimodule over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔾i)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{G}}_{i}) which is oriented, graded, and Novikov. Let 𝕐{\mathbb{Y}} be a multimodule over (𝔾1,…,𝔾n,𝔾′)({\mathbb{G}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{G}}_{n};{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}) which is oriented, graded, and Novikov. Then one can consider the concatenation 𝕏∘i𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}} which is a multimodule over (𝔾1,…,𝔾i−1,𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔾i+1,…,𝔾n,𝔾′)({\mathbb{G}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{G}}_{i-1},{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m},{\mathbb{G}}_{i+1},\ldots,{\mathbb{G}}_{n};{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}). Lemma 7.7 implies that the concatenation is Novikov. Lemma 7.14 says that the concatenation 𝕏∘i𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}} is coherently oriented. Hence one obtains a chain map
Φ~𝕏∘i𝕐:C(𝔾1)⊗ℤ^⋯⊗ℤ^C(𝔾i−1)⊗ℤ^C(𝔽1)⊗ℤ^⋯⊗ℤ^C(𝔽m)⊗ℤ^C(𝔾i+1)⊗ℤ^⋯⊗ℤ^C(𝔾n)→C(𝔾′).\tilde{\Phi}^{{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}}}:C({\mathbb{G}}_{1})\widehat{\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}}\cdots\widehat{\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}}C({\mathbb{G}}_{i-1})\widehat{\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}}C({\mathbb{F}}_{1})\widehat{\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}}\cdots\widehat{\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}}C({\mathbb{F}}_{m})\widehat{\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}}C({\mathbb{G}}_{i+1})\widehat{\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}}\cdots\widehat{\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}}C({\mathbb{G}}_{n})\to C({\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}).
Lemma 7.19.
There holds
Φ~𝕏∘i𝕐(y1,⋯,yi−1,x1,⋯xm,yi+1,⋯,yn)=Φ~𝕐(y1,⋯,yi−1,Φ~𝕏(x1,⋯,xm),yi+1,⋯,yn).\tilde{\Phi}^{{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}}}(y_{1},\cdots,y_{i-1},x_{1},\cdots x_{m},y_{i+1},\cdots,y_{n})=\tilde{\Phi}^{\mathbb{Y}}(y_{1},\cdots,y_{i-1},\tilde{\Phi}^{\mathbb{X}}(x_{1},\cdots,x_{m}),y_{i+1},\cdots,y_{n}).
Proof.
One only needs to verify this identity for xα=pαx_{\alpha}=p_{\alpha} and yβ=rβy_{\beta}=r_{\beta} for generators of the involved chain complexes. Fix r′∈Ob​𝔾′r^{\prime}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}. The r′r^{\prime}-coefficient of the left is the signed count of the disjoint union
Mp1⋯pm;ri𝕏×Mr1⋯rn;r′𝕐.M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};r_{i}}^{\mathbb{X}}\times M_{r_{1}\cdots r_{n};r^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{Y}}.
By our orientation conventions (note that the moduli spaces are zero-dimensional), it is equal to
np1⋯pm;p′𝕏np′r1⋯rn;r′𝕐.n_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}}n_{p^{\prime}r_{1}\cdots r_{n};r^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{Y}}.
As only zero dimensional moduli spaces contribute, the sign above is positive; therefore, the induced count produces the right hand side.
∎
Lastly, suppose 𝕏0,𝕏1{\mathbb{X}}_{0},{\mathbb{X}}_{1} be two, unobstructed, oriented, ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-graded Novikov multimodules over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}) enriched in 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}} of the same degree nn, and ℍ{\mathbb{H}} is an oriented, unobstructed, Novikov homotopy from 𝕏0{\mathbb{X}}_{0} to 𝕏1{\mathbb{X}}_{1}. For each tuple (p1⋯pm;p′)(p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}), the orientation on Mp1⋯pm;p′ℍM_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{H}} induces an integral count
np1⋯pm;p′ℍ∈ℤ.n_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{H}}\in{\mathbb{Z}}.
Define a linear map
Ψ~ℍ:C∗(𝔽1)⊗ℤ⋯⊗ℤC∗(𝔽m)→C∗(𝔽′)\tilde{\Psi}^{\mathbb{H}}:C_{*}({\mathbb{F}}_{1})\underset{{\mathbb{Z}}}{\otimes}\cdots\underset{{\mathbb{Z}}}{\otimes}C_{*}({\mathbb{F}}_{m})\to C_{*}({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime})
by ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-linearly extending
p1⊗⋯⊗pm↦∑p′np1⋯pm;p′ℍp′.p_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes p_{m}\mapsto\sum_{p^{\prime}}n_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{H}}p^{\prime}.
Using the conditions stated in Definition 7.15, the following statement is immediate.
Lemma 7.20.
Ψ~ℍ\tilde{\Psi}^{\mathbb{H}} extends to C(𝔽1)⊗ℤ^⋯⊗ℤ^C(𝔽m)C({\mathbb{F}}_{1})\widehat{\underset{{\mathbb{Z}}}{\otimes}}\cdots\widehat{\underset{{\mathbb{Z}}}{\otimes}}C({\mathbb{F}}_{m}) and is a chain homotopy from Φ~𝕏0\tilde{\Phi}^{{\mathbb{X}}_{0}} to Φ~𝕏1\tilde{\Phi}^{{\mathbb{X}}_{1}}.
7.3. Symmetries on flow categories, multimodules, and homotopies
In the geometric situations considered in this paper, there are three types of symmetries on flow categories, multimodules, and homotopies. The first is the typical kind of Novikov symmetry, which is basically the symmetry related to changing cappings of contractible periodic orbits. The second and the third only appear in the equivariant case. The second type is the symmetry on the Borel model S∞≅E​ℤ𝗉S^{\infty}\cong E{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}, given by the monoid ℤ≥0{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}, which shifts the coordinates, rather than the group ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}. The third is symmetry by a finite group ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}.
7.3.1. Twisted Novikov groups
Definition 7.21 (Novikov groups).
(1)
A Novikov group consists of a free abelian group Π\mathbb{\Pi} together with morphisms
λ=(λ1,…,λk):Π→ℝk,\displaystyle\ \lambda=(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{k}):\mathbb{\Pi}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{k},\
μ:Π→2​ℤ\displaystyle\ \mu:\mathbb{\Pi}\to 2{\mathbb{Z}}
A morphism of Novikov groups from (Π,λ,μ)(\mathbb{\Pi},\lambda,\mu) to (Π′,λ′,μ′)(\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime},\lambda^{\prime},\mu^{\prime}) consists of a group homomorphism ρ:Π→Π′\rho:\mathbb{\Pi}\to\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime} and a linear map σ:ℝk→ℝk′\sigma:{\mathbb{R}}^{k}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{k^{\prime}} such that the following diagrams commute.
Π\textstyle{\mathbb{\Pi}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}λ\scriptstyle{\lambda}ρ\scriptstyle{\rho}ℝk\textstyle{{\mathbb{R}}^{k}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}σ\scriptstyle{\sigma}Π′\textstyle{\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}λ′\scriptstyle{\lambda^{\prime}}ℝk′\textstyle{{\mathbb{R}}^{k^{\prime}}}
Π\textstyle{\mathbb{\Pi}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}μ\scriptstyle{\mu}ρ\scriptstyle{\rho}ℤ\textstyle{{\mathbb{Z}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}Id\scriptstyle{\rm Id}Π′\textstyle{\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}μ′\scriptstyle{\mu^{\prime}}ℤ\textstyle{{\mathbb{Z}}}
(2)
The category of Novikov groups admits finite products, denoted by
(Π,λ,μ)⊕(Π′,λ′,μ′)=(Π⊕Π′,λ⊕λ′,μ+μ′).(\mathbb{\Pi},\lambda,\mu)\oplus(\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime},\lambda^{\prime},\mu^{\prime})=(\mathbb{\Pi}\oplus\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime},\lambda\oplus\lambda^{\prime},\mu+\mu^{\prime}).
(3)
An twisted Novikov group, denoted by Π⋊G\mathbb{\Pi}\rtimes G, consists of a Novikov group Π\mathbb{\Pi} together with a finite group GG acting on Π\mathbb{\Pi} by isomorphisms of Novikov groups. Notice that the semi-direct product Π⋊G\mathbb{\Pi}\rtimes G is a not necessarily abelian.
Example 7.22.
(1)
Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a symplectic manifold. Then
Π=π2​(X)ker​ω∩ker​c1\Pi=\frac{\pi_{2}(X)}{{\rm ker}\omega\cap{\rm ker}c_{1}}
together with the symplectic area λ⁡(a)=ω⁡(a)\lambda(a)=\omega(a) and twice the Chern number μ⁡(a)=2​c1​(a)\mu(a)=2c_{1}(a) is a Novikov group.
(2)
ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} with the inclusion λ:ℤ↪ℝ\lambda:{\mathbb{Z}}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{R}} and the multiplication by two μ:ℤ→2​ℤ↪ℤ\mu:{\mathbb{Z}}\to 2{\mathbb{Z}}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}} is a Novikov group.
(3)
Any finite group is a twisted Novikov group.
7.3.2. Novikov rings
Let RR be a commutative ring with unit, typically ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} or 𝐅𝗉{\bf F}_{\sf p}. Let (Π,λ,μ)(\mathbb{\Pi},\lambda,\mu) be a Novikov group. We define the Novikov ring ΛRΠ\Lambda_{R}^{\mathbb{\Pi}} as follows. Define
ΛRΠ:={f:Π→R|∀α=1,…,k,inf{λα​(a)|f⁡(a)≠0}>−∞,∀c>0,#{a∈Π|f(a)≠0,λα(a)<c,α=1,…,k}<∞}.\Lambda_{R}^{\mathbb{\Pi}}:=\left\{f:\mathbb{\Pi}\to R\ \left|\ \begin{array}[]{l}\forall\alpha=1,\ldots,k,\ \displaystyle\inf\{\lambda_{\alpha}(a)\ |\ f(a)\neq 0\}>-\infty,\\
\forall c>0,\ \#\big\{a\in\mathbb{\Pi}\ |\ f(a)\neq 0,\ \lambda_{\alpha}(a)<c,\ \alpha=1,\ldots,k\big\}<\infty\end{array}\right.\right\}.
(7.4)
Lemma 7.23.
ΛRΠ\Lambda_{R}^{\mathbb{\Pi}} is a graded unital commutative ring.
Proof.
We can grade ΛRΠ\Lambda_{R}^{\mathbb{\Pi}} by dualizing the grading on Π{\mathbb{\Pi}} induced by the morphism μ:Π→ℤ\mu:{\mathbb{\Pi}}\to{\mathbb{Z}}. The product structure is defined as follows. Choose f′,f′′∈ΛRΠf^{\prime},f^{\prime\prime}\in\Lambda_{R}^{\mathbb{\Pi}}. Define formally f′​f′′:Π→Rf^{\prime}f^{\prime\prime}:\mathbb{\Pi}\to R by
f′​f′′​(a)=∑a′+a′′=af′​(a′)​f′′​(a′′).f^{\prime}f^{\prime\prime}(a)=\sum_{a^{\prime}+a^{\prime\prime}=a}f^{\prime}(a^{\prime})f^{\prime\prime}(a^{\prime\prime}).
(7.5)
which is commutative in f′f^{\prime} and f′′f^{\prime\prime}. We claim that this is a finite sum. If not, then there is a sequence (ai′,ai′′)∈Π×Π(a_{i}^{\prime},a_{i}^{\prime\prime})\in\mathbb{\Pi}\times\mathbb{\Pi} such that ai′+ai′′=aa_{i}^{\prime}+a_{i}^{\prime\prime}=a and f′​(ai′),f′′​(ai′′)≠0f^{\prime}(a_{i}^{\prime}),f^{\prime\prime}(a_{i}^{\prime\prime})\neq 0. Then
λα​(ai′)+λα​(ai′′)=λα​(a)\lambda_{\alpha}(a_{i}^{\prime})+\lambda_{\alpha}(a_{i}^{\prime\prime})=\lambda_{\alpha}(a)
which is independent of ii. Then
supiλα​(ai′′)=λα​(a)−infiλα​(ai′)<∞.\sup_{i}\lambda_{\alpha}(a_{i}^{\prime\prime})=\lambda_{\alpha}(a)-\inf_{i}\lambda_{\alpha}(a_{i}^{\prime})<\infty.
The finiteness condition in the definition of ΛRΠ\Lambda_{R}^{\mathbb{\Pi}} shows that there are only finitely many distinct ai′′a_{i}^{\prime\prime} in this sequence. As ai′=a−ai′′a_{i}^{\prime}=a-a_{i}^{\prime\prime}, there are also only finitely many distinct ai′a_{i}^{\prime} in this sequence. Hence the sum (7.5) is indeed finite. Therefore, f′​f′′f^{\prime}f^{\prime\prime} is defined. It is also straightforward to check that f′​f′′f^{\prime}f^{\prime\prime} satisfies the definition of ΛRΠ\Lambda_{R}^{\mathbb{\Pi}}. Using this definition, one can easily see that the unit is given by the map which assigns the identity element of Π{\mathbb{\Pi}} to the multiplicative unit in RR and 00 otherwise.
∎
We also define the subring
ΛR,0Π:={f∈ΛRΠ|f(a)≠0⟹λα(ai)≥0,α=1,…,k}.\Lambda_{R,0}^{\mathbb{\Pi}}:=\left\{f\in\Lambda_{R}^{\mathbb{\Pi}}\ |\ f(a)\neq 0\Longrightarrow\lambda_{\alpha}(a_{i})\geq 0,\ \alpha=1,\ldots,k\right\}.
Now we consider the tensor product of Novikov rings. If Π1\mathbb{\Pi}_{1}, Π2\mathbb{\Pi}_{2} are two Novikov groups, then the Novikov ring
ΛRΠ1⊕Π2\Lambda_{R}^{\mathbb{\Pi}_{1}\oplus\mathbb{\Pi}_{2}}
is a certain completion of the tensor product ΛRΠ1⊗RΛRΠ2\Lambda_{R}^{\mathbb{\Pi}_{1}}\otimes_{R}\Lambda_{R}^{\mathbb{\Pi}_{2}}. We denote the completed tensor product by ⊗^\widehat{\otimes}. More generally, if Π1,…,Πm\mathbb{\Pi}_{1},\ldots,\mathbb{\Pi}_{m} are Novikov groups, then there is a natural identification
ΛΠ1R⊗𝑅^⋯⊗𝑅^ΛΠmR≅ΛRΠ1⊕⋯⊕Πm.\Lambda^{\mathbb{\Pi}_{1}}_{R}\widehat{\underset{R}{\otimes}}\cdots\widehat{\underset{R}{\otimes}}\Lambda^{\mathbb{\Pi}_{m}}_{R}\cong\Lambda_{R}^{\mathbb{\Pi}_{1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathbb{\Pi}_{m}}.
Lastly, suppose one has a morphism of Novikov groups ρ:Π→Π′\rho:\mathbb{\Pi}\to\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime}. Then there is a natural ring map
ΛRΠ→ΛRΠ′\Lambda_{R}^{\mathbb{\Pi}}\to\Lambda_{R}^{\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime}}
making the latter an algebra over ΛRΠ\Lambda_{R}^{\mathbb{\Pi}}.
7.3.3. Symmetries on flow categories
We introduce the concepts related to symmetries on flow categories, multimodules, and homotopies which appear everywhere in the Floer-theoretic setting.
Definition 7.24.
Let Π⋊G\mathbb{\Pi}\rtimes G be a twisted Novikov group of rank kk. Remark 7.25.
(1)
Notice that the last condition of Definition 7.24 implies that (𝔽,𝒜)({\mathbb{F}},{\mathcal{A}}) is a locally finite flow category.
(2)
If Πi\mathbb{\Pi}_{i} are Novikov groups and (𝔽i,𝒜i)({\mathbb{F}}_{i},{\mathcal{A}}_{i}) are Πi\mathbb{\Pi}_{i}-equivariant Novikov flow categories, then the direct product
(𝔽1×⋯×𝔽m,𝒜1×⋯×𝒜m)({\mathbb{F}}_{1}\times\cdots\times{\mathbb{F}}_{m},{\mathcal{A}}_{1}\times\cdots\times{\mathcal{A}}_{m})
is a Π1×⋯×Πm\mathbb{\Pi}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{\Pi}_{m}-equivariant weak Novikov flow category. When all factors are equal to a Π\mathbb{\Pi}-equivariant Novikov flow category (𝔽,𝒜)({\mathbb{F}},{\mathcal{A}}), the power (𝔽×⋯×𝔽,𝒜×⋯×𝒜)({\mathbb{F}}\times\cdots\times{\mathbb{F}},{\mathcal{A}}\times\cdots\times{\mathcal{A}}) is Πm⋊ℤm\mathbb{\Pi}^{m}\rtimes{\mathbb{Z}}_{m}-equivariant where ℤm{\mathbb{Z}}_{m} acts on Πm\mathbb{\Pi}^{m} by permuting the factors.
7.3.4. Symmetries on multimodules and homotopies

The case of multimodules can be obtained from the case of weak bimodules.

Note that incorporating GG-symmetry for flow multimodules and bimodule homotopies is straightforward. We do not spell out the details because they are not needed for this paper.
7.4. Algebraic structures with symmetry
In the previous two subsections, we provide separate treatments of convergence of structural maps of chain complexes and Novikov rings with geometric origin. As usual, in the concrete setting of Floer theory, the two structures interact with each other in the form that recapping of periodic orbits corresponds to multiplication by Novikov variables. Abstractly, equivariance under Novikov groups of flow categories, multimodules, and homotopies leads to linearity of differentials and chain maps under Novikov rings, and local finiteness of orbits under the Novikov group action is compatible with the convergence assumption. We record these classical observations here formally.
7.4.1. Flow categories and bimodules
Suppose (𝔽,𝒜)({\mathbb{F}},{\mathcal{A}}) is a ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-graded, oriented, unobstructed, Novikov flow category enriched in 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}, then we have obtained previously the complex C⁡(𝔽)C({\mathbb{F}}) as a free abelian group.
Proposition 7.30.
Let (Π⋊G,λ,μ)(\mathbb{\Pi}\rtimes G,\lambda,\mu) be a twisted Novikov group. If (𝔽,𝒜)({\mathbb{F}},{\mathcal{A}}) is Π⋊\mathbb{\Pi}\rtimes-equivariant, then C⁡(𝔽)C({\mathbb{F}}) has the structure of a ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-graded ΛℤΠ\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\mathbb{\Pi}}-module with a GG-action and the differential is GG-equivariant and ΛℤΠ\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\mathbb{\Pi}}-linear.
Proof.
The Π\mathbb{\Pi}-equivariance condition on 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} implies that C⁡(𝔽)C({\mathbb{F}}) has a natural ΛℤΠ\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\mathbb{\Pi}}-module structure. Moreover, the Π\mathbb{\Pi}-equivariance on the flow category implies that dd is a ΛℤΠ\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\mathbb{\Pi}}-module map. In the presence of the finite group GG, it follows from definition that the chain complex C⁡(𝔽)C({\mathbb{F}}) is GG-equivariant.
∎
The following proposition is straightforward.
Proposition 7.31.
Let Π⋊G\mathbb{\Pi}\rtimes G and Π′⋊G\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime}\rtimes G be twisted Novikov groups with a GG-equivariant morphism ρ:Π→Π′\rho:\mathbb{\Pi}\to\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime}. Let (𝔽,𝒜)({\mathbb{F}},{\mathcal{A}}) resp. (𝔽′,𝒜′)({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime},{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}) be a Π⋊G\mathbb{\Pi}\rtimes G-equivariant resp. Π′⋊G\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime}\rtimes G-equivariant ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-graded, oriented, unobstructed flow categories enriched in 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}. Let 𝔹{\mathbb{B}} be a ρ\rho-equivariant graded, oriented, and unobstructed bimodule over (𝔽;𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}). Then the chain map
Φ~𝔹:C⁡(𝔽)→C⁡(𝔽′)\tilde{\Phi}^{\mathbb{B}}:C({\mathbb{F}})\to C({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime})
extends to a ΛΠ′\Lambda^{{\mathbb{\Pi}}^{\prime}}-linear chain map
Φ~𝔹:C⁡(𝔽)​⊗ΛΠ​ΛΠ′→C⁡(𝔽′)\tilde{\Phi}^{\mathbb{B}}:C({\mathbb{F}})\underset{\Lambda^{\mathbb{\Pi}}}{\otimes}\Lambda^{{\mathbb{\Pi}}^{\prime}}\to C({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime})
which is equivariant with respect to the GG-actions.
7.4.2. Multimodules and homotopies
Recall that by Proposition 7.18, given a ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-graded, oriented, unobstructed multimodule, and locally finite 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}) enriched in 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}, one has obtained a chain map
Φ~𝕏:C(𝔽1)⊗ℤ^⋯⊗ℤ^C(𝔽m)→C(𝔽′)\tilde{\Phi}^{\mathbb{X}}:C({\mathbb{F}}_{1})\widehat{\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}}\cdots\widehat{\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}}C({\mathbb{F}}_{m})\to C({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime})
To obtain a chain map as modules over the Novikov ring, one needs to make use of the equivariance condition.
Proposition 7.32.
Suppose (𝔽i,𝒜i),i=1,…,m({\mathbb{F}}_{i},{\mathcal{A}}_{i}),i=1,\ldots,m is equivariant with respect to the action of an (untwisted) Novikov group (Πi,λi,μi)(\mathbb{\Pi}_{i},\lambda_{i},\mu_{i}). Then the tensor product
C(𝔽1)⊗ℤ^⋯⊗ℤ^C(𝔽m)C({\mathbb{F}}_{1})\widehat{\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}}\cdots\widehat{\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}}C({\mathbb{F}}_{m})
is a differential graded module over
ΛℤΠ1⊗ℤ^⋯⊗ℤ^ΛℤΠm≅ΛℤΠ1⊕⋯⊕Πm.\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\mathbb{\Pi}_{1}}\widehat{\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}}\cdots\widehat{\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}}\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\mathbb{\Pi}_{m}}\cong\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\mathbb{\Pi}_{1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathbb{\Pi}_{m}}.
Suppose 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} is equivariant with respect to a Novikov group morphism ρ:Π1⊕⋯⊕Πm→Π′\rho:\mathbb{\Pi}_{1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathbb{\Pi}_{m}\to\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime}, then the chain map Φ~𝕏\tilde{\Phi}^{\mathbb{X}} induces a ΛℤΠ′\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime}}-linear chain map
Φ~𝕏:(C∗(𝔽1)⊗ℤ^⋯⊗ℤ^C∗(𝔽m))⊗ΛℤΠ1⊕⋯⊕ΠmΛℤΠ′→C∗(𝔽′).\tilde{\Phi}^{\mathbb{X}}:\left(C_{*}({\mathbb{F}}_{1})\widehat{\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}}\cdots\widehat{\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}}C_{*}({\mathbb{F}}_{m})\right)\underset{\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\mathbb{\Pi}_{1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathbb{\Pi}_{m}}}{\otimes}\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime}}\to C_{*}({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}).
In addition, if 𝕏0{\mathbb{X}}_{0} and 𝕏1{\mathbb{X}}_{1} are two such multimodules and there exists a ρ\rho-equivariant unobstructed and oriented homotopy from 𝕏0{\mathbb{X}}_{0} to 𝕏1{\mathbb{X}}_{1}, then the corresponding chain maps Φ𝕏0\Phi^{{\mathbb{X}}_{0}} and Φ𝕏1\Phi^{{\mathbb{X}}_{1}} are homotopic as ΛℤΠ′\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}^{{\mathbb{\Pi}}^{\prime}}-linear chain maps.
Proof.
It follows from the same reasoning as in Lemma 7.30.
∎
Remark 7.33.
There is a specific case corresponding to the equivariant pair-of-pants product which we would like to address in Section 24 and Section 26 in a more concrete setting rather than the current abstract setting.
7.5. Quantitative theories
7.5.1. Nonarchimedean linear algebra
We recall some basic notions about nonarchimedean linear algebra systematically used in [69]. Let (Π,λ)(\Pi,\lambda) be an ungraded Novikov group; the relevant discussion is insensitive to ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-grading so we only consider a ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}-graded theory. Let 𝐊{\bf K} be a field. Then on the Novikov field Λ𝐊Π\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi} there is the standard valuation
𝔳⁡(∑i=1∞ci​Tai):=inf{λ⁡(ai)|ci≠0}∈ℝ∪{+∞}.{\mathfrak{v}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}c_{i}T^{a_{i}}\right):=\inf\Big\{\lambda(a_{i})\ |\ c_{i}\neq 0\Big\}\in{\mathbb{R}}\cup\{+\infty\}.
Then Λ𝐊Π\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi} is a nonarchimedean field. Notice that in the setting of [69] one requires Π⊆ℝ\Pi\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}. We slightly relax this setting to better fit our discussion. To translate to the setting of [69], denote
|Π|:=λ⁡(Π)⊆ℝ.|\Pi|:=\lambda(\Pi)\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}.
(7.6)
Then Λ𝐊|Π|\Lambda_{\bf K}^{|\Pi|} is an algebra over Λ𝐊Π\Lambda_{{\bf K}}^{\Pi}.
A nonarchimedean normed vector space of Λ𝐊Π\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi} (cf. [69, Definition 2.2]) is a pair (C,ℓ)(C,\ell) where CC is a Λ𝐊Π\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi}-vector space and ℓ:C→{−∞}∪ℝ\ell:C\to\{-\infty\}\cup{\mathbb{R}} be a function satisfying
(1)
ℓ⁡(x)=−∞⟹x=0\ell(x)=-\infty\Longrightarrow x=0.
(2)
ℓ⁡(λ​x)=ℓ⁡(x)−𝔳⁡(λ)\ell(\lambda x)=\ell(x)-{\mathfrak{v}}(\lambda).
(3)
ℓ⁡(x+y)≤max⁡{ℓ⁡(x),ℓ⁡(y)}\ell(x+y)\leq\max\{\ell(x),\ \ell(y)\}.
There is a notion called orthogonalizability on nonarchimedean normed vector spaces ([69, Definition 2.10]) over Λ𝐊|Π|\Lambda_{{\bf K}}^{|\Pi|}, which is satisfied by all concrete cases considered in Floer theory. Finally, Usher–Zhang defined the notion called Floer-type complex which is crucial in their abstract discussion on barcodes. As the consideration does not necessarily involve grading, we slightly modify the original definition.
Definition 7.34.
(cf.[69, Definition 4.1]) Let (Π,λ)(\Pi,\lambda) be an ungraded Novikov group and 𝐊{\bf K} be a field.
(1)
A nonarchimedean normed vector space (C,ℓC)(C,\ell_{C}) over Λ𝐊Π\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi} is called orthogonalizable if the tensor product C⊗Λ𝐊|Π|C\otimes\Lambda_{\bf K}^{|\Pi|} is orthogonalizable over Λ𝐊|Π|\Lambda_{\bf K}^{|\Pi|}.
(2)
A Floer-type complex over Λ𝐊Π\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi} consists of a ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}-graded orthogonalizable Λ𝐊Π\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi}-space CC together with an odd Λ𝐊Π\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi}-differential dC:C→Cd_{C}:C\to C satisfying
ℓC​(dC​x)≤ℓC​(x).\ell_{C}(d_{C}x)\leq\ell_{C}(x).
Remark 7.35.
There is another notion called Floer–Novikov complex defined in [70]. It requires that the differential strictly decreases the nonarchimedean norm. On the other hand, that notion allows one to consider Novikov rings with coefficients in a general Noetherian ring and the exponents Γ\Gamma to be a general finite-rank free abelian group. In the Floer setup, the Floer complex can be made both a Floer–Novikov complex and a Floer-type complex with appropriate Novikov coefficients.
Next we have two notions about chain maps and chain homotopies.
Definition 7.36.
(cf. [69, Definition 4.5])
Let CC and DD be two Floer-type complexes over Λ𝐊Π\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi}.
(1)
A linear map Φ:C→D\Phi:C\to D is said to preserve the filtration if
ℓD​(Φ⁡(x))≤ℓC​(x)​∀x∈C.\ell_{D}(\Phi(x))\leq\ell_{C}(x)\ \forall x\in C.
(2)
CC and DD are said to be filtered isomorphic if there is an isomorphism Φ:C→D\Phi:C\to D of chain complexes such that
ℓD​(Φ⁡(x))=ℓC​(x)​∀x∈C.\ell_{D}(\Phi(x))=\ell_{C}(x)\ \forall x\in C.
(3)
Two chain maps Φ,Ψ:C→D\Phi,\Psi:C\to D are said to be filtered chain homotopic if 1) both Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi preserve the filtration and 2) there exists a homotopy K:C→DK:C\to D between Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi which also preserves the filtration. Two Floer-type complexes are filtered chain homotopy equivalent if there exists a filtered chain homotopy Φ:C→D\Phi:C\to D and a filtered homotopy inverse Ψ:D→C\Psi:D\to C such that Φ∘Ψ\Phi\circ\Psi is filtered chain homotopic to IdD{\rm Id}_{D} and Ψ∘Φ\Psi\circ\Phi is filtered chain homotopic to IdC{\rm Id}_{C}.
One uses the following notion to compare Floer type complexes.
Definition 7.37.
Let (C,ℓC,dC)(C,\ell_{C},d_{C}) and (D,ℓD,dC)(D,\ell_{D},d_{C}) be two Floer-type complexes and δ≥0\delta\geq 0. A δ\delta-quasiequivalence between CC and DD is a quadruple (Φ,Ψ,KC,KD)(\Phi,\Psi,K_{C},K_{D}) where Φ:C→D\Phi:C\to D, Ψ:D→C\Psi:D\to C are chain maps, KCK_{C}, KDK_{D} are chain homotopies as
Ψ∘Φ−IdC=dC∘KC+KC∘dC,\displaystyle\ \Psi\circ\Phi-{\rm Id}_{C}=d_{C}\circ K_{C}+K_{C}\circ d_{C},\
Φ∘Ψ−IdD=dD∘KD+KD∘dD\displaystyle\ \Phi\circ\Psi-{\rm Id}_{D}=d_{D}\circ K_{D}+K_{D}\circ d_{D}
satisfying for all x∈Cx\in C and y∈Dy\in D,
ℓD​(Φ⁡(x))≤ℓC​(x)+δ,\displaystyle\ \ell_{D}(\Phi(x))\leq\ell_{C}(x)+\delta,\
ℓC​(Ψ⁡(y))≤ℓD​(y)+δ,\displaystyle\ \ell_{C}(\Psi(y))\leq\ell_{D}(y)+\delta,
and
ℓC​(KC​(x))≤ℓC​(x)+2​δ,\displaystyle\ \ell_{C}(K_{C}(x))\leq\ell_{C}(x)+2\delta,\
ℓD​(KD​(y))≤ℓD​(y)+2​δ.\displaystyle\ \ell_{D}(K_{D}(y))\leq\ell_{D}(y)+2\delta.
The quasiequivalence distance between two Floer-type complexes is the infimum of δ\delta for which there exists a δ\delta-quasiequivalence between them.
Below we show that the complex obtained from a Novikov flow category is indeed a Floer-type complex, once we use field coefficients.
Proposition 7.38.
Let Π\Pi be a finitely generated Novikov group and let (𝔽,𝒜)({\mathbb{F}},{\mathcal{A}}) be a Π\Pi-equivariant Novikov flow category enriched in 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}} satisfying in addition
(1)
The action λ\lambda on Π\Pi is ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-valued and 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-valued.
(2)
Ob​𝔽/Π{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}/\Pi is finite.
Then these data together with the differential on the chain complex C⁡(𝔽)C({\mathbb{F}}) define a filtered Floer–Novikov complex in the sense of [70, Definition 1.1].
Moreover, for any field 𝐊{\bf K}, the complex
C⁡(𝔽)⊗Λ𝐊ΠC({\mathbb{F}})\otimes\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi}
together with the norm ℓ:=𝒜\ell:={\mathcal{A}} is a Floer-type complex over Λ𝐊Π\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi} in the sense of Definition 7.34.
Proof.
The first claim is straightforward where we take Ob⁡(𝔽̊){\rm Ob}(\mathring{\mathbb{F}}) under the Π\Pi-action equipped with the action 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, and we use the incidence coefficients of the differential. For the second, see [69, Section 12].
∎
7.5.2. Filtration and spectral invariants
For any Floer-type complex (C,ℓC,dC)(C,\ell_{C},d_{C}), one can consider the filtration defined by
C≤τ={x∈C|ℓC​(x)≤τ},\displaystyle\ C^{\leq\tau}=\Big\{x\in C\ |\ \ell_{C}(x)\leq\tau\Big\},\
C<τ:={x∈C|ℓC​(x)<τ}.\displaystyle\ C^{<\tau}:=\Big\{x\in C\ |\ \ell_{C}(x)<\tau\Big\}.
As dCd_{C} respects the norm, C≤τC^{\leq\tau} is a subcomplex. Then for any interval I⊆ℝI\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}, one has a corresponding complex defined in a typical way. For example, when I=[a,b]I=[a,b], CIC^{I} is the quotient complex
CI:=C≤b/C<aC^{I}:=C^{\leq b}/C^{<a}
For each x∈H⁡(C)x\in H(C), define the spectral number to be
c⁡(x):=inf{τ∈ℝ|x∈Im⁡(H⁡(C<τ)→H⁡(C))}∈ℝ∪{−∞}.c(x):=\inf\Big\{\tau\in{\mathbb{R}}\ |\ x\in{\rm Im}\Big(H(C^{<\tau})\to H(C)\Big)\Big\}\in{\mathbb{R}}\cup\{-\infty\}.
When the complex CC comes from a flow category 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} enriched in 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}, denote the spectral number by
c𝔽​(x)c_{{\mathbb{F}}}(x)
where the coefficient ring is understood from the context.
Usher [70] provided an abstract argument showing the finiteness of spectral numbers and existence of spectral carriers.
Theorem 7.39 (cf. [70]).
Under the assumption of Proposition 7.38, for any Noetherian ring RR, and a∈H∗​(𝔽)≠0a\in H_{*}({\mathbb{F}})\neq 0, τ⁡(a):=c𝔽​(a)>−∞\tau(a):=c_{\mathbb{F}}(a)>-\infty. Moreover, aa is represented by a cycle contained in C∗​(𝔽)≤τ⁡(a)C_{*}({\mathbb{F}})^{\leq\tau(a)}.
Proof.
The theorem follows from Proposition 7.38 and [70, Theorem 1.3].
∎
7.5.3. Barcodes
By the nonarchimedean Gram–Schmidt process established in [69, Definition 6.3], given a Floer-type complex (C,ℓC,dC)=(C,ℓ,d)(C,\ell_{C},d_{C})=(C,\ell,d), the map d:C→Cd:C\to C of the ungraded complex factors through C→ker⁡(d)⊆CC\to\ker(d)\subseteq C, so we can find an orthogonal basis y1,…,yny_{1},\ldots,y_{n} of CC and an orthogonal basis of x1,…,xmx_{1},\ldots,x_{m} of ker⁡(d){\rm ker}(d) such that one can write d:C→ker⁡(d)d:C\to\ker(d) in the block-matrix form
[Ir000]\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}I_{r}&0\\
0&0\end{array}\right]
where r≤nr\leq n is the rank of dd and such that
ℓ⁡(y1)−ℓ⁡(x1)≥⋯≥ℓ⁡(yr)−ℓ⁡(xr).\ell(y_{1})-\ell(x_{1})\geq\cdots\geq\ell(y_{r})-\ell(x_{r}).
The verbose barcode of (C,d,ℓ)(C,d,\ell) is the multiset of elements (ℝ/Γ)×[0,+∞]({\mathbb{R}}/\Gamma)\times[0,+\infty] consisting of
(1)
a pair (ℓ⁡(xi)​mod​Γ,ℓ⁡(yi)−ℓ⁡(xi))(\ell(x_{i})\ {\rm mod}\ \Gamma,\ell(y_{i})-\ell(x_{i})) for i=1,…,ri=1,\ldots,r.
(2)
a pair (ℓ⁡(xi)​mod​Γ,∞)(\ell(x_{i})\ {\rm mod}\ \Gamma,\infty) for i=r+1,…,mi=r+1,\ldots,m.
Each element of this multiset is called a bar while the second variable is called the bar-length. The concise barcode is the submultiset obtained by removing bars of length zero. It was proved ([69, Theorem 7.1]) that the verbose barcode of a Floer-type complex does not depend on the choice of the singular value decomposition, hence is well-defined.
Theorem 7.40.
Let CC and DD be two Floer-type complexes over Λ𝐊Π\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi}.
(1)
If CC and DD are filtered isomorphic, then they have identical verbose barcodes.
(2)
If CC and DD are filtered homotopy equivalent, then they have identical concise barcodes.
Proof.
By [69, Theorem A, B], this is true if the Novikov group Π\Pi is contained in ℝ{\mathbb{R}}. In our setting, the conclusion holds after tensoring with Λ𝐊|Π|\Lambda_{\bf K}^{|\Pi|}.
∎
7.5.4. Continuity
Now we consider the case of tensor product and discuss quantitative aspects of chain maps. Let (𝔽1,𝒜1),…,(𝔽m,𝒜m)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},{\mathcal{A}}_{1}),\ldots,({\mathbb{F}}_{m},{\mathcal{A}}_{m}) be locally finite flow categories enriched in 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}} so there are the associated chain complexes C⁡(𝔽j)C({\mathbb{F}}_{j}). Recall that one can consider the completed tensor product (over ℤ{\mathbb{Z}})
C(𝔽1)⊗^⋯⊗^C(𝔽m)C({\mathbb{F}}_{1})\widehat{\otimes}\cdots\widehat{\otimes}C({\mathbb{F}}_{m})
whose elements are formal sums
∑i=1∞ai(pi1⊗⋯⊗pim)\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}a_{i}\big(p_{i_{1}}\otimes\cdots\otimes p_{i_{m}}\big)
with ai∈Ra_{i}\in R such that
limi→∞(𝒜1​(pi1)+⋯+𝒜m​(pim))=−∞.\lim_{i\to\infty}\big({\mathcal{A}}_{1}(p_{i_{1}})+\cdots+{\mathcal{A}}_{m}(p_{i_{m}})\big)=-\infty.
Then there is a similar filtration on the tensor product and for τ1,…,τm∈ℝ\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{m}\in{\mathbb{R}}, an inclusion
C≤τ1(𝔽1)⊗^⋯⊗^C≤τm(𝔽m)→(C(𝔽1)⊗^⋯⊗^C(𝔽m))≤τ1+⋯+τmC^{\leq\tau_{1}}({\mathbb{F}}_{1})\widehat{\otimes}\cdots\widehat{\otimes}C^{\leq\tau_{m}}({\mathbb{F}}_{m})\to\big(C({\mathbb{F}}_{1})\widehat{\otimes}\cdots\widehat{\otimes}C({\mathbb{F}}_{m})\big)^{\leq\tau_{1}+\cdots+\tau_{m}}
Definition 7.41.
Let 𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m},{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} be Novikov flow categories with ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-valued actions 𝒜1,…,𝒜m,𝒜′{\mathcal{A}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathcal{A}}_{m},{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}.
(1)
Let 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} be a Novikov multimodule over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}). The threshold of 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} is the number
ϵ𝕏:=inf{𝒜1(p1)+⋯+𝒜m(pm)−𝒜′(p′)|Mp1⋯pm;p′𝕏≠∅}∈[−∞,∞].\epsilon^{\mathbb{X}}:=\inf\Big\{{\mathcal{A}}_{1}(p_{1})+\cdots+{\mathcal{A}}_{m}(p_{m})-{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}(p^{\prime})\ |\ M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}}\neq\emptyset\Big\}\in[-\infty,\infty].
(2)
Let 𝕏0{\mathbb{X}}_{0} and 𝕏1{\mathbb{X}}_{1} be two Novikov multimodules over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}). Let ℍ{\mathbb{H}} be a Novikov homotopy from 𝕏0{\mathbb{X}}_{0} to 𝕏1{\mathbb{X}}_{1}. The threshold of ℍ{\mathbb{H}} is the number
δℍ:=inf{𝒜1(p1)+⋯+𝒜m(pm)−𝒜′(p′)|Mp1⋯pm;p′ℍ≠∅}∈[−∞,+∞].\delta^{\mathbb{H}}:=\inf\Big\{{\mathcal{A}}_{1}(p_{1})+\cdots+{\mathcal{A}}_{m}(p_{m})-{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}(p^{\prime})\ |\ M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{H}}\neq\emptyset\Big\}\in[-\infty,+\infty].
By the Novikov property of multimodules (see Definition 7.2), ϵ𝕏≠−∞\epsilon^{\mathbb{X}}\neq-\infty and δℍ≠−∞\delta^{\mathbb{H}}\neq-\infty.
Proposition 7.42.
In the situation of Definition 7.41, the chain map
Φ𝕏:C(𝔽1)⊗^⋯⊗^C(𝔽m)→C(𝔽′)\Phi^{\mathbb{X}}:C({\mathbb{F}}_{1})\widehat{\otimes}\cdots\widehat{\otimes}C({\mathbb{F}}_{m})\to C({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime})
satisfies
Φ𝕏((C(𝔽1)⊗^⋯⊗^C(𝔽m))≤τ)⊆C∗≤τ−ϵ𝕏(𝔽′).\Phi^{\mathbb{X}}\left(\big(C({\mathbb{F}}_{1})\widehat{\otimes}\cdots\widehat{\otimes}C({\mathbb{F}}_{m})\big)^{\leq\tau}\right)\subseteq C_{*}^{\leq\tau-\epsilon^{\mathbb{X}}}({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}).
The chain homotopy
Φℍ:C(𝔽1)⊗^⋯⊗^C(𝔽m)→C(𝔽′)\Phi^{\mathbb{H}}:C({\mathbb{F}}_{1})\widehat{\otimes}\cdots\widehat{\otimes}C({\mathbb{F}}_{m})\to C({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime})
satisfies
Φℍ((C(𝔽1)⊗^⋯⊗^C(𝔽m))≤τ)⊆C∗≤τ−δℍ(𝔽′).\Phi^{\mathbb{H}}\left(\big(C({\mathbb{F}}_{1})\widehat{\otimes}\cdots\widehat{\otimes}C({\mathbb{F}}_{m})\big)^{\leq\tau}\right)\subseteq C_{*}^{\leq\tau-\delta^{\mathbb{H}}}({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}).
Proof.
Straightforward check.
∎
8. FOP Perturbations
In this section we review the technique of FOP perturbations. The original idea was proposed by Fukaya–Ono in [29], and further explored by Parker [54]. In [13] the authors rigorously established this technique and defined integer-valued Gromov–Witten invariants for general compact symplectic manifolds. In [14] the authors further proved the integral Arnold conjecture; see [11] for another application.
8.1. FOP perturbations
Definition 8.1 (Perturbations on derived orbifolds).
Given a derived orbifold 𝒟=(𝒰,ℰ,𝒮){\mathcal{D}}=({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}},{\mathcal{S}}), a perturbation of 𝒟{\mathcal{D}} (or of 𝒮{\mathcal{S}}) is a smooth section 𝒮′:𝒰→ℰ{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}:{\mathcal{U}}\to{\mathcal{E}} such that if 𝒮−1​(0){\mathcal{S}}^{-1}(0) is compact, then (𝒮′)−1​(0)({\mathcal{S}}^{\prime})^{-1}(0) is also compact.
We recall the main “black-box” type theorem proved in [13].
Theorem 8.2.
[13, Theorem 1.1]
Suppose 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} is an NC orbifold without boundary1414
14
When discussing FOP transverse sections for orbifolds with boundaries and corners, the behavior near boundary and corner strata are predetermined. and ℰ→𝒰{\mathcal{E}}\to{\mathcal{U}} is an NC vector bundle. Let Γ⁡(𝒰,ℰ)\Gamma({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}}) be the space of smooth sections. Then there is a C0C^{0}-dense subset ΓFOP​(𝒰,ℰ)⊆Γ⁡(𝒰,ℰ)\Gamma^{\rm FOP}({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}})\subseteq\Gamma({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}}) whose elements are called FOP transverse sections satisfying the following properties.
(1)
(Classical transversality) If 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} is a manifold, FOP transversality is equivalent to classical transversality.
(2)
(Locality Property) The restrictions of FOP transverse sections to open subsets are still FOP transverse.
(3)
(Extension Property) For any pair of closed subsets 𝒴⊆𝒴′{\mathcal{Y}}\subseteq{\mathcal{Y}}^{\prime} and open neighborhoods 𝒱⊆𝒰{\mathcal{V}}\subseteq{\mathcal{U}} of 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} and 𝒱′⊆𝒰{\mathcal{V}}^{\prime}\subseteq{\mathcal{U}} of 𝒴′{\mathcal{Y}}^{\prime}, if 𝒮∈ΓFOP​(𝒱,ℰ|𝒱){\mathcal{S}}\in\Gamma^{\rm FOP}({\mathcal{V}},{\mathcal{E}}|_{{\mathcal{V}}}), then there exists 𝒮′∈ΓFOP​(𝒱′,ℰ|𝒱′){\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}\in\Gamma^{\rm FOP}({\mathcal{V}}^{\prime},{\mathcal{E}}|_{{\mathcal{V}}^{\prime}}) which agrees with 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} near 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}}.
(4)
(Product Property) Let 𝒰′{\mathcal{U}}^{\prime} be another normally complex orbifold and ℰ′→𝒰′{\mathcal{E}}^{\prime}\to{\mathcal{U}}^{\prime} be a normally complex vector bundle. Then the product map
Γ⁡(𝒰,ℰ)×Γ⁡(𝒰′,ℰ′)→Γ⁡(𝒰×𝒰′,ℰ⊞ℰ′)\Gamma({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}})\times\Gamma({\mathcal{U}}^{\prime},{\mathcal{E}}^{\prime})\to\Gamma({\mathcal{U}}\times{\mathcal{U}}^{\prime},{\mathcal{E}}\boxplus{\mathcal{E}}^{\prime})
sends products of FOP transverse sections to FOP transverse sections.
(5)
(Stabilization Property) If πℱ:ℱ→𝒰\pi_{\mathcal{F}}:{\mathcal{F}}\to{\mathcal{U}} is rigid complex vector bundle1515
15
This condition was stated in [13] for more general normally complex vector bundles. When ℱ{\mathcal{F}} is a rigid bundle, the total space ℱ{\mathcal{F}} carries a canonical NC structure., then the stabilization map
Γ⁡(𝒰,ℰ)→Γ⁡(ℱ,πℱ∗​ℰ⊕πℱ∗​ℱ),𝒮↦πℱ∗​𝒮⊕τℱ,\Gamma({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}})\to\Gamma({\mathcal{F}},\pi_{\mathcal{F}}^{*}{\mathcal{E}}\oplus\pi_{\mathcal{F}}^{*}{\mathcal{F}}),\quad\quad{\mathcal{S}}\mapsto\pi_{\mathcal{F}}^{*}{\mathcal{S}}\oplus\tau_{\mathcal{F}},
where τℱ:ℱ→πℱ∗​ℱ\tau_{\mathcal{F}}:{\mathcal{F}}\to\pi_{\mathcal{F}}^{*}{\mathcal{F}} is the tautological section, sends FOP transverse sections to FOP transverse sections.
(6)
(Main stratum) For each 𝒮∈ΓFOP​(𝒰,ℰ){\mathcal{S}}\in\Gamma^{\rm FOP}({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}}), the closure
𝒮−1​(0)∩𝒰free¯\overline{{\mathcal{S}}^{-1}(0)\cap{\mathcal{U}}_{\rm free}}
is a pseudomanifold (whose dimension is dim​𝒰−rank​ℰ{\rm dim}{\mathcal{U}}-{\rm rank}{\mathcal{E}}).
Definition 8.3.
Let 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯FOP\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{\rm FOP} resp. 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigFOP\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{\rm FOP}_{\rm rig} be the category whose objects are
𝒟̊:=(𝒰,ℰ,𝒮,𝒮′)\mathring{\mathcal{D}}:=({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}},{\mathcal{S}},{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime})
where 𝒟:=(𝒰,ℰ,𝒮){\mathcal{D}}:=({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}},{\mathcal{S}}) is an NC derived orbifold and 𝒮′:𝒰→ℰ{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}:{\mathcal{U}}\to{\mathcal{E}} is an FOP transverse perturbation. The morphism from 𝒟̊1:=(𝒰1,ℰ1,𝒮1,𝒮1′)\mathring{\mathcal{D}}_{1}:=({\mathcal{U}}_{1},{\mathcal{E}}_{1},{\mathcal{S}}_{1},{\mathcal{S}}_{1}^{\prime}) to 𝒟̊2:=(𝒰2,ℰ2,𝒮2,𝒮2′)\mathring{\mathcal{D}}_{2}:=({\mathcal{U}}_{2},{\mathcal{E}}_{2},{\mathcal{S}}_{2},{\mathcal{S}}_{2}^{\prime}) is an embedding of underlying stratified orbifolds covered by a bundle embedding 𝜾21=(ι21,ι^21):(𝒰1,ℰ1)→(𝒰2,ℰ2){\bm{\iota}}_{21}=(\iota_{21},\widehat{\iota}_{21}):({\mathcal{U}}_{1},{\mathcal{E}}_{1})\to({\mathcal{U}}_{2},{\mathcal{E}}_{2}) such that it induces both a morphism of 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯NC\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{\rm NC} resp. 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{\rm NC}_{\rm rig} from 𝒟1:=(𝒰1,ℰ1,𝒮1){\mathcal{D}}_{1}:=({\mathcal{U}}_{1},{\mathcal{E}}_{1},{\mathcal{S}}_{1}) to 𝒟2:=(𝒰2,ℰ2,𝒮2){\mathcal{D}}_{2}:=({\mathcal{U}}_{2},{\mathcal{E}}_{2},{\mathcal{S}}_{2}) and a morphism with 𝒮i{\mathcal{S}}_{i} replaced by 𝒮i′{\mathcal{S}}_{i}^{\prime}.
Notice that there are natural forgetful functors
by forgetting the perturbation part 𝒮′{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime} resp. taking the closure of (𝒮′)−1​(0)∩𝒰free({\mathcal{S}}^{\prime})^{-1}(0)\cap{\mathcal{U}}_{\rm free}.
By using Theorem 8.2 inductively, one can construct FOP transverse perturbations on stratified derived orbifolds which respect collars.
Lemma 8.4.
Let AA be a regular poset and 𝒟=(𝒰,ℰ,𝒮){\mathcal{D}}=({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}},{\mathcal{S}}) be an AA-stratified object of ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯NC{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{\rm NC}. Let A′⊆AA^{\prime}\subseteq A be an Alexandrov closed subset and
∂A′𝒟\partial^{A^{\prime}}{\mathcal{D}}
be the corresponding A′A^{\prime}-stratified derived orbifold. Suppose 𝒮A′:∂A′𝒰→ℰ{\mathcal{S}}_{A^{\prime}}:\partial^{A^{\prime}}{\mathcal{U}}\to{\mathcal{E}} is an FOP transverse perturbation so that
(∂A′𝒰,ℰ,𝒮,𝒮A′)(\partial^{A^{\prime}}{\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}},{\mathcal{S}},{\mathcal{S}}_{A^{\prime}})
is an A′A^{\prime}-stratified object of ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯FOP{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{\rm FOP}. Then there exists an FOP transverse perturbation 𝒮′:𝒰→ℰ{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}:{\mathcal{U}}\to{\mathcal{E}} which extends 𝒮A′{\mathcal{S}}_{A^{\prime}} such that (𝒰,ℰ,𝒮,𝒮′)({\mathcal{U}},{\mathcal{E}},{\mathcal{S}},{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}) is an object of ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯FOP{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{\rm FOP}.
8.2. FOP perturbations on flow categories, multimodules, and homotopies
Now we prove a major result of this paper stating the general procedure of constructing FOP perturbations on flow categories, multimodules, and homotopies.
Theorem N.
Flow categories, multimodules, and homotopies in this proposition are assumed to be unobstructed (Definition 7.1) and locally compact (Definition 7.2, 7.5, 7.6, and 7.8). We also assume that all charts have compact zero locus.
(1)
(FOP perturbation for equivariant flow categories) Let Π⋊G\mathbb{\Pi}\rtimes G be a twisted Novikov group (Definition 7.21) and let 𝔽~\tilde{\mathbb{F}} be a free Π⋊G\mathbb{\Pi}\rtimes G-equivariant flow category enriched in ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm NC}. Then there exists a Π⋊G\mathbb{\Pi}\rtimes G-equivariant FOP perturbation 𝔽̊\mathring{\mathbb{F}} on 𝔽~\tilde{\mathbb{F}}.
(2)
(FOP perturbation for equivariant multimodules) Let Π1,…,Πm;Π′\mathbb{\Pi}_{1},\ldots,\mathbb{\Pi}_{m};\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime} be Novikov groups and GG be a finite group acting on Π1×⋯×Πm\mathbb{\Pi}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{\Pi}_{m} and on Π′\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime}. Let
ρ:Π1×⋯×Πm→Π′\rho:\mathbb{\Pi}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{\Pi}_{m}\to\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime}
be a GG-equivariant morphism of Novikov groups.
