Let 𝔽~1,…,𝔽~m\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{m} be Πi\mathbb{\Pi}_{i}-equivariant flow categories enriched in ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm NC} such that the weak flow category 𝔽~1×⋯×𝔽~m\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{1}\times\cdots\times\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{m} has a free (Π1×⋯×Πm)⋊G(\mathbb{\Pi}_{1}\times\cdots\times{\mathbb{\Pi}}_{m})\rtimes G-action. Let 𝔽~′\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} be a free Π′⋊G\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime}\rtimes G-equivariant flow category enriched in ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm NC}. Let 𝕏~\tilde{\mathbb{X}} be a ρ\rho-equivariant multimodule over (𝔽~1,…,𝔽~m,𝔽~′)(\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{m};\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}). Let 𝔽̊i\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{i} resp. 𝔽̊′\mathring{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} be a Πi\mathbb{\Pi}_{i}-equivariant resp. Π′\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime}-equivariant FOP perturbation on 𝔽~i\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{i} resp. 𝔽~′\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} such that 𝔽̊1×⋯×𝔽̊m\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{m} resp. 𝔽̊′\mathring{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} is also GG-equivariant. Then there exists a ρ\rho-equivariant FOP perturbation 𝕏̊\mathring{\mathbb{X}} on 𝕏~\tilde{\mathbb{X}} as an equivariant multimodule over (𝔽̊1,…,𝔽̊m,𝔽̊′)(\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{m};\mathring{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}).
(3)
(FOP perturbation for equivariant multimodule homotopies) Let Π1,…,Πm\mathbb{\Pi}_{1},\ldots,\mathbb{\Pi}_{m}, Π′\mathbb{\Pi}^{\prime}, GG, ρ\rho, 𝔽~1,…,𝔽~m,𝔽~′\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{m},\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}, and 𝔽̊1,…,𝔽̊m,𝔽̊′\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{m},\mathring{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} be as in the above situation. Let 𝕏~0\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{0} and 𝕏~1\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{1} be two ρ\rho-equivariant multimodules over (𝔽~1,…,𝔽~m,𝔽~′)(\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{m};\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}) and ℍ~\tilde{\mathbb{H}} be a ρ\rho-equivariant homotopy from 𝕏~0\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{0} to 𝕏~1\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{1}. Let 𝕏̊0\mathring{\mathbb{X}}_{0} and 𝕏̊1\mathring{\mathbb{X}}_{1} be FOP perturbations on 𝕏~0\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{0} and 𝕏~1\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{1} respectively as ρ\rho-equivariant multimodules over (𝔽̊1,…,𝔽̊m,𝔽̊′)(\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{m};\mathring{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}). Then there exists a ρ\rho-equivariant FOP perturbation ℍ̊\mathring{\mathbb{H}} on ℍ~\tilde{\mathbb{H}} as a homotopy from 𝕏̊0\mathring{\mathbb{X}}_{0} to 𝕏̊1\mathring{\mathbb{X}}_{1}.
Proof of Theorem N.
We construct the FOP perturbations inductively. In general, the Novikov conditions of Definition 7.2, Definition 7.5, and Definition 7.24 allow us to choose a beginning of the induction process. The freeness assumed in Theorem N allows us to achieve equivariant transversality.
—The case of flow categories— We say a pair of objects p<qp<q is minimal if Mp​q𝔽~≠∅M_{pq}^{\tilde{\mathbb{F}}}\neq\emptyset and there does not exist a third object rr such that both Mp​r𝔽~M_{pr}^{\tilde{\mathbb{F}}} and Mr​q𝔽~M_{rq}^{\tilde{\mathbb{F}}} are nonempty. By (2) of Definition 7.24, unless all morphism spaces are empty, minimal pairs exist. Moreover, the Π\mathbb{\Pi}-equivariance condition implies that minimal pairs form a union of Π\mathbb{\Pi}-orbits.
Now we perturb Mp​q𝔽~=(𝒰p​q,ℰp​q,𝒮p​q)M_{pq}^{\tilde{\mathbb{F}}}=({\mathcal{U}}_{pq},{\mathcal{E}}_{pq},{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}) for minimal pairs p<qp<q. We claim that 𝒮p​q−1​(0){\mathcal{S}}_{pq}^{-1}(0) is strictly contained in the union of top strata of 𝒟p​q{\mathcal{D}}_{pq}. If it is not the case, then there exists a codimension one stratum which intersects 𝒮p​q−1​(0){\mathcal{S}}_{pq}^{-1}(0). By the unobstructedness assumption, such a stratum comes from the product of two other morphism spaces. This contradicts the assumption that p<qp<q is a minimal pair. Hence our claim is correct.
Then by Theorem 8.2, there exists an FOP transverse perturbation 𝒮p​q′{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}^{\prime}. Then using the free Π\mathbb{\Pi}-action, we translate this perturbation to charts Mp′​q′𝔽~M_{p^{\prime}q^{\prime}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{F}}} with all (p′,q′)(p^{\prime},q^{\prime}) in the same Π\mathbb{\Pi}-orbit of (p,q)(p,q). We apply such perturbation constructions independently for all Π\mathbb{\Pi}-orbits of minimal pairs.
Now we set up the induction. Recall that the Novikov flow category 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} carries an ℝk{\mathbb{R}}^{k}-valued action 𝒜=(𝒜1,…,𝒜k){\mathcal{A}}=({\mathcal{A}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathcal{A}}_{k}). Define
|𝒜|=𝒜1+⋯+𝒜m:Ob​𝔽→ℝ.|{\mathcal{A}}|={\mathcal{A}}_{1}+\cdots+{\mathcal{A}}_{m}:{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}\to{\mathbb{R}}.
Choose an increasing sequence c1<c2<⋯c_{1}<c_{2}<\cdots satisfying the following conditions.
(1)
clc_{l} goes to infinity.
(2)
For each pair p<qp<q with cl−1≤|𝒜​|(p)−|​𝒜|(q)<clc_{l-1}\leq|{\mathcal{A}}|(p)-|{\mathcal{A}}|(q)<c_{l}, if p<r<qp<r<q, then |𝒜|​(p)−|𝒜|​(r)<cl−1|{\mathcal{A}}|(p)-|{\mathcal{A}}|(r)<c_{l-1} and |𝒜|​(r)−|𝒜|​(q)<cl−1|{\mathcal{A}}|(r)-|{\mathcal{A}}|(q)<c_{l-1}.
(3)
If p<qp<q, then |𝒜|​(p)−|𝒜|​(q)≥c1|{\mathcal{A}}|(p)-|{\mathcal{A}}|(q)\geq c_{1}.
Now we state the following induction hypothesis: suppose for clc_{l} in this sequence, we have constructed FOP transverse perturbations
𝒮p​q′:𝒰p​q→ℰp​q{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}^{\prime}:{\mathcal{U}}_{pq}\to{\mathcal{E}}_{pq}
for all pairs p<qp<q with |𝒜|​(p)−|𝒜|​(q)<cl|{\mathcal{A}}|(p)-|{\mathcal{A}}|(q)<c_{l} for all α=1,…,k\alpha=1,\ldots,k, which satisfy the following conditions.
(1)
The perturbations are Π\mathbb{\Pi}-equivariant.
(2)
Whenever p<r<qp<r<q, the restriction of 𝒮p​q′{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}^{\prime} to ∂p​r​q𝒰p​q\partial^{prq}{\mathcal{U}}_{pq} coincides with the stabilization of the product of 𝒮p​r′{\mathcal{S}}_{pr}^{\prime} and 𝒮r​q′{\mathcal{S}}_{rq}^{\prime} under the compositions of 𝔽~\tilde{\mathbb{F}}.
(3)
If p<qp<q is minimal, then 𝒮p​q′{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}^{\prime} is the one we have already constructed.
Our choice of c1c_{1} implies that the base case is established. Suppose the induction hypothesis holds for cl−1c_{l-1}.
Consider a pair p<qp<q with |𝒜|​(p)−|𝒜|​(q)∈[cl−1,cl)|{\mathcal{A}}|(p)-|{\mathcal{A}}|(q)\in[c_{l-1},c_{l}). If the pair (p,q)(p,q) is minimal, then we take 𝒮p​q′{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}^{\prime} to be the one we constructed before the induction setup. Suppose it is not minimal. By the induction hypothesis, for each rr with p<r<qp<r<q, one has constructed FOP transverse perturbations
𝒮p​r′:𝒰p​r→ℰp​r,\displaystyle\ {\mathcal{S}}_{pr}^{\prime}:{\mathcal{U}}_{pr}\to{\mathcal{E}}_{pr},\
𝒮r​q′:𝒰r​q→ℰr​q.\displaystyle\ {\mathcal{S}}_{rq}^{\prime}:{\mathcal{U}}_{rq}\to{\mathcal{E}}_{rq}.
As the structural map
Mp​r𝔽×Mr​q𝔽→∂p​r​qMp​q𝔽M_{pr}^{\mathbb{F}}\times M_{rq}^{\mathbb{F}}\to\partial^{prq}M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}
is a rigidified embedding of normally complex derived orbifolds, there is a canonical extension of the product 𝒮p​r′×𝒮r​q′{\mathcal{S}}_{pr}^{\prime}\times{\mathcal{S}}_{rq}^{\prime} to ∂p​r​q𝒰p​q\partial^{prq}{\mathcal{U}}_{pq}. The induction hypothesis also implies that for all such rr, these canonical extensions agree on strata of the form ∂p​r1​r2​q𝒰p​q\partial^{pr_{1}r_{2}q}{\mathcal{U}}_{pq}. Hence one obtains an object in ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigFOP{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm FOP} stratified by the true boundary of Ap​q𝔽~A_{pq}^{\tilde{\mathbb{F}}}. Then using Lemma 8.4, there exists an FOP transverse perturbation 𝒮α:∂α𝒰p​q→ℰp​q{\mathcal{S}}_{\alpha}:\partial^{\alpha}{\mathcal{U}}_{pq}\to{\mathcal{E}}_{pq} which is compatible with the existing ones.
As the Π\mathbb{\Pi}-action is free, one can translate 𝒮p​q′{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}^{\prime} to all pairs on the same Π\mathbb{\Pi}-orbit. Apply the same procedure for all Π\mathbb{\Pi}-orbits of pairs p′,q′p^{\prime},q^{\prime} with |𝒜|​(p′)−|𝒜|​(q′)∈[cl−1,cl)|{\mathcal{A}}|(p^{\prime})-|{\mathcal{A}}|(q^{\prime})\in[c_{l-1},c_{l}). This implies that the induction can be carried out. Hence the case of flow categories of Theorem N is established.
—The case of multimodules— We follow a similar inductive process. Consider the set Ob𝔽~1×⋯×Ob𝔽~m×Ob𝔽~′{\rm Ob}\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{1}\times\cdots\times{\rm Ob}\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{m}\times{\rm Ob}\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}, whose objects are denoted by (p1,…,pm,p′)(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m};p^{\prime}). Then Π1×⋯×Πm\mathbb{\Pi}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{\Pi}_{m} acts freely on this set via the morphism ρ\rho; in the situation of item (3), the group Γ\Gamma also acts on this set and the Γ\Gamma-action commutes with Π1×⋯×Πm\mathbb{\Pi}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{\Pi}_{m}. We say a tuple (p1,…,pm,p′)(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m};p^{\prime}) is minimal if 1) there does not exist ii and pi<qip_{i}<q_{i} in 𝔽~i\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{i} such that Mp1⋯pi−1qipi+1⋯pm;p′𝕏~≠∅M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1}q_{i}p_{i+1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{X}}}\neq\emptyset and 2) there does not exist q′<p′q^{\prime}<p^{\prime} in 𝔽~′\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} such that Mp1⋯pm;q′𝕏~≠∅M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};q^{\prime}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{X}}}\neq\emptyset. When (p1,…,pm,p′)(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m};p^{\prime}) is minimal, similar to the flow category case, the unobstructedness assumption implies that one can construct an FOP transverse perturbation
𝒮p1⋯pm;p′′:𝒰p1⋯pm;p′→ℰp1⋯pm;p′{\mathcal{S}}_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\prime}:{\mathcal{U}}_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}\to{\mathcal{E}}_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}
which can be translated to orbits of Π1×⋯×Πm×Γ\mathbb{\Pi}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{\Pi}_{m}\times\Gamma.
Now we set up an induction scheme. For each tuple (p1,…,pm,p′)(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m};p^{\prime}), define
|p1⋯pm;p′|=|𝒜1|(p1)+⋯+|𝒜m|(pm)−|𝒜′|(p′)∈ℝ.|p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}|=|{\mathcal{A}}_{1}|(p_{1})+\cdots+|{\mathcal{A}}_{m}|(p_{m})-|{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}|(p^{\prime})\in{\mathbb{R}}.
Lemma 8.5.
There exists a sequences of real numbers
c1<c2<⋯c_{1}<c_{2}<\cdots
satisfying the following conditions.
(1)
clc_{l} goes to infinity.
(2)
If |p1⋯pm;p′|∈[cl−1,cl)|p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}|\in[c_{l-1},c_{l}) with pi<qip_{i}<q_{i} in 𝔽~i\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{i} such that Mp1⋯pi−1qipi+1⋯pm;p′𝕏~≠∅M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1}q_{i}p_{i+1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{X}}}\neq\emptyset, then |p1⋯pi−1qipi+1⋯pm;p′|<cl−1|p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1}q_{i}p_{i+1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}|<c_{l-1}.
(3)
If |p1⋯pm;p′|∈[cl−1,cl)|p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}|\in[c_{l-1},c_{l}) with q′<p′q^{\prime}<p^{\prime} in 𝔽~′\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} such that Mp1⋯pm;q′𝕏~≠∅M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};q^{\prime}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{X}}}\neq\emptyset, then |p1⋯pm;q′|<cl−1|p_{1}\cdots p_{m};q^{\prime}|<c_{l-1}.
(4)
If Mp1⋯pm;p′𝕏~≠∅M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{X}}}\neq\emptyset, then |p1⋯pm;p′|≥c1|p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}|\geq c_{1}.
Proof.
It follows from the definition of equivariant Novikov flow categories (Definition 7.24) that for each ii, one has
inf{|𝒜i|​(pi)−|𝒜i|​(qi)|Mpi​qi𝔽~i≠∅}>0.\inf\Big\{|{\mathcal{A}}_{i}|(p_{i})-|{\mathcal{A}}_{i}|(q_{i})\ |\ M_{p_{i}q_{i}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{i}}\neq\emptyset\Big\}>0.
Similarly
inf{|𝒜′|​(p′)−|𝒜′|​(q′)|Mp′​q′𝔽~′≠∅}>0.\inf\Big\{|{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}|(p^{\prime})-|{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}|(q^{\prime})\ |\ M_{p^{\prime}q^{\prime}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}\neq\emptyset\Big\}>0.
Let ϵ\epsilon be the minimum of these lower bounds. Then we can take cl=l​ϵc_{l}=l\epsilon.
∎
Now we state the induction hypothesis: for a clc_{l} in this sequence, we have constructed FOP transverse perturbations
𝒮p1⋯pm;p′′:𝒰p1⋯pm;p′→ℰp1⋯pm;p′{\mathcal{S}}_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\prime}:{\mathcal{U}}_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}\to{\mathcal{E}}_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}
for all tuples (p1,…,pm,p′)(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m};p^{\prime}) satisfying |p1⋯pm;p′|<cl|p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}|<c_{l} which satisfy the following conditions.
(1)
The perturbations are Π1×⋯×Πm\mathbb{\Pi}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{\Pi}_{m}-equivariant.
(2)
Whenever pi<qip_{i}<q_{i} in 𝔽~i\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{i}, the morphism
ιp1⋯pi−1(piqi)pi+1⋯pm;p′𝕏~:Mpi​qi𝔽~i×Mp1⋯pi−1qipi+1⋯pm;p′𝕏~→Mp1⋯pm;p′𝕏~\iota_{p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1}(p_{i}q_{i})p_{i+1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{X}}}:M_{p_{i}q_{i}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{i}}\times M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1}q_{i}p_{i+1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{X}}}\to M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{X}}}
is also a morphism in ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigFOP{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm FOP}.
(3)
Whenever q′<p′q^{\prime}<p^{\prime} in 𝔽~′\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}, the morphism
ιp1⋯pm;q′p′𝕏~:Mp1⋯pm;q′𝕏~×Mq′​p′𝔽~′→Mp1⋯pm;p′𝕏~\iota_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};q^{\prime}p^{\prime}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{X}}}:M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};q^{\prime}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{X}}}\times M_{q^{\prime}p^{\prime}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}\to M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{X}}}
is also a morphism in ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigFOP{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm FOP}.
(4)
When (p1,…,pm,p′)(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m};p^{\prime}) is minimal, 𝒮p1⋯pm;p′′{\mathcal{S}}_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\prime} is the one we have already constructed before the induction.
Our choice of c1c_{1} implies that the base case is established. Suppose the induction hypothesis holds for cl−1c_{l-1}. Consider a tuple (p1,…,pm,p′)(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m};p^{\prime}) with |p1⋯pm;p′|∈[cl−1,cl)|p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}|\in[c_{l-1},c_{l}). If it is minimal, then the perturbation has been constructed. If not, then the induction hypothesis and the conditions on the sequence clc_{l} implies that an FOP transverse perturbation has been constructed compatibly on each lower stratum of 𝒰p1⋯pm;p′{\mathcal{U}}_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}. One can extend it using the collar structure to a neighborhood of the boundary. Then by (3) of Theorem 8.2, one can extend to an FOP transverse perturbation 𝒮p1⋯pm;p′′:𝒰p1⋯pm;p′→ℰp1⋯pm;p′{\mathcal{S}}_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\prime}:{\mathcal{U}}_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}\to{\mathcal{E}}_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}.
Using the free Π1×⋯×Πm\mathbb{\Pi}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{\Pi}_{m}-action, one can translate this perturbation to all tuples on the same orbit. Apply the same procedure to all orbits of tuples within this energy window. Therefore the induction can be carried out. Hence the multimodule case of Theorem N is established.
The homotopy case of Theorem N is almost identical to the case of multimodules, hence is omitted.
∎
8.3. FOP perturbation and multimodule concatenations
Recall that although multimodule concatenation can be canonically done for multimodules enriched in 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}, in practice we will have non-canonical concatenations (involving extra stabilizations).
Proposition 8.6.
Let 𝔽̊1,…,𝔽̊m,𝔾̊1,…,𝔾̊n,𝔾̊′\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{m},\mathring{\mathbb{G}}_{1},\ldots,\mathring{\mathbb{G}}_{n},\mathring{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime} be Novikov flow categories enriched in ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigFOP{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm FOP}. Let 𝕏̊\mathring{\mathbb{X}} be a Novikov multimodule over (𝔽̊1,…,𝔽̊m,𝔾̊i)(\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{m};\mathring{\mathbb{G}}_{i}) and 𝕐̊\mathring{\mathbb{Y}} be a Novikov multimodule over (𝔾̊1,…,𝔾̊n,𝔾̊′)(\mathring{\mathbb{G}}_{1},\ldots,\mathring{\mathbb{G}}_{n};\mathring{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}). Let 𝕏~\tilde{\mathbb{X}} resp. 𝕐~\tilde{\mathbb{Y}} be their descents to ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm NC}. Suppose 𝕏~∘i𝕐~\tilde{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}\tilde{\mathbb{Y}} is a concatenation of 𝕏~\tilde{\mathbb{X}} and 𝕐~\tilde{\mathbb{Y}} at 𝔾~i\tilde{\mathbb{G}}_{i}. Then this concatenation has a lift to ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm NC} as a concatenation 𝕏̊∘i𝕐̊\mathring{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}\mathring{\mathbb{Y}}. Moreover, the concatenation respects the functor
⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigFOP→⌊𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯.{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm FOP}\to{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}.
Proof.
By Definition 6.13, the concatenation 𝕏~∘i𝕐~\tilde{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}\tilde{\mathbb{Y}} contains codimension zero morphisms
Mp1⋯pm;ri𝕏~×Mr1⋯rn;r′𝕐~→Mr1⋯ri−1p1⋯pmri+1⋯rn;r′𝕏~∘i𝕐~M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};r_{i}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{X}}}\times M_{r_{1}\cdots r_{n};r^{\prime}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{Y}}}\to M_{r_{1}\cdots r_{i-1}p_{1}\cdots p_{m}r_{i+1}\cdots r_{n};r^{\prime}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}\tilde{\mathbb{Y}}}
(8.1)
where the three items above are objects of ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm NC} and the morphism is a collared rigidified embedding of NC derived orbifolds. Then by the (Product Property) of Theorem 8.2, the product of existing FOP perturbations on Mp1⋯pm;ri𝕏~M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};r_{i}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{X}}} and on Mr1⋯rn;r′𝕐~M_{r_{1}\cdots r_{n};r^{\prime}}^{\tilde{\mathbb{Y}}} is an FOP perturbation on the source of the morphism (8.1). Then after certain stabilization by a rigid orbifold vector bundle, by the (Stabilization Property) of Theorem 8.2, the product has a canonical germ of FOP transverse extensions to the (corresponding open stratum) of the target of (8.1). The condition that the FOP perturbations are collared and respect the rigidifications guarantees that the extensions agree on adjacent strata. Therefore, one obtains a concatenation 𝕏̊∘i𝕐̊\mathring{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}\mathring{\mathbb{Y}} lifting 𝕏~∘i𝕐~\tilde{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}\tilde{\mathbb{Y}}. It is easy to verify that the concatenation is compatible with the concatenation of multimodules enriched in 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}} and the forgetful functor ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigFOP→⌊𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm FOP}\to{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}.
∎
Part II GEOMETRIC FLOW CATEGORIES, BIMODULES, AND HOMOTOPIES
Outline of Part 2
In this part, we describe flow categories, bimodules, and homotopies that will appear in (most of) the settings of Hamiltonian Floer theory. We then state the main theorems about the construction of their lifts to the category of normally complex Kuranishi spaces, which induce lifts to normally complex derived orbifolds. Using the the counting scheme described in Section 8, we prove the main theorems except for those in the ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant setting. The technical constructions of the regularization of the moduli spaces are deferred to the next Part.
9. Geometric Flow Categories
9.1. Morse flow category
Given a closed oriented Riemannian manifold (M,g)(M,g) and a Morse function f:M→ℝf:M\to{\mathbb{R}}, the Morse flow category, denoted by
𝕄⁡(f,g)\mathbb{M}(f,g)
and usually abbreviated as 𝕄\mathbb{M}, has critical points of ff as its objects and the moduli spaces of unparametrized (broken) downward gradient trajectories as its morphism spaces. We always assume that (f,g)(f,g) is Morse–Smale and that near critical points ff is a quadratic function and gg is the Euclidean metric with respect to a certain coordinate system near each critical point. In this way, for any two critical points p,q∈crit​fp,q\in{\rm crit}f, the moduli space ℳ¯p​q𝕄\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{pq}^{\mathbb{M}} is a smooth manifold with corners [71].
The partial order of Ob​𝕄{\rm Ob}\mathbb{M} is defined as
p≤q⟺ℳ¯p​q𝕄≠∅p\leq q\Longleftrightarrow\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{pq}^{\mathbb{M}}\neq\emptyset
and the poset stratifying ℳ¯p​q𝕄\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{pq}^{\mathbb{M}} (when p≠qp\neq q)
Ap​q𝕄={p<r1<⋯<rk<q}.A_{pq}^{\mathbb{M}}=\{p<r_{1}<\cdots<r_{k}<q\}.
Then ℳ¯p​q𝕄\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{pq}^{\mathbb{M}} is an object of 𝐒𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{\bf SMan}}.
We also define composition maps as the natural inclusion
ℳ¯p​r𝕄×ℳ¯r​q𝕄→ℳ¯p​q𝕄\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{pr}^{\mathbb{M}}\times\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{rq}^{\mathbb{M}}\to\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{pq}^{\mathbb{M}}
which is a morphism of 𝐒𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{\bf SMan}}. Therefore, we obtained a flow category enriched in 𝐒𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{\bf SMan}}. In fact, the standard exponential decay estimate implies that the moduli spaces are indeed objects of 𝐒𝐌𝐚𝐧¯adm\underline{\smash{\bf SMan}}_{\rm adm}. Therefore, its outercollaring still lives in the same category.
The flow category 𝕄⁡(f,g)\mathbb{M}(f,g) admits a grading which assigns to each critical point pp the its Morse index. By assigning orientations on unstable manifolds and counting elements of zero-dimensional moduli spaces, one obtains a Morse–Smale–Witten complex C​M∗​(f,g)CM_{*}(f,g) over integers freely generated by critical points, whose homology is isomorphic to the singular homology of MM.
9.2. Floer flow category
We now describe a central object considered in this paper. We will assign to each compact symplectic manifold together with a nondegenerate Hamiltonian and an almost complex structure a flow category, called the Floer flow category, typically denoted by 𝔽{\mathbb{F}}. More precisely, let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a compact symplectic manifold. Recall
Π=π2​(X)ker​c1∩ker​ω\Pi=\frac{\pi_{2}(X)}{{\rm ker}c_{1}\cap{\rm ker}\omega}
which is an abelian group (monoid). We make it a Novikov monoid (Definition 7.21) by defining
λ:Π→ℝ,λ⁡(a)=ω⁡(a),\lambda:\Pi\to{\mathbb{R}},\ \lambda(a)=\omega(a),
and
μ:Π→ℤ,μ⁡(a)=2​c1​(a).\mu:\Pi\to{\mathbb{Z}},\ \mu(a)=2c_{1}(a).
Let H:M×S1→XH:M\times S^{1}\to X be a (time-dependent) 11-periodic family of Hamiltonians which induces a 1-parameter family of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms
ϕHt∈Ham⁡(X,ω).\phi_{H}^{t}\in{\rm Ham}(X,\omega).
We assume that HH is nondegenerate. Let 𝒫~​(H)\tilde{\mathcal{P}}(H) be the set of pairs (u,x)(u,x) where u:𝔻2→Xu:{\mathbb{D}}^{2}\to X is a smooth map and x=u|∂𝔻2:S1→Xx=u|_{\partial\mathbb{D}^{2}}:S^{1}\to X is a 1-periodic orbit of HH. Define
(u,x)∼(u′,x′)⟺x=x′,∫𝔻2u∗​ω=∫𝔻2(u′)∗​ω,⟨c1​(T​X),u⁡(𝔻2)∪(−u′​(𝔻2))⟩=0.(u,x)\sim(u^{\prime},x^{\prime})\Longleftrightarrow x=x^{\prime},\ \int_{{\mathbb{D}}^{2}}u^{*}\omega=\int_{{\mathbb{D}}^{2}}(u^{\prime})^{*}\omega,\ \langle c_{1}(TX),u({\mathbb{D}}^{2})\cup(-u^{\prime}({\mathbb{D}}^{2}))\rangle=0.
Define
𝒫(H):=𝒫~(H)/∼{\mathcal{P}}(H):=\tilde{\mathcal{P}}(H)/\sim
whose elements are called capped 1-periodic orbits. Notice that there are well-defined action
𝒜H:𝒫⁡(H)→ℝ{\mathcal{A}}_{H}:{\mathcal{P}}(H)\to{\mathbb{R}}
and well-defined Conley–Zehnder index
deg:𝒫⁡(H)→ℤ.{\rm deg}:{\mathcal{P}}(H)\to{\mathbb{Z}}.
Moreover, Π\Pi acts on 𝒫⁡(H){\mathcal{P}}(H) freely with a finite quotient set, satisfying
𝒜H​(a​p)=𝒜H​(p)−λ⁡(a),\displaystyle\ {\mathcal{A}}_{H}(ap)={\mathcal{A}}_{H}(p)-\lambda(a),\
deg⁡(a​p)=deg⁡(p)−μ⁡(a).\displaystyle\ {\rm deg}(ap)={\rm deg}(p)-\mu(a).
The Floer flow category 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} has object set
Ob​𝔽=𝒫⁡(H).{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}={\mathcal{P}}(H).
Choose an ω\omega-compatible almost complex structure JJ. For each pair p,q∈𝒫⁡(H)p,q\in{\mathcal{P}}(H), one has the moduli space ℳ¯p​q𝔽\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}} of stable Floer trajectories. A partial order on 𝒫⁡(H){\mathcal{P}}(H) is induced by:
p≤q⟺ℳ¯p​q𝔽≠∅.p\leq q\Longleftrightarrow\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}\neq\emptyset.
The moduli space ℳ¯p​q𝔽\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}} is stratified by the regular poset Ap​q𝔽A_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}} which is (when p≠qp\neq q)
Ap​q𝔽:={p<r1<⋯<rk<q}.A_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}:=\{p<r_{1}<\cdots<r_{k}<q\}.
This provides a flow category which is denoted by 𝔽⁡(X,ω,H,J)\mathbb{F}(X,\omega,H,J), often abbreviated by 𝔽{\mathbb{F}}. At this moment this flow category is only enriched in 𝐓𝐨𝐩¯\underline{\smash{\bf Top}}.
We summarize the above setup in the following situation.
Situation Flow(i).
(X,ω)(X,\omega) is a compact symplectic manifold. 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} is the Floer flow category associated to a nondegenerate 11-periodic Hamiltonian and a 1-periodic family of ω\omega-compatible almost complex structure JJ.
We summarize the usual properties of the Floer flow category.
Proposition 9.1.
In Situation Flow(i), the Floer flow category 𝔽{\mathbb{F}}, together with the symplectic action 𝒜H{\mathcal{A}}_{H} and the Conley–Zehnder index, is a ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-graded Π\Pi-equivariant Novikov flow category.
9.3. The pearly flow category
To compare Floer homology and Morse homology, we introduce a version of the pearly flow category. A priori, this flow category induces a chain complex which is not quasi-isomorphic to the Morse chain complex, as least not in the most naive way.
Let (X,ω,J)(X,\omega,J) be a compact almost Kähler manifold. For each a∈Πa\in\Pi, consider the moduli space
ℳ(a)ℝ0,2{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}^{\mathbb{R}}(a)
which is a variant of the moduli space ℳ(a)0,2{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}(a) of JJ-holomorphic maps with two marked points in degree dd. It is defined to be the moduli space of unparametrized Floer trajectories for the Hamiltonian H≡0H\equiv 0. By singularity removal, ℳ(a)ℝ0,2{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}^{\mathbb{R}}(a) can be alternatively described as the moduli space of JJ-holomorphic spheres of class aa with 22 marked points such that the 22 marked points are equipped with asymptotic markers with the same angular coordinate.
There is a natural compactification
ℳ¯(a)ℝ0,2\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}^{\mathbb{R}}(a)
which is naturally stratified by (ordered) decompositions a=a1+⋯+aka=a_{1}+\cdots+a_{k} with ω⁡(ai)>0\omega(a_{i})>0. The strata of the above moduli space ℳ¯(a)ℝ0,2\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}^{\mathbb{R}}(a) can be labelled by the so-called linear trees. These are oriented trees whose vertices have valence at most 2, hence have a unique incoming vertex (the input) and a unique outgoing vertex (the output). The degrees a1,…,ak∈Πa_{1},\ldots,a_{k}\in\Pi are viewed as extra decorations on the vertices. We then can allow the edges of the tree to acquire length, allowing the lengths to vary, and allowing the edges to break when the lengths approach infinity. Choose a Morse–Smale pair (f,g)(f,g) on XX. We then add additional variables which are negative gradient segments of (f,g)(f,g) defined on the edges of varying length. For the input sphere resp. output sphere we also add a semi-infinite edge on which is supported a negative gradient ray. The natural matching conditions at nodes are required. By choosing an incoming resp. outgoing critical point x¯\underline{\smash{x}} resp. y¯\underline{\smash{y}} of ff, one can consider the pearly moduli space and its compactification
ℳ¯(a)ℙx¯​y¯.\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{\underline{\smash{x}}\underline{\smash{y}}}^{\mathbb{P}}(a).
The underlying poset is not as simple as the Morse or Floer case. For x=(x¯,a)x=(\underline{\smash{x}},a) and y=(x¯,b)y=(\underline{\smash{x}},b) in crit​f×Π{\rm crit}f\times\Pi, define Ax​yℙA_{xy}^{\mathbb{P}} to be the set of (possibly broken) linear trees whose breakings are labelled by critical points of ff, whose vertices are labelled by elements of Π\Pi (with sum being a−ba-b), and whose finite edges have either zero or positive lengths. This is a regular poset, whose maximal elements are those unbroken trees whose edges all have positive length. The depth function is given by the number of breakings plus the number of edges with length zero.
Definition 9.2.
The pearly flow category ℙ\mathbb{P} associated to X,J,f,gX,J,f,g as above, is the flow category enriched in 𝐓𝐨𝐩¯\underline{\smash{\bf Top}} which is defined as follows.
(1)
The set of objects is Ob​ℙ=crit​f×Π{\rm Ob}\mathbb{P}={\rm crit}f\times\Pi.
(2)
For any pair of objects x=(x¯,a)x=(\underline{\smash{x}},a) and y=(y¯,b)y=(\underline{\smash{y}},b), the morphism space is the moduli space
ℳ¯(a−b)ℙx¯​y¯.\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{\underline{\smash{x}}\underline{\smash{y}}}^{\mathbb{P}}(a-b).
(3)
The composition map is given by the concatenation of pearly solutions.
Remark 9.3.
The pearly flow category ℙ\mathbb{P} should be distinguished from the pearly bimodule introduced in [14, Section 4.4], which is a flow bimodule between Morse flow categories. ℙ\mathbb{P} here is used to set up the Morse–Bott homology of the constant Hamiltonian H≡0H\equiv 0.
9.4. Coupling of geometric flow categories
Given symplectic manifolds (Xj,ωj)(X^{j},\omega^{j}), j=1,…,kj=1,\ldots,k and Floer flow categories 𝔽j\mathbb{F}^{j} associated to pairs (Hj,Jj)(H^{j},J^{j}), their coupling is defined to be the Floer flow category of the product manifold with the product Hamiltonians and almost complex structure. However, it is difficult to describe this construction on the abstract level for a collection of flow categories. The more abstract packaging would require building a symmetric monoidal structure on the (infinity) category of flow categories, cf. [2] and its follow-up work. Here we describe certain “coupling” that arises geometrically.
Running Assumption. Let 𝔽j\mathbb{F}^{j}, j=1,…,kj=1,\ldots,k be a collection of flow categories. Each of them is either a Floer, Morse, or pearly flow category on a compact (symplectic) manifold.
We define their coupling, denoted as
𝔽:=𝔽1∗⋯∗𝔽k,{\mathbb{F}}:={\mathbb{F}}^{1}\ast\cdots\ast{\mathbb{F}}^{k},
as follows. Its set of objects is
Ob𝔽=Ob𝔽1×⋯×Ob𝔽k{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}={\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}^{1}\times\cdots\times{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}^{k}
whose elements are written as 𝐩=(p1,…,pk){\bf p}=(p^{1},\ldots,p^{k}). The morphism space M𝐩𝐪M_{{\bf p}{\bf q}} is the moduli space of solutions 𝐮=(u1,…,uk){\bf u}=(u^{1},\ldots,u^{k}) where uju^{j} is a (stable) Floer/Morse/pearly trajectory connecting pjp^{j} and qjq^{j}, depending on the geometric origin of 𝔽j\mathbb{F}^{j}. We take the quotient by the “synchronized” ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-action, i.e., for any s∈ℝs\in{\mathbb{R}}, we identify tuples of parametrized trajectories
(u1(⋅),…,uk(⋅))∼(u1(⋅+s),…,uk(⋅+s)),(u^{1}(\cdot),\dots,u^{k}(\cdot))\sim(u^{1}(\cdot+s),\dots,u^{k}(\cdot+s)),
and compactify by allowing sphere bubbling and breaking of trajectories. Notice that this formulation means that breakings in each factor happen simultaneously. For example, when all 𝔽j{\mathbb{F}}^{j} are Floer flow categories, this coupling is the same as the Floer flow category of the product manifold with respect to the product Hamiltonian and product almost complex structure. Notice that if 𝔽j{\mathbb{F}}^{j} is equivariant with respect to an abelian group Πj\Pi^{j}, then 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} is equivariant with respect to the natural action by the product Π=Π1×⋯×Πk\Pi=\Pi^{1}\times\cdots\times\Pi^{k}.
In the discussion of equivariant Floer theory, one often needs to take self-coupling. For any kk, denote
𝔽∗k:=𝔽∗⋯∗𝔽⏟k,{\mathbb{F}}^{\ast k}:=\underbrace{{\mathbb{F}}\ast\cdots\ast{\mathbb{F}}}_{k},
which is equivariant with respect to the action by the product Π×⋯×Π\Pi\times\cdots\times\Pi of kk copies of Π\Pi. On the other hand, ℤk{\mathbb{Z}}_{k} acts on this flow category by cyclically permuting the factors. This ℤk{\mathbb{Z}}_{k}-action commutes with the action by the diagonal Π\Pi. Hence this coupled flow category is equivariant with respect to an action by Π×ℤk\Pi\times{\mathbb{Z}}_{k}.
10. Geometric Multimodules
Next, we describe bimodules and multimodules that lead to continuation maps, PSS and SSP maps, pair-of-pants products, and Künneth maps.
10.1. Floer data and Floer domains
Definition 10.1.
A punctured surface is a compact oriented surface (not necessarily connected) with finitely many points removed, usually denoted by Σ\Sigma. We also include as part of data a decomposition of the punctures into negative ends and positive ends. The negative ends are usually denoted by z−1,…,z−k−z_{-}^{1},\ldots,z_{-}^{k_{-}}, and the positive ends are usually denoted by z+1,…,z+k+z_{+}^{1},\ldots,z_{+}^{k_{+}}.
A cylindrical end on a punctured surface Σ\Sigma around a negative resp. positive puncture z±jz_{\pm}^{j} is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism between ℝ±×S1{\mathbb{R}}^{\pm}\times S^{1} and a punctured neighborhood of z±jz_{\pm}^{j}; two cylindrical ends are regarded as equivalent if they differ by a translation. An equivalence class is called a germ of cylindrical ends.
A cylindrical surface is a punctured surface equipped with germs of cylindrical ends around all punctures. To save notations such an object is still denoted by Σ\Sigma.
Definition 10.2.
Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a symplectic manifold. A Floer datum over a cylindrical surface Σ\Sigma, denoted by σ=(j,J,α)\sigma=(j,J,\alpha), consists of a complex structure jj on Σ\Sigma, a smooth family JzJ_{z} of ω\omega-compatible almost complex structures on XX, and a smooth 1-form (called the Hamiltonian connection)
α∈Γ⁡(X×Σ,T∗​Σ)\alpha\in\Gamma(X\times\Sigma,T^{*}\Sigma)
such that
(1)
For any cylindrical end φ±j:ℝ±×St1→Σ\varphi_{\pm}^{j}:{\mathbb{R}}^{\pm}\times S^{1}_{t}\to\Sigma at z±jz_{\pm}^{j}, it is holomorphic with respect to jj near infinity where ℝ±×S1{\mathbb{R}}^{\pm}\times S^{1} is equipped with the standard complex structure.
(2)
Near the infinity of the cylindrical end around z±jz_{\pm}^{j}, we have (φ±j)∗​α=H±j​d​t(\varphi_{\pm}^{j})^{*}\alpha=H_{\pm}^{j}dt where H±jH_{\pm}^{j} is either a nondegenerate 1-periodic Hamiltonian or zero. In the former resp. latter case we say this end is of Floer type resp. Morse type.
(3)
Near the infinity of the cylindrical end around z±jz_{\pm}^{j}, the almost complex structure JzJ_{z} coincides with a fixed almost complex structure J±jJ_{\pm}^{j} on XX.
A cylindrical surface Σ\Sigma equipped with a Floer datum σ\sigma is called a Floer domain, which we still denote by Σ\Sigma for brevity.
Given a Floer domain (Σ,σ=(j,J,α))(\Sigma,\sigma=(j,J,\alpha)) and a smooth map u:Σ→Xu:\Sigma\to X, one can take the form
∂¯σ​u:=(d​u+Xσ​(u))0,1∈Ω0,1​(Σ,u∗​T​X)\overline{\partial}_{\sigma}u:=(du+X_{\sigma}(u))^{0,1}\in\Omega^{0,1}(\Sigma,u^{*}TX)
where XσX_{\sigma} is defined via
ω⁡(Xσ,−)=dX​α,\omega(X_{\sigma},-)=d_{X}\alpha,
where dXd_{X} is the differentiation along the XX direction, and (⋅)0,1(\cdot)^{0,1} is the projection onto the (0,1)(0,1)-part determined by the domain complex structure jj and the target almost complex structure JJ.
10.2. Multimodules from smooth domains
Now we can define a particular kind of multimodules coming from Floer domains. Let Σ\Sigma be a connected Floer domain with mm negative ends and nn positive ends such that all cylindrical ends are of Floer type (see Definition 10.2), with limiting Hamiltonians H1,…,HmH_{1},\ldots,H_{m} on the mm negative ends and H1′,…,Hn′H_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,H_{n}^{\prime} on the positive ends. Let J1,…,JmJ_{1},\ldots,J_{m} be the limiting almost complex structures on the negative ends and J1′,…,Jn′J_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,J_{n}^{\prime} be the limiting almost complex structures on the positive ends. Let 𝔽1,…,𝔽m{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m} resp. 𝔽1′,…,𝔽n′{\mathbb{F}}_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{n}^{\prime} be Floer flow category associated to (H1,J1),…,(Hm,Jm)(H_{1},J_{1}),\ldots,(H_{m},J_{m}) resp. (H1′,J1′),…,(Hn′,Jn′)(H_{1}^{\prime},J_{1}^{\prime}),\ldots,(H_{n}^{\prime},J_{n}^{\prime}). Then the Floer domain Σ\Sigma defines a multimodule 𝕏Σ{\mathbb{X}}^{\Sigma} over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽1′,…,𝔽n′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{n}^{\prime}). More precisely, given any tuple 𝔭=(p1,…,pm){\mathfrak{p}}=(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m}) of objects of 𝔽1,…,𝔽m{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m} and 𝔭′=(p1′,…,pn′){\mathfrak{p}}^{\prime}=(p_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,p_{n}^{\prime}) of objects of 𝔽1′,…,𝔽n′{\mathbb{F}}_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{n}^{\prime}, consider the space of solutions to
u:Σ→X,∂¯σ​u=0u:\Sigma\to X,\ \overline{\partial}_{\sigma}u=0
which are asymptotic to pip_{i} near the ii-th negative end and to pj′p_{j}^{\prime} near the jj-th positive end. We compactify this space by allowing sphere bubbles and Floer trajectory breakings, and denote the compactified space by
M𝔭;𝔭′𝕏Σ.M_{{\mathfrak{p}};{\mathfrak{p}}^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}^{\Sigma}}.
Then there are natural structural maps
Mpi​qi𝔽i×Mp1⋯pi−1qipi+1⋯pm;𝔭′𝕏Σ→M𝔭;𝔭′𝕏ΣM_{p_{i}q_{i}}^{{\mathbb{F}}_{i}}\times M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1}q_{i}p_{i+1}\cdots p_{m};{\mathfrak{p}}^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}^{\Sigma}}\to M_{{\mathfrak{p}};{\mathfrak{p}}^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}^{\Sigma}}
and
M𝔭;p1′⋯pj−1′qj′pj+1′⋯pn′𝕏Σ×Mqj′​pj′𝔽j′→M𝔭;𝔭′𝕏Σ.M_{{\mathfrak{p}};p_{1}^{\prime}\cdots p_{j-1}^{\prime}q_{j}^{\prime}p_{j+1}^{\prime}\cdots p_{n}^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}^{\Sigma}}\times M_{q_{j}^{\prime}p_{j}^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{F}}_{j}^{\prime}}\to M_{{\mathfrak{p}};{\mathfrak{p}}^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}^{\Sigma}}.
It is straightforward to see that the collection of moduli spaces M𝔭;𝔭′𝕏ΣM_{{\mathfrak{p}};{\mathfrak{p}}^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}^{\Sigma}} and the above maps satisfy the requirement for a multimodule over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽1′,…,𝔽n′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{n}^{\prime}). Moreover, both 𝔽i{\mathbb{F}}_{i} and 𝔽j′{\mathbb{F}}_{j}^{\prime} have a free Π\Pi-action, hence ∏𝔽i\prod{\mathbb{F}}_{i} resp. ∏𝔽j′\prod{\mathbb{F}}_{j}^{\prime} has a free action by Πm\Pi^{m} resp. Πn\Pi^{n}. Then it is easy to see that the multimodule 𝕏Σ{\mathbb{X}}^{\Sigma} is equivariant with respect to the diagonal embeddings Π→Πm\Pi\to\Pi^{m} and Π→Πn\Pi\to\Pi^{n}. We summarize the properties of this multimodule.
Situation Module(i).
(X,ω)(X,\omega) is a compact symplectic manifold. 𝔽1,…,𝔽m;𝔽′{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} 1616
16
Here mm is allowed to be 00, the situation of the cigar bimodule described in Subsubsection 10.3.6. are Floer flow categories associated to pairs (H1,J1),…,(Hm,Jm);(H′,J′)(H_{1},J_{1}),\ldots,(H_{m},J_{m});(H^{\prime},J^{\prime}). 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} is the multimodule over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}) associated to a smooth Floer domain Σ𝕏\Sigma^{\mathbb{X}} with mm negative cylindrical ends and one positive cylindrical end. Moreover, the Floer datum on Σ𝕏\Sigma^{\mathbb{X}} coincides with (Hj​d​t,Jj)(H_{j}dt,J_{j}) on the jj-th negative end and (H′​d​t,J′)(H^{\prime}dt,J^{\prime}) on the positive end.
Proposition 10.3.
In Situation Module(i), the multimodule 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} is a Π\Pi-equivariant Novikov multimodule over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}).
We give examples of a few concrete cases which appear naturally in applications.
10.2.1. Bimodules for continuation maps
The first one is the bimodule coming from the continuation map construction. Given Floer flow categories 𝔽±\mathbb{F}^{\pm} associated to a pair (H±,J±)(H_{\pm},J_{\pm}) on the same symplectic manifold (X,ω)(X,\omega), a homotopy of the Floer data
(j0,Hsdt,Js,t),lims→±∞Hs=H±,lims→±Js,t=J±(j_{0},H_{s}dt,J_{s,t}),\quad\quad\quad\lim_{s\to\pm\infty}H_{s}=H_{\pm},\ \lim_{s\to\pm}J_{s,t}=J_{\pm}
over the infinite cylinder, where j0j_{0} is the standard complex structure on ℝ×S1\mathbb{R}\times S^{1}, is a special case of Floer data over an arbitrary punctured sphere. Hence one obtains an (𝔽−,𝔽+)({\mathbb{F}}^{-},{\mathbb{F}}^{+})-module, usually called the bimodule of continuation maps.
There is a special one corresponding to the constant Floer datum on the infinite cylinder.
Definition 10.4.
The diagonal bimodule of a Floer flow category 𝔽\mathbb{F} associated to (H,J)(H,J) is the bimodule for continuation maps associated to the ss-independent Floer data (j0,H​d​t,J)(j_{0},Hdt,J) on the infinite cylinder. It is denoted by Δ𝔽​𝔽\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}}.
10.2.2. Poincaré duality multimodule
Consider a surface ΣPD\Sigma^{\rm PD} with two negative cylindrical ends and no positive ends. Let σPD\sigma^{\rm PD} be a Floer datum on ΣPD\Sigma^{\rm PD} which converges to H1​d​tH_{1}dt and H2​d​tH_{2}dt on the two negative ends. Let 𝔽1{\mathbb{F}}_{1} and 𝔽2{\mathbb{F}}_{2} be the Hamiltonian Floer flow categories associated to H1H_{1} and H2H_{2}. On the other hand, consider the trivial flow category 𝕆{\mathbb{O}} whose objects are elements of Π\Pi and the only morphisms are identities. Then we describe a multimodule 𝕏PD{\mathbb{X}}^{\rm PD} over (𝔽1,𝔽2,𝕆)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},{\mathbb{F}}_{2};{\mathbb{O}}). Given objects p1∈Ob​𝔽1p_{1}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{1}, p2∈Ob​𝔽2p_{2}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{2}, and a∈Π≅Ob​𝕆a\in\Pi\cong{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{O}}, consider the moduli spaces of maps u:ΣPD→Xu:\Sigma^{\rm PD}\to X solving ∂¯σPD​u=0\overline{\partial}_{\sigma^{\rm PD}}u=0 which converges to the (uncapped) orbits p¯1\underline{\smash{p}}_{1} and p¯2\underline{\smash{p}}_{2} at the two negative ends; moreover, the spherical class obtained by adding the cappings has symplectic area a∈Πa\in\Pi. We compactify the space by allowing sphere bubbles as well as Floer breakings at the two negative ends, and denote the compactified space by
Mp1​p2;a𝕏PD.M_{p_{1}p_{2};a}^{{\mathbb{X}}^{\rm PD}}.
Then there are natural maps
Mp1​q1𝔽1×Mq1​p2;a𝕏PD→Mp1​p2;a𝕏PDM_{p_{1}q_{1}}^{{\mathbb{F}}_{1}}\times M_{q_{1}p_{2};a}^{{\mathbb{X}}^{\rm PD}}\to M_{p_{1}p_{2};a}^{{\mathbb{X}}^{\rm PD}}
and
Mp2​q2𝔽2×Mp1​q2;a𝕏PD→Mp1​p2;a𝕏PDM_{p_{2}q_{2}}^{{\mathbb{F}}_{2}}\times M_{p_{1}q_{2};a}^{\mathbb{X}^{\rm PD}}\to M_{p_{1}p_{2};a}^{{\mathbb{X}}^{\rm PD}}
making it a multimodule over (𝔽1,𝔽2,𝕆)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},{\mathbb{F}}_{2};{\mathbb{O}}). We call it a Poincaré duality multimodule.
10.3. PSS type bimodules
In order to establish the relation between the Floer homology and the integral homology of the symplectic manifold, one typically considers the PSS (Piunikhin–Salamon–Schwarz [55]) maps. In the current situation, we need to consider a few similar constructions. In terms of the formal terms, we describe bimodules among the three flow categories: Floer, Morse, and Pearly flow categories.
10.3.1. Deformed Morse-to-Morse bimodule
Let (f,g)(f,g) be a Morse–Smale pair on the almost Kähler manifold (X,ω,J)(X,\omega,J). Let 𝕄¯\underline{\smash{\mathbb{M}}} be the Morse flow category associated to (f,g)(f,g) whose objects are critical points of ff. Let 𝕄{\mathbb{M}} be the trivial product of 𝕄¯\underline{\smash{\mathbb{M}}} with Π\Pi. Instead of the identity bimodule from 𝕄{\mathbb{M}} to itself, we consider a bimodule involving holomorphic spheres. Indeed, for each a∈Πa\in\Pi, consider the space of JJ-holomorphic maps u:S2→Xu:S^{2}\to X representing the class aa with two fixed marked points z−,z+z_{-},z_{+}. Denote its Gromov compactification by ℳ¯(X,J,a)parametrized0,2\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}^{\rm parametrized}(X,J,a), consisting of genus zero stable JJ-holomorphic spheres with two marked points with energy aa with a rigid component. Let the two markings be z−z_{-} and z+z_{+}. There are two evaluation maps
ev±:ℳ¯(X,J,a)parametrized0,2→X.{\rm ev}_{\pm}:\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}^{\rm parametrized}(X,J,a)\to X.
Then for each pair of ojects x=(ax,x¯),y=(by,y¯)∈Ob​𝕄x=(a_{x},\underline{\smash{x}}),y=(b_{y},\underline{\smash{y}})\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{M}}, define
Mx;y𝕄​𝕄:=ev−−1(Wx¯us¯)∩ev+−1(Wy¯st¯)∩ℳ¯(X,J,ax−by)parametrized0,2.M_{x;y}^{\mathbb{MM}}:={\rm ev}_{-}^{-1}(\overline{W_{\underline{\smash{x}}}^{\rm us}})\cap{\rm ev}_{+}^{-1}(\overline{W_{\underline{\smash{y}}}^{\rm st}})\cap\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}^{\rm parametrized}(X,J,a_{x}-b_{y}).
There are obvious structural maps coming from breaking of Morse trajectories:
Mx​z𝕄×Mz;y𝕄​𝕄→Mx;y𝕄​𝕄,\displaystyle\ M_{xz}^{\mathbb{M}}\times M_{z;y}^{\mathbb{MM}}\to M_{x;y}^{\mathbb{MM}},\
Mx;w𝕄​𝕄×Mw​y𝕄→Mx;y𝕄​𝕄\displaystyle\ M_{x;w}^{\mathbb{MM}}\times M_{wy}^{\mathbb{M}}\to M_{x;y}^{\mathbb{MM}}
forming a bimodule over (𝕄,𝕄)({\mathbb{M}},{\mathbb{M}}). We call it the deformed Morse-to-Morse bimodule, denoted by Δ𝕄​𝕄\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{MM}}.
10.3.2. Floer-to-Morse and Morse-to-Floer bimodules
We describe two bimodules relating the Morse flow category 𝕄{\mathbb{M}} and the Floer flow category 𝔽{\mathbb{F}}, which will be denoted by 𝔹𝕄​𝔽{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{MF}} and 𝔹𝔽​𝕄\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{FM}}. Fix a compact almost complex manifold (X,ω,J)(X,\omega,J). Let 𝕄¯\underline{\smash{\mathbb{M}}} be the Morse flow category associated to a Morse–Smale pair (f,g)(f,g) on XX whose objects are critical points of ff. Let 𝕄{\mathbb{M}} be the trivial product of 𝕄¯\underline{\smash{\mathbb{M}}} with Π\Pi. Let 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} be the Floer flow category associated to a nondegenerate Hamiltonian HH.
Let Σ𝕄​𝔽\Sigma^{\mathbb{MF}} be ℂ{\mathbb{C}} with ∞\infty viewed as a positive end with canonical cylindrical coordinates. Choose a Hamiltonian connection σ𝕄​𝔽\sigma^{\mathbb{MF}} which is equal to H​d​tHdt near ∞\infty and which is zero near 00. Then for each object p∈Ob​𝔽p\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}, one can consider the equation
u:Σ𝕄​𝔽→X,∂¯σ𝕄​𝔽​u=0,u:\Sigma^{\mathbb{MF}}\to X,\ \overline{\partial}_{\sigma^{\mathbb{MF}}}u=0,
such that uu is asymptotic to the 1-periodic orbit underlying pp and the map uu represents the capped orbit pp. Compactify this space by allowing sphere bubblings and Floer trajectory breakings on the positive ends. Denote the compactified moduli space by ℳ¯p𝕄​𝔽\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{p}^{\mathbb{MF}}. There is an evaluation map
ev0:ℳ¯p𝕄​𝔽→X{\rm ev}_{0}:\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{p}^{\mathbb{MF}}\to X
at the point 0∈Σ𝕄​𝔽0\in\Sigma^{\mathbb{MF}}. Then for each pair of objects x∈Ob​𝕄x\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{M}}, p∈Ob​𝔽p\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}, if x=(ax,x¯)x=(a_{x},\underline{\smash{x}}) where ax∈Πa_{x}\in\Pi and x¯∈crit​f\underline{\smash{x}}\in{\rm crit}f, then define
Mx;p𝕄​𝔽:=ev0−1(Wx¯us¯)∩ℳ¯.𝕄​𝔽(−ax)⋅pM_{x;p}^{\mathbb{MF}}:={\rm ev}_{0}^{-1}(\overline{W_{\underline{\smash{x}}}^{\rm us}})\cap\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{(-a_{x})\cdot p}^{\mathbb{MF}}.
Here Wx¯usW_{\underline{\smash{x}}}^{\rm us} is the unstable manifold of x¯\underline{\smash{x}} and Wx¯us¯\overline{W_{\underline{\smash{x}}}^{\rm us}} is its compactification. Then there are natural structural maps
Mx​y𝕄×My;p𝕄​𝔽→Mx;p𝕄​𝔽,\displaystyle\ M_{xy}^{\mathbb{M}}\times M_{y;p}^{\mathbb{MF}}\to M_{x;p}^{\mathbb{MF}},\
Mx;q𝕄​𝔽×Mq​p𝔽→Mx;p𝕄​𝔽\displaystyle\ M_{x;q}^{\mathbb{MF}}\times M_{qp}^{\mathbb{F}}\to M_{x;p}^{\mathbb{MF}}
defining a bimodule 𝔹𝕄​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{MF}} over (𝕄;𝔽)({\mathbb{M}};{\mathbb{F}}).
Similarly, if we let Σ𝔽​𝕄\Sigma^{\mathbb{FM}} be ℂ{\mathbb{C}} with ∞\infty viewed as a negative end and if we choose a Hamiltonian connection σ𝔽​𝕄\sigma^{\mathbb{FM}} on this domain which is equal to H​d​tHdt on the cylindrical end, then we can define moduli spaces Mp;x𝔽​𝕄M_{p;x}^{\mathbb{FM}} similarly, giving a bimodule 𝔹𝔽​𝕄{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{FM}} over (𝔽;𝕄)({\mathbb{F}};{\mathbb{M}}).
10.3.3. The Pearly-to-Floer and Floer-to-Pearly bimodules
Suppose we have fixed data for the Pearly flow category ℙ{\mathbb{P}} and the Floer flow category on the almost Kähler manifold (X,ω,J)(X,\omega,J). In particular, one has a Morse–Smale pair (f,g)(f,g). Then for the moduli space of solutions to
∂¯σ𝕄​𝔽​u=0,u:Σ𝕄​𝔽→X\overline{\partial}_{\sigma^{\mathbb{MF}}}u=0,\ u:\Sigma^{\mathbb{MF}}\to X
we can take the “pearly compactification” in the same way as defining the pearly flow category. Indeed, we treat 0∈Σ𝕄​𝔽0\in\Sigma^{\mathbb{MF}} as a special marked point around which there is the standard cylindrical coordinates (s,t)(s,t). When compactifying the moduli space, sphere bubbles at 00 are taken only modulo translation in ss. Then one can insert gradient segments to obtain the corresponding pearly compactification. For each pair of objects x∈Ob​ℙ=Ob​𝔽x\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{P}}={\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}, p∈Ob​𝔽p\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}, there is the moduli space Mx;pℙ​𝔽M_{x;p}^{\mathbb{PF}} together with structural maps
Mx​yℙ×My;pℙ​𝔽→Mx;pℙ​𝔽,\displaystyle\ M_{xy}^{\mathbb{P}}\times M_{y;p}^{\mathbb{PF}}\to M_{x;p}^{\mathbb{PF}},\
Mx;qℙ​𝔽×Mq​p𝔽→Mx;pℙ​𝔽\displaystyle\ M_{x;q}^{\mathbb{PF}}\times M_{qp}^{\mathbb{F}}\to M_{x;p}^{\mathbb{PF}}
giving a bimodule 𝔹ℙ​𝔽{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{PF}} over (ℙ,𝔽)({\mathbb{P}},{\mathbb{F}}). Similarly, one also has the Floer-to-Pearly bimodule 𝔹𝔽​ℙ{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{FP}}.
10.3.4. Morse-to-Pearly and Pearly-to-Morse bimodules
We describe a bimodule 𝔹ℙ​𝕄\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{PM}} over (ℙ,𝕄)({\mathbb{P}},{\mathbb{M}}) and a bimodule 𝔹𝕄​ℙ{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{MP}} over (𝕄,ℙ)({\mathbb{M}},{\mathbb{P}}). For simplicity, we assume 𝕄{\mathbb{M}} and ℙ{\mathbb{P}} share the same Morse–Smale pair, though we can certainly take different ones.
Given a pair of objects x=(ax,x¯)∈Ob​ℙx=(a_{x},\underline{\smash{x}})\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{P}} and y=(by,y¯)∈Ob​𝕄y=(b_{y},\underline{\smash{y}})\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{M}}, consider the moduli space of JJ-holomorphic maps u:ℝ×S1u:{\mathbb{R}}\times S^{1} of symplectic area ax−by∈Πa_{x}-b_{y}\in\Pi such that
u⁡(−∞)∈Wx¯us,u⁡(+∞)∈Wy¯st.u(-\infty)\in W_{\underline{\smash{x}}}^{\rm us},\ u(+\infty)\in W_{\underline{\smash{y}}}^{\rm st}.
When compactifying these moduli spaces, the bubbling at negative ends are taken modulo only the translation in ℝ{\mathbb{R}} while bubbling at positive ends are taken modulo both translation and rotations; moreover, we also insert gradient segments at nodes connecting −∞-\infty and the principal component. In this way, one obtains a compact stratified space
Mx;yℙ​𝕄M_{x;y}^{\mathbb{PM}}
with structural maps
Mx​wℙ×Mw;yℙ​𝕄→Mx;yℙ​𝕄,\displaystyle\ M_{xw}^{\mathbb{P}}\times M_{w;y}^{\mathbb{PM}}\to M_{x;y}^{\mathbb{PM}},\
Mx;wℙ​𝕄×Mw​y𝕄→Mx;yℙ​𝕄\displaystyle\ M_{x;w}^{\mathbb{PM}}\times M_{wy}^{\mathbb{M}}\to M_{x;y}^{\mathbb{PM}}
giving a bimodule 𝔹ℙ​𝕄{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{PM}} over (ℙ,𝕄)({\mathbb{P}},{\mathbb{M}}). Similarly one has a bimodule 𝔹𝕄​ℙ{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{MP}} over (𝕄,ℙ)({\mathbb{M}},{\mathbb{P}}) by taking “half pearly” compactifications at the positive end instead of the negative one.
10.3.5. Pearly-to-Pearly bimodule
We describe a bimodule Δℙ​ℙ\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{PP}} over (ℙ,ℙ)(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{P}) where ℙ\mathbb{P} is associated to a Morse–Smale pair (f,g)(f,g) on (X,ω,J)(X,\omega,J). Given a pair of critical points x¯,y¯∈crit​f\underline{\smash{x}},\underline{\smash{y}}\in{\rm crit}f and a∈Πa\in\Pi, consider the space of JJ-holomorphic maps u:ℝ×S1→Xu:{\mathbb{R}}\times S^{1}\to X with symplectic area aa such that u⁡(−∞)∈Wx¯usu(-\infty)\in W_{\underline{\smash{x}}}^{\rm us} and u⁡(+∞)∈Wy¯stu(+\infty)\in W_{\underline{\smash{y}}}^{\rm st}. We take the “pearly compactification,” namely, when sphere bubbles at ±∞\pm\infty, the bubbles are taken modulo only the ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-translation. Moreover, we insert (possibly broken) gradient segments at nodes connecting the distinguished marked points ±∞\pm\infty. Denote the compactified moduli space by
ℳ¯(X,J,a)ℙ​ℙx¯;y¯.\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{\underline{\smash{x}};\underline{\smash{y}}}^{\mathbb{PP}}(X,J,a).
A typical configuration of this moduli space is shown in Figure 3.
Figure 3. Configurations in Δℙ​ℙ\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{PP}}.
Then for each pair of objects x=(x¯,ax),y=(y¯,ay)x=(\underline{\smash{x}},a_{x}),y=(\underline{\smash{y}},a_{y}) of ℙ\mathbb{P}, define
Mx;yℙ​ℙ:=ℳ¯x¯​y¯ℙ​ℙ​(X,J,ax−ay).M_{x;y}^{\mathbb{PP}}:=\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{\underline{\smash{x}}\underline{\smash{y}}}^{\mathbb{PP}}(X,J,a_{x}-a_{y}).
Then there are natural maps
Mx​x′ℙ×Mx′;yℙ​ℙ→Mx;yℙ​ℙ,\displaystyle\ M_{xx^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{P}}\times M_{x^{\prime};y}^{\mathbb{PP}}\to M_{x;y}^{\mathbb{PP}},\
Mx;y′ℙ​ℙ×My′​yℙ→Mx;yℙ​ℙ\displaystyle\ M_{x;y^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{PP}}\times M_{y^{\prime}y}^{\mathbb{P}}\to M_{x;y}^{\mathbb{PP}}
defining the structural maps of a bimodule over (ℙ,ℙ)(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{P}). We call this bimoulde the Pearly-to-Pearly bimodule, denoted by Δℙ​ℙ\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{PP}}. Notice that there is a “classical part” which corresponds to the diagonal bimodule of the Morse flow category.
10.3.6. Cigar module
To construct a multiplicative identity of the Floer homology, we consider an analogue of the PSS moduli space where we do not have interior markings or Morse trajectories. Let Σcigar≅ℂ\Sigma^{\rm cigar}\cong{\mathbb{C}} be the open Riemann surface with a cylindrical end. Let 𝔽\mathbb{F} be the Floer flow category on (X,ω,J)(X,\omega,J) associated to a nondegenerate Hamiltonian HH. On the other hand, let 𝕆{\mathbb{O}} be the “trivial” flow category consisting of a single object o∈Ob​𝕆o\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{O}} with self-morphism space being a single point.
Choose a Floer datum on Σcigar\Sigma^{\rm cigar} which coincides with HH near the infinity. Let 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} be the Floer flow category associated to HH. The cigar module is a bimodule 𝔹cigar{\mathbb{B}}^{\rm cigar} over (𝕆,𝔽)({\mathbb{O}},{\mathbb{F}}) whose morphism spaces consist of solutions to the Floer equation on Σ\Sigma. More precisely, for each object p∈Ob​𝔽p\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}, consider the space of solutions to
u:Σcigar→X,∂¯σcigar​u=0u:\Sigma^{\rm cigar}\to X,\ \overline{\partial}_{\sigma^{\rm cigar}}u=0
such that uu converges to the 1-periodic orbit p¯\underline{\smash{p}} underlying pp and such that uu represents the capped orbit pp. Moreover, compactify this moduli space by allowing sphere bubbling and Floer trajectory breakings. Let the compactified space be Mo;pcigarM_{o;p}^{\rm cigar}. Then there are structural maps
Mo;qcigar×Mq​p𝔽→Mo;pcigar,M_{o;q}^{\rm cigar}\times M_{qp}^{\mathbb{F}}\to M_{o;p}^{\rm cigar},
making a bimodule over (𝕆;𝔽)({\mathbb{O}};{\mathbb{F}}).
10.4. Concatenations
We describe the situation corresponding to concatenating Floer data on different domains.
Situation Concatenation(i).
(X,ω)(X,\omega) is a compact symplectic manifold. 𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔾1,…,𝔾n,𝔾′{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m},{\mathbb{G}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{G}}_{n},{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime} are Floer flow categories associated to pairs (H1,J1),…,(Hm,Jm),(G1,I1),…,(Gn,In),(G′,I′)(H_{1},J_{1}),\ldots,(H_{m},J_{m}),(G_{1},I_{1}),\ldots,(G_{n},I_{n}),(G^{\prime},I^{\prime}) respectively. 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} resp. 𝕐{\mathbb{Y}} is a multimodule over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔾i)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{G}}_{i}) resp. over (𝔾1,…,𝔾n,𝔾′)({\mathbb{G}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{G}}_{n};{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}) associated to smooth Floer domain Σ𝕏\Sigma^{\mathbb{X}} resp. Σ𝕐\Sigma^{\mathbb{Y}} as described in Situation Module(i).
Proposition 10.5.
In Situation Concatenation(i), the concatenation 𝕏∘i𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}} is a Π\Pi-equivariant Novikov multimodule over (𝔾1,…,𝔾i−1,𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔾i+1,…,𝔾n,𝔾′)({\mathbb{G}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{G}}_{i-1},{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m},{\mathbb{G}}_{i+1},\ldots,{\mathbb{G}}_{n};{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}).
Proof.
Straightforward.
∎
11. Homotopies of Multimodules
In this section we descibe several geometrically defined bimodule homotopies. As we only use bimodule homotopies to show certain chain maps are canonically defined up to homotopy, we will not provide the most general treatment. Hence, we only give a minimal descriptions of bimodules which will be used in this paper.
11.1. Homotopies from varying Floer data
Recall the notions of Floer data and Floer domains (Definition 10.2).
Definition 11.1.
A smooth 1-parameter family of Floer domain consists of the following objects.
(1)
A smooth genus zero surface Σ\Sigma.
(2)
A smooth 1-parameter family of domain complex structures jτj_{\tau}, τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1], such that there exists an open and precompact region Σ0⊆Σ\Sigma_{0}\subseteq\Sigma and diffeomorphisms
ϕi±:ℝ±×S1→Ui±⊆Σ∖Σ0,i=1,…,l±,\phi_{i}^{\pm}:{\mathbb{R}}_{\pm}\times S^{1}\to U_{i}^{\pm}\subseteq\Sigma\setminus\Sigma_{0},\ i=1,\ldots,l_{\pm},
where Ui±U_{i}^{\pm} are all open subsets of Σ∖Σ0\Sigma\setminus\Sigma_{0}, such that ϕi±\phi_{i}^{\pm} is biholomorphic with respect to all jτ|Ui±j_{\tau}|_{U_{i}^{\pm}}. Each Ui±U_{i}^{\pm} is called a positive/negative cylindrical end. Two cylindrical ends are germ-equivalent if they differ by a translation.
(3)
A smooth 1-parameter family of Hamiltonian connections στ\sigma_{\tau} on Σ\Sigma such that on each Ui±U_{i}^{\pm}, using the cylindrical coordinates provided by ϕi±\phi_{i}^{\pm}, we have στ=Hi±​d​t\sigma_{\tau}=H_{i}^{\pm}dt near ∞\infty, where Hi±H_{i}^{\pm} is a nondegenerate 1-periodic Hamiltonian on XX.
(4)
A smooth 1-parameter family of domain-dependent, ω\omega-compatible almost complex structures JτJ_{\tau} on XX such that on each Ui±U_{i}^{\pm}, using the cylindrical coordinates, Jτ=Ji±J_{\tau}=J_{i}^{\pm} near ∞\infty where Ji±J_{i}^{\pm} is a fixed almost complex structure on XX.
Denote such a 1-parameter family of Floer domains by Σtℍ\Sigma_{t}^{\mathbb{H}}, where ℍ{\mathbb{H}} stands for homotopy.
Given Σℍ\Sigma^{\mathbb{H}}, which has the family of incoming Floer flow categories
𝔽1,…,𝔽m{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m}
and the collection of outgoing Floer flow categories
𝔽1′,…,𝔽n′.{\mathbb{F}}_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{n}^{\prime}.
For each pair of collections of objects
pj∈Ob𝔽j,j=1,…,m,\displaystyle\ p_{j}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{j},\ j=1,\ldots,m,\
pi′∈Ob𝔽i′,i=1,…,n\displaystyle\ p_{i}^{\prime}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{i}^{\prime},\ i=1,\ldots,n
we consider the moduli space
Mp1⋯pm;p1′⋯pn′ℍM_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p_{1}^{\prime}\cdots p_{n}^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{H}}
which is the Gromov–Floer compactification of
{(τ,u)|τ∈[0,1],u:Σ→X,∂¯στu=0,lims→−∞u|Uj(s,t)=pj,j=1,…,m,lims→+∞u|Ui′=pi′,i=1,…,n}.\left\{(\tau,u)\ \left|\ \begin{array}[]{l}\tau\in[0,1],u:\Sigma\to X,\ \overline{\partial}_{\sigma_{\tau}}u=0,\\
\displaystyle\lim_{s\to-\infty}u|_{U_{j}}(s,t)=p_{j},j=1,\ldots,m,\\
\displaystyle\lim_{s\to+\infty}u|_{U_{i}^{\prime}}=p_{i}^{\prime},\ i=1,\ldots,n\end{array}\right.\right\}.
This is a compact topological space stratified by a regular poset Ap1⋯pm;p1′⋯pn′ℍA_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p_{1}^{\prime}\cdots p_{n}^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{H}}.
Notice that the subset of pairs (τ,u)(\tau,u) with τ=0\tau=0 resp. τ=1\tau=1 defines a multimodule 𝕏0{\mathbb{X}}_{0} resp. 𝕏1{\mathbb{X}}_{1} over (𝔽1,⋯,𝔽m,𝔽1′,⋯,𝔽n′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\cdots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}_{1}^{\prime},\cdots,{\mathbb{F}}_{n}^{\prime}). Then there are natural structural maps
Mpj​qj𝔽j×Mp1⋯pj−1qjpj+1⋯pm;p1′⋯pi−1′qi′pi+1′⋯pn′ℍ×Mqi′​pi′𝔽i′→Mp1⋯pm;p1′⋯pn′ℍM_{p_{j}q_{j}}^{{\mathbb{F}}_{j}}\times M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{j-1}q_{j}p_{j+1}\cdots p_{m};p_{1}^{\prime}\cdots p_{i-1}^{\prime}q_{i}^{\prime}p_{i+1}^{\prime}\cdots p_{n}^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{H}}\times M_{q_{i}^{\prime}p_{i}^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{F}}_{i}^{\prime}}\to M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p_{1}^{\prime}\cdots p_{n}^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{H}}
and
Mp1⋯pm;p1′⋯pn′𝕏0⊔Mp1⋯pm;p1′⋯pn′𝕏1→Mp1⋯pm;p1′⋯pn′ℍ.M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p_{1}^{\prime}\cdots p_{n}^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}_{0}}\sqcup M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p_{1}^{\prime}\cdots p_{n}^{\prime}}^{{\mathbb{X}}_{1}}\to M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p_{1}^{\prime}\cdots p_{n}^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{H}}.
One can then check that ℍ{\mathbb{H}} together with these structural maps defines a homotopy from 𝕏0{\mathbb{X}}_{0} to 𝕏1{\mathbb{X}}_{1}, enriched in 𝐓𝐨𝐩¯\underline{\smash{\bf Top}}.
We will mainly consider the case when n=1n=1. We summarize the setting in the following situation.
Situation Homotopy(i).
(X,ω)(X,\omega) is a compact symplectic manifold. Σtℍ,t∈[0,1]\Sigma_{t}^{\mathbb{H}},t\in[0,1] is a smooth 1-parameter family of Floer domains with mm negative cylindrical ends and 11 positive cylindrical end. ℍ{\mathbb{H}} is a homotopy from the multimodule 𝕏0{\mathbb{X}}_{0} over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}) defined by Σ0ℍ\Sigma_{0}^{\mathbb{H}} to the multimodule 𝕏1{\mathbb{X}}_{1} defined by Σ1ℍ\Sigma_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}.
11.2. Homotopies from gluing
Recall the notion of multimodule concatenations. Let Σ𝕏\Sigma^{\mathbb{X}} and Σ𝕐\Sigma^{\mathbb{Y}} be Floer domains defining Floer multimodules 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} and 𝕐{\mathbb{Y}} which can be composed to a multimodule 𝕏∘i𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}}. We assume that there is only one breaking on the surface Σ𝕏∘iΣ𝕐\Sigma^{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}\Sigma^{\mathbb{Y}}, see Figure 4. Then depending on choosing the cylindrical ends on both sides of that breaking, there is a canonical way to construct a 1-parameter family of Floer domains Σ𝕏∘S𝕐\Sigma^{{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{S}{\mathbb{Y}}} for S∈[S0,+∞)S\in[S_{0},+\infty), where SS parametrizes the neck-length, such that when S→+∞S\to+\infty, the Floer domain degenerates to the nodal Σ𝕏∘iΣ𝕐\Sigma^{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}\Sigma^{\mathbb{Y}}. Denote this family by Σℍ\Sigma^{\mathbb{H}}. Choose a smooth function τ↦S\tau\mapsto S which sends τ=0\tau=0 to S0S_{0} and τ=1\tau=1 to ∞\infty. Let Στ\Sigma^{\tau} be the corresponding Floer domain. For τ∈[0,1)\tau\in[0,1), let 𝕏∘S⁡(τ)𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{S(\tau)}{\mathbb{Y}} be the multimodule coming from the Floer domain Στ\Sigma^{\tau}.
Then for any collection of incoming objects 𝔭−{\mathfrak{p}}^{-} and outgoing objects 𝔭+{\mathfrak{p}}^{+}, one has the moduli space M𝔭−​𝔭+ℍM_{{\mathfrak{p}}^{-}{\mathfrak{p}}^{+}}^{\mathbb{H}}, which is the natural compactification of
{(τ,u)|τ∈[0,1],u:Στ→X,∂¯στu=0,lims→±∞u|U±i(s,t)=pi±}.\Big\{(\tau,u)\ |\ \tau\in[0,1],\ u:\Sigma^{\tau}\to X,\ \overline{\partial}_{\sigma^{\tau}}u=0,\ \lim_{s\to\pm\infty}u|_{U_{\pm}^{i}}(s,t)=p_{i}^{\pm}\Big\}.

As usual, we have the natural structural maps

(X,ω)(X,\omega) is a compact symplectic manifold. 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} and 𝕐{\mathbb{Y}} are Floer multimodules as described in Situation Concatenation(i). 11.3. Homotopies associated to PSS type moduli spaces
On a symplectic manifold, consider the three geometric flow categories: a Floer flow category 𝔽{\mathbb{F}}, a Morse flow category 𝕄{\mathbb{M}}, and a pearly flow category ℙ{\mathbb{P}}. Consider the following diagram
𝔽\textstyle{\mathbb{F}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}Δ𝔽​𝔽\scriptstyle{{\mathbb{\Delta}}^{\mathbb{FF}}}𝔹𝔽​𝕄\scriptstyle{{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{FM}}}𝔹𝔽​ℙ\scriptstyle{{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{FP}}}𝕄\textstyle{\mathbb{M}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}Δ𝕄​𝕄\scriptstyle{{\mathbb{\Delta}}^{\mathbb{MM}}}𝔹𝕄​𝔽\scriptstyle{{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{MF}}}𝔹𝕄​ℙ\scriptstyle{{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{MP}}}ℙ\textstyle{\mathbb{P}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}Δℙ​ℙ\scriptstyle{{\mathbb{\Delta}}^{\mathbb{PP}}}𝔹ℙ​𝔽\scriptstyle{{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{PF}}}𝔹ℙ​𝕄\scriptstyle{{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{PM}}}
(11.1)
where the arrows are bimodules. Notice that we can compose bimodules in this diagram following the arrows. We say a triangle in this diagram is commutative if the composed bimodule from two edges is homotopic to the third bimodule. We will explain 1) why the concatenation 𝔹𝔽​ℙ∘𝔹ℙ​𝔽{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{FP}}\circ{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{PF}} resp. 𝔹𝔽​ℙ∘𝔹ℙ​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{FP}}\circ\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{PF}} is homotopic to Δ𝔽​𝔽{\mathbb{\Delta}}^{\mathbb{FF}} resp. Δℙ​ℙ\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{PP}}, whose construction actually can show all triangle whose concatenation happens at 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} or ℙ{\mathbb{P}} commutes, 2) why the concatenation 𝔹𝕄​ℙ∘𝔹ℙ​𝕄\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{MP}}\circ\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{PM}} is homotopic to Δℙ​ℙ\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{PP}}, and 3) why the concatenation 𝔹𝔽​𝕄∘𝔹𝕄​𝔽{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{FM}}\circ{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{MF}} resp. 𝔹ℙ​𝕄∘𝔹𝕄​ℙ\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{PM}}\circ\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{MP}} is not (at least not obviously) homotopic to Δ𝔽​𝔽{\mathbb{\Delta}}^{\mathbb{FF}} resp. Δ𝕄​𝕄\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{MM}}.
11.3.1. Floer-to-Pearly, Pearly-to-Floer bimodules, and their concatenations
Choose a 1-parameter family of Floer data on the infinite cylinder, parametrized by τ∈[0,1)\tau\in[0,1), given by a Hamiltonian connection στ\sigma_{\tau} supported in a region of length about −1/logτ-1/\log\tau when τ\tau is close to 11, and converges to zero when τ→0\tau\to 0, and such that when τ\tau is close to 11, over the long cylinder it is equal to H​d​tHdt where HH is a nondegenerate 1-periodic Hamiltonian. Given a pair x=(x¯,ax),y=(y¯,ay)x=(\underline{\smash{x}},a_{x}),y=(\underline{\smash{y}},a_{y}) of objects of ℙ{\mathbb{P}}, consider the moduli space
{(τ,u)|τ∈[0,1),u:ℝ×S1→X,∂¯στu=0,lims→−∞u⁡(s,t)∈Wx¯us,lims→+∞u⁡(s,t)∈Wy¯st,ω⁡(u)=ax−ay}.\left\{(\tau,u)\ \left|\ \begin{array}[]{c}\tau\in[0,1),\ u:{\mathbb{R}}\times S^{1}\to X,\ \overline{\partial}_{\sigma_{\tau}}u=0,\\
\displaystyle\lim_{s\to-\infty}u(s,t)\in W^{\rm us}_{\underline{\smash{x}}},\ \lim_{s\to+\infty}u(s,t)\in W^{\rm st}_{\underline{\smash{y}}},\ \omega(u)=a_{x}-a_{y}\end{array}\right.\right\}.
We consider the pearly compactification at ±∞\pm\infty and meanwhile allowing τ→1\tau\to 1, which means the map uu should break along Hamiltonian orbits as −1/logτ→∞-1/\log\tau\to\infty (see Figure 5, where the neck length −1/logτ-1/\log\tau is denoted by SS).
Figure 5. The homotopy from Δℙ​ℙ\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{PP}} to 𝔹𝔽​ℙ∘𝔹ℙ​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{FP}}\circ\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{PF}}.
Then the restriction to the τ=1\tau=1 slice gives moduli spaces of the bimodule concatenation 𝔹𝔽​ℙ∘𝔹ℙ​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{FP}}\circ\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{PF}} (concatenation at Floer flow category). On the other hand, the restriction to the τ=0\tau=0 slice gives moduli spaces of the bimodule Δℙ​ℙ\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{PP}}. Denote this homotopy by
ℍℙ​𝔽​∘~​𝔽​ℙ{\mathbb{H}}^{\mathbb{PF}\tilde{\circ}\mathbb{FP}}
The concatenation at the Pearly flow category and its homotopy to Δ𝔽​𝔽\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}} is a bit more complicated. It is the concatenation of two homotopies.
First, consider the infinite cylinder equipped with a 1-parameter family of Floer data, parametrized by τ∈[0,1)\tau\in[0,1) such that when τ=0\tau=0, the Hamiltonian connection is the flat one H​d​tHdt, which gives rise to the diagonal bimodule Δ𝔽​𝔽\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}}, while as τ\tau increases, there is a long cylinder of length growing to ∞\infty on which the Hamiltonian connection is trivial. Then for each pair of objects p,p′∈Ob​𝔽p,p^{\prime}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}, consider the space
{(τ,u)|τ∈[0,1),u:ℝ×S1→X,∂¯στu=0,lims→−∞u⁡(s,t)=p,lims→+∞u⁡(s,t)=p′}\left\{(\tau,u)\left|\begin{array}[]{cc}\tau\in[0,1),\ u:{\mathbb{R}}\times S^{1}\to X,\ \overline{\partial}_{\sigma_{\tau}}u=0,\\
\displaystyle\lim_{s\to-\infty}u(s,t)=p,\ \lim_{s\to+\infty}u(s,t)=p^{\prime}\end{array}\right.\right\}
We compactify it naturally by adding sphere bubbles, Floer trajectory breakings at both negative and positive ends, and allowing cylindrical breakings when τ→1\tau\to 1. When the cylinder breaks off, we only quotient by the translation symmetry but not the rotation symmetry. This provides a compact moduli space
Mp​p′𝔽​ℙ​∘~​ℙ​𝔽,1M_{pp^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{FP}\tilde{\circ}\mathbb{PF},1}
and gives a homotopy from Δ𝔽​𝔽\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}} to an intermediate bimodule, denoted by 𝔹𝔽∙𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{F}\bullet\mathbb{F}}, denoted by ℍ𝔽​ℙ​∘~​ℙ​𝔽,1\mathbb{H}^{\mathbb{FP}\tilde{\circ}\mathbb{PF},1} (see Figure 6).
Figure 6. The homotopy between Δ𝔽​𝔽\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}} and 𝔹𝔽​ℙ∘𝔹ℙ​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{FP}}\circ\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{PF}}.
Next, we introduce a homotopy from 𝔹𝔽∙𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{F}\bullet\mathbb{F}} to 𝔹𝔽​ℙ∘ℙ​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{FP}\circ\mathbb{PF}}.
First, given a nonnegative real number ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0, we can consider the notion of telephone (see Figure 6) of length ℓ\ell, which is a pearly-type configuration with two ends being solutions to a Floer equation while the surfaces in between are holomorphic cylinders connected by Morse flow segments of total length ℓ\ell. By compactifying the moduli space while allowing ℓ→∞\ell\to\infty (meaning the Morse trajectories will break one or more times), one obtains moduli spaces
Mp​p′𝔽​ℙ​∘~​ℙ​𝔽,2M_{pp^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{FP}\tilde{\circ}\mathbb{PF},2}
providing a homotopy from 𝔹𝔽∙𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{F}\bullet\mathbb{F}} to 𝔹𝔽​ℙ∘𝔹ℙ​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{FP}}\circ\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{PF}}, denoted by ℍ𝔽​ℙ​∘~​ℙ​𝔽,2\mathbb{H}^{\mathbb{FP}\tilde{\circ}\mathbb{PF},2}. Then define
ℍ=ℍ𝔽​ℙ​∘~​ℙ​𝔽,1∪ℍ𝔽​ℙ​∘~​ℙ​𝔽,2\mathbb{H}=\mathbb{H}^{\mathbb{FP}\tilde{\circ}\mathbb{PF},1}\cup\mathbb{H}^{\mathbb{FP}\tilde{\circ}\mathbb{PF},2}
which is a homotopy from Δ𝔽​𝔽\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}} to 𝔹𝔽​ℙ∘𝔹ℙ​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{FP}}\circ\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{PF}}. We call it the telephone homotopy.
Remark 11.2.
The homotopy ℍ𝔽​ℙ​∘~​ℙ​𝔽,2\mathbb{H}^{\mathbb{FP}\tilde{\circ}\mathbb{PF},2} is used to relate two different constructions of the Morse–Bott theory for the constant Hamiltonian H=0H=0. The pearl flow category includes choosing a Morse function over the critical submanifolds and corresponds to the “cascades model” (see, e.g., [16]) of Morse–Bott theory. In contrast, the natural output of the bimodule ℍ𝔽​ℙ​∘~​ℙ​𝔽,1\mathbb{H}^{\mathbb{FP}\tilde{\circ}\mathbb{PF},1} corresponds to the “fiber product model” (see [8] for an early incarnation). The point of our construction is to compare the “Morse version” of Floer theory, coming from the flow category 𝔽\mathbb{F} that is associated with a nondegenerate Hamiltonian, with the Morse–Bott version, which uses pearly trajectories, using the fiber product model as an intermediate gadget.
11.3.2. Other concatenations along Pearly flow categories
We can also construct a homotopy from 𝔹𝕄​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{MF}} to the concatenation 𝔹𝕄​ℙ∘𝔹ℙ​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{MP}}\circ\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{PF}}, denoted by ℍ𝕄​ℙ​∘~​ℙ​𝔽{\mathbb{H}}^{\mathbb{MP}\tilde{\circ}\mathbb{PF}} and a homotopy from 𝔹𝔽​𝕄\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{FM}} to the concatenation 𝔹𝔽​ℙ∘𝔹ℙ​𝕄\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{FP}}\circ\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{PM}}, denoted by ℍ𝔽​ℙ​∘~​ℙ​𝕄\mathbb{H}^{\mathbb{FP}\tilde{\circ}\mathbb{PM}}. Since the two cases are dual to each other, we only explain the definition of the first homotopy.
Consider the bimodule 𝔹𝕄​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{MF}} given by the collection of moduli spaces
Mx​p𝕄​𝔽M_{xp}^{\mathbb{MF}}
which is the natural compactification of the space of solutions to the Floer equation on the infinite cylinder with a Hamiltonian connection σ\sigma which is zero near −∞-\infty and which is H​d​tHdt near +∞+\infty. We deform σ\sigma to a 1-parameter family στ\sigma_{\tau}, τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1] such that when τ→1\tau\to 1, the support of στ\sigma_{\tau} is pushed to +∞+\infty. Then as τ=1\tau=1, one obtains a bimodule consisting of moduli spaces whose configurations are similar to the third picture of Figure 6. Then one can continue the homotopy by inserting gradient segments of lengths which vary from 00 to +∞+\infty. The very end of this homotopy is the concatenation 𝔹𝕄​ℙ∘𝔹ℙ​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{MP}}\circ\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{PF}}.
11.3.3. Remarks on concatenation at the Morse flow category
One can also form the concatenation at the Morse flow category, for example, 𝔹𝔽​𝕄∘𝔹𝕄​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{FM}}\circ\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{MF}}. In the category 𝐓𝐨𝐩¯\underline{\smash{\bf Top}}, it is homotopic to the bimodule Δ𝔽​𝔽\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}}, firstly by gluing broken Morse trajectories and secondly by gluing holomorphic curves. However, it is hard to regularize such a homotopy. In particular, when gluing holomorphic curves at a node, unlike the Pearly case, the gluing has a complex gluing parameter. This does not fit very well with our framework. This is the reason why we need to go through the Pearly flow category in order to prove the invertibility of the PSS and SSP maps.
12. Main Theorems on AMS Lifts
In this section, we state the main results regarding regularizations of moduli spaces introduced in the previous section. The proof will be presented in the next part.
12.1. Main statements for Floer flow categories
We state the main theorem about global charts of Floer flow categories and other types of flow categories. The constructions depend on many choices. Most of the dependence of the choices can be absorbed via the global chart construction of bimodules; however, the dependence of the outercollaring width and the choice of the so-called integral action (Definition 15.1) cannot be absorbed easily. Hence in the statement, we emphasize the dependence of these two choices.
Theorem O.
In Situation Flow(i), given any outercollaring width ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and a choice of integral action on 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} (Definition 15.1) on 𝔽{\mathbb{F}}, the ϵ\epsilon-outercollaring of 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} admits a set of lifts 𝔽~\tilde{\mathbb{F}} to ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯NCrig{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{\rm NC}_{\rm rig} (Definition 3.12) as a Π\Pi-equivariant Novikov flow category. Each individual lift in this set is called an AMS lift subject to the outercollaring width and the integral action. The AMS lifts admit coherent orientations in the sense of Definition 7.12. Moreover, for any ϵ′>0\epsilon^{\prime}>0, the ϵ′\epsilon^{\prime}-outercollaring of 𝔽~\tilde{\mathbb{F}} is an AMS lift of 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} subject to the outercollaring width ϵ+ϵ′\epsilon+\epsilon^{\prime} and the same integral action.
Proof.
See Section 18 except for the last statement, which is a straightforward consequence of the constructions.
∎
Remark 12.1.
In fact what we mean by an AMS lift does not only mean the resulting flow category 𝔽~\tilde{\mathbb{F}}, but also all the choices made in the process of construction. When an follow-up construction depends on a given AMS lift, it means the construction a priori depends on the choices made for the AMS lift.
The (in)dependence on the choice of the integral action is characterized by the following theorem. Recall that for the Floer flow category 𝔽{\mathbb{F}}, there is a bimodule Δ𝔽​𝔽\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}} over (𝔽;𝔽)({\mathbb{F}};{\mathbb{F}}) associated to the continuation map from (J,H)(J,H) to (J,H)(J,H) with the trivial Floer data.
Proposition 12.2.
In Situation Flow(i), let 𝔽~1\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{1} and 𝔽~2\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{2} be two AMS lifts of 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} subject to the same outercollaring width and two different integral actions, provided by Theorem O. Then there exists a class of lifts of the corresponding outercollaring of Δ𝔽​𝔽\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}} to ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm NC} as a bimodule over (𝔽~1;𝔽~2)(\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{1};\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{2}). Moreover, with respect to the coherent orientations on 𝔽~1,𝔽~2\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{2}, the lift is coherently oriented.
Proof.
See Section 20.
∎
The (in)dependence on other choices for the AMS lift is included in the theorem on multimodules (Theorem P).
12.2. Multimodules and homotopies
Next, we state the main theorems concerning regularizing flow multimodules and homotopies.
First, we formulate the theorem on lifts for multimodules. Due to technical reasons, we must consider the dependence on a specific choice, namely, that of integral actions (Definition 15.1 and Definition 15.2) in the construction.
Theorem P.
Suppose 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} is a multimodule associated a smooth Floer domain Σ𝕏\Sigma^{\mathbb{X}} with m≥0m\geq 0 negative ends and n≥0n\geq 0 positive ends satisfying
n∈{0,1},n=0⟹m=2​and​m=0⟹n=1.n\in\{0,1\},\ n=0\Longrightarrow m=2\ {\rm and}\ m=0\Longrightarrow n=1.
It is a multimodule over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}) where 𝔽1,…,𝔽m{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m} are Floer flow categories and 𝔽′{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} is a Floer flow category when n=1n=1 and the trivial flow category when n=0n=0. When m=0m=0 and n=1n=1, 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} is a cigar bimodule over (𝕆;𝔽′)({\mathbb{O}};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}).
Choose a common outercollaring width and compatible integral actions on the involved Floer flow categories (see Definition 15.2). Let 𝔽~1,…,𝔽~m,𝔽~′\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{m},\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} be AMS lifts to ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯NCrig{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{\rm NC}_{\rm rig} of 𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m},{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} subject to the fixed outercollaring width and these integral actions provided by Theorem O (when 𝔽′=𝕆{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}={\mathbb{O}}, take 𝔽~′=𝕆\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}={\mathbb{O}}).
(1)
There exists a set of lifts of 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} to ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯NCrig{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{\rm NC}_{\rm rig}, denoted by 𝕏~\tilde{\mathbb{X}} (called an AMS lift subject to the chosen integral actions), which is a multimodule over (𝔽~1,…,𝔽~k,𝔽~′)(\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{k};\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}). Moreover, with respect to the coherent orientations on 𝔽~1,…,𝔽~m,𝔽~′\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{m},\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}, the lift 𝕏~\tilde{\mathbb{X}} is coherently oriented.
(2)
Any two AMS lifts of 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} (subject to the same set of integral actions) are homotopic as multimodules enriched in ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm NC} via a lift of the the trivial homotopy from the outercollaring of 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} to itself and the homotopy is coherently oriented.
Proof.
See Section 18.
∎
Notice that Theorem P depends on choosing an integral action. For comparing different choices, we consider a particular homotopy. Recall that Δ𝔽j​𝔽j\mathbb{\Delta}^{{\mathbb{F}}_{j}\mathbb{F}_{j}}, Δ𝔽′​𝔽′\mathbb{\Delta}^{{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}} are the diagonal bimodules. There is an obvious homotopy ℍ{\mathbb{H}} from the concatenation (as concatenations of weak bimodules)
(Δ𝔽1​𝔽1×⋯×Δ𝔽m​𝔽m)∘𝕏∘Δ𝔽′​𝔽′\Big(\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{F}_{1}\mathbb{F}_{1}}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{F}_{m}\mathbb{F}_{m}}\Big)\circ\mathbb{X}\circ\mathbb{\Delta}^{{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}\mathbb{F}^{\prime}}
to 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} by simultaneously gluing at both positive and negative ends. When n=0n=0 and m=2m=2, we replace the above concatenation by
(Δ𝔽1​𝔽1×Δ𝔽2​𝔽2)∘𝕏.\Big(\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{F}_{1}\mathbb{F}_{1}}\times\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{F}_{2}\mathbb{F}_{2}}\Big)\circ\mathbb{X}.
Proposition 12.3.
Under the assumption of Theorem P, fix an outercollaring width.
(1)
When n=1n=1, let
𝒜𝔽jΩ(s),𝒜𝔽′Ω(s),s=0,1{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{F}_{j}}^{\Omega_{(s)}},\ {\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}^{\Omega_{(s)}},\ s=0,1
be two compatible sets of integral actions. Let 𝕏~(s)\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{(s)} be an AMS lift subject to the fixed outercollaring width and one set of integral actions. Here the source and target flow categories are all Floer flow categories associated to the limiting Hamiltonians on the two Floer domains. Recall that the concatenation 𝕏∘i𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}{\mathbb{Y}} is a multimodule over (𝔾1,…,𝔾i−1,𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔾i+1,…,𝔾n,𝔾′)({\mathbb{G}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{G}}_{i-1},{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m},{\mathbb{G}}_{i+1},\ldots,{\mathbb{G}}_{n};{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}).

Remark 12.5.
We do not discuss comparing non-homotopic choices in the constructions of lifts of homotopies. We only use homotopies to ensure well-defineness of operations induced by flow multimodules, so we stop our discussion on non-homotopic choices at multimodules.

12.3.2. The triangle of Morse, Floer and pearly flow categories
Recall that in Subsection 10.3, besides the Morse-to-Floer and Floer-to-Morse bimodules, we also described a few other bimodules, namely the Pearly-to-Floer bimodule 𝔹ℙ​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{PF}}, the Floer-to-Pearly bimodule 𝔹𝔽​ℙ{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{FP}}, the Pearly-to-Morse bimodule 𝔹ℙ​𝕄{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{PM}}, and the Morse-to-Pearly bimodule 𝔹𝕄​ℙ{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{MP}}. Moreover, one has the diagonal bimodules Δ𝔽​𝔽\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}} (which is a special case for the continuation map bimodule), Δℙ​ℙ\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{PP}}, and Δ𝕄​𝕄\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{MM}} (a deformation of the diagonal bimodule of the classical Morse flow category).
