13. Proof of the Main Theorems
In this section we prove (most of) the main theorems using previously stated theorems on Kuranishi lifts of various flow categories, bimodules, homotopies and the theorem on FOP perturbations (Theorem N). The proofs are mostly formal consequences of the existence of the regularizations and coherent FOP perturbations thereon, following the general theme of Floer theory which turns bordifications of moduli spaces into algebraic structures.
13.1. Proof of Theorem A
Suppose we are in Situation Flow(i). Theorem O provides, depending on a choice, an AMS lift 𝔽~\tilde{\mathbb{F}} enriched in ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯NCrig{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{{\rm NC}}_{\rm rig} together with a coherent orientation. As the Floer flow category is an unobstructed (Definition 7.1) and Π\Pi-equivariant Novikov flow category (Definition 7.2 and Definition 7.24), Theorem N provides a Π\Pi-equivariant lift, i.e., an FOP perturbation 𝔽̊\mathring{\mathbb{F}} on 𝔽~\tilde{\mathbb{F}}, which is a flow category enriched in ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯FOPrig{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{\rm FOP}_{\rm rig}. Then apply the forgetful functor (i.e., taking the closure of the isotropy-free locus of the Kuranishi section)
⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯FOPrig→𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯,{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{\rm FOP}_{\rm rig}\to\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}},
one obtains a flow category enriched in 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}. Using the coherent orientation and the ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-grading by the Conley–Zehnder index, by Proposition 7.16 and Proposition 7.30, one obtains a canonically associated chain complex
C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ):=C∗​(𝔽̊)CF_{*}(H,J;\Xi):=C_{*}(\mathring{\mathbb{F}})
generated by objects of 𝔽\mathbb{F}, which has the structure of a graded ΛℤΠ\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\Pi}-module. Here Ξ\Xi denotes all choices made in constructing the AMS lift and the FOP perturbation; in particular, Ξ\Xi includes the information of the outercollaring width and the integral action. We call this process the basic construction for Floer complex.
We prove that the Floer chain complex has a well-defined chain homotopy type. Let Ξ(0)\Xi_{(0)}, Ξ(1)\Xi_{(1)} be two different sets of choices, including outercollaring widths, integral actions, and choices made for the two AMS lifts 𝔽~(0)\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{(0)}, 𝔽~(1)\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{(1)} and the FOP perturbations 𝔽̊(0)\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{(0)}, 𝔽̊(1)\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{(1)}.
Lemma 13.1.
There exists a chain homotopy equivalence
Ψ(01):C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ(0))→C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ(1))\Psi_{(01)}:CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi_{(0)})\to CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi_{(1)})
whose chain homotopy type is well-defined.
Proof.
By the part of Theorem O about outercollaring width, one can reduce the comparison to the case that the outercollaring widths are equal. Then by Proposition 12.2, there exists a lift of the outercollaring of the diagonal bimodule Δ𝔽​𝔽\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}} to ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm NC} as a bimodule over (𝔽~(0);𝔽~(1))(\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{(0)};\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{(1)}). Then by Theorem N, the FOP perturbations 𝔽̊(0)\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{(0)} and 𝔽̊(1)\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{(1)} can be extended to an FOP perturbation Δ̊𝔽​𝔽\mathring{\mathbb{\Delta}}^{\mathbb{FF}} on Δ~𝔽​𝔽\tilde{\mathbb{\Delta}}^{\mathbb{FF}}. Then by Proposition 7.31, one obtains the chain map
Ψ(01):C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ(0))→C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ(1)).\Psi_{(01)}:CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi_{(0)})\to CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi_{(1)}).
Using the part of Proposition 12.2 stating that two lifts of Δ𝔽​𝔽{\mathbb{\Delta}}^{\mathbb{FF}} are homotopic and Theorem N, one can prove that the homotopy type of Ψ(01)\Psi_{(01)} is well-defined.
It remains to prove that Ψ(01)\Psi_{(01)} is a homotopy equivalence. Indeed, for each object p∈Ob​𝔽p\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}, the bimodule moduli space Mp;p𝔽​𝔽M_{p;p}^{\mathbb{FF}} consists of a single point corresponding to the constant trajectory at pp. This moduli space has no lower strata, hence coincides with its outercollaring. Moreover, it is transversely cut out, so the FOP perturbation can be chosen to be the same as the original Kuranishi section. We can then choose the FOP perturbation Δ̊𝔽​𝔽\mathring{\mathbb{\Delta}}^{\mathbb{FF}} inductively such that we do not perturb for Mp;p𝔽​𝔽M_{p;p}^{\mathbb{FF}}. For such a choice of FOP perturbation, the count np;p𝔽​𝔽n_{p;p}^{\mathbb{FF}} needed to define the corresponding coefficient of the chain map is 11. With respect to the natural identification of the chain groups C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ(0))≅C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ(1))CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi_{(0)})\cong CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi_{(1)}), Ψ(01)\Psi_{(01)} is a higher order perturbation of the identity in terms of TT-valuation. Therefore, Ψ(01)\Psi_{(01)} is an invertible chain map, hence a chain homotopy equivalence.
∎
This finishes the proof of Theorem A.
13.2. General construction of chain maps and homotopics
13.2.1. Chain maps associated to smooth Floer domains
Suppose we are in Situation Module(i). Choose an outercollaring width and a compatible set of integral actions
𝒜𝔽jΩ:Ob​𝔽j→ℤ,\displaystyle\ {\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}_{j}}^{\Omega}:{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{j}\to{\mathbb{Z}},\
𝒜𝔽′Ω:Ob​𝔽′→ℤ.\displaystyle\ {\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}^{\Omega}:{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}\to{\mathbb{Z}}.
Let C​F∗​(Hj,Jj,Ξj)CF_{*}(H_{j},J_{j},\Xi_{j}) resp. C​F∗​(H′,J′,Ξ′)CF_{*}(H^{\prime},J^{\prime},\Xi^{\prime}) be Floer chain complexes associated to the Floer flow categories 𝔽j{\mathbb{F}}_{j} resp. 𝔽′{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}, which depend on the choices Ξj\Xi_{j} resp. Ξ′\Xi^{\prime}, including the information of the chosen outercollaring width, the integral actions, the construction of the AMS lifts 𝔽~j\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{j} reps. 𝔽~′\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}, and FOP perturbations 𝔽̊j\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{j} resp. 𝔽̊′\mathring{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}. Then by Theorem P, there exists an AMS lift 𝕏~\tilde{\mathbb{X}} of 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} subject to the outercollaring width and the integral actions as a multimodule over (𝔽~1,…,𝔽~m,𝔽~′)(\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{m};\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}). By Theorem N, the FOP perturbations 𝔽̊j\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{j} and 𝔽̊′\mathring{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} can be extended to an FOP perturbation 𝕏̊\mathring{\mathbb{X}} on 𝕏~\tilde{\mathbb{X}}. Then by Proposition 7.31, one obtains a chain map
Φ𝕏​(Θ):⨂1≤j≤mC​F∗​(Hj,Jj,Ξj)→C​F∗​(H′,J′,Ξ′)\Phi^{\mathbb{X}}(\Theta):\bigotimes_{1\leq j\leq m}CF_{*}(H_{j},J_{j},\Xi_{j})\to CF_{*}(H^{\prime},J^{\prime},\Xi^{\prime})
where Θ\Theta contains the information of all choices made in order to define such a chain map.
In practice, the multimodule 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} could be either a bimodule needed for establishing the continuation map, the multimodule needed for defining the pair-of-pants product, or the multimodule for defining the Poincaré duality etc. We need to prove that it is well-defined up to homotopy. Again, one can reduce the comparison to the case when the outercollaring widths are the same.
Lemma 13.2.
Fix the outercollaring width and the compatible set of integral actions on the involved flow categories. Let C​F∗​(Hj,Jj,Ξj)CF_{*}(H_{j},J_{j},\Xi_{j}) resp. C​F∗​(H′,J′,Ξ′)CF_{*}(H^{\prime},J^{\prime},\Xi^{\prime}) be Floer chain complexes associated to these flow categories. Let
Φ𝕏​(Θ0),Φ𝕏​(Θ1):⨂1≤j≤mC​F∗​(Hj,Jj,Ξj)→C​F∗​(H′,J′,Ξ′)\Phi^{\mathbb{X}}(\Theta_{0}),\ \Phi^{{\mathbb{X}}}(\Theta_{1}):\bigotimes_{1\leq j\leq m}CF_{*}(H_{j},J_{j},\Xi_{j})\to CF_{*}(H^{\prime},J^{\prime},\Xi^{\prime})
be two chain maps defined via two differet sets of choices made for two AMS lifts 𝕏~0\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{0} resp. 𝕏~1\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{1} and two FOP perturbations 𝕏̊0\mathring{\mathbb{X}}_{0} resp. 𝕏̊1\mathring{\mathbb{X}}_{1}. Then Φ𝕏​(Θ0)\Phi^{{\mathbb{X}}}(\Theta_{0}) and Φ𝕏​(Θ1)\Phi^{{\mathbb{X}}}(\Theta_{1}) are chain homotopic.
Proof.
Consider the trivial homotopy ℍ\mathbb{H} from 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} to itself. The set of integral actions remain compatible with respect to ℍ{\mathbb{H}}. Therefore, by part (2) of Theorem P, there exists a homotopy ℍ~\tilde{\mathbb{H}} from 𝕏~0\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{0} to 𝕏~1\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{1} as a lift of the outercollaring of ℍ{\mathbb{H}}. By Theorem N, the FOP perturbations 𝔽̊j\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{j}, 𝔽̊′\mathring{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}, 𝕏̊0\mathring{\mathbb{X}}_{0}, 𝕏̊1\mathring{\mathbb{X}}_{1} can be extended to an FOP perturbation ℍ̊\mathring{\mathbb{H}} on ℍ~\tilde{\mathbb{H}}. Then by Proposition 7.32 one obtains a chain homotopy between Φ𝕏​(Θ0)\Phi^{{\mathbb{X}}}(\Theta_{0}) and Φ𝕏​(Θ1)\Phi^{{\mathbb{X}}}(\Theta_{1}).
∎
Next we compare different choices of integral actions.
Lemma 13.3.
Fix an outercollaring width. Let
𝒜𝔽jΩ(s),𝒜𝔽′Ω(s),s=0,1{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}_{j}}^{\Omega_{(s)}},\ {\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}^{\Omega_{(s)}},\ s=0,1
be two compatible sets of integral actions. Let
C​F∗​(Hj,Jj,Ξj,(s)),C​F∗​(H′,J′,Ξ(s)′)CF_{*}(H_{j},J_{j},\Xi_{j,(s)}),\ CF_{*}(H^{\prime},J^{\prime},\Xi_{(s)}^{\prime})
be Floer complexes whose constructions are subject to one of the sets of compatible integral actions, including the construction of the AMS lifts 𝔽~j,(s)\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{j,(s)} and 𝔽~(s)′\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{(s)}^{\prime} and FOP perturbations 𝔽̊j,(s)\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{j,(s)}, 𝔽̊(s)′\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{(s)}^{\prime}. Let
Φ𝕏​(Θ(s)):⨂1≤j≤mC​F∗​(Hj,Jj,Ξj,(s))→C​F∗​(H′,J′,Ξ(s)′)\Phi^{{\mathbb{X}}}(\Theta_{(s)}):\bigotimes_{1\leq j\leq m}CF_{*}(H_{j},J_{j},\Xi_{j,(s)})\to CF_{*}(H^{\prime},J^{\prime},\Xi_{(s)}^{\prime})
be the chain map defined via two different AMS constructions subject to the two sets of integral actions, including the AMS lifts 𝕏~(s)\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{(s)} and the FOP perturbation 𝕏̊(s)\mathring{\mathbb{X}}_{(s)}.
Moreover, let
Ψj,(01):C​F∗​(Hj,Jj,Ξj,(0))→C​F∗​(Hj,Jj,Ξj,(1))\Psi_{j,(01)}:CF_{*}(H_{j},J_{j},\Xi_{j,(0)})\to CF_{*}(H_{j},J_{j},\Xi_{j,(1)})
and
Ψ(10)′:C​F∗​(H′,J′,Ξ(1)′)→C​F∗​(H′,J′,Ξ(0)′)\Psi_{(10)}^{\prime}:CF_{*}(H^{\prime},J^{\prime},\Xi_{(1)}^{\prime})\to CF_{*}(H^{\prime},J^{\prime},\Xi_{(0)}^{\prime})
be the chain maps induced from the continuation maps provided by Proposition 12.2. Then there exists a chain homotopy between Φ𝕏​(Θ(0))\Phi^{\mathbb{X}}(\Theta_{(0)}) and the composition
Ψ(10)′∘Φ𝕏(Θ(1))∘(Ψ1,(01)⊗⋯⊗Ψm,(01)).\Psi_{(10)}^{\prime}\circ\Phi^{\mathbb{X}}(\Theta_{(1)})\circ\Big(\Psi_{1,(01)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Psi_{m,(01)}\Big).
Proof.
This is essentially a consequence of Proposition 12.3. Indeed, the assumption of this lemma can be plugged into the assumption of Proposition 12.3. Then one obtains a homotopy ℍ~\tilde{\mathbb{H}} from 𝕏~(0)\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{(0)} to the concatenation
(Δ~(01)𝔽1​𝔽1×⋯×Δ~(01)𝔽m​𝔽m)∘𝕏~(1)∘Δ~(10)𝔽′​𝔽′.\Big(\tilde{\mathbb{\Delta}}_{(01)}^{\mathbb{F}_{1}\mathbb{F}_{1}}\times\cdots\times\tilde{\mathbb{\Delta}}_{(01)}^{\mathbb{F}_{m}\mathbb{F}_{m}}\Big)\circ\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{(1)}\circ\tilde{\mathbb{\Delta}}_{(10)}^{\mathbb{F}^{\prime}\mathbb{F}^{\prime}}.
Then by Theorem N, the existing FOP perturbations can be extended to an FOP perturbation ℍ̊\mathring{\mathbb{H}} on ℍ~\tilde{\mathbb{H}}. The conclusion then follows.
∎
13.2.2. Homotopy
We prove the following basic chain-level consequence of homotopies of multimodules from varying Floer data.
Lemma 13.4.
In Situation Homotopy(i), fix an outercollaring width and a compatible set of integral actions on involved Floer flow categories. Let
C​F∗​(Hj,Jj,Ξj),\displaystyle\ CF_{*}(H_{j},J_{j},\Xi_{j}),\
C​F∗​(H′,J′,Ξ′)\displaystyle\ CF_{*}(H^{\prime},J^{\prime},\Xi^{\prime})
be Floer chain complexes provided by Theorem A subject to the outercollaring width and the integral actions. Let
Φ𝕏0​(Θ0),Φ𝕏1​(Θ1):⨂1≤j≤mC​F∗​(Hj,Jj,Ξj)→C​F∗​(H′,J′,Ξ′)\Phi^{{\mathbb{X}}_{0}}(\Theta_{0}),\ \Phi^{{\mathbb{X}}_{1}}(\Theta_{1}):\bigotimes_{1\leq j\leq m}CF_{*}(H_{j},J_{j},\Xi_{j})\to CF_{*}(H^{\prime},J^{\prime},\Xi^{\prime})
be chain maps provided by the basic construction of chain maps. Then these two chain maps are homotopic.
Proof.
The construction of the Floer chain complexes involves choosing AMS lifts 𝔽~1,…,𝔽~m;𝔽~′\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{m};\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} and FOP perturbations 𝔽̊1,…,𝔽̊m;𝔽̊′\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{m};\mathring{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}. Then the chain maps are constructed by choosing AMS lifts 𝕏~0\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{0} and 𝕏~1\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{1}
as multimodules over (𝔽~1,…,𝔽~m,𝔽~′)(\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{m};\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}), and FOP perturbations 𝕏̊0\mathring{\mathbb{X}}_{0}, 𝕏̊1\mathring{\mathbb{X}}_{1} as multimodules over (𝔽̊1,…,𝔽̊m,𝔽̊′)(\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{m};\mathring{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}). Then by Theorem Q, there exists an AMS lift ℍ~\tilde{\mathbb{H}} as a homotopy from 𝕏~0\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{0} to 𝕏~1\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{1}. Then by Theorem N, the existing FOP perturbations can be extended to an FOP perturbation ℍ̊\mathring{\mathbb{H}} on ℍ~\tilde{\mathbb{H}}. Then Proposition 7.32 implies that the chain maps are homotopic via a concrete homotopy from ℍ̊\mathring{\mathbb{H}}.
∎
13.2.3. Concatenation and gluing
Now we consider the situation of concatenation.
Lemma 13.5.
In Situation Glue(i), fix an outercollaring width and a 1-parameter family of lateral lines in the domains. Suppose
𝒜𝔽1Ω,…,𝒜𝔽mΩ,\displaystyle\ {\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}_{1}}^{\Omega},\ldots,{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}_{m}}^{\Omega},\
𝒜𝔾1Ω,…,𝒜𝔾nΩ,𝒜𝔾′Ω\displaystyle\ {\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{G}}_{1}}^{\Omega},\ldots,{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{G}}_{n}}^{\Omega},{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}}^{\Omega}
are integral actions on the involved flow categories which are compatible with respect to 𝕏{\mathbb{X}}, 𝕐{\mathbb{Y}}, 𝕄{\mathbb{M}}, and the homotopy ℍ{\mathbb{H}}. Subject to these choices, let
C​F​(H1,J1,Ξ1),…,C​F​(Hm,Jm,Ξm)CF(H_{1},J_{1},\Xi_{1}),\ldots,CF(H_{m},J_{m},\Xi_{m})
and
C​F​(G1,I1,Λ1),…,C​F​(Gn,In,Λn),C​F​(G′,I′,Λ′)CF(G_{1},I_{1},\Lambda_{1}),\ldots,CF(G_{n},I_{n},\Lambda_{n}),CF(G^{\prime},I^{\prime},\Lambda^{\prime})
be Floer chain complexes provided by Theorem A. Let
Φ𝕏:⨂1≤j≤mC​F∗​(Hj,Jj,Ξj)→C​F∗​(Gi,Ii,Λi),\Phi^{{\mathbb{X}}}:\bigotimes_{1\leq j\leq m}CF_{*}(H_{j},J_{j},\Xi_{j})\to CF_{*}(G_{i},I_{i},\Lambda_{i}),
Φ𝕐:⨂1≤l≤nC​F​(Gl,Il,Λl)→C​F​(G′,I′,Λ′),\Phi^{\mathbb{Y}}:\bigotimes_{1\leq l\leq n}CF(G_{l},I_{l},\Lambda_{l})\to CF(G^{\prime},I^{\prime},\Lambda^{\prime}),
and
Φ𝕄:⨂l<iC​F​(Gl,Il,Λl)⊗⨂1≤j≤mC​F​(Hj,Jj,Ξj)⊗⨂l>iC​F​(Gl,Il,Λl)→C​F​(G′,I′,Λ′)\Phi^{{\mathbb{M}}}:\bigotimes_{l<i}CF(G_{l},I_{l},\Lambda_{l})\otimes\bigotimes_{1\leq j\leq m}CF(H_{j},J_{j},\Xi_{j})\otimes\bigotimes_{l>i}CF(G_{l},I_{l},\Lambda_{l})\to CF(G^{\prime},I^{\prime},\Lambda^{\prime})
be chain maps provided by the general construction of Floer chain maps. Then the last chain map is homotopic to the composition
(y1,⋯,yi−1,x1,…,xm,yi+1,…,yn)↦Φ𝕐​(y1,…,yi−1,Φ𝕏​(x1,…,xm),yi+1,…,yn).(y_{1},\cdots,y_{i-1},x_{1},\ldots,x_{m},y_{i+1},\ldots,y_{n})\mapsto\Phi^{{\mathbb{Y}}}(y_{1},\ldots,y_{i-1},\Phi^{\mathbb{X}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}),y_{i+1},\ldots,y_{n}).
Proof.
Subject to the integral actions and outercollaring widths, the construction of the Floer chain complexes depends on the AMS lifts 𝔽~1,…,𝔽~m\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{m} and 𝔾~1,…,𝔾~n,𝔾~′\tilde{\mathbb{G}}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{\mathbb{G}}_{n},\tilde{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime} and FOP perturbations 𝔽̊1,…,𝔽̊m\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{m} and 𝔾̊1,…,𝔾̊n,𝔾̊′\mathring{\mathbb{G}}_{1},\ldots,\mathring{\mathbb{G}}_{n},\mathring{\mathbb{G}}^{\prime}. The chain maps Φ𝕏\Phi^{\mathbb{X}}, Φ𝕐\Phi^{\mathbb{Y}}, and Φ𝕄\Phi^{\mathbb{M}} also depend on corresponding AMS lifts and FOP perturbations. One can also choose concatenations 𝕏~∘i𝕐~\tilde{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}\tilde{\mathbb{Y}} and 𝕏̊∘i𝕐̊\mathring{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}\mathring{\mathbb{Y}} (provided by Theorem 12.4 and Proposition 8.6).
Then by Theorem R, there exists a lift ℍ~\tilde{\mathbb{H}} of the outercollaring of ℍ{\mathbb{H}} as a homotopy from 𝕏~∘i𝕐~\tilde{\mathbb{X}}\circ_{i}\tilde{\mathbb{Y}} to 𝕄~\tilde{\mathbb{M}}. By Theorem N, one can find an FOP perturbation ℍ̊\mathring{\mathbb{H}} on ℍ~\tilde{\mathbb{H}} as a homotopy from 𝕏~∘𝕐~\tilde{\mathbb{X}}\circ\tilde{\mathbb{Y}} to 𝕄~\tilde{\mathbb{M}}. Then one obtains the desired chain homotopy.
∎
13.3. Proof of Theorem B
Assume we are in Situation Flow(i). Above, we have defined the Floer chain complex
C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ)CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi)
which appears to depend on the outercollaring width, the integral action, choices made for constructing the AMS lift 𝔽~\tilde{\mathbb{F}}, and the FOP perturbation 𝔽̊\mathring{\mathbb{F}}. We have already proved (see Lemma 13.1) that the chain homotopy type only depends on (H,J)(H,J), but not on the system of choices Ξ\Xi. It remains to construct the continuation map.
13.3.1. Definition of the continuation map
Let 𝔽′{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} be another Floer flow category associated to another pair (H′,J′)(H^{\prime},J^{\prime}). Choose a 1-parameter family of Floer data interpolating between (H,J)(H,J) and (H′,J′)(H^{\prime},J^{\prime}), resulting in a bimodule 𝔹{\mathbb{B}} from 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} to 𝔽′{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}. Then we are in a special case of Situation Module(i). Then, using the above construction, upon choosing an outercollaring width and a pair of integral actions on 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} and 𝔽′{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} compatible with respect to 𝔹{\mathbb{B}}, after AMS constructions of 𝔽~\tilde{\mathbb{F}}, 𝔽~′\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime},𝔹~\tilde{\mathbb{B}}, and choosing FOP perturbations 𝔽̊\mathring{\mathbb{F}}, 𝔽̊′\mathring{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}, and 𝔹̊\mathring{\mathbb{B}}, one obtains a chain map
Φ𝔹​(Θ):C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ)→C​F∗​(H′,J′,Ξ′)\Phi^{\mathbb{B}}(\Theta):CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi)\to CF_{*}(H^{\prime},J^{\prime},\Xi^{\prime})
whose homotopy class only depends on the bimodule 𝔹{\mathbb{B}} and the choices of the integral actions (see Lemma 13.2).
13.3.2. Independence of the integral actions
We first would like to reduce the dependence to 𝔹{\mathbb{B}} but not the integral actions. Indeed, if 𝒜𝔽Ω(s){\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}}^{\Omega_{(s)}}, 𝒜𝔽′Ω(s){\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}^{\Omega_{(s)}}, s=0,1s=0,1 are two compatible pairs of integral actions, then by Lemma 13.3, the diagram
C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ(0))\textstyle{CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi_{(0)})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}Φ𝔹​(Θ(0))\scriptstyle{\Phi^{{\mathbb{B}}}(\Theta_{(0)})}Ψ(01)𝔽\scriptstyle{\Psi_{(01)}^{\mathbb{F}}}C​F∗​(H′,J′,Ξ(0)′)\textstyle{CF_{*}(H^{\prime},J^{\prime},\Xi_{(0)}^{\prime})}C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ(1))\textstyle{CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi_{(1)})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}Φ𝔹​(Θ(1))\scriptstyle{\Phi^{{\mathbb{B}}}(\Theta_{(1)})}C​F∗​(H′,J′,Ξ(1)′)\textstyle{CF_{*}(H^{\prime},J^{\prime},\Xi_{(1)}^{\prime})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}Ψ(10)𝔽′\scriptstyle{\Psi_{(10)}^{{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}}
commutes up to homotopy. Therefore, the homotopy class only depends on the bimodule 𝔹{\mathbb{B}}.
13.3.3. Independence of the interpolation of Floer data
Next we would like to prove the homotopy independence of the bimodule 𝔹{\mathbb{B}}. Suppose 𝔹0{\mathbb{B}}_{0} and 𝔹1{\mathbb{B}}_{1} are two such bimodules over (𝔽;𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}). Since 𝔹0{\mathbb{B}}_{0} and 𝔹1{\mathbb{B}}_{1} are both defined via varying Floer data, one can construct a homotopy ℍ{\mathbb{H}} from 𝔹0{\mathbb{B}}_{0} to 𝔹1{\mathbb{B}}_{1}. Then by Proposition 15.4, one can find a pair of integral actions 𝒜𝔽Ω{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}}^{\Omega}, 𝒜𝔽′Ω{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}^{\Omega} compatible with respect to ℍ{\mathbb{H}}. This leads to the setup of Lemma 13.4. Let
C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ),\displaystyle\ CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi),\
C​F∗​(H′,J′,Ξ′)\displaystyle\ CF_{*}(H^{\prime},J^{\prime},\Xi^{\prime})
be Floer chain complexes constructed subject to these integral actions and let
Φ𝔹0​(Θ0),Φ𝔹1​(Θ1):C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ)→C​F∗​(H′,J′,Ξ′)\Phi^{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}}(\Theta_{0}),\ \Phi^{{\mathbb{B}}_{1}}(\Theta_{1}):CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi)\to CF_{*}(H^{\prime},J^{\prime},\Xi^{\prime})
be continuation maps associated to these two bimodules constructed as above. Then by Lemma 13.4, the two continuation maps are homotopic. This proves that the continuation map does not depend on the bimodule either.
13.3.4. Composition of continuation maps
We prove that the composition of continuation maps is homotopic to another continuation map.
Proposition 13.6.
Suppose 𝔽0,𝔽1,𝔽2{\mathbb{F}}_{0},{\mathbb{F}}_{1},{\mathbb{F}}_{2} are Floer flow categories associated to three pairs (Hi,Ji)(H_{i},J_{i}) for i=0,1,2i=0,1,2. Let 𝔹01{\mathbb{B}}_{01} resp. 𝔹12{\mathbb{B}}_{12} be a bimodule over (𝔽0;𝔽1)({\mathbb{F}}_{0};{\mathbb{F}}_{1}) resp. over (𝔽1;𝔽2)({\mathbb{F}}_{1};{\mathbb{F}}_{2}) associated to Floer data σ01\sigma_{01} resp. σ12\sigma_{12} on the infinite cylinder. Let ℍ{\mathbb{H}} be a homotopy associated to gluing σ01\sigma_{01} and σ12\sigma_{12}, as a homotopy from the composition 𝔹01∘𝔹12{\mathbb{B}}_{01}\circ{\mathbb{B}}_{12} to a bimodule 𝔹02{\mathbb{B}}_{02} over (𝔽0;𝔽2)({\mathbb{F}}_{0};{\mathbb{F}}_{2}) associated to a Floer datum σ02\sigma_{02}. Then there exist continuation maps
Φ𝔹01:C​F∗​(H0,J0,Ξ0)→C​F∗​(H1,J1,Ξ1)\Phi^{{\mathbb{B}}_{01}}:CF_{*}(H_{0},J_{0},\Xi_{0})\to CF_{*}(H_{1},J_{1},\Xi_{1})
Φ𝔹12:C​F∗​(H1,J1,Ξ1)→C​F∗​(H2,J2,Ξ2)\Phi^{{\mathbb{B}}_{12}}:CF_{*}(H_{1},J_{1},\Xi_{1})\to CF_{*}(H_{2},J_{2},\Xi_{2})
and
Φ𝔹02:C​F∗​(H0,J0,Ξ0)→C​F∗​(H2,J2,Ξ2)\Phi^{\mathbb{B}_{02}}:CF_{*}(H_{0},J_{0},\Xi_{0})\to CF_{*}(H_{2},J_{2},\Xi_{2})
such that the last one is homotopic to the composition Φ𝔹12∘Φ𝔹01\Phi^{{\mathbb{B}}_{12}}\circ\Phi^{\mathbb{B}_{01}}.
Proof.
By Proposition 15.4, we can choose integral actions on the three Floer categories which are compatible with respect to 𝔹01{\mathbb{B}}_{01}, 𝔹12{\mathbb{B}}_{12}, 𝔹02{\mathbb{B}}_{02}, and the homotopy ℍ{\mathbb{H}}. Then we are in the situation of Lemma 13.5, which implies the desired homotopy.
∎
13.3.5. Continuation maps are homotopy equivalences
Corollary 13.7.
Any chain-level continuation map is a homotopy equivalence.
Proof.
Using the notations in Proposition 13.6, take 𝔽2=𝔽0{\mathbb{F}}_{2}={\mathbb{F}}_{0} and denote 𝔹12{\mathbb{B}}_{12} by 𝔹10{\mathbb{B}}_{10}. Let 𝔹02{\mathbb{B}}_{02} be the diagonal bimodule Δ𝔽0​𝔽0\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{F}_{0}\mathbb{F}_{0}} associated to the trivial Floer datum on the cylinder. Choose a homotopy ℍ{\mathbb{H}} from 𝔹01∘𝔹10\mathbb{B}_{01}\circ\mathbb{B}_{10} to Δ𝔽0​𝔽0\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{F}_{0}\mathbb{F}_{0}} by gluing Floer data and varying in a one-parameter family, Proposition 13.6 provides a chain homotopy between the composition Φ01∘Φ10\Phi_{01}\circ\Phi_{10} and the chain map associated to an AMS lift of Δ𝔽0​𝔽0\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{F}_{0}\mathbb{F}_{0}}. Notice that the latter has the form
ΦΔ𝔽​𝔽=Id+higher​order​in​T\Phi^{{\mathbb{\Delta}}^{\mathbb{FF}}}={\rm Id}+{\rm higher\ order\ in\ }T
hence is an invertible chain map. Therefore, by a similar argument switching the roles of Φ01\Phi_{01} and Φ10\Phi_{10}, the continuation maps Φ01\Phi_{01} and Φ10\Phi_{10} are homotopy inverses to each other.
∎
Lastly, we prove
Corollary 13.8.
The chain map from C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ)→C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ)CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi)\to CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi) induced from an AMS lift of the diagonal bimodule Δ𝔽​𝔽\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}} is chain homotopic to the identity.
Proof.
The same argument of the proof of Lemma 13.1 also applies here, resulting in a chain map associated to an AMS lift of the bimodule Δ𝔽​𝔽\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}} of the form
Φ=Id+A.\Phi={\rm Id}+A.
Notice that Id{\rm Id} is also a chain map in this case. Now since Δ𝔽​𝔽∘Δ𝔽​𝔽\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}}\circ\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}} is homotopic to Δ𝔽​𝔽\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}}, Proposition 13.6 implies that
(Id+A)2−(Id+A)=A⁡(Id+A)=d​ρ+ρ​d({\rm Id}+A)^{2}-({\rm Id}+A)=A({\rm Id}+A)=d\rho+\rho d
for some linear map ρ\rho. As Id+A{\rm Id}+A is an invertible chain map, one has
A=(d​ρ+ρ​d)​(Id+A)−1=d⁡(ρ​(Id+A)−1)+(ρ​(Id+A)−1)​dA=(d\rho+\rho d)({\rm Id}+A)^{-1}=d(\rho({\rm Id}+A)^{-1})+(\rho({\rm Id}+A)^{-1})d
meaning that Id+A{\rm Id}+A is chain homotopic to Id{\rm Id}.
∎
13.4. Proof of Theorem C
13.4.1. Definition of the pair-of-pants products
The setting of Theorem C falls into Situation Module(i). Let Σ𝕏\Sigma^{\mathbb{X}} be a smooth pair-of-pants with two negative ends and one positive end equipped with a Floer datum which are asymptotic to H1​d​tH_{1}dt and H2​d​tH_{2}dt on the negative ends and to H′​d​tH^{\prime}dt on the positive end. To simplify the argument, use a fixed almost complex structure JJ; more general cases can be treated with the help of continuation maps. Hence we omit the reference to almost complex structures. Let 𝔽1,𝔽2,𝔽′{\mathbb{F}}_{1},{\mathbb{F}}_{2},{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} be the Floer flow categories associated to H1H_{1}, H2H_{2}, and H′H^{\prime} respectively.
We fix an outercollaring width and will not mention it anymore in this subsection. Let 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} be the multimodule associated to Σ𝕏\Sigma^{\mathbb{X}}. Then by Proposition 15.4, one can choose a triple of integral actions 𝒜𝔽1Ω,𝒜𝔽2Ω{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}_{1}}^{\Omega},{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}_{2}}^{\Omega}, 𝒜𝔽′Ω{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}^{\Omega}. Then one obtains Floer chain complexes
C​F∗​(H1,Ξ1),C​F∗​(H2,Ξ2),C​F∗​(H′,Ξ′)CF_{*}(H_{1},\Xi_{1}),CF_{*}(H_{2},\Xi_{2}),CF_{*}(H^{\prime},\Xi^{\prime})
which depend on the AMS lifts 𝔽~1,𝔽~2,𝔽~′\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\tilde{\mathbb{F}}_{2},\tilde{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime} subject to the integral actions and their FOP perturbations 𝔽̊1,𝔽̊2,𝔽̊′\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{1},\mathring{\mathbb{F}}_{2},\mathring{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}. Upon choosing a pair of lateral lines in Σ𝕏\Sigma^{\mathbb{X}}, the basic construction provides a chain map
Φ𝕏​(Θ):C​F∗​(H1,Ξ1)⊗C​F∗​(H2,Ξ2)→C​F∗​(H′,Ξ′)\Phi^{\mathbb{X}}(\Theta):CF_{*}(H_{1},\Xi_{1})\otimes CF_{*}(H_{2},\Xi_{2})\to CF_{*}(H^{\prime},\Xi^{\prime})
which depends on an AMS lift 𝕏~\tilde{\mathbb{X}} and an FOP perturbation 𝕏̊\mathring{\mathbb{X}}.
13.4.2. Well-defined homotopy class
Now we prove Part (1) of Theorem C. Similar to the case of continuation maps, by Lemma 13.2, the homotopy class of Φ𝕏​(Θ)\Phi^{{\mathbb{X}}}(\Theta) does not depend on choices made for constructing the AMS lift 𝕏~\tilde{\mathbb{X}} and FOP perturbation 𝕏̊\mathring{\mathbb{X}}, so a priori only depends on the integral actions and the choices of lateral lines. These dependence is removed (up to homotopy) by Lemma 13.3. Hence the homotopy class of Φ𝕏​(Θ)\Phi^{{\mathbb{X}}}(\Theta) a priori only depends on the Floer data defining 𝕏{\mathbb{X}}. Lastly, if 𝕏0{\mathbb{X}}_{0} and 𝕏1{\mathbb{X}}_{1} are multimodules defined by two different Floer data on the pair-of-pants (including different cylindrical ends), then one can build a homotopy ℍ{\mathbb{H}} from 𝕏0{\mathbb{X}}_{0} to 𝕏1{\mathbb{X}}_{1} by varying the Floer data. Then Lemma 13.4 implies that the corresponding chain maps Φ𝕏0​(Θ0)\Phi^{{\mathbb{X}}_{0}}(\Theta_{0}) and Φ𝕏1​(Θ1)\Phi^{{\mathbb{X}}_{1}}(\Theta_{1}) are also homotopic.
13.4.3. Compatibility with the continuation maps
We only treat the case with composing continuation maps at the positive end, and the other cases follow from the same reasoning. Let 𝔽′′{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime\prime} be a fourth Floer flow category associated to (H′′,J′′)(H^{\prime\prime},J^{\prime\prime}). We assume that the almost complex structure is fixed and drop it from the notation; the general case when JJ is domain-dependent can be treated using continuation maps. Let 𝔹𝔽′​𝔽′′\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{F}^{\prime}\mathbb{F}^{\prime\prime}} be a bimodule over (𝔽′;𝔽′′)({\mathbb{F}}^{\prime};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime\prime}) provided by continuation map Floer data on the cylinder. Consider the concatenation 𝕏∘𝔹𝔽′​𝔽′′{\mathbb{X}}\circ\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{F}^{\prime}\mathbb{F}^{\prime\prime}}. Then by gluing the Floer domains, one obtains a homotopy ℍ{\mathbb{H}} from 𝕏∘𝔹𝔽′​𝔽′′{\mathbb{X}}\circ\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{F}^{\prime}\mathbb{F}^{\prime\prime}} to a multimodule 𝕐{\mathbb{Y}} over (𝔽1,𝔽2,𝔽′′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},{\mathbb{F}}_{2};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime\prime}) defined on the pair-of-pants with another Floer datum.
Then by Proposition 15.4, one can choose integral actions on involved Floer flow categories which are compatible with respect to 𝕏\mathbb{X}, 𝔹𝔽′​𝔽′′\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{F}^{\prime}\mathbb{F}^{\prime\prime}}, 𝕐{\mathbb{Y}}, and ℍ{\mathbb{H}}. Then we are in the situation of Lemma 13.5, which provides specific chain complexes
C​F∗​(H1,Ξ1),C​F∗​(H2,Ξ2),C​F∗​(H′,Ξ′),C​F∗​(H′′,Ξ′′)CF_{*}(H_{1},\Xi_{1}),CF_{*}(H_{2},\Xi_{2}),CF_{*}(H^{\prime},\Xi^{\prime}),CF_{*}(H^{\prime\prime},\Xi^{\prime\prime})
chain maps
Φ𝕏:C​F∗​(H1,Ξ1)⊗C​F∗​(H2,Ξ2)→C​F∗​(H′,Ξ′),Φ𝔽′​𝔽′′:C​F∗​(H′,Ξ′)→C​F∗​(H′′,Ξ′′),Φ𝕐:C​F∗​(H1,Ξ1)⊗C​F∗​(H2,Ξ2)→C​F∗​(H′′,Ξ′′).\begin{split}\Phi^{\mathbb{X}}:CF_{*}(H_{1},\Xi_{1})\otimes CF_{*}(H_{2},\Xi_{2})\to&\ CF_{*}(H^{\prime},\Xi^{\prime}),\\
\Phi^{\mathbb{F}^{\prime}\mathbb{F}^{\prime\prime}}:CF_{*}(H^{\prime},\Xi^{\prime})\to&\ CF_{*}(H^{\prime\prime},\Xi^{\prime\prime}),\\
\Phi^{\mathbb{Y}}:CF_{*}(H_{1},\Xi_{1})\otimes CF_{*}(H_{2},\Xi_{2})\to&\ CF_{*}(H^{\prime\prime},\Xi^{\prime\prime}).\end{split}
The Lemma 13.5 shows that Φ𝕐\Phi^{\mathbb{Y}} is chain homotopic to the composition Φ𝔽′​𝔽′′∘Φ𝕏\Phi^{\mathbb{F}^{\prime}\mathbb{F}^{\prime\prime}}\circ\Phi^{\mathbb{X}}. This is Theorem C (2).
13.4.4. Associativity
Associativity follows from Lemma 13.4 and 13.5. In the notations of chain complexes, we drop the dependence on JJ.
Choose Hamiltonians H1,H2,H3,H′H_{1},H_{2},H_{3},H^{\prime}, H12H_{12}, H23H_{23} independently. One can build a homotopy of two concatenated multimodules as shown in Figure 7. One can choose integral actions on all involved Floer flow categories which are compatible with respect to this homotopy. Then apply Lemma 13.5 twice, one obtains the following diagram in which each triangle commutes up to homotopy.
C​F∗​(H1,Ξ1)⊗C​F∗​(H2,Ξ2)⊗C​F∗​(H3,Ξ3)\textstyle{CF_{*}(H_{1},\Xi_{1})\otimes CF_{*}(H_{2},\Xi_{2})\otimes CF_{*}(H_{3},\Xi_{3})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}C​F∗​(H1,Ξ1)⊗C​F∗​(H23,Ξ23)\textstyle{CF_{*}(H_{1},\Xi_{1})\otimes CF_{*}(H_{23},\Xi_{23})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}C​F∗​(H12,Ξ12)⊗C​F∗​(H3,Ξ3)\textstyle{CF_{*}(H_{12},\Xi_{12})\otimes CF_{*}(H_{3},\Xi_{3})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}C​F∗​(H′,Ξ′)\textstyle{CF_{*}(H^{\prime},\Xi^{\prime})}
Here the diagonal arrow is provided by a multimodule with three source flow categories. As the homotopy types of continuation maps are well-defined, the associativity is proved. This is Theorem C (3).
Figure 7. The homotopy between two concatenations.
13.4.5. Identity element
There is a natural multiplicative identity of the pair-of-pants product coming from the cigar bimodule (see Subsection 10.3.6). Let 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} be the Floer flow category associated to a nondegenerate Hamiltonian HH on the almost Kähler manifold (X,ω,J)(X,\omega,J). On the other hand, let 𝕆{\mathbb{O}} be the trivial flow category consisting of only one object. Then the cigar bimodule is a bimodule 𝔹𝕆​𝔽{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{OF}} associated to a Floer data on ℂ{\mathbb{C}} which is asymptotic to H​d​tHdt near ∞\infty. Then this is a special case of Situation Module(i).
By Proposition 15.4, one can choose an integral action 𝒜𝔽Ω{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{F}}^{\Omega} on 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} which is compatible with respect to 𝔹𝕆​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{OF}}. Choose an outercollaring width. Let
C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ)CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi)
be the associated Floer chain complex depending an AMS lift 𝔽~\tilde{\mathbb{F}} subject to the outercollaring width, the integral action, and an FOP perturbation 𝔽̊\mathring{\mathbb{F}}. The basic construction for multimodules then provides a chain map
Φ𝕆​𝔽​(Θ):ℤ≅C∗​(𝕆)→C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ)\Phi^{\mathbb{OF}}(\Theta):{\mathbb{Z}}\cong C_{*}({\mathbb{O}})\to CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi)
which depends on an AMS lift 𝔹~𝕆​𝔽\tilde{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{OF}} and an FOP perturbation 𝔹̊𝕆​𝔽\mathring{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{OF}}.
Following the same argument as before, one can prove that the homotopy class of the chain map Φ𝕆​𝔽​(Θ)\Phi^{\mathbb{OF}}(\Theta) is well-defined, independent of all choices as well as the Floer data responsible for the bimodule 𝔹𝕆​𝔽{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{OF}}. Moreover, Φ𝕆​𝔽​(Θ)\Phi^{\mathbb{OF}}(\Theta) is compatible with continuation maps up to homotopy. As the differential of C∗​(𝕆)C_{*}(\mathbb{O}) is trivial, the image of 1∈ℤ1\in{\mathbb{Z}} is closed and its homology class is well-defined. Therefore, one obtains a well-defined element
𝟏∈H​F∗​(X,ω,ΛℤΠ).{\bf 1}\in HF_{*}(X,\omega;\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\Pi}).
We prove that 𝟏{\bf 1} is the multiplicative identity. This follows from a particular concatenation of multimodules and Lemma 13.5. Consider the concatenation of the bimodule 𝔹𝕆​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{OF}} with a multimodule 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} over (𝔽,𝔽′,𝔽′′)({\mathbb{F}},{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime\prime}) for pair-of-pants product. One can see that by gluing the Floer data, the concatenation is homotopic to a bimodule for continuation map 𝔹𝔽′​𝔽′′\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{F}^{\prime}\mathbb{F}^{\prime\prime}}, hence a special case of Situation Glue(i). Therefore, by following similar argument as previous situations where gluing is concerned, one can prove that 𝟏{\bf 1} is a multiplicative identity. We omit the details. This is Theorem C (4) and we conclude the proof.
13.5. Proof of Theorem D
We establish the Floer-theoretic Poincaré duality. Consider the punctured Riemann sphere ΣPD\Sigma^{\rm PD} which has two negative ends and no positive end. A Floer datum whose restrictions to the two negative ends are (Hi​d​t,Ji)(H_{i}dt,J_{i}), i=1,2i=1,2, leads to the multimodule 𝕏P​D{\mathbb{X}}^{PD} over (𝔽1,𝔽2,𝕆~)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},{\mathbb{F}}_{2};\tilde{\mathbb{O}}) where 𝕆~\tilde{\mathbb{O}} is the Π\Pi-covering of the trivial flow category 𝕆{\mathbb{O}}. In particular, Ob​𝕆~≅Π{\rm Ob}\tilde{\mathbb{O}}\cong\Pi.
Now we define hte Poincaré pairing on the chain level. By Proposition 15.4, one can choose integral actions on 𝔽1{\mathbb{F}}_{1}, 𝔽2{\mathbb{F}}_{2} compatible with respect to 𝕏PD{\mathbb{X}}^{\rm PD}. Fix an outercollaring width. By Theorem A, one obtains chain complexes
C​F∗​(H1,J1,Ξ1),C​F∗​(H2,J2,Ξ2).CF_{*}(H_{1},J_{1},\Xi_{1}),\ CF_{*}(H_{2},J_{2},\Xi_{2}).
Then the general construction of chain maps provided in Subsection 13.2 provides
ΦPD:C​F∗​(H1,J1,Ξ1)⊗C​F∗​(H2,J2,Ξ2)→C∗​(𝕆~)≅ΛΠ.\Phi^{\rm PD}:CF_{*}(H_{1},J_{1},\Xi_{1})\otimes CF_{*}(H_{2},J_{2},\Xi_{2})\to C_{*}(\tilde{\mathbb{O}})\cong\Lambda^{\Pi}.
In the same way as proving independence of choices, one can see that ΦPD\Phi^{\rm PD} has a well-defined homotopy type which does not depend on choices made for the AMS construction and FOP perturbations. It is also compatible with continuation maps, and compatible with the comparison between different choices of integral actions (here we do not need lateral lines). Hence the Poincaré pairing is well-defined.
We need to prove the compatibility between the Poincaré pairing and the pair-of-pants product. In fact this is similar to the proof of the associativity of the pair-of-pants product, using the concatenation of a multimodule 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} (for the pair-of-pants products) and 𝕏PD{\mathbb{X}}^{\rm PD} and a gluing construction, utilizing Lemma 13.4 and Lemma 13.5. We omit the details.
Lastly, we prove the nondegeneracy of the Poincaré pairing with field coefficients. We only need to prove it on the homology level. We make use of the PSS map Φ𝕄​𝔽\Phi^{\mathbb{MF}} regarded as a map on homology. One can see that the composition
ΦPD∘(Φ𝕄​𝔽⊗Φ𝕄​𝔽)\Phi^{\rm PD}\circ(\Phi^{\mathbb{MF}}\otimes\Phi^{\mathbb{MF}})
is a bilinear pairing on H∗​(M,Λ𝐊Π)H_{*}(M;\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi}). The pairing has a leading order term which can be identified with the classical Poincaré pairing on the integral homology of XX. Hence the induced pairing is still nondegenerate on the Morse homology (tensoring with Λ𝐊Π\Lambda_{\bf K}^{\Pi}). As the PSS map is an isomorphism on homology (Theorem F), it implies that the Poincaré pairing on the Floer homology is also nondegenerate. This finishes the proof of Theorem D.
13.6. Proof of Theorem E
The definition of the PSS and the SSP maps are simply special cases of general chain maps induced from bimodules. Fix a Floer flow category 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} on (X,ω)(X,\omega) associated to a pair (H,J)(H,J). To simplify the argument we assume JJ is time-independent; the general case can be treated with continuation maps. The same data provide the diagonal bimodule Δ𝔽​𝔽\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}}. Choose a Morse–Smale pair (f,g)(f,g) on MM. Then one has the Morse flow category 𝕄{\mathbb{M}} associated to (f,g)(f,g). Choosing an interpolation between HH and 00, one obtains a Floer-to-Morse bimodule 𝔹𝔽​𝕄\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{FM}}; a backward interpolation provides a Morse-to-Floer bimodule 𝔹𝕄​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{MF}}.
Fix a common outercollaring width. Choose an integral action 𝒜𝔽Ω{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{F}}^{\Omega} on 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} which are compatible with all bimodules and homotopies involved in the discussion. Then Theorem A provides a Floer complex C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ)CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi) depending on choices, which involve an AMS lift 𝔽~\tilde{\mathbb{F}} subject to the outercollaring width and the integral action, and an FOP perturbation 𝔽̊\mathring{\mathbb{F}}. Then by Theorem S, one can find AMS lifts 𝔹~𝕄​𝔽\tilde{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{MF}} and 𝔹~𝔽​𝕄\tilde{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{FM}} (which are enriched in ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯NCrig{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}^{\rm NC}_{\rm rig}) of 𝔹𝕄​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{MF}} and 𝔹𝔽​𝕄\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{FM}}. Notice that ⌊𝕄{}_{\lfloor}{\mathbb{M}} can be viewed as enriched in ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigFOP{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm FOP}. Then the FOP perturbation 𝔽̊\mathring{\mathbb{F}} can be extended, by Theorem N, to an FOP perturbation 𝔹̊𝕄​𝔽\mathring{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{MF}} and an FOP perturbation 𝔹̊𝔽​𝕄\mathring{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{FM}}. Then one obtains chain maps
Φ𝕄​𝔽:C​M∗​(f,g)→C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ),\displaystyle\ \Phi^{\mathbb{MF}}:CM_{*}(f,g)\to CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi),\
Φ𝔽​𝕄:C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ)→C​M∗​(f,g).\displaystyle\ \Phi^{\mathbb{FM}}:CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi)\to CM_{*}(f,g).
We call them the chain-level PSS map and the chain-level SSP map.
Using similar argument as the case of continuation maps, based on part of Theorem S and Theorem 12.6, one can show that the homotopy classes of the PSS and SSP maps are independent of the choices made for constructing the AMS lifts or the FOP lifts. Moreover, using homotopies realized by gluing Floer cylinders, one can show that the PSS and SSP maps are compatible with continuation maps. Namely, the composition of a chain-level PSS map resp. a chain-level SSP map with a chain-level continuation map (in the right way) is homotopic to a chain-level PSS resp. a chain-level SSP map. This finishes the proof of Theorem E.
13.7. Proof of Theorem F
To prove Theorem F, what remains to show is that the PSS and SSP maps are chain homotopy equivalences. We remind the reader again that the PSS and SSP maps are not known to be homotopy inverses to each other. To make the comparison, we need to go through the pearly flow category ℙ\mathbb{P}.
Keep the data fixed in the proof of Theorem E. Then the Morse–Smale pair (f,g)(f,g) and the almost complex structure JJ also determines the pearly flow category ℙ\mathbb{P} (see Subsection 9.3). Meanwhile, one has the diagonal bimodules
Δ𝔽​𝔽,Δ𝕄​𝕄,Δℙ​ℙ\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}},\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{MM}},\ \mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{PP}}
and the Morse-to-pearly bimodule 𝔹𝕄​ℙ\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{MP}}, pearly-to-Morse bimodule 𝔹ℙ​𝕄\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{PM}}. Using the same Floer data on the infinite cylinder defining the bimodules 𝔹𝕄​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{MF}}, 𝔹𝔽​𝕄\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{FM}} also provides the Floer-to-pearly bimodule 𝔹𝔽​ℙ\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{FP}} and the pearly-to-Floer bimodule 𝔹ℙ​𝔽\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{PF}}. Moreover, one can build homotopies realizing the commutativity-up-to-homotopy of each triangle of the diagram (11.1).
Fix an outercollaring width. Choose an integral action on 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} which is compatible with respect to all involved bimodules and homotopies. Then upon making choices, one obtains the Floer chain complex C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ)CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi) by Theorem A and the PSS and SSP maps as in the proof of Theorem E.
Moreover, by Theorem 12.7, upon making choices, one can construct an AMS lift of the outercollaring of ℙ{\mathbb{P}} to ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm NC}, denoted by ℙ~\tilde{\mathbb{P}}. By choosing an FOP perturbation ℙ̊\mathring{\mathbb{P}} (granted by Theorem N), one obtains a chain complex
C​P∗​(f,g,J,Θ)CP_{*}(f,g,J,\Theta)
where Θ\Theta represents all the choices, including the outercollaring width, the integral symplectic form contained in 𝒜𝔽Ω{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{F}}^{\Omega}, the choices made for constructing ℙ~\tilde{\mathbb{P}}, and the FOP perturbation. Then Theorem 12.7 also provides a lift Δ~ℙ​ℙ\tilde{\mathbb{\Delta}}^{\mathbb{PP}} of the outercollaring of Δℙ​ℙ\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{PP}} as a bimodule over (ℙ~;ℙ~)(\tilde{\mathbb{P}};\tilde{\mathbb{P}}). Then Theorem N allows us to extend the FOP perturbations ℙ̊\mathring{\mathbb{P}} to an FOP perturbation Δ̊ℙ​ℙ\mathring{\mathbb{\Delta}}^{\mathbb{PP}}. Then one obtains a chain map
Φℙ​ℙ:C​P∗​(f,g,J,Θ)→C​P∗​(f,g,J,Θ).\Phi^{\mathbb{PP}}:CP_{*}(f,g,J,\Theta)\to CP_{*}(f,g,J,\Theta).
Based on the above constructions and choices, Theorem T guarantees the existence of chain maps
Φ𝔽​ℙ:C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ)→C​P∗​(f,g,J,Θ),\displaystyle\ \Phi^{\mathbb{FP}}:CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi)\to CP_{*}(f,g,J,\Theta),\
Φℙ​𝔽:C​P∗​(f,g,J,Θ)→C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ).\displaystyle\ \Phi^{\mathbb{PF}}:CP_{*}(f,g,J,\Theta)\to CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi).
and
Φℙ​𝕄:C​P∗​(f,g,J,Θ)→C​M∗​(f,g)⊗ΛΠ,\displaystyle\ \Phi^{\mathbb{PM}}:CP_{*}(f,g,J,\Theta)\to CM_{*}(f,g)\otimes\Lambda^{\Pi},\
Φ𝕄​ℙ:C​M∗​(f,g)⊗ΛΠ→C​P∗​(f,g,J,Θ).\displaystyle\ \Phi^{\mathbb{MP}}:CM_{*}(f,g)\otimes\Lambda^{\Pi}\to CP_{*}(f,g,J,\Theta).
Lemma 13.9.
Φ𝔽​𝕄\Phi^{\mathbb{FM}} is chain homotopic to Φℙ​𝕄∘Φ𝔽​ℙ\Phi^{\mathbb{PM}}\circ\Phi^{\mathbb{FP}} and Φ𝕄​𝔽\Phi^{\mathbb{MF}} is chain homotopic to Φℙ​𝔽∘Φ𝕄​ℙ\Phi^{\mathbb{PF}}\circ\Phi^{\mathbb{MP}}.
Proof.
One has fixed a specific homotopy ℍ\mathbb{H} from the concatenation 𝔹𝔽​ℙ∘𝔹ℙ​𝕄\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{FP}}\circ\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{PM}} to 𝔹𝔽​𝕄\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{FM}}. By Theorem 12.4, there exists a concatenation 𝔹~𝔽​ℙ∘𝔹~ℙ​𝕄\tilde{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{FP}}\circ\tilde{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{PM}} enriched in ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm NC}. Then by Theorem 19.5, there exists a lift ℍ~\tilde{\mathbb{H}} of the outercollaring of ℍ{\mathbb{H}} to ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm NC} as a homotopy from 𝔹~𝔽​ℙ∘𝔹~ℙ​𝕄\tilde{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{FP}}\circ\tilde{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{PM}} to 𝔹~𝔽​𝕄\tilde{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{FM}}. Moreover, Proposition 8.6 allows us to have a concatenation 𝔹̊𝔽​ℙ∘𝔹̊ℙ​𝕄\mathring{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{FP}}\circ\mathring{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{PM}}. Then Theorem N allows us to extend this concatenation and the FOP perturbation 𝔹̊𝔽​𝕄\mathring{\mathbb{B}}^{\mathbb{FM}} to an FOP perturbation ℍ̊\mathring{\mathbb{H}} on ℍ~\tilde{\mathbb{H}}. Then one obtains a chain homotopy between Φ𝔽​𝕄\Phi^{\mathbb{FM}} to Φℙ​𝕄∘Φ𝔽​ℙ\Phi^{\mathbb{PM}}\circ\Phi^{\mathbb{FP}}. The other chain homotopy can be established in the same way.
∎
Lemma 13.10.
Φ𝔽​ℙ\Phi^{\mathbb{FP}} and Φℙ​𝔽\Phi^{\mathbb{PF}} are invertible after passing to homology.
Proof.
Similar to the above lemma, by Theorem T, using FOP perturbations, one obtains a chain homotopy between Φℙ​𝔽∘Φ𝔽​ℙ\Phi^{\mathbb{PF}}\circ\Phi^{\mathbb{FP}} and the chain-level continuation map associated to the diagonal bimodule Δ𝔽​𝔽\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{FF}}, which is invertible after passing to homology. Via the reversed gluing along the Floer flow category, one obtains a chain homotopy between Φ𝔽​ℙ∘Φℙ​𝔽\Phi^{\mathbb{FP}}\circ\Phi^{\mathbb{PF}} and the chain map Φℙ​ℙ\Phi^{\mathbb{PP}} associated to the diagonal bimodule Δℙ​ℙ\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{PP}}, which is also invertible. Hence Φℙ​𝔽\Phi^{\mathbb{PF}} and Φ𝔽​ℙ\Phi^{\mathbb{FP}} are both invertible after passing to homology.
∎
Lemma 13.11.
Φℙ​𝕄\Phi^{\mathbb{PM}} and Φ𝕄​ℙ\Phi^{\mathbb{MP}} are invertible chain maps.
Proof.
Notice that the objects of ℙ\mathbb{P} and 𝕄\mathbb{M} are identical. Moreover, both Φℙ​𝕄\Phi^{\mathbb{PM}} and Φ𝕄​ℙ\Phi^{\mathbb{MP}} have leading order term being the identity map. Hence both these two chain maps are invertible.
∎
Now by the previous three lemmas, Φ𝔽​𝕄\Phi^{\mathbb{FM}} and Φ𝕄​𝔽\Phi^{\mathbb{MF}} are chain homotopic to invertible chain maps. Hence they are chain homotopy equivalences. This finishes the proof of Theorem F.
13.8. Proof of Theorem G
By Hofer–Salamon [35] and Ono [50] (see also [23] and [46]), one can choose a time-independent JJ and suitable nondegenerate HH satisfying
(1)
All simple nonconstant JJ-holomorphic sphere u:S2→Xu:S^{2}\to X is transverse.
(2)
When deg⁡(p)−deg⁡(q)≤1{\rm deg}(p)-{\rm deg}(q)\leq 1, Mp​q𝔽M_{pq}^{{\mathbb{F}}} is transverse and consists of stable Floer trajectories without sphere bubbles.
(3)
When deg⁡(p)−deg⁡(q)=0{\rm deg}(p)-{\rm deg}(q)=0, Mp​q𝔽M_{pq}^{{\mathbb{F}}} consists of maps defined over smooth cylinders.
To proceed, one needs to carefully make choices when constructing the AMS lift 𝔽~\tilde{\mathbb{F}}, especially the smooth structure. Choose an outercollaring width and an integral action on 𝔽{\mathbb{F}}. Let 𝔽^\hat{\mathbb{F}} be a relatively NC AMS lift of 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} to ⌊𝐒rel​𝐊𝐮𝐫¯rigNC{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf S^{\rm rel}Kur}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm NC}. Let Kp​q=(Gp​q,Vp​q/Bp​q,Ep​q,Sp​q)K_{pq}=(G_{pq},V_{pq}/B_{pq},E_{pq},S_{pq}) be the corresponding relative Kuranishi space.
Notice that for pair p<qp<q, there is an open subset
M̊p​q𝔽⊆Mp​q𝔽\mathring{M}_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}\subseteq M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}
corresponding to smooth Floer trajectories. By the above assumption on HH and JJ, we see that when deg⁡(p)−deg⁡(q)≤0{\rm deg}(p)-{\rm deg}(q)\leq 0, Mp​q𝔽=M̊p​q𝔽M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}=\mathring{M}_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}. There is also the corresponding open subset
V̊p​q/B̊p​q.\mathring{V}_{pq}/\mathring{B}_{pq}.
We know that V̊p​q\mathring{V}_{pq} has a canonical smooth structure such that the map V̊p​q→B̊p​q\mathring{V}_{pq}\to\mathring{B}_{pq} is a smooth submersion. Moreover, S̊p​q:=Sp​q|V̊p​q\mathring{S}_{pq}:=S_{pq}|_{\mathring{V}_{pq}} is smooth.
Recall that the stable smoothing of 𝔽^\hat{\mathbb{F}} should be given by a Gp​qG_{pq}-smoothing on stabilizations V^p​q:=Vp​q×Wp​q\hat{V}_{pq}:=V_{pq}\times W_{pq} where Wp​qW_{pq} is a linear representation of Gp​qG_{pq}. The open set V̊p​q×Wp​q\mathring{V}_{pq}\times W_{pq} has a canonical smooth structure.
Lemma 13.12.
There exists a stable smoothing 𝔽^^\hat{\vphantom{\rule{1.0pt}{5.71527pt}}\smash{\hat{\mathbb{F}}}} of 𝔽^\hat{\mathbb{F}} satisfying the following conditions. If p<qp<q and deg⁡(p)≤deg⁡(q){\rm deg}(p)\leq{\rm deg}(q), then V^p​q\hat{V}_{pq} is equivariantly diffeomorphic to V̊p​q×Wp​q\mathring{V}_{pq}\times W_{pq} near Sp​q−1​(0)S_{pq}^{-1}(0). In particular, the stabilization S^p​q\hat{S}_{pq} is smooth near its zero locus and transverse in the classical sense.
Proof.
This is because the smoothing can be done locally and extend (cf. [14, Theorem B.3]).
∎
Now consider the AMS lift 𝔽~\tilde{\mathbb{F}} of the outercollaring of 𝔽{\mathbb{F}}. In order to define the Floer chain complex using FOP transverse perturbations, one needs to construct the perturbations inductively.
Lemma 13.13.
There exists an FOP perturbation 𝔽̊\mathring{\mathbb{F}} of 𝔽~\tilde{\mathbb{F}} satisfying the following conditions. Let 𝒮p​q′:𝒰p​q→ℰp​q{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}^{\prime}:{\mathcal{U}}_{pq}\to{\mathcal{E}}_{pq} be the FOP transverse perturbation. If p<qp<q and deg⁡(p)−deg⁡(q)≤0{\rm deg}(p)-{\rm deg}(q)\leq 0, then (𝒮p​q′)−1​(0)=(𝒮p​q)−1​(0)({\mathcal{S}}_{pq}^{\prime})^{-1}(0)=({\mathcal{S}}_{pq})^{-1}(0) and 𝒮p​q′{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}^{\prime} agrees with 𝒮p​q{\mathcal{S}}_{pq} near the zero locus.
Proof.
For the proof, except for the conditions listed in the statement, we further ask that for any p<qp<q such that deg⁡(p)<deg⁡(q){\rm deg}(p)<{\rm deg}(q), the FOP transverse perturbation satisfies ‖𝒮p​q′−𝒮p​q‖C0<12​‖𝒮p​q‖C0\|{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}_{pq}-{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}\|_{C^{0}}<\frac{1}{2}\|{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}\|_{C^{0}}. We consider the inductive procedure provided in the proof of Theorem N. Consider a pair p<qp<q. Let 𝒟p​q=(𝒰p​q,ℰp​q,𝒮p​q){\mathcal{D}}_{pq}=({\mathcal{U}}_{pq},{\mathcal{E}}_{pq},{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}) be the normally complex derived orbifold obtained from the AMS construction.
For the base case of the induction argument, we assume that (p,q)(p,q) is minimal, i.e., Mp​q𝔽M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}} does not contain broken trajectories. Then we can choose an FOP transverse perturbation 𝒮p​q′{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}^{\prime} independent of other pairs. In this case, if deg⁡(p)−deg⁡(q)<0{\rm deg}(p)-{\rm deg}(q)<0, note that 𝒮p​q{\mathcal{S}}_{pq} is nowhere vanishing. Using the C0C^{0}-density of FOP sections (cf. Theorem 8.2), via a partition-of-unity argument, we can choose a smooth FOP transverse perturbation 𝒮p​q′{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}_{pq} such that ‖𝒮p​q′−𝒮p​q‖C0<12​‖𝒮p​q‖C0\|{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}_{pq}-{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}\|_{C^{0}}<\frac{1}{2}\|{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}\|_{C^{0}}. Then, in particular, 𝒮p​q{\mathcal{S}}_{pq} is nowhere vanishing. If deg⁡(p)=deg⁡(q){\rm deg}(p)={\rm deg}(q), then 𝒮p​q{\mathcal{S}}_{pq} vanishes at finitely many points which correspond to smooth solutions to the Floer equation. In this case, our stable smoothing for such Kuranishi spaces carry the original smooth structure (see Lemma 13.12), the original section 𝒮p​q{\mathcal{S}}_{pq} is smooth near the zero locus and transverse in the classical sense. Moreover, 𝒰p​q{\mathcal{U}}_{pq} is a manifold near its zero locus. Hence (Classical Transversality) condition of Theorem 8.2, 𝒮p​q{\mathcal{S}}_{pq} is also FOP transverse near the zero loucs. Hence one can choose 𝒮p​q′{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}^{\prime} to agree with 𝒮p​q{\mathcal{S}}_{pq} near its zero locus without creating more zeroes. If deg⁡(p)−deg⁡(q)≥1{\rm deg}(p)-{\rm deg}(q)\geq 1, we choose an arbitrary FOP transverse perturbation 𝒮p​q′{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}^{\prime}.
Inductively, suppose we have chosen FOP transverse perturbations 𝒮r​s′{\mathcal{S}}_{rs}^{\prime} satisfying our requirement for all pairs r,sr,s such that 𝒜H​(r)−𝒜H​(s)<𝒜H​(p)−𝒜H​(q){\mathcal{A}}_{H}(r)-{\mathcal{A}}_{H}(s)<{\mathcal{A}}_{H}(p)-{\mathcal{A}}_{H}(q). To continue the induction, we analyze the induced perturbation near the boundary strata of 𝒰p​q{\mathcal{U}}_{pq}. We first consider the case when deg⁡(p)−deg⁡(q)<0{\rm deg}(p)-{\rm deg}(q)<0. For any triple p<r<qp<r<q, one of the factors of Mp​r𝔽×Mr​q𝔽M_{pr}^{\mathbb{F}}\times M_{rq}^{\mathbb{F}} has negative virtual dimension. Without loss of generality, we can assume that deg⁡(p)−deg⁡(r)<0{\rm deg}(p)-{\rm deg}(r)<0. By the inductive hypothesis, we know that ‖𝒮p​r−𝒮p​r′‖C0<12​‖𝒮p​r‖C0\|{\mathcal{S}}_{pr}-{\mathcal{S}}_{pr}^{\prime}\|_{C^{0}}<\frac{1}{2}\|{\mathcal{S}}_{pr}\|_{C^{0}}. By the compatibility requirement, the putative perturbation 𝒮p​q′{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}^{\prime} is obtained from 𝒮p​r′×𝒮r​q′{\mathcal{S}}_{pr}^{\prime}\times{\mathcal{S}}_{rq}^{\prime} via a stabilization, which implies that the condition ‖𝒮p​q′−𝒮p​q‖C0<12​‖𝒮p​q‖C0\|{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}_{pq}-{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}\|_{C^{0}}<\frac{1}{2}\|{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}\|_{C^{0}} is already met near the boundary stratum ∂p​r​q𝒰p​q\partial^{prq}{\mathcal{U}}_{pq}. Because this induced section is nowhere vanishing, it is FOP transverse. Then we can apply the (Extension Property) of Theorem 8.2 together with the C0C^{0}-density of FOP transverse perturbations to construct 𝒮p​q′{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}_{pq} which argees with the induced section near ∂p​r​q𝒰p​q\partial^{prq}{\mathcal{U}}_{pq} with ‖𝒮p​q′−𝒮p​q‖C0<12​‖𝒮p​q‖C0\|{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}_{pq}-{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}\|_{C^{0}}<\frac{1}{2}\|{\mathcal{S}}_{pq}\|_{C^{0}}. In particular, we see that 𝒮p​q′{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}_{pq} is nowhere vanishing.
As for the case deg⁡(p)=deg⁡(q){\rm deg}(p)={\rm deg}(q), if we have p<r<qp<r<q, we can similarly analyze the induced section near ∂p​r​q𝒰p​q\partial^{prq}{\mathcal{U}}_{pq} to see that it is nowhere vanishing near ∂p​r​q𝒰p​q\partial^{prq}{\mathcal{U}}_{pq}. As for the interior part of 𝒰p​q{\mathcal{U}}_{pq}, similar to the above discussion, we know that the original section 𝒮p​q{\mathcal{S}}_{pq} vanishes at finitely many points, near which the Kuranishi spaces carry the original smooth structure with respect to which 𝒮p​q{\mathcal{S}}_{pq} is smooth, thereby being an FOP transverse section. So we can choose the perturbation 𝒮p​q′{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}_{pq} to agree with 𝒮p​q{\mathcal{S}}_{pq} near 𝒮p​q−1​(0){\mathcal{S}}^{-1}_{pq}(0) and to satisfy the inductive compatibility near the boundary strata such that (𝒮)p​q−1​(0)=(𝒮′)p​q−1​(0)({\mathcal{S}})^{-1}_{pq}(0)=({\mathcal{S}}^{\prime})^{-1}_{pq}(0).
Finally, if deg⁡(p)−deg⁡(q)≥1{\rm deg}(p)-{\rm deg}(q)\geq 1, we choose 𝒮p​q′{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}_{pq} such that it satisfies the compatibility condition near the boundary strata as in the proof of Theorem N. This finishes the inductive step and we conclude the proof.
∎
Proof of Theorem G.
By Lemma 13.13, there exists an FOP transverse perturbation 𝔽̊\mathring{\mathbb{F}} such that the associated counts (with respect to the natural orientations) of zeros coincides with the counts of zero-dimensional moduli spaces using the classical method. Then the chain complexes defined using the FOP perturbation agrees with the classical one.
∎
13.9. Proof of Theorem L
We verify each item of Theorem L. In fact the verification is similar to the case of Hamiltonian Floer spectral invariants defined via the Floer chain complex over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}} (see for example [26]). The argument here is a rather straightforward adaptation to the current setting.
(1)
The (Spectrality) follows from Usher’s abstract result (Theorem 7.39). Notice that the argument requires that C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ)CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi) is a Floer–Novikov complex, which is proved in Proposition 7.38.
(2)
The (Shifting property) follows from the fact that the multiplication by a∈ΛRΠa\in\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi} is an isomorphism of chain complexes from C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ)≤τCF_{*}(H,J,\Xi)^{\leq\tau} to C​F∗​(H,J,Ξ)≤τ−𝔳⁡(a)CF_{*}(H,J,\Xi)^{\leq\tau-\mathfrak{v}(a)}.
(3)
The (Lipschitz Continuity) is a straightforward consequence of Theorem K (2), where we recall that the Hofer distance between Hamiltonians H1H_{1} and H2H_{2} is
∫01maxx∈M⁡(H1​(x,t)−H2​(x,t))​𝑑t−∫01minx∈M⁡(H1​(x,t)−H2​(x,t))​𝑑t,\int_{0}^{1}\max_{x\in M}(H_{1}(x,t)-H_{2}(x,t))dt-\int_{0}^{1}\min_{x\in M}(H_{1}(x,t)-H_{2}(x,t))dt,
which is an upper bound for the threshold (cf. Definition 7.41) of the continuation maps.
(4)
The (Isotopy invariance) following from the continuation map construction. Let H1,H2H_{1},H_{2} induce the same Hamiltonian isotopy ϕ~∈H​am~​(X,ω)\tilde{\phi}\in{\rm H}\widetilde{\rm am}(X,\omega) and J1J_{1}, J2J_{2} be two ω\omega-compatible almost complex structure. Then there exists a Floer data on the infinite cylinder connecting H1​d​tH_{1}dt and H2​d​tH_{2}dt and a family of compatible almost complex structures connecting J1J_{1} and J2J_{2}. Let 𝔽1,𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{1},\mathbb{F}_{2} be the associated Floer flow categories. Then the Floer data described here defines a bimodule 𝔹12{\mathbb{B}}_{12} from 𝔽1{\mathbb{F}}_{1} to 𝔽2{\mathbb{F}}_{2}. Theorem P together with the FOP perturbation provides a chain map
Φ𝔹01:C​F∗​(H1,J1,Ξ1)→C​F∗​(H2,J2,Ξ2).\Phi^{\mathbb{B}_{01}}:CF_{*}(H_{1},J_{1},\Xi_{1})\to CF_{*}(H_{2},J_{2},\Xi_{2}).
The Hamiltonian connection can be chosen to be flat precisely because the Hamiltonian isotopies induced from H1H_{1} and H2H_{2} are isotopic. Hence the threshold of the chain map Φ𝔹01\Phi^{\mathbb{B}_{01}} (Definition 7.41) is zero. The same is true for a continuation map in the reversed direction. Hence we obtain the equality between the spectral numbers.
(5)
For the (Symplectic invariance) property, fix a symplectomorphism ρ:X→X\rho:X\to X. Let JρJ_{\rho} and HρH_{\rho} be the pullback almost complex structure and Hamiltonian. Let 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} resp. 𝔽ρ{\mathbb{F}}_{\rho} be the Floer flow category associated to (H,J)(H,J) resp. (Hρ,Jρ)(H_{\rho},J_{\rho}). Then ρ\rho induces an isomorphism of Floer flow categories 𝔽→𝔽ρ\mathbb{F}\to\mathbb{F}_{\rho}. The the AMS+FOP construction for 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} can be pulled back to 𝔽ρ\mathbb{F}_{\rho}, providing an isomorphic chain complex C​F∗​(Hρ,Jρ,Ξρ)CF_{*}(H_{\rho},J_{\rho},\Xi_{\rho}). This isomorphism also preserves the symplectic action and the filtration on the chain complexes.
(6)
The (Triangle inequality) follows from the chain-level pair-of-pants product construction provided by Theorem C. Let H1,H2H_{1},H_{2} be nondegenerate Hamiltonians generating ϕ~1,ϕ~2∈H​am~​(X,ω)\tilde{\phi}_{1},\tilde{\phi}_{2}\in{\rm H}\widetilde{\rm am}(X,\omega) such that ϕ~1∘ϕ~2\tilde{\phi}_{1}\circ\tilde{\phi}_{2} is also nondegenerate. Then there is a composition H1​♮​H2H_{1}\natural H_{2} generating the composition ϕ~1∘ϕ~2\tilde{\phi}_{1}\circ\tilde{\phi}_{2}. Moreover, on the pair-of-pants Σpants\Sigma^{\rm pants}, there exists a flat Hamiltonian connection σ\sigma which converges to H1​d​tH_{1}dt, H2​d​tH_{2}dt on the two negative ends and converges to H3​d​t:=H1​♮​H2​d​tH_{3}dt:=H_{1}\natural H_{2}dt on the positive ends. Let 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} be the corresponding multimodule, which is an equivariant Novikov multimodule. Let 𝔽i{\mathbb{F}}_{i}, i=1,2,3i=1,2,3 be the Floer flow categories associated to HiH_{i}. Then it is well-known that the curvature of σ\sigma gives the threshold of the Novikov multimodule (Definition 7.41), and the curvature can be taken to be zero. Therefore, by Proposition 7.42, one has
c𝔽3​(𝔵1⋆𝔵2)≤c𝔽1​(𝔵1)+c𝔽2​(𝔵2).c_{{\mathbb{F}}_{3}}({\mathfrak{x}}_{1}\star{\mathfrak{x}}_{2})\leq c_{{\mathbb{F}}_{1}}({\mathfrak{x}}_{1})+c_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}({\mathfrak{x}}_{2}).
(7)
The (Poincaré duality) property follows from the chain-level construction of the Poincaré duality and the spectral invariant continuatity result (Proposition 7.42). The argument also follows that of [51, Lemma 5.1].
Fix an almost complex structure JJ and omit it from the argument from now on. Let HH be a nondegenerate Hamiltonian on XX and 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} be the associated Floer flow category. Let H¯\overline{H} be the reversal of HH, which has an induced Floer flow category 𝔽¯\overline{\mathbb{F}}. Then on the domain Σℙ​𝔻\Sigma^{\mathbb{PD}} which has two negative ends and no positive end, there exists a flat Hamiltonian connection σℙ​𝔻\sigma^{\mathbb{PD}} which is H​d​tHdt on one end and H¯​d​t\overline{H}dt on the other. Consider this specific Poincaré duality multimodule 𝕏ℙ​𝔻{\mathbb{X}}^{\mathbb{PD}} (over (𝔽,𝔽¯,𝕆)({\mathbb{F}},\overline{{\mathbb{F}}};{\mathbb{O}})). Notice that the involved moduli spaces are identical to moduli spaces for the diagonal bimodule Δ𝔽​𝔽\mathbb{\Delta}^{\mathbb{F}{\mathbb{F}}}.
Notice that 𝕆{\mathbb{O}} contains a special object, or rather a subcategory 𝕆¯\underline{\smash{\mathbb{O}}} corresponding to the trivial element of Π\Pi. Let 𝕏0PD{\mathbb{X}}_{0}^{\rm PD} be the restriction to 𝕆¯\underline{\smash{\mathbb{O}}}, which is a multimodule over (𝔽,𝔽¯,𝕆¯)({\mathbb{F}},\overline{\mathbb{F}};\underline{\smash{\mathbb{O}}}). Let
Φ0PD:C​F​(H)⊗C​F​(H¯)→𝐊\Phi_{0}^{\rm PD}:CF(H)\otimes CF(\overline{H})\to{\bf K}
be the chain-level pairing. Notice that Φ0PD\Phi_{0}^{\rm PD} only comes from trivial Floer cylinders, hence is obviously a nondegenerate pairing (in both variables).
Now we start to prove Poincaré duality property of spectral invariants. Fix x∈H​F​(X)x\in HF(X).
(a)
We first prove that
cH(x)≥−inf{cH¯(y)|Φ0PD(x,y)≠0}c_{H}(x)\geq-\inf\Big\{c_{\overline{H}}(y)\ |\ \Phi_{0}^{\rm PD}(x,y)\neq 0\Big\}
Indeed, the multimodule 𝕏0ℙ​𝔻{\mathbb{X}}_{0}^{\mathbb{PD}} has a threshold 00 (see Definition 7.41). So for any y∈H​F​(X)y\in HF(X), if Φ0PD​(x,y)≠0\Phi_{0}^{\rm PD}(x,y)\neq 0, then there exist cycles 𝔵{\mathfrak{x}} and 𝔶{\mathfrak{y}} representing them such that the chain-level pairing between 𝔵{\mathfrak{x}} and 𝔶{\mathfrak{y}} is nonzero. Then by Proposition 7.42, one has
𝒜H​(𝔵)+𝒜H¯​(𝔶)≥0.{\mathcal{A}}_{H}({\mathfrak{x}})+{\mathcal{A}}_{\overline{H}}({\mathfrak{y}})\geq 0.
As 𝒜H​(𝔵){\mathcal{A}}_{H}({\mathfrak{x}}) and 𝒜H¯​(𝔶){\mathcal{A}}_{\overline{H}}({\mathfrak{y}}) can approximate cH​(x)c_{H}(x) and cH¯​(y)c_{\overline{H}}(y) respectively, one has
Φ0PD​(x,y)≠0⟹cH​(x)+cH¯​(y)≥0.\Phi_{0}^{\rm PD}(x,y)\neq 0\Longrightarrow c_{H}(x)+c_{\overline{H}}(y)\geq 0.
Then one has
cH​(x)≥sup{−cH¯​(y)|Φ0PD​(x,y)=0}.c_{H}(x)\geq\sup\Big\{-c_{\overline{H}}(y)\ |\ \Phi_{0}^{\rm PD}(x,y)=0\Big\}.
(b)
We prove that for all ϵ>0\epsilon>0,
cH​(x)<ϵ−inf{cH¯​(y)|Φ0PD​(x,y)≠0}.c_{H}(x)<\epsilon-\inf\Big\{c_{\overline{H}}(y)\ |\ \Phi_{0}^{\rm PD}(x,y)\neq 0\Big\}.
Choose ϵ\epsilon such that α:=ϵ−cH​(x)∉Spec⁡(H¯)\alpha:=\epsilon-c_{H}(x)\notin{\rm Spec}(\overline{H}). By energy consideration, the restriction of the chain-level pairing Φ0PD\Phi_{0}^{\rm PD} to
C​F​(H)<β⊗C​F​(H¯)<γ→𝐊CF(H)^{<\beta}\otimes CF(\overline{H})^{<\gamma}\to{\bf K}
vanishes when β+γ<0\beta+\gamma<0. Hence one obtains a well-defined nondegenerate pairing
Φ0,αPD:H​F​(H)>−α⊗H​F​(H¯)<α→𝐊.\Phi_{0,\alpha}^{\rm PD}:HF(H)^{>-\alpha}\otimes HF(\overline{H})^{<\alpha}\to{\bf K}.
As −α=cH​(x)−ϵ<cH​(x)-\alpha=c_{H}(x)-\epsilon<c_{H}(x),
x∉Im⁡(H​F​(H)<−α→H​F​(X)).x\notin{\rm Im}\Big(HF(H)^{<-\alpha}\to HF(X)\Big).
Therefore, the image of xx under
H​F​(X)→H​F​(H)>−αHF(X)\to HF(H)^{>-\alpha}
denoted by xαx_{\alpha}, is nonzero. By the nondegeneracy of the pairing Φ0,αPD\Phi_{0,\alpha}^{\rm PD}, there exists yα∈H​F​(H¯)<αy_{\alpha}\in HF(\overline{H})^{<\alpha} such that Φ0,αPD​(xα,yα)≠0\Phi_{0,\alpha}^{\rm PD}(x_{\alpha},y_{\alpha})\neq 0. Choose a cycle 𝔵∈C​F​(H)≤cH​(x){\mathfrak{x}}\in CF(H)^{\leq c_{H}(x)} representing xx and a cycle 𝔶∈C​F​(H¯)<α{\mathfrak{y}}\in CF(\overline{H})^{<\alpha} representing yαy_{\alpha}. Then the chain level pairing Φ0PD​(𝔵,𝔶)\Phi_{0}^{\rm PD}({\mathfrak{x}},{\mathfrak{y}}) is nonzero. As 𝔵{\mathfrak{x}} is closed, 𝔶{\mathfrak{y}} is not a boundary. Hence the map H​F​(H¯)<α→H​F​(X)HF(\overline{H})^{<\alpha}\to HF(X) does not annihilate yαy_{\alpha}. Denote the image by yy. Then Φ0PD​(x,y)≠0\Phi_{0}^{\rm PD}(x,y)\neq 0. Then one has
cH¯​(y)≤α=ϵ−cH​(x)⟹cH​(x)≤ϵ−cH¯​(y)≤ϵ−inf{cH¯​(y)|Φ0PD​(x,y)≠0}.c_{\overline{H}}(y)\leq\alpha=\epsilon-c_{H}(x)\Longrightarrow c_{H}(x)\leq\epsilon-c_{\overline{H}}(y)\leq\epsilon-\inf\Big\{c_{\overline{H}}(y)\ |\ \Phi_{0}^{\rm PD}(x,y)\neq 0\Big\}.
Combining (a) and (b), we conclude that Poincaré duality holds.
Part III THE AMS CONSTRUCTION
Outline of Part 3
We go through the AMS construction of lifts of various geometric flow categories, multimodules, and homotopies to the category of (collared rigidified) smooth normally complex Kuranishi spaces.
14. The Flow Categories, Multimodules, and Homotopies of Domains
The Abouzaid–McLean–Smith (AMS) construction of global charts for genus zero Gromov–Witten theory [3] uses certain auxiliary moduli spaces of rational curves in projective spaces. To extend such construction to the case of Floer moduli spaces, we consider an analogy, which is an auxiliary flow category. The final goal of this section is to describe a flow category enriched in an intermediate category. The discussion in this section and subsequent ones has certain overlap with [14, Section 5], but we include these expositions to make the paper self-contained and various technical aspects more streamlined.
14.1. Monotone flow categories, multimodules, and homotopies
14.1.1. Monotone flow category
We introduce the technical notion of monotone flow categories to simplify the discussions.
We introduce the following normal poset used frequently in this paper. For each d≥0d\geq 0, define
Ad={{(d0,…,dl)|di>0,d0+⋯+dl=d},d≠0,{(0)},d=0.A_{d}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}\Big\{(d_{0},\ldots,d_{l})\ |\ d_{i}>0,\ d_{0}+\cdots+d_{l}=d\Big\},&\ d\neq 0,\\
\{(0)\},&\ d=0.\end{array}\right.
The depth function is the number ll. There are also homogeneous inclusions of degree 11
Ad×Ad′→Ad+d′A_{d}\times A_{d^{\prime}}\to A_{d+d^{\prime}}
(14.1)
defined by the natural concatenation.
Definition 14.1.
Let 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}} be a regular stratification category. A monotone flow category enriched in 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}, denoted by 𝕗{\mathbb{f}}, consists of for each d≥0d\geq 0 an object Md𝕗M_{d}^{\mathbb{f}} in 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}} together with morphisms
ιd​d′𝕗:Md𝕗×Md′𝕗→Md+d′𝕗\iota_{dd^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{f}}:M_{d}^{\mathbb{f}}\times M_{d^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{f}}\to M_{d+d^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{f}}
satisfying the following conditions.
(1)
For d=0d=0, Md𝕗M_{d}^{\mathbb{f}} is a singleton in 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}.
(2)
The associativity: for d,d′,d′′≥0d,d^{\prime},d^{\prime\prime}\geq 0, the following diagram commutes.
Md𝕗×Md′𝕗×Md′′𝕗\textstyle{M_{d}^{\mathbb{f}}\times M_{d^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{f}}\times M_{d^{\prime\prime}}^{\mathbb{f}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}Md+d′𝕗×Md′′𝕗\textstyle{M_{d+d^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{f}}\times M_{d^{\prime\prime}}^{\mathbb{f}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}Md𝕗×Md′+d′′𝕗\textstyle{M_{d}^{\mathbb{f}}\times M_{d^{\prime}+d^{\prime\prime}}^{\mathbb{f}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}Md+d′+d′′𝕗\textstyle{M_{d+d^{\prime}+d^{\prime\prime}}^{\mathbb{f}}}
Remark 14.2.
Notice that given a monotone flow category 𝕗\mathbb{f}, one obtains an ordinary flow category, denoted by 𝔽{\mathbb{F}}, whose object set is ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}. The partial order is the opposite of the natural one on ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}. The space of morphisms from aa to bb (with a≥ba\geq b) is
Ma​b𝔽=Ma−b𝕗.M_{ab}^{\mathbb{F}}=M_{a-b}^{\mathbb{f}}.
Moreover, the flow category 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} has a free action by ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}.
Remark 14.3.
One can generalize the notion of monotone flow categories by replacing ℤ≥0{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0} with certain other abelian monoids. One option is ℤ≥0k{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}^{k}, where the k=2k=2 case will be used to prove Proposition 12.2. The corresponding flow category has object set being ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}. The other is the effective cone
Πeff={a∈Π|ω⁡(a)>0}∪{0}\Pi^{\rm eff}=\{a\in\Pi\ |\ \omega(a)>0\}\cup\{0\}
of a symplectic manifold. The corresponding flow category has object set being Π\Pi.
14.1.2. Monotone flow multimodules and homotopies
Now we discuss the case of multimodules.
Definition 14.4.
Let 𝕗1,…,𝕗m\mathbb{f}_{1},\ldots,\mathbb{f}_{m} resp. 𝕗′{\mathbb{f}}^{\prime} be monotone flow categories enriched in a regular stratification category 𝐂¯\underline{\smash{\bf C}}. Notice that the monotone multimodule 𝕩{\mathbb{x}} induces an ordinary multimodule 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} over (𝔽1,…,𝔽m,𝔽′)({\mathbb{F}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbb{F}}_{m};{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}) with

and structural maps induced from structural maps of 𝕩{\mathbb{x}}. Moreover, it is equivariant with respect to the natural group morphism

The case of homotopies is similar and stated as follows.
