14.2. The category of curves
The following definition may not be the most canonical one. However, as we will consider only very concrete objects, the ad hoc description suffices our purpose. We should remind the reader that the following definition goes beyond the algebro-geometric situation as the base BB is typically only a stratified smooth manifold.
Definition 14.6.
An equivariant families of curves is a triple 𝒞=(𝒢,B,C){\mathcal{C}}=({\mathcal{G}},B,C) where 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} is a (not necessarily reductive) complex Lie group containing a maximal compact subgroup G⊆𝒢G\subseteq{\mathcal{G}}, BB and CC are stratified smooth 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}-manifolds, with a 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}-equivariant map C→BC\to B, and the structure of a prestable genus zero complex curve on each fiber Cϕ⊆CC_{\phi}\subseteq C. This triple needs to satisfy the following conditions.
(1)
For any g∈𝒢g\in{\mathcal{G}} and ϕ∈B\phi\in B, the map g:Cϕ→Cg​ϕg:C_{\phi}\to C_{g\phi} is an isomorphism of complex curves.
(2)
Let C̊⊆C\mathring{C}\subseteq C be the complement of fiberwise nodes. Then C̊\mathring{C} is a stratified 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}-manifold and the map C̊→B\mathring{C}\to B is a submersion.
For each object 𝒞=(𝒢,B,C){\mathcal{C}}=({\mathcal{G}},B,C), we introduce
P𝒞=𝒢/G,\displaystyle\ P_{\mathcal{C}}={\mathcal{G}}/G,\
Q𝒞=Lie⁡(𝒢)/Lie​G.\displaystyle\ Q_{\mathcal{C}}={\rm Lie}({\mathcal{G}})/{\rm Lie}G.
We can also add additional structures to an equivariant family of curves, such as a collection of marked points, which are precisely 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}-equivariant sections of C→BC\to B avoiding nodes and each other. Another structure we will use all the time is the cylindrical ends around markings and nodes, which are choices of germs of cylindrical coordinates.
We define morphisms of the category of equivariant families of curves.
Definition 14.7.
Let 𝒞=(𝒢,B,C){\mathcal{C}}=({\mathcal{G}},B,C) be an equivariant family of curves.
(1)
A group enlargement of 𝒞=(𝒢,B,C){\mathcal{C}}=({\mathcal{G}},B,C) is an equivariant family of curves 𝒞′=(𝒢′,B′,C′){\mathcal{C}}^{\prime}=({\mathcal{G}}^{\prime},B^{\prime},C^{\prime}) where 𝒢→𝒢′{\mathcal{G}}\to{\mathcal{G}}^{\prime} is a complex Lie group embedding which sends the compact group GG into G′G^{\prime} with B′=𝒢′×𝒢BB^{\prime}={\mathcal{G}}^{\prime}\times_{\mathcal{G}}B and C′=𝒢′×𝒢CC^{\prime}={\mathcal{G}}^{\prime}\times_{\mathcal{G}}C. We denote the group enlargement as such by
𝒢′×𝒢𝒞.{\mathcal{G}}^{\prime}\times_{\mathcal{G}}{\mathcal{C}}.
(2)
A strict morphism from 𝒞1=(𝒢1,B1,C1){\mathcal{C}}_{1}=({\mathcal{G}}_{1},B_{1},C_{1}) to 𝒞2=(𝒢2,B2,C2){\mathcal{C}}_{2}=({\mathcal{G}}_{2},B_{2},C_{2}), denoted by ζ21:𝒞1→𝒞2\zeta_{21}:{\mathcal{C}}_{1}\to{\mathcal{C}}_{2}, consists of a complex Lie group embedding ζ21𝒢:𝒢1→𝒢2\zeta_{21}^{{\mathcal{G}}}:{\mathcal{G}}_{1}\to{\mathcal{G}}_{2} which restricts to a group map ζ21G:G1→G2\zeta_{21}^{G}:G_{1}\to G_{2} and an equivariant commutative diagram
C1\textstyle{C_{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}ζ21C\scriptstyle{\zeta_{21}^{C}}C2\textstyle{C_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}B1\textstyle{B_{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}ζ21B\scriptstyle{\zeta_{21}^{B}}B2\textstyle{B_{2}}
satisfying 1) the map ζ21B:B1→B2\zeta_{21}^{B}:B_{1}\to B_{2} is a stratified smooth map; 2) the map ζ21C:C1→C2\zeta_{21}^{C}:C_{1}\to C_{2} is continuous such that the restricted map C̊1→C̊2\mathring{C}_{1}\to\mathring{C}_{2} is smooth and such that for each ϕ1∈B1\phi_{1}\in B_{1} sent to ϕ2∈B2\phi_{2}\in B_{2}, the induced map C̊ϕ1→C̊ϕ2\mathring{C}_{\phi_{1}}\to\mathring{C}_{\phi_{2}} is an isomorphism (of complex curves together with extra structures such as germs of cylindrical ends and marked points). Notice that a strict morphism 𝒞1→𝒞2{\mathcal{C}}_{1}\to{\mathcal{C}}_{2} induces a strict morphism from 𝒢2×𝒢1𝒞1{\mathcal{G}}_{2}\times_{{\mathcal{G}}_{1}}{\mathcal{C}}_{1} into 𝒞2{\mathcal{C}}_{2}.
(3)
A strict morphism is called a strict embedding if the induced map 𝒢2×𝒢1𝒞1→𝒞2{\mathcal{G}}_{2}\times_{{\mathcal{G}}_{1}}{\mathcal{C}}_{1}\to{\mathcal{C}}_{2} is an isomorphism.
(4)
A unitary conjugation of (𝒢,B,C)({\mathcal{G}},B,C) is a strict morphism induced from an element g∈Gg\in G which lifts the conjugation action of gg on 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}.
(5)
An embedding of equivariant families of curves is a unitary conjugacy class of strict embeddings, where we declare that two strict embeddings 𝒞1→𝒞2{\mathcal{C}}_{1}\to{\mathcal{C}}_{2} are equivalent if one can be taken to another via a unitary conjugation of g∈G2g\in G_{2}.
(6)
The category of equivariant families of curves, denoted by 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}, is the category whose objects are equivariant families of curves and whose morphisms are embeddings.
Notice that the category 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}} is monoidal: given two object 𝒞i=(𝒢i,Bi,Ci){\mathcal{C}}_{i}=({\mathcal{G}}_{i},B_{i},C_{i}), the product 𝒞1×𝒞2{\mathcal{C}}_{1}\times{\mathcal{C}}_{2} is (𝒢1×𝒢2,B1×B2,C1⊔C2)({\mathcal{G}}_{1}\times{\mathcal{G}}_{2},B_{1}\times B_{2},C_{1}\sqcup C_{2}) where the fiber of C1⊔C2C_{1}\sqcup C_{2} over (ϕ1,ϕ2)∈B1×B2(\phi_{1},\phi_{2})\in B_{1}\times B_{2} is the disjoint union Cϕ1⊔Cϕ2C_{\phi_{1}}\sqcup C_{\phi_{2}}. The initial object, which is ∅\emptyset-stratified (see Definition 2.10), is the object with 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} being the trivial group, BB being the singleton, and CC being empty.
Notice that the category 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}} also allows outercollaring.
14.2.1. Lateral lines
We introduce the notation of lateral lines, which are used for gluing domains of solutions to Floer equations in various flow-category constructions.
Definition 14.8.
(1)
Let Σ\Sigma be a smooth genus zero curve with cylindrical ends. A lateral line in Σ\Sigma is a real curve ℝ≅ℓ⊆Σ{\mathbb{R}}\cong\ell\subseteq\Sigma satisfying: near ±∞\pm\infty, ℓ\ell is contained in a cylindrical end of Σ\Sigma and in cylindrical coordinates, is parametrized by (s,0)(s,0). In particular, for domains of Floer trajectories, this amounts to an ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-orbit of the translation action on the cylinder.
(2)
Let 𝒞=(𝒢,B,C){\mathcal{C}}=({\mathcal{G}},B,C) be an equivariant family of curves equipped with marked points and cylindrical ends. A family of lateral lines is a collection of lateral lines ℓϕ⊆Cϕ\ell_{\phi}\subseteq C_{\phi} such that ℓg​ϕ=g⁡(ℓϕ)\ell_{g\phi}=g(\ell_{\phi}) for all ϕ∈B\phi\in B and g∈𝒢g\in{\mathcal{G}}.
By abuse of notations, we use 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}} to denote the category of equivariant family of curves equipped with cylindrical ends and lateral lines. It is easy to see that lateral lines can be concatenated (as we always require the angular coordinate to be 0∈S10\in S^{1}), which also guarantees their existence by induction.
14.2.2. Rigidifications
To fit into the construction of Kuranishi charts and FOP perturbations, we need to introduce the more refined category 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rig\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}. Comparing to other “rigidified” morphisms in categories such as 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}} or 𝐊𝐮𝐫¯\underline{\smash{\bf Kur}}, the difference between the domain and target of an embedding in 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}} is caused typically by the enlargement of the complex Lie group. So the rigidification becomes more specific.
Definition 14.9.
Let ζ21:(𝒢1,B1,C1)→(𝒢2,B2,C2)\zeta_{21}:({\mathcal{G}}_{1},B_{1},C_{1})\to({\mathcal{G}}_{2},B_{2},C_{2}) be a strict embedding in 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}. A rigidification of ζ21\zeta_{21} consists of an orthogonal representation Q21Q_{21} of G1G_{1} and
a germ of ζ21G\zeta_{21}^{G}-equivariant maps
θ21:B1×Q21ϵ→B2\theta_{21}:B_{1}\times Q_{21}^{\epsilon}\to B_{2}
(where G1G_{1} acts diagonally on the domain) whose restriction to B1×{0}B_{1}\times\{0\} coincides with ζ21B\zeta_{21}^{B}, such that the map
G2×G1(B1×Q21ϵ)→B2,[g2,(b1,η21)]↦g2​θ21​(b1,η21)\begin{split}G_{2}\times_{G_{1}}(B_{1}\times Q_{21}^{\epsilon})\to&\ B_{2},\\
[g_{2},(b_{1},\eta_{21})]\mapsto&\ g_{2}\theta_{21}(b_{1},\eta_{21})\end{split}
is a diffeomorphism onto an open neighborhood of the image of ζ21B\zeta_{21}^{B}. A strict rigidified embedding is a strict embedding together with a rigidification.
Notice that the group embedding ι21𝒢:𝒢1→𝒢2\iota_{21}^{\mathcal{G}}:{\mathcal{G}}_{1}\to{\mathcal{G}}_{2} induces a linear injection
Q𝒞1→Q𝒞2Q_{{\mathcal{C}}_{1}}\to Q_{{\mathcal{C}}_{2}}
and Q21Q_{21} is necessarily isomorphic to its cokernel.
Each group element g2∈G2g_{2}\in G_{2} induces a strict rigidified embedding from 𝒞2{\mathcal{C}}_{2} to itself.
Lemma 14.10.
Strict rigidified embeddings can be composed.
Proof.
Suppose 𝒞i=(𝒢i,Bi,Ci){\mathcal{C}}_{i}=({\mathcal{G}}_{i},B_{i},C_{i}), i=1,2,3i=1,2,3 are three equivariant families. Let ζ21:𝒞1→𝒞2\zeta_{21}:{\mathcal{C}}_{1}\to{\mathcal{C}}_{2} and ζ32:𝒞2→𝒞3\zeta_{32}:{\mathcal{C}}_{2}\to{\mathcal{C}}_{3} be strict embeddings with rigidifications
θ21:B1×Q21ϵ→𝒢2,\displaystyle\ \theta_{21}:B_{1}\times Q_{21}^{\epsilon}\to{\mathcal{G}}_{2},\
θ32:B2×Q32ϵ→𝒢3.\displaystyle\ \theta_{32}:B_{2}\times Q_{32}^{\epsilon}\to{\mathcal{G}}_{3}.
The composed rigidification consists of the representation Q21⊕Q32Q_{21}\oplus Q_{32}, the neighborhood Q21ϵ⊕Q32ϵQ_{21}^{\epsilon}\oplus Q_{32}^{\epsilon}, and the map
θ31:B1×Q21ϵ×Q32ϵ→𝒢3,(b1,η21,η32)↦θ32​(θ21​(b1,η21),η32).\begin{split}\theta_{31}:B_{1}\times Q_{21}^{\epsilon}\times Q_{32}^{\epsilon}\to&\ {\mathcal{G}}_{3},\\
(b_{1},\eta_{21},\eta_{32})\mapsto&\ \theta_{32}\Big(\theta_{21}(b_{1},\eta_{21}),\eta_{32}\Big).\end{split}
The property that the induced map is a diffeomorphism onto a neighborhood of ζ31B​(B1)\zeta_{31}^{B}(B_{1}) is an obvious consequence of the corresponding properties for the two rigidified embeddings.
∎
Definition 14.11.
𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rig\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig} has morphisms being conjugacy classes of strict rigidified embeddings.
Notice that we can naturally define the collared version of 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rig\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}, denoted by
⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rig.{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}.
14.2.3. Stable complex structure
We would like to define a category 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯ℂ\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}^{\mathbb{C}} of equivariant families of curves whose bases have equivariant stable complex structures.
Definition 14.12.
A stable complex structure on an equivariant family of curves 𝒞=(𝒢,B,C){\mathcal{C}}=({\mathcal{G}},B,C) is a GG-equivariant stable complex structure of the tangent bundle T​BTB (see Definition 3.17). Recall that it consists of a 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}-equivariant complex vector bundle I→BI\to B and a 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}-equivariant stable isomorphism
τ:T​B​→𝑠​I.\tau:TB\overset{s}{\to}I.
To define morphisms of stably complex objects, note the following fact. Let ζ21:(𝒢1,B1,C1)→(𝒢2,B2,C2)\zeta_{21}:({\mathcal{G}}_{1},B_{1},C_{1})\to({\mathcal{G}}_{2},B_{2},C_{2}) be a strict embedding of equivariant families of curves. Notice that there are 𝒢2{\mathcal{G}}_{2}-equivariant vector bundles
𝒢2×𝒢1T​B1,\displaystyle\ {\mathcal{G}}_{2}\times_{{\mathcal{G}}_{1}}TB_{1},\
π∗​T​(𝒢2/𝒢1)\displaystyle\ \pi^{*}T({\mathcal{G}}_{2}/{\mathcal{G}}_{1})
where π:𝒢2×𝒢1B1→𝒢2/𝒢1\pi:{\mathcal{G}}_{2}\times_{{\mathcal{G}}_{1}}B_{1}\to{\mathcal{G}}_{2}/{\mathcal{G}}_{1} temporarily denotes the natural projection.
Via ζ21\zeta_{21}, one can see that there is a 𝒢2{\mathcal{G}}_{2}-equivariant bundle isomorphism
T​B2≅π∗​T​(𝒢2/𝒢1)⊕(𝒢2×𝒢1T​B1)TB_{2}\cong\pi^{*}T({\mathcal{G}}_{2}/{\mathcal{G}}_{1})\oplus({\mathcal{G}}_{2}\times_{{\mathcal{G}}_{1}}TB_{1})
(14.2)
where the first summand is complex. Hence a stable complex structure on 𝒞1{\mathcal{C}}_{1} naturally induces a stable complex structure on 𝒞2{\mathcal{C}}_{2} via the strict embedding ζ21\zeta_{21}. One can see that the induced one is invariant under unitary conjugations of strict embeddings. Hence one can make the following definition.
Definition 14.13.
A strict embedding of equivariant families of curves with stably complex structures from (𝒢1,B1,C1,I1,τ1)({\mathcal{G}}_{1},B_{1},C_{1},I_{1},\tau_{1}) to (𝒢2,B2,C2,I2,τ2)({\mathcal{G}}_{2},B_{2},C_{2},I_{2},\tau_{2}) is a strict embedding ζ21\zeta_{21} from (𝒢1,B1,C1)({\mathcal{G}}_{1},B_{1},C_{1}) to (𝒢2,B2,C2)({\mathcal{G}}_{2},B_{2},C_{2}) such that the bundle isomorphism (14.2) respects the 𝒢2{\mathcal{G}}_{2}-equivariant stable complex structures. The category 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯ℂ\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}^{\mathbb{C}} consists of objects being equivariant families of curves with stable complex structures whose morphisms are unitary conjugacy classes of strict embeddings.
One can also define rigidifications for strict embeddings in 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯ℂ\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}^{\mathbb{C}}. Indeed, suppose
(𝒢1,B1,C1,I1,τ1),(𝒢2,B2,C2,I2,τ2)∈Ob​𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯ℂ({\mathcal{G}}_{1},B_{1},C_{1},I_{1},\tau_{1}),\ ({\mathcal{G}}_{2},B_{2},C_{2},I_{2},\tau_{2})\in{\rm Ob}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}^{\mathbb{C}}
and
ζ21:(𝒢1,B1,C1)→(𝒢2,B2,C2)\zeta_{21}:({\mathcal{G}}_{1},B_{1},C_{1})\to({\mathcal{G}}_{2},B_{2},C_{2})
is a strict embedding. Suppose
θ21:B1×Q21ϵ→𝒢2\theta_{21}:B_{1}\times Q_{21}^{\epsilon}\to{\mathcal{G}}_{2}
is a rigidification of ζ21\zeta_{21} as a strict embedding in 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}. Consider the image
B2ϵ:=Im⁡(G2×G1(B1×Q21ϵ)→B2)B_{2}^{\epsilon}:={\rm Im}(G_{2}\times_{G_{1}}(B_{1}\times Q_{21}^{\epsilon})\to B_{2})
which is a G2G_{2}-invariant open subset of B2B_{2}. There is a projection
B2ϵ→G2×G1B1.B_{2}^{\epsilon}\to G_{2}\times_{G_{1}}B_{1}.
We say that the rigidification θ21\theta_{21} respects the stable complex structure if over B2ϵB_{2}^{\epsilon}, the stable complex structure on B2B_{2} is pulled back from its restriction to G2×G1B1G_{2}\times_{G_{1}}B_{1} via the above projection. This provides a category 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}}. One also has the corresponding collared version ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}}.
14.3. Construction of the domain flow categories
The purpose of the rest of this section is to construct monotone flow categories (Definition 14.1) enriched in the category ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}}, as well as monotone flow bimodules and homotopies.
14.3.1. Some Lie groups and homogeneous spaces
We will consider variants of U⁡(d)U(d) and G​L​(d)GL(d). Inside P​G​L​(d+1)PGL(d+1), there are two complex subgroups
𝒢d−:=PGL−(d+1)={[1∗0∗]∈PGL(d+1)}{\mathcal{G}}_{d}^{-}:=PGL^{-}(d+1)=\left\{\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}1&*\\
0&*\end{array}\right]\in PGL(d+1)\right\}
and
𝒢d+:=PGL+(d+1)={[∗01]∈PGL(d+1)}.{\mathcal{G}}_{d}^{+}:=PGL^{+}(d+1)=\left\{\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}*&0\\
&1\end{array}\right]\in PGL(d+1)\right\}.
In this paper we will use exclusively the positive version1919
19
This preference is due to the fact that the domains of multimodules always have a unique output. However, for Floer flow categories, using the negative version is also possible., hence we simply denote 𝒢d=𝒢d+{\mathcal{G}}_{d}={\mathcal{G}}_{d}^{+}. The unitary group Gd:=U⁡(d)G_{d}:=U(d) embeds into 𝒢d{\mathcal{G}}_{d} by
U⁡(d)∋g↦[g001]∈𝒢d.U(d)\ni g\mapsto\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}g&0\\
0&1\end{array}\right]\in{\mathcal{G}}_{d}.
One needs to consider certain specific group embeddings for different dd’s. The embedding
Gd1×Gd2=U⁡(d1)×U⁡(d2)→Gd1+d2=U⁡(d1+d2)G_{d_{1}}\times G_{d_{2}}=U(d_{1})\times U(d_{2})\to G_{d_{1}+d_{2}}=U(d_{1}+d_{2})
is obvious. For the corresponding complex Lie group 𝒢d{\mathcal{G}}_{d}, there are corresponding embeddings. For example, for d1=d2=2d_{1}=d_{2}=2, the embedding 𝒢2×𝒢2→𝒢4{\mathcal{G}}_{2}\times{\mathcal{G}}_{2}\to{\mathcal{G}}_{4} reads
([a11a120a21a220a31a321],[b11b120b21b220b31b321])↦[a11a12000a21a2200000b11b12000b21b220a31a32b31b321].\left(\left[\begin{array}[]{ccc}a_{11}&a_{12}&0\\

b_{21}&b_{22}&0\\

0&0&b_{21}&b_{22}&0\\

We set up the following notations for later purposes. Denote
Pd:=𝒢d/Gd.P_{d}:={\mathcal{G}}_{d}/G_{d}.
The tangent space at the identity coset is the quotient of Lie algebras
Qd:=𝔤dℂ/𝔤d.Q_{d}:={\mathfrak{g}}_{d}^{\mathbb{C}}/{\mathfrak{g}}_{d}.
There are canonical GdG_{d}-invariant metrics on QdQ_{d} making the linear embeddings
Qd1⊕Qd2→Qd1+d2Q_{d_{1}}\oplus Q_{d_{2}}\to Q_{d_{1}+d_{2}}
isometric. Denote
Qd1,d2:=Qd1+d2/(Qd1⊕Qd2).Q_{d_{1},d_{2}}:=Q_{d_{1}+d_{2}}/(Q_{d_{1}}\oplus Q_{d_{2}}).
(14.3)
14.3.2. Moduli spaces of cylinders in projective spaces
For d≥1d\geq 1, we will describe an object 𝒞d=(𝒢d,Bd,Cd){\mathcal{C}}_{d}=({\mathcal{G}}_{d},B_{d},C_{d}) in 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}. Consider the moduli space of holomorphic maps
u:ℝ×S1→ℙdu:{\mathbb{R}}\times S^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{d}
of degree dd, modulo the translation in ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-direction (but not the S1S^{1}-rotation). Let
ℳ¯(ℙd,d)ℝ0,2\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}^{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{P}^{d},d)
be the natural compactification of this moduli space (cf. [14, Definition 5.14] for an explanation of this notation). Then the group P​U​(d+1)PU(d+1) acts on ℳ¯(ℙd,d)ℝ0,2\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}^{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{P}^{d},d). Let
ℳ¯(ℙd,d)ℝ,+0,2⊆ℳ¯(ℙd,d)ℝ0,2\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}^{{\mathbb{R}},+}({\mathbb{P}}^{d},d)\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}^{\mathbb{R}}({\mathbb{P}}^{d},d)
be the subset satisfying the constraint:
u⁡(z+)=[0,…,0,1]u(z_{+})=[0,\ldots,0,1]
(14.4)
which is invariant under Gd=U⁡(d)G_{d}=U(d), where z+={∞}∈ℙ1⊇ℝ×S1z_{+}=\{\infty\}\in\mathbb{P}^{1}\supseteq{\mathbb{R}}\times S^{1}. Let
Bd⊆ℳ¯(ℙd,d)ℝ,+0,2B_{d}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}^{{\mathbb{R}},+}(\mathbb{P}^{d},d)
be the open subset of curves uu whose image is not contained in any hyperplane of ℙd\mathbb{P}^{d}. It is easy to calculate the dimension of BdB_{d}, which is
dimℝ​Bd=2​d​(d+1)−1=dimℝ​𝒢d−1.{\rm dim}_{\mathbb{R}}B_{d}=2d(d+1)-1={\rm dim}_{\mathbb{R}}{\mathcal{G}}_{d}-1.
Further, let Cd→BdC_{d}\to B_{d} be the universal curve; notice that fibers also carry canonical germs of cylindrical ends.
The moduli space BdB_{d} is stratified by the poset AdA_{d} (cf. the notations introduced in Section 14.1.1): for any τ=(d0⋯dr)∈Ad\tau=(d_{0}\cdots d_{r})\in A_{d}, the stratum ∂τBd\partial^{\tau}B_{d} is the subspace of curves in ℙd\mathbb{P}^{d} which breaks into r+1r+1 stable cylinders such that the ii-th one has degree did_{i}. Therefore, one obtains an object
𝒞d=(𝒢d,Bd,Cd){\mathcal{C}}_{d}=({\mathcal{G}}_{d},B_{d},C_{d})
in the category 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}.
Remark 14.14.
There is a refinement of the above stratification, namely, the stratification by combinatorial types, and each stratum is preserved by the 𝒢d{\mathcal{G}}_{d}-action.
14.3.3. Orientations
The smooth part of the moduli space ℳ¯0,2​(ℙd,d)\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,2}({\mathbb{P}}^{d},d) is a complex manifold, which is canonically oriented. The interior of BdB_{d} has a natural S1S^{1}-action by reparametrizing the cylinders so that the quotient Int​Bd/S1{\rm Int}B_{d}/S^{1} is identified with an open subset of ℳ¯0,2​(ℙd,d)\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,2}({\mathbb{P}}^{d},d). Hence we can orient BdB_{d} by regarding the infinitesimal S1S^{1}-direction as positively oriented.
14.3.4. Concatenation of cylinders
We would like to define the structural maps, i.e., morphisms
ζd,d′:𝒞d×𝒞d′→𝒞d+d′,d,d′>0\zeta_{d,d^{\prime}}:{\mathcal{C}}_{d}\times{\mathcal{C}}_{d^{\prime}}\to{\mathcal{C}}_{d+d^{\prime}},\ d,d^{\prime}>0
in the category 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}} such that they satisfy associativity. In this way, one obtains a monotone flow category enriched in 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}.
We describe the definition as follows. Given two points ϕ∈Bd\phi\in B_{d}, ϕ′∈Bd′\phi^{\prime}\in B_{d^{\prime}} represented by maps u:Σ→ℙdu:\Sigma\to{\mathbb{P}}^{d}, u′:Σ′→ℙd′u^{\prime}:\Sigma^{\prime}\to{\mathbb{P}}^{d^{\prime}}, let Σ​#​Σ′\Sigma\#\Sigma^{\prime} be the prestable cylinder obtained by identifying the output of Σ\Sigma with the input Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}. The map uu can be represented by sections
h0,…,hd∈H0​(Σ,u∗​𝒪ℙd​(1)).h_{0},\ldots,h_{d}\in H^{0}(\Sigma,u^{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{d}}(1)).
We abbreviate Lu:=u∗​𝒪ℙd​(1)L_{u}:=u^{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{d}}(1) and extend it by trivial bundle to Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}. Then h0,…,hdh_{0},\ldots,h_{d} are sections over Σ​#​Σ′\Sigma\#\Sigma^{\prime}. Similarly, the map u′u^{\prime} can be represented by sections h0′,…,hd′′h_{0}^{\prime},\ldots,h_{d^{\prime}}^{\prime} of the pullback bundle Lu′→Σ′L_{u^{\prime}}\to\Sigma^{\prime} which can be extended to the whole of Σ​#​Σ′\Sigma\#\Sigma^{\prime}.
For each ϕ′∈Bd′\phi^{\prime}\in B_{d^{\prime}}, we choose the lateral line, a (broken) real curve
ℓϕ′⊆Cϕ′\ell_{\phi^{\prime}}\subseteq C_{\phi^{\prime}}
(14.5)
which is parametrized by (s,0)(s,0) in the cylindrical coordinates in all cylindrical components. Along ℓϕ′\ell_{\phi^{\prime}}, the parallel transport with respect to the Chern connection on Lu′L_{u^{\prime}} sends the (nonzero) vector hd′​(z+)∈Lu′|z+h_{d^{\prime}}(z_{+})\in L_{u^{\prime}}|_{z_{+}} to a nonzero vector τu′∈Lu′|z−\tau_{u^{\prime}}\in L_{u^{\prime}}|_{z_{-}}. Then consider 1+d+d′1+d+d^{\prime} sections of Lu⊗Lu′→Σ​#​Σ′L_{u}\otimes L_{u^{\prime}}\to\Sigma\#\Sigma^{\prime} given by
h0⊗τu′,…,hd−1⊗τu′,hd⊗h0′,…,hd⊗hd′.h_{0}\otimes\tau_{u^{\prime}},\ldots,h_{d-1}\otimes\tau_{u^{\prime}},h_{d}\otimes h_{0}^{\prime},\ldots,h_{d}\otimes h_{d^{\prime}}.
It is easy to check that it is base-point-free, hence defines a map
(ϕ​#​ϕ′):Σ​#​Σ′→ℙd+d′(\phi\#\phi^{\prime}):\Sigma\#\Sigma^{\prime}\to\mathbb{P}^{d+d^{\prime}}
which represents a point in Bd+d′B_{d+d^{\prime}}. Moreover, it is straightforward to see that the equivalence class of u​#​u′u\#u^{\prime} is independent of the choice of the representatives uu and u′u^{\prime}. Therefore, one obtains a well-defined map
ζd,d′B:Bd×Bd′→Bd+d′.\zeta_{d,d^{\prime}}^{B}:B_{d}\times B_{d^{\prime}}\to B_{d+d^{\prime}}.
Lemma 14.15.
The map ζd,d′B:Bd×Bd′→Bd+d′\zeta_{d,d^{\prime}}^{B}:B_{d}\times B_{d^{\prime}}\to B_{d+d^{\prime}} is smooth and equivariant with respect to the group embedding
ζd,d′𝒢:𝒢d×𝒢d′→𝒢d+d′,\zeta_{d,d^{\prime}}^{\mathcal{G}}:{\mathcal{G}}_{d}\times{\mathcal{G}}_{d^{\prime}}\to{\mathcal{G}}_{d+d^{\prime}},
and satisfying the associativity, i.e., the following diagram commutes.
Bd1×Bd2×Bd3\textstyle{B_{d_{1}}\times B_{d_{2}}\times B_{d_{3}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}Bd1+d2×Bd3\textstyle{B_{d_{1}+d_{2}}\times B_{d_{3}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}Bd1×Bd2+d3\textstyle{B_{d_{1}}\times B_{d_{2}+d_{3}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}Bd1+d2+d3\textstyle{B_{d_{1}+d_{2}+d_{3}}}
Furthermore, the maps ζd,d′B\zeta_{d,d^{\prime}}^{B} can be lifted canonically to a strict morphism
ζd,d′:𝒞d×𝒞d′→𝒞d+d′\zeta_{d,d^{\prime}}:{\mathcal{C}}_{d}\times{\mathcal{C}}_{d^{\prime}}\to{\mathcal{C}}_{d+d^{\prime}}
in the category 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}} such that the following diagram commutes.
𝒞d1×𝒞d2×𝒞d3\textstyle{{\mathcal{C}}_{d_{1}}\times{\mathcal{C}}_{d_{2}}\times{\mathcal{C}}_{d_{3}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}𝒞d1+d2×𝒞d3\textstyle{{\mathcal{C}}_{d_{1}+d_{2}}\times{\mathcal{C}}_{d_{3}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}𝒞d1×𝒞d2+d3\textstyle{{\mathcal{C}}_{d_{1}}\times{\mathcal{C}}_{d_{2}+d_{3}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}𝒞d1+d2+d3\textstyle{{\mathcal{C}}_{d_{1}+d_{2}+d_{3}}}
Proof.
All elements in the definition depend smoothly on the variables ϕ\phi and ϕ′\phi^{\prime}. From the explicit definition of u​#​u′u\#u^{\prime} given above, the equivariance follows immediately. The associativity can also be checked directly. See [14, §5.2.4] for more details.
∎
We need to prove that the morphisms are strict embeddings into the corresponding stratum.
Proposition 14.16.
The morphism ζd,d′\zeta_{d,d^{\prime}} is a strict embedding into the stratum ∂d,d′𝒞d+d′\partial^{d,d^{\prime}}{\mathcal{C}}_{d+d^{\prime}}.
Proof.
What we need to show is that the induced strict morphism
𝒢d+d′×𝒢d×𝒢d′(𝒞d×𝒞d′)→∂d,d′𝒞d+d′{\mathcal{G}}_{d+d^{\prime}}\times_{{\mathcal{G}}_{d}\times{\mathcal{G}}_{d^{\prime}}}\left({\mathcal{C}}_{d}\times{\mathcal{C}}_{d^{\prime}}\right)\to\partial^{d,d^{\prime}}{\mathcal{C}}_{d+d^{\prime}}
is an isomorphism. Indeed, given any curve in ∂d,d′Bd+d′\partial^{d,d^{\prime}}B_{d+d^{\prime}}, it is represented by a holomorphic map u:Σ​#​Σ′→ℙd+d′u:\Sigma\#\Sigma^{\prime}\to\mathbb{P}^{d+d^{\prime}} such that the restriction of uu to Σ\Sigma resp. Σ′\Sigma^{\prime} has degree dd resp. d′d^{\prime}. After applying a transformation in 𝒢d+d′{\mathcal{G}}_{d+d^{\prime}}, one can make u⁡(Σ)u(\Sigma) be contained in the special ℙd⊆ℙd+d′{\mathbb{P}}^{d}\subseteq{\mathbb{P}}^{d+d^{\prime}} with last d′d^{\prime} coordinates vanish, and make u⁡(Σ′)u(\Sigma^{\prime}) be contained in a ℙd′⊆ℙd+d′{\mathbb{P}}^{d^{\prime}}\subseteq{\mathbb{P}}^{d+d^{\prime}} which is spanned by the last d′d^{\prime} coordinates as well as a line contained in the special ℙd{\mathbb{P}}^{d}. Such curves are exactly in the image of ζd,d′B\zeta_{d,d^{\prime}}^{B}.
∎
14.3.5. Rigidification
Lastly we construct the rigidifications (see Definition 14.9).
Proposition 14.17.
The monotone flow category ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom} by taking the outer-collaring of the monotone flow category which has objects 𝒞d{\mathcal{C}}_{d} and morphisms ζd,d′\zeta_{d,d^{\prime}} admits a lift to ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rig{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}.
Proof.
We first explain why a single embedding ζd1,d2:𝒞d1×𝒞d2→∂d1,d2𝒞d1+d2\zeta_{d_{1},d_{2}}:{\mathcal{C}}_{d_{1}}\times{\mathcal{C}}_{d_{2}}\to\partial^{d_{1},d_{2}}{\mathcal{C}}_{d_{1}+d_{2}} can be rigidified (before outer-collaring). (See Definition 14.9) the representation of G1=Gd1×Gd2G_{1}=G_{d_{1}}\times G_{d_{2}} is Qd1,d2Q_{d_{1},d_{2}} given by (14.3). Roughly, Qd1,d2Q_{d_{1},d_{2}} is the normal direction to Gd1+d2​(𝒢d1×𝒢d2)G_{d_{1}+d_{2}}({\mathcal{G}}_{d_{1}}\times{\mathcal{G}}_{d_{2}}) inside 𝒢d1+d2{\mathcal{G}}_{d_{1}+d_{2}}. To be more specific, one can choose a GdG_{d}-invariant germ of maps
θd1,d2:Qd1,d2→𝒢d1+d2\theta_{d_{1},d_{2}}:Q_{d_{1},d_{2}}\to{\mathcal{G}}_{d_{1}+d_{2}}
sending 00 to the identity (such as the restriction of an exponential map) which is orthogonal to Gd1+d2​(𝒢d1×𝒢d2)G_{d_{1}+d_{2}}({\mathcal{G}}_{d_{1}}\times{\mathcal{G}}_{d_{2}}).
By the definition of embeddings in 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}, there is an isomorphism
𝒢d1+d2×𝒢d1×𝒢d2(𝒞d1×𝒞d2)→∂d1,d2𝒞d1+d2.{\mathcal{G}}_{d_{1}+d_{2}}\times_{{\mathcal{G}}_{d_{1}}\times{\mathcal{G}}_{d_{2}}}({\mathcal{C}}_{d_{1}}\times{\mathcal{C}}_{d_{2}})\to\partial^{d_{1},d_{2}}{\mathcal{C}}_{d_{1}+d_{2}}.
Then the map
Qd1,d2×(Bd1×Bd2)→∂d1,d2Bd1+d2(v,x1,x2)↦θd1,d2​(v)​(ζd1,d2B​(x1,x2))\begin{split}Q_{d_{1},d_{2}}\times(B_{d_{1}}\times B_{d_{2}})&\ \to\partial^{d_{1},d_{2}}B_{d_{1}+d_{2}}\\
(v,x_{1},x_{2})&\ \mapsto\theta_{d_{1},d_{2}}(v)(\zeta_{d_{1},d_{2}}^{B}(x_{1},x_{2}))\end{split}
is a local diffeomorphism after equivariantize by Gd1+d2G_{d_{1}+d_{2}}.
We need to choose rigidifications for all such embeddings so that they satisfy the requirement for flow categories. For this one can allow θd1,d2\theta_{d_{1},d_{2}} to depend on (x1,x2)∈Bd1×Bd2(x_{1},x_{2})\in B_{d_{1}}\times B_{d_{2}} so θd1,d2\theta_{d_{1},d_{2}} is a germ of equivariant bundle maps
Qd1,d2×Bd1×Bd2→𝒢d1+d2×Bd1×Bd2Q_{d_{1},d_{2}}\times B_{d_{1}}\times B_{d_{2}}\to{\mathcal{G}}_{d_{1}+d_{2}}\times B_{d_{1}}\times B_{d_{2}}
over Bd1×Bd2B_{d_{1}}\times B_{d_{2}}. All such rigidifications of the embedding ζd1,d2\zeta_{d_{1},d_{2}} are equivariantly homotopic. The collaring region allows us to connect different choices.
∎
We choose such a lift of ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom} to ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rig{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig} and still denote it by ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}. The effect of such a lift to later constructions needs to be addressed in the following way. Roughly, the resulting Kuranishi spaces of the AMS construction have symmetry groups being compact Lie groups GG while the domains we constructed here have symmetry groups being corresponding complex Lie groups 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}. This redundance will be removed by using a notion called group reduction (see Definition 15.7), which later becomes part of the Kuranishi section.
Consider a strict embedding
ζ21:𝒞1=(𝒢1,B1,C1)→𝒞2=(𝒢2,B2,C1)\zeta_{21}:{\mathcal{C}}_{1}=({\mathcal{G}}_{1},B_{1},C_{1})\to{\mathcal{C}}_{2}=({\mathcal{G}}_{2},B_{2},C_{1})
of equivariant families of curves. Denote by
ζ21P:P1=𝒢1/G1→P2=𝒢2/G2\zeta_{21}^{P}:P_{1}={\mathcal{G}}_{1}/G_{1}\to P_{2}={\mathcal{G}}_{2}/G_{2}
the induced embedding of homogeneous spaces and
ζ21Q:Q1=𝔤1ℂ/𝔤1→Q2=𝔤2ℂ/𝔤2\zeta_{21}^{Q}:Q_{1}={\mathfrak{g}}_{1}^{\mathbb{C}}/{\mathfrak{g}}_{1}\to Q_{2}={\mathfrak{g}}_{2}^{\mathbb{C}}/{\mathfrak{g}}_{2}
the linearization of ζ21P\zeta_{21}^{P}.
Lemma 14.18.
Let ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom} be the monotone flow category enriched in ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rig{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig} we constructed above. There exist a collection of germs of Gd×GdG_{d}\times G_{d}-equivariant maps
λd:⌊Bd×Qd→⌊Bd×Pd\lambda_{d}:{}_{\lfloor}B_{d}\times Q_{d}\to{}_{\lfloor}B_{d}\times P_{d}
as bundle maps over ⌊Bd{}_{\lfloor}B_{d} satisfying the following conditions.
(1)
For each ϕ∈⌊Bd\phi\in{}_{\lfloor}B_{d}, the restriction of λd\lambda_{d} to {ϕ}×Qd\{\phi\}\times Q_{d} is a local diffeomorphism onto an open neighborhood of [1]∈Pd[1]\in P_{d}.
(2)
λd\lambda_{d} is collared, i.e., λd\lambda_{d} is determined over the collar neighborhood by its restriction to the boundary strata via the projections.
(3)
For each decomposition d=d1+d2d=d_{1}+d_{2}, the following diagram commutes.
(Bd1⌊×Qd1)×(Bd2⌊×Qd2)\textstyle{\big({}_{\lfloor}B_{d_{1}}\times Q_{d_{1}}\big)\times\big({}_{\lfloor}B_{d_{2}}\times Q_{d_{2}}\big)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}λd1×λd2\scriptstyle{\lambda_{d_{1}}\times\lambda_{d_{2}}}ζd1,d2B×ζd1,d2Q\scriptstyle{\zeta_{d_{1},d_{2}}^{B}\times\zeta_{d_{1},d_{2}}^{Q}}(Bd1⌊×Pd1)×(Bd2⌊×Pd2)\textstyle{\big({}_{\lfloor}B_{d_{1}}\times P_{d_{1}}\big)\times\big({}_{\lfloor}B_{d_{2}}\times P_{d_{2}}\big)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}ζd1,d2B×ζd1,d2P\scriptstyle{\zeta_{d_{1},d_{2}}^{B}\times\zeta_{d_{1},d_{2}}^{P}}∂d1,d2⌊Bd×Qd\textstyle{\partial^{d_{1},d_{2}}{}_{\lfloor}B_{d}\times Q_{d}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}λd1+d2\scriptstyle{\lambda_{d_{1}+d_{2}}}∂d1,d2⌊Bd×Pd\textstyle{\partial^{d_{1},d_{2}}{}_{\lfloor}B_{d}\times P_{d}}
(4)
For each decomposition d=d1+d2d=d_{1}+d_{2}, x1∈⌊Bd1x_{1}\in{}_{\lfloor}B_{d_{1}}, x2∈⌊Bd2x_{2}\in{}_{\lfloor}B_{d_{2}}, q1∈Qd1q_{1}\in Q_{d_{1}}, q2∈Qd2q_{2}\in Q_{d_{2}}, and v∈Qd1,d2v\in Q_{d_{1},d_{2}} with |v||v| sufficiently small, one has
λd​(ζd1,d2B​(x1,x2),(q1,q2,v))=(1,θd1,d2​(x1,x2,v))⋅(ζd1,d2B​(x1,x2),ζd1,d2P​(λd1​(x1,q1),λd2​(x2,q2)))\lambda_{d}(\zeta_{d_{1},d_{2}}^{B}(x_{1},x_{2}),(q_{1},q_{2},v))=(1,\theta_{d_{1},d_{2}}(x_{1},x_{2},v))\cdot\Big(\zeta_{d_{1},d_{2}}^{B}(x_{1},x_{2}),\zeta_{d_{1},d_{2}}^{P}(\lambda_{d_{1}}(x_{1},q_{1}),\lambda_{d_{2}}(x_{2},q_{2}))\Big)
(14.6)
where ⋅\cdot denots the 𝒢d×𝒢d{\mathcal{G}}_{d}\times{\mathcal{G}}_{d}-action on Bd×PdB_{d}\times P_{d}.
Proof.
The proof, which is similar to that of Proposition 14.17, is based on induction and homotopies over the collar region. For d=1d=1, choose an arbitrary λ1\lambda_{1} which realizes the local diffeomorphism Q1Q_{1} with P1P_{1}. The formula (14.6) allows us to define λd\lambda_{d} on boundary. The condition that λd\lambda_{d} is collared implies that the boundary values of λd\lambda_{d} determine its values near the boundary. One can then extend to the interior of ⌊Bd{}_{\lfloor}B_{d}.
∎
14.3.6. Stable complex structure
As the first step towards constructing the stable complex structure for the AMS construction, we have the following “natural” stable complex structure on the monotone flow category of curves.
Proposition 14.19.
The monotone flow category ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞{}_{\lfloor}{\mathbb{Dom}} (enriched in ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rig{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}) admits a natural lift to ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}}.
Proof.
Notice that the smooth part ℳ¯(ℂℙd,d)∗0,2⊆ℳ¯(ℂℙd,d)0,2\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}^{*}(\mathbb{CP}^{d},d)\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}(\mathbb{CP}^{d},d) has a P​G​L​(d+1)PGL(d+1)-invariant complex structure. The constraint at the negative or the positive marking does not affect this complex structure. Notice that the interior of BdB_{d} has a projection map Bd→ℳ¯(ℂℙd,d)0,2B_{d}\to\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}(\mathbb{CP}^{d},d) whose fibers are the S1S^{1}-rotations (which has no fixed point); moreover, the 𝒢d{\mathcal{G}}_{d}-action sends S1S^{1}-orbits to S1S^{1}-orbits. Hence we can define IBd→BdI_{B_{d}}\to B_{d} as the pullback of the tangent bundle of ℳ¯(ℂℙd,d)∗0,2\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}^{*}(\mathbb{CP}^{d},d) so that there is a 𝒢d{\mathcal{G}}_{d}-equivariant vector bundle isomorphism
T​Bd⊕ℝ¯≅IBdTB_{d}\oplus\underline{\smash{\mathbb{R}}}\cong I_{B_{d}}
where the trivial bundle ℝ¯\underline{\smash{\mathbb{R}}} is the subbundle coming from the S1S^{1}-orbits.
Now we consider the structural maps. Given d1,d2≥1d_{1},d_{2}\geq 1, recall one has the map
ζd1,d2B:Bd1×Bd2→∂d1,d2Bd1+d2.\zeta_{d_{1},d_{2}}^{B}:B_{d_{1}}\times B_{d_{2}}\to\partial^{d_{1},d_{2}}B_{d_{1}+d_{2}}.
The differential reads
T​Bd1⊕T​Bd2→T​∂d1,d2Bd1+d2.TB_{d_{1}}\oplus TB_{d_{2}}\to T\partial^{d_{1},d_{2}}B_{d_{1}+d_{2}}.
On the other hand, one can see from the construction of ζd1,d2B\zeta_{d_{1},d_{2}}^{B} that it induces a complex analytic embedding
ℳ¯(ℂℙd1,d1)∗0,2×ℳ¯(ℂℙd2,d2)∗0,2→ℳ¯(ℂℙd1+d2,d1+d2)∗0,2.\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}^{*}(\mathbb{CP}^{d_{1}},d_{1})\times\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}^{*}(\mathbb{CP}^{d_{2}},d_{2})\to\overline{\mathcal{M}}{}_{0,2}^{*}(\mathbb{CP}^{d_{1}+d_{2}},d_{1}+d_{2}).
Therefore, the map ζd1,d2B\zeta_{d_{1},d_{2}}^{B} respects the corresponding stable complex structures.
∎
14.3.7. Orientation and concatenation
Recall that each BdB_{d} is oriented in a canonical way. Hence for d=d1+d2d=d_{1}+d_{2}, there is a product orientation on Bd1×Bd2B_{d_{1}}\times B_{d_{2}}. As 𝒢d{\mathcal{G}}_{d} is a complex Lie group, 𝒢d×𝒢d1×𝒢d2(Bd1×Bd2){\mathcal{G}}_{d}\times_{{\mathcal{G}}_{d_{1}}\times{\mathcal{G}}_{d_{2}}}(B_{d_{1}}\times B_{d_{2}}) has the induced product orientation. On the other hand, it is a codimension one boundary of BdB_{d}, hence has a corresponding boundary orientation.
Lemma 14.20.
The product orientation and the boundary orientation coincide.
Proof.
We only consider the interior of the moduli spaces Bd1B_{d_{1}} and Bd2B_{d_{2}}. Recall that Bd1/S1B_{d_{1}}/S^{1} and Bd2/S1B_{d_{2}}/S^{1} are open subsets of complex manifolds. There are also orientation-preserving gluing maps
Bd1/S1×Δ×Bd2/S1→Bd/S1B_{d_{1}}/S^{1}\times\Delta\times B_{d_{2}}/S^{1}\to B_{d}/S^{1}
where Δ\Delta is a small disk of gluing parameters. By explicitly writing down the gluing map in terms of representative and the effect of reparametrizations, one can see that the induced map
Bd1×[0,ϵ)×Bd2→BdB_{d_{1}}\times[0,\epsilon)\times B_{d_{2}}\to B_{d}
is orientation preserving. Because all BdB_{d} are odd-dimensional, our convention on induced boundary orientation leads to the conclusion.
∎
14.4. Multimodules and homotopies for smooth domains
In this subsection, we describe the multimodules of domain curves which will be used for the AMS construction for moduli spaces for pair-of-pants products.
We would like to specify a class of constructions as follows. Fix a common outercollaring width. Choose (independently) lifts of the outercollared domain flow category ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞1,…,⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞m,⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞′{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}_{1},\ldots,{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}_{m},{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\prime} to ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}}.2020
20
When we treat the cigar bimodule and the Poincaré duality multimodule, one does not need ⌊𝔻​𝕠​𝕞¯′{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\mathbb{Dom}}}^{\prime}. However the method can be easily modified to suit those cases.
(1)
For any smooth genus zero curve Σ\Sigma with mm negative cylindrical ends and one positive cylindrical end, we construct a class of monotone multimodule ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞Σ{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\Sigma} over (𝔻⌊𝕠𝕞1,…,𝔻⌊𝕠𝕞m;𝔻⌊𝕠𝕞′)({}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}_{1},\ldots,{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}_{m};{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\prime}) enriched in ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}}.
(2)
Let Σt\Sigma_{t}, t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] be a smooth family of smooth genus zero curves with mm negative cylindrical ends and one positive cylindrical end. Let ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞Σ0{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\Sigma_{0}}, ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞Σ1{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\Sigma_{1}} be two monotone multimodules as above. be the subspace satisfying the positive constraint

14.4.1. Structural maps
To describe the structural maps, we need to choose the corresponding lateral lines on Σ\Sigma.2121

Similarly, we also define the concatenation map. Consider the concatenation at the two negative ends of Σ\Sigma. Let ϕj∈Bdj\phi^{j}\in B_{d^{j}}, j=1,2j=1,2, be represented by maps uj:Σj→ℙdju^{j}:\Sigma^{j}\to\mathbb{P}^{d^{j}}. Then they pullback line bundles Lu1,Lu2→ΣL_{u^{1}},L_{u^{2}}\to\Sigma with frames
(h01,…,hd11),(h02,…,hd22).(h_{0}^{1},\ldots,h_{d^{1}}^{1}),\ (h_{0}^{2},\ldots,h_{d^{2}}^{2}).
The positive constraint is that
h01​(z+)=⋯=hd1−11​(z+)=0,\displaystyle\ h_{0}^{1}(z_{+})=\cdots=h_{d^{1}-1}^{1}(z_{+})=0,\
h02​(z+)=⋯=hd2−12​(z+)=0.\displaystyle\ h_{0}^{2}(z_{+})=\cdots=h_{d^{2}-1}^{2}(z_{+})=0.
On the other hand, suppose the point ϕ∈BdΣ\phi\in B_{d}^{\Sigma} is represented by a map u:Σ→ℙdu:\Sigma\to{\mathbb{P}}^{d}, which pulls back a bundle Lu→ΣL_{u}\to\Sigma having a frame
h0,…,hdh_{0},\ldots,h_{d}
satisfying
h0​(z+)=⋯=hd−1​(z+)=0.h_{0}(z_{+})=\cdots=h_{d-1}(z_{+})=0.
The parallel transport along the two lateral lines induces nonzero vectors τ1∈Lu​(z−1)\tau^{1}\in L_{u}(z_{-}^{1}), τ2∈Lu​(z−2)\tau^{2}\in L_{u}(z_{-}^{2}). Then consider the prestable curve
Σ~:=(Σ1⊔Σ2)​#​Σ.\tilde{\Sigma}:=(\Sigma^{1}\sqcup\Sigma^{2})\#\Sigma.
We extend the bundles Lu1→Σ1L_{u^{1}}\to\Sigma^{1}, Lu2→Σ2L_{u^{2}}\to\Sigma^{2}, and Lu→ΣL_{u}\to\Sigma to other components by trivial bundle extension. Then all the sections extend by constants. Then define L=Lu1⊗Lu2⊗LuL=L_{u^{1}}\otimes L_{u^{2}}\otimes L_{u} and consider the collection of sections (written in three groups)
(h01⊗hd22⊗τ1,…,hd1−11⊗hd22⊗τ1,hd11⊗h02⊗τ2,…,hd11⊗hd2−12⊗τ2,hd11⊗hd22⊗h0,…,hd11⊗hd22⊗hd).\Big(h_{0}^{1}\otimes h_{d^{2}}^{2}\otimes\tau^{1},\ldots,h_{d^{1}-1}^{1}\otimes h_{d^{2}}^{2}\otimes\tau^{1};h_{d^{1}}^{1}\otimes h_{0}^{2}\otimes\tau^{2},\ldots,h_{d^{1}}^{1}\otimes h_{d^{2}-1}^{2}\otimes\tau^{2};h_{d^{1}}^{1}\otimes h_{d^{2}}^{2}\otimes h_{0},\ldots,h_{d^{1}}^{1}\otimes h_{d^{2}}^{2}\otimes h_{d}\Big).
Then it is easy to see that this collection forms a basis of H0​(L)H^{0}(L). In particular, it is base-point-free. Hence it defines a holomorphic map
u~:Σ→ℙd1+d2+d.\tilde{u}:\Sigma\to\mathbb{P}^{d^{1}+d^{2}+d}.
One can also see that this is independent of the choices of the representatives. Hence one obtains a well-defined map
ζd1,d2;dB:Bd1×Bd2×BdΣ→Bd1+d2+dΣ.\zeta_{d^{1},d^{2};d}^{B}:B_{d^{1}}\times B_{d^{2}}\times B_{d}^{\Sigma}\to B_{d^{1}+d^{2}+d}^{\Sigma}.
It is easy to see that the map is equivariant with respect to the group embedding.
The associativity is more subtle than the previous case. Choose da1,db1,da2,db2,dd^{1}_{a},d^{1}_{b},d_{a}^{2},d_{b}^{2},d. Denote d~=db1+db2+d\tilde{d}=d_{b}^{1}+d_{b}^{2}+d. Let’s compare the following two elements
ζda1+db1,da2+db2;dB​(ζda1,db1B​(ϕa1,ϕb1),ζda2,db2B​(ϕa2,ϕb2),ϕ)​vs.ζda1,da2;d~B​(ϕa1,ϕa2,ζϕb1,ϕb2;dB​(ϕb1,ϕb2,ϕ)).\zeta_{d^{1}_{a}+d_{b}^{1},d^{2}_{a}+d_{b}^{2};d}^{B}\left(\zeta_{d_{a}^{1},d_{b}^{1}}^{B}(\phi^{1}_{a},\phi^{1}_{b}),\zeta_{d_{a}^{2},d_{b}^{2}}^{B}(\phi^{2}_{a},\phi^{2}_{b});\phi\right)\ {\rm vs.}\ \zeta_{d_{a}^{1},d_{a}^{2};\tilde{d}}^{B}\left(\phi_{a}^{1},\phi_{a}^{2};\zeta_{\phi_{b}^{1},\phi_{b}^{2};d}^{B}(\phi_{b}^{1},\phi_{b}^{2};\phi)\right).
They indeed differ by a conjugation. In fact, the diagram
U⁡(da1)×U⁡(db1)×U⁡(da2)×U⁡(db2)×U⁡(d)\textstyle{U(d_{a}^{1})\times U(d_{b}^{1})\times U(d_{a}^{2})\times U(d_{b}^{2})\times U(d)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}U⁡(da1+db1)×U⁡(da2+db2)×U⁡(d)\textstyle{U(d_{a}^{1}+d_{b}^{1})\times U(d_{a}^{2}+d_{b}^{2})\times U(d)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}U⁡(da1)×U⁡(da2)×U⁡(d~)\textstyle{U(d_{a}^{1})\times U(d_{a}^{2})\times U(\tilde{d})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}U⁡(da1+da2+db1+db2+d)\textstyle{U(d_{a}^{1}+d_{a}^{2}+d_{b}^{1}+d_{b}^{2}+d)}
commutes up to an element in U⁡(da1+da2+db1+db2+d)U(d_{a}^{1}+d_{a}^{2}+d_{b}^{1}+d_{b}^{2}+d) which is the matrix permuting corresponding coordinates. Therefore, the above diagram commutes up to a conjugation.
One can extend the above construction to the general case when Σ\Sigma is smooth with multiple inputs.
Proposition 14.21.
The collections of equivariant family of curves 𝒞dΣ{\mathcal{C}}_{d}^{\Sigma} together with the structural maps
𝒞d1×⋯×𝒞dm×𝒞dΣ×𝒞d′→𝒞d1+⋯+dm+d+d′Σ{\mathcal{C}}_{d_{1}}\times\cdots\times{\mathcal{C}}_{d_{m}}\times{\mathcal{C}}_{d}^{\Sigma}\times{\mathcal{C}}_{d^{\prime}}\to{\mathcal{C}}_{d_{1}+\cdots+d_{m}+d+d^{\prime}}^{\Sigma}
define a monotone multimodule over (𝔻​𝕠​𝕞,…,𝔻​𝕠​𝕞,𝔻​𝕠​𝕞)(\mathbb{Dom},\ldots,\mathbb{Dom};\mathbb{Dom}).
14.4.2. Rigidification and stable complex structure
We can construct a rigidification of any outercollaring of the multimodule 𝔻​𝕠​𝕞Σ\mathbb{Dom}^{\Sigma} in the same way as constructing the rigidification of the domain flow category (see Proposition 14.17).
Proposition 14.22.
Given lifts of ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞1,…,⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞m,⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞′{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}_{1},\ldots,{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}_{m},{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\prime} to ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}}, there exists a lift of ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞Σ{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\Sigma} to ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}} as a monotone multimodule over the given lifts of the monotone flow categories. Moreover, for all dd there exist 𝒢d{\mathcal{G}}_{d}-invariant orientations on BdΣB_{d}^{\Sigma} satisfying
(1)
For each i∈{1,…,m}i\in\{1,\ldots,m\} and di>0d_{i}>0, the map
𝒢di+d×𝒢di×𝒢d(Bdi×BdΣ)→∂di,dBd+diΣ{\mathcal{G}}_{d_{i}+d}\times_{{\mathcal{G}}_{d_{i}}\times{\mathcal{G}}_{d}}(B_{d_{i}}\times B_{d}^{\Sigma})\to\partial^{d_{i},d}B_{d+d_{i}}^{\Sigma}
is orientation preserving.
(2)
For each d′>0d^{\prime}>0, the map
𝒢d+d′×𝒢d×𝒢d′(BdΣ×Bd′)→∂d,d′Bd+d′Σ{\mathcal{G}}_{d+d^{\prime}}\times_{{\mathcal{G}}_{d}\times{\mathcal{G}}_{d^{\prime}}}(B_{d}^{\Sigma}\times B_{d^{\prime}})\to\partial^{d,d^{\prime}}B_{d+d^{\prime}}^{\Sigma}
is orientation reversing.
Proof.
The construction of the rigidification can be carried out as done in the proof of Proposition 14.17. The construction of stable complex structure can be carried out similarly as in the proof of Proposition 14.19. As for the orientation, the argument is similar to Lemma 14.20. However, notice that BdB_{d} has an odd dimension and BdΣB_{d}^{\Sigma} has an even dimension, which make the difference in the two cases as one has to interchange the [0,ϵ)[0,\epsilon) factor with either BdiB_{d_{i}} or BdΣB_{d}^{\Sigma}.
∎
14.4.3. Homotopies
Flow homotopies associated to a 1-parameter family of variations of domain Floer data is indeed quite trivial. Indeed, let Σt\Sigma_{t}, t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] be a smooth family of Floer domains with mm negative ends and 11 positive end. Then there are m+1m+1 copies of the monotone flow categories 𝔻​𝕠​𝕞\mathbb{Dom} corresponding to the mm inputs and 1 output. Suppose Σt\Sigma_{t} is equipped with a smooth family of lateral lines. Then Σ0\Sigma_{0} and Σ1\Sigma_{1} correspond to monotone multimodules 𝔻​𝕠​𝕞Σ0\mathbb{Dom}^{\Sigma_{0}} and 𝔻​𝕠​𝕞Σ1\mathbb{Dom}^{\Sigma_{1}} over (𝔻​𝕠​𝕞,…,𝔻​𝕠​𝕞,𝔻​𝕠​𝕞)(\mathbb{Dom},\ldots,\mathbb{Dom};\mathbb{Dom}). Moreover, by allowing tt to vary, one naturally obtains a monotone homotopy 𝔻​𝕠​𝕞ℍ\mathbb{Dom}^{\mathbb{H}} from 𝔻​𝕠​𝕞Σ0\mathbb{Dom}^{\Sigma_{0}} to 𝔻​𝕠​𝕞Σ1\mathbb{Dom}^{\Sigma_{1}}. Upon choosing any outercollaring width, these items become corresponding collared versions. The following proposition demonstrates that the choices of rigidifications and stable complex structures can also be carried inductively.
Proposition 14.23.
Let ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞1,…,⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞m;⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞′{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}_{1},\ldots,{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}_{m};{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\prime} be monotone flow categories enriched in ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}} obtained from the monotone flow category 𝔻​𝕠​𝕞\mathbb{Dom} by outercollaring and possibly different rigidifications. Let
⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞Σ0,\displaystyle\ {}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\Sigma_{0}},\
⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞Σ1\displaystyle\ {}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\Sigma_{1}}
be monotone multimodules over (𝔻⌊𝕠𝕞1,…,𝔻⌊𝕠𝕞m;𝔻⌊𝕠𝕞′)({}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}_{1},\ldots,{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}_{m};{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\prime}) enriched in ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}} constructed above. Then the outercollaring ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞ℍ{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\mathbb{H}} admits a lift to ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}} as a monotone homotopy from ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞Σ0{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\Sigma_{0}} to ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞Σ1{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\Sigma_{1}}.
Proof.
Routine verification of the inductive constructions.
∎

14.4.4. The case of cigar bimodule
Let Σcigar\Sigma^{\rm cigar} be the complex plane ℂ{\mathbb{C}} equipped with a cylindrical end. It is used to construct the cigar bimodule and eventually lead to the multiplicative identity of the pair-of-pants product. The construction of the corresponding monotone bimodule, denoted by ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞cigar{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\rm cigar}, is slightly different from the general case.
We shall regard ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞cigar{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\rm cigar} not as a bimodule, but only a right module over ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}. This means it consists of objects
𝒞dcigar∈⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{\mathcal{C}}_{d}^{\rm cigar}\in{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}}
together with structural maps
𝒞dcigar×𝒞d′→𝒞d+d′cigar{\mathcal{C}}_{d}^{\rm cigar}\times{\mathcal{C}}_{d^{\prime}}\to{\mathcal{C}}_{d+d^{\prime}}^{\rm cigar}
which satisfy the obvious associativity relation. The construction of the object 𝒞dcigar{\mathcal{C}}_{d}^{\rm cigar} is the same as before. Indeed, consider the moduli space of degree dd maps
ϕ:Σcigar→ℂ​ℙd\phi:\Sigma^{\rm cigar}\to\mathbb{CP}^{d}
satisfying the constraint
ϕ⁡(∞)=[0,…,0,1]∈ℙd\phi(\infty)=[0,\ldots,0,1]\in\mathbb{P}^{d}
and such that the image of ϕ\phi is not contained in any hyperplane. After compactification in the standard way, one obtains a moduli space BdcigarB_{d}^{\rm cigar} equipped with a 𝒢d{\mathcal{G}}_{d}-action and a universal curve Cdcigar→BdcigarC_{d}^{\rm cigar}\to B_{d}^{\rm cigar}, hence provides an object
𝒞dcigar=(𝒢d,Bdcigar,Cdcigar){\mathcal{C}}_{d}^{\rm cigar}=({\mathcal{G}}_{d},B_{d}^{\rm cigar},C_{d}^{\rm cigar})
stratified by the poset
Adcigar={(d0,d1,…,dl)|d0+⋯+dl=d,di≥1}.A_{d}^{\rm cigar}=\{(d_{0},d_{1},\ldots,d_{l})\ |\ d_{0}+\cdots+d_{l}=d,\ d_{i}\geq 1\}.
The difference from the previous case is the definition of the structural maps. In the current situation, we do not need a lateral line in Σcigar\Sigma^{\rm cigar}. Other constructions are the same. This provides a monotone right module 𝔻​𝕠​𝕞cigar\mathbb{Dom}^{\rm cigar} over 𝔻​𝕠​𝕞\mathbb{Dom}. Then after outercollaring and choosing a lift of ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom} to ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}}, one can find a rigidification of the outercollaring ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞cigar{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\rm cigar}.
14.4.5. The case of Poincaré duality multimodule
Now let ΣPD\Sigma^{\rm PD} be the smooth Floer domain with two negative ends and no positive ends, which is responsible for defining the Poincaré duality for Floer theory. One can similar define a monotone multimodule ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞PD{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\rm PD} enriched in ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}} as above, whose construction slightly differ from previous cases.
In this case, the structure we build is better called a double left module, meaning a collection of objects
𝒞dPD∈⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{\mathcal{C}}_{d}^{\rm PD}\in{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}}
together with two structural maps
𝒞d1×𝒞dPD→𝒞d1+dPD,𝒞d2×𝒞dPD→𝒞d2+dPD\displaystyle\ {\mathcal{C}}_{d_{1}}\times{\mathcal{C}}_{d}^{\rm PD}\to{\mathcal{C}}_{d_{1}+d}^{\rm PD},\ {\mathcal{C}}_{d_{2}}\times{\mathcal{C}}_{d}^{\rm PD}\to{\mathcal{C}}_{d_{2}+d}^{\rm PD}
corresponding to breakings at the two negative ends, which satisfy similar associativity conditions as a general monotone multimodule.
We first consider the moduli space of degree dd stable maps
ϕ:ΣPD→ℂ​ℙd\phi:\Sigma^{\rm PD}\to\mathbb{CP}^{d}
whose images are not contained in any hyperplane. As the cylindrical ends are on the negative side, in the current convention we do not impose any evaluation constraint. After the standard compactification, one obtains such a moduli space
BdPDB_{d}^{\rm PD}
which has a 𝒢d{\mathcal{G}}_{d}-action and a universal curve CdPD→BdPDC_{d}^{\rm PD}\to B_{d}^{\rm PD}, providing an object
𝒞dPD=(𝒢d,BdPD,CdPD).{\mathcal{C}}_{d}^{\rm PD}=({\mathcal{G}}_{d},B_{d}^{\rm PD},C_{d}^{\rm PD}).
The structural maps are also defined similarly, but without using lateral lines. We omit the details. Hence one obtains a monotone double left module 𝔻​𝕠​𝕞PD\mathbb{Dom}^{\rm PD} over (𝔻​𝕠​𝕞,𝔻​𝕠​𝕞)(\mathbb{Dom},\mathbb{Dom}). Then after outercollaring, upon choosing two independent lifts ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞1,⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞2{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}_{1},{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}_{2} to ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}}, one can construct a lift ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞PD{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\rm PD} to ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}}. We omit the details.
15. Relatively Smooth AMS lifts
In this section we carry out perhaps the most complex part of the AMS construction. We demonstrate how to lift an outercollaring of a Floer flow category 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} to ⌊𝐒rel​𝐊𝐮𝐫¯rig{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf S^{\rm rel}Kur}}_{\rm rig}, the category of (collared and rigidified) relatively smooth Kuranishi spaces. In fact, we will construct a lift to ⌊𝐊𝐮𝐫¯rig{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Kur}}_{\rm rig}, the category of collared and rigidified topological Kuranishi spaces. The lift to relatively smooth version is automatic. The collared-and-rigidified feature is always preserved in the construction as it is a basic prerequisite for inductively construct perturbations.
15.1. Integral modification of topological energy
We generalize the method of Rezchikov [57] of modifying the topological energy. First, there is a way to modify the symplectic form.
Definition 15.1.
Let 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} be the Floer flow category associated to a nondegenerate Hamiltonian HH on (X,ω,J)(X,\omega,J). An integral action on 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} is a function
𝒜𝔽Ω:Ob​𝔽→ℤ{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{F}}^{\Omega}:{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}\to{\mathbb{Z}}
satisfying the following conditions.
(1)
There exists an integral symplectic form Ω∈Ω2​(X)\Omega\in\Omega^{2}(X) tamed by JJ such that ker​Ω=ker​ω⊆π2​(X){\rm ker}\Omega={\rm ker}\omega\subseteq\pi_{2}(X) and for each A∈ΠA\in\Pi and p∈Ob​𝔽p\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}
𝒜𝔽Ω​(A⋅p)=𝒜𝔽Ω​(p)−Ω⁡(A).{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{F}}^{\Omega}(A\cdot p)={\mathcal{A}}^{\Omega}_{\mathbb{F}}(p)-\Omega(A).
(2)
There exists C>0C>0 such that whenever p≠qp\neq q and Mp​q𝔽≠∅M_{pq}^{\mathbb{F}}\neq\emptyset, one has
0<C⁡(𝒜H​(p)−𝒜H​(q))≤𝒜𝔽Ω​(p)−𝒜𝔽Ω​(q).0<C\left({\mathcal{A}}_{H}(p)-{\mathcal{A}}_{H}(q)\right)\leq{\mathcal{A}}^{\Omega}_{\mathbb{F}}(p)-{\mathcal{A}}^{\Omega}_{\mathbb{F}}(q).
We need similar notions for multimodules and homotopies.
Definition 15.2.
Consider a smooth genus zero Riemann surface with cylindrical ends Σ\Sigma together with a family of Floer data σw\sigma_{w} parametrized continuously by ww in a compact topological space such that for all ww, the Floer data is asymptotic to (Hi​d​t,Ji)(H_{i}dt,J_{i}) on the ii-th negative end (i=1,…,mi=1,\ldots,m) and asymptotic to (Hj′​d​t,Jj′)(H_{j}^{\prime}dt,J_{j}^{\prime}) on the jj-th positive end (j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n). A compatible collection of integral actions consists of integral actions
𝒜𝔽iΩ:Ob​𝔽i→ℤ⁡(i=1,…,m),\displaystyle\ {\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}_{i}}^{\Omega}:{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{i}\to{\mathbb{Z}}\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\
𝒜𝔽j′Ω:Ob​𝔽j′→ℤ\displaystyle\ {\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}_{j}^{\prime}}^{\Omega}:{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{j}^{\prime}\to{\mathbb{Z}}
on the Floer flow categories 𝔽i{\mathbb{F}}_{i} resp. 𝔽j′{\mathbb{F}}_{j}^{\prime} associated to (Hi,Ji)(H_{i},J_{i}) resp. (Hj′,Jj′)(H_{j}^{\prime},J_{j}^{\prime}) satisfying the following conditions.
(1)
The integral actions induce the same integral symplectic form Ω\Omega.
(2)
For each parameter ww and each point z∈Σz\in\Sigma, Ω\Omega is tamed by the almost complex structure Jw,zJ_{w,z}.
(3)
For objects pi∈Ob​𝔽ip_{i}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{i} and pj′∈Ob​𝔽j′p_{j}^{\prime}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{j}^{\prime}, let Mp1⋯pm;p1′⋯pn′M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p_{1}^{\prime}\cdots p_{n}^{\prime}} denote temporarily the moduli space of stable solutions of Floer equation for all parameter ss asymptotic to the labeling objects. Then
Mp1⋯pm;p1′⋯pn′≠∅⟹∑i=1m𝒜𝔽iΩ(pi)>∑j=1n𝒜𝔽j′Ω(pj′)M_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p_{1}^{\prime}\cdots p_{n}^{\prime}}\neq\emptyset\Longrightarrow\sum_{i=1}^{m}{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}_{i}}^{\Omega}(p_{i})>\sum_{j=1}^{n}{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}_{j}^{\prime}}^{\Omega}(p_{j}^{\prime})
One can then specialize to multimodules and homotopies.
Definition 15.3.
(1)
In Situation Module(i), integral actions 𝒜𝔽1Ω,…,𝒜𝔽mΩ;𝒜𝔽′Ω{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}_{1}}^{\Omega},\ldots,{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}_{m}}^{\Omega};{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}^{\Omega} on the involved flow categories are called compatible with respect to 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} if it is compatible with respect to the fixed Floer data σ𝕏\sigma^{\mathbb{X}} on Σ𝕏\Sigma^{\mathbb{X}}.
(2)
In Situation Homotopy(i), integral actions 𝒜𝔽1Ω,…,𝒜𝔽mΩ,𝒜𝔽′Ω{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}_{1}}^{\Omega},\ldots,{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}_{m}}^{\Omega},{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}^{\Omega} are called compatible with respect to ℍ{\mathbb{H}} if it is compatible with respect to the 1-parameter family of Floer data.
Proposition 15.4.
In the setting of Definition 15.2, there exist compatible integral actions on involved Floer flow categories.
Proof.
It was proved in [57, Lemma 16] that given any collection H1,…,HmH_{1},\ldots,H_{m} of nondegenerate 1-periodic Hamiltonians on (X,ω)(X,\omega), there exists an open subset U⊆XU\subseteq X containing the images of all 1-periodic orbits of all HiH_{i} and for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, a rational symplectic form Ω∈Ω2​(M)\Omega\in\Omega^{2}(M) satisfying the following conditions.
(1)
Ω|U=ω|U\Omega|_{U}=\omega|_{U}.
(2)
‖Ω−ω‖C0​(X)≤ϵ\|\Omega-\omega\|_{C^{0}(X)}\leq\epsilon.
(3)
ker​Ω=ker​ω⊆π2​(X){\rm ker}\Omega={\rm ker}\omega\subseteq\pi_{2}(X).
Now consider a Floer domain Σ\Sigma with the Hamiltonian connection σ\sigma. Let Σ0⊆Σ\Sigma_{0}\subseteq\Sigma be a compact region such that Σ∖Σ0\Sigma\setminus\Sigma_{0} is a union of half cylinders. Let (s,t)(s,t) be the cylindrical coordinates and let Hi​d​tH_{i}dt be the restriction of σ\sigma to the ii-th cylindrical end UiU_{i}, where HiH_{i} is nondegenerate.
Let U⊆XU\subseteq X be the open subset provided by Rezchikov’s lemma. Let Ω\Omega be a symplectic form which agrees with ω\omega within UU and which is C0C^{0}-close to ω\omega so Ω\Omega tames Jw,zJ_{w,z} for all almost complex structures appearing. Then there exists ϵ0>0\epsilon_{0}>0 satisfying
∀i∀ρ:S1→X,∫S1|ρ′​(t)−XHi,t​(ρ⁡(t))|2​𝑑t≤ϵ0⟹Im⁡(ρ)⊆U.\forall i\ \ \forall\rho:S^{1}\to X,\ \int_{S^{1}}|\rho^{\prime}(t)-X_{H_{i,t}}(\rho(t))|^{2}dt\leq\epsilon_{0}\Longrightarrow{\rm Im}(\rho)\subseteq U.
(15.1)
For each capped 1-periodic orbit pp of HiH_{i} where the capping is a map u:𝔻2→Xu:{\mathbb{D}}^{2}\to X, define
𝒜HiΩ(γ,u)=−∫𝔻2u∗Ω−∫S1Hi(γ(t))dt.{\mathcal{A}}_{H_{i}}^{\Omega}(\gamma,u)=-\int_{{\mathbb{D}}^{2}}u^{*}\Omega-\int_{S^{1}}H_{i}(\gamma(t))dt.
Let |⋅|Ω|\cdot|_{\Omega} be the norm on the tangent bundle T​XTX determined by Ω\Omega and Jw,zJ_{w,z}. For any map u:Σ→Xu:\Sigma\to X, define
∇σ,Ω(u)=∇u+XσΩ​(u)\nabla^{\sigma,\Omega}(u)=\nabla u+X_{\sigma}^{\Omega}(u)
where XσΩX_{\sigma}^{\Omega} is the 1-form on Σ\Sigma taking values in Hamiltonian vector fields associated to Ω\Omega. In any local coordinate z=s+𝐢​tz=s+{\bf i}t one can write σ=σs​d​s+σt​d​t\sigma=\sigma_{s}ds+\sigma_{t}dt and
∇σ,Ωu=∇sσ,Ωu​d​s+∇tσ,Ωu​d​t.\nabla^{\sigma,\Omega}u=\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\Omega}uds+\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\Omega}udt.
The difference of the covariant derivatives between Ω\Omega and ω\omega is
∇σ,Ωu−∇σ,ωu=(XσsΩ​(u)−Xσsω​(u))​d​s+(XσtΩ​(u)−Xσtω​(u))​d​t=:XσsΩ−ω​(u)​d​s+XσtΩ−ω​(u)​d​t\nabla^{\sigma,\Omega}u-\nabla^{\sigma,\omega}u=(X_{\sigma_{s}}^{\Omega}(u)-X_{\sigma_{s}}^{\omega}(u))ds+(X_{\sigma_{t}}^{\Omega}(u)-X_{\sigma_{t}}^{\omega}(u))dt=:X_{\sigma_{s}}^{\Omega-\omega}(u)ds+X_{\sigma_{t}}^{\Omega-\omega}(u)dt
which is linear in the difference Ω−ω\Omega-\omega.
Define the energy density of the map uu as
12​|∇σ,ω(u)|Ω2​dvolΣ.\frac{1}{2}|\nabla^{\sigma,\omega}(u)|_{\Omega}^{2}{\rm dvol}_{\Sigma}.
Then one has the calculation (see [46, Lemma 2.2.1])
12​|∇σ,ω(u)|Ω2​dvolΣ=|(∇σ,ω(u))0,1|2​dvolΣ+12​(Ω⁡(∇sσ,ωu,∇tσ,ωu)+Ω⁡(J​∇sσ,ωu,J​∇tσ,ωu))​d​s​d​t.\frac{1}{2}|\nabla^{\sigma,\omega}(u)|_{\Omega}^{2}{\rm dvol}_{\Sigma}=|(\nabla^{\sigma,\omega}(u))^{0,1}|^{2}{\rm dvol}_{\Sigma}+\frac{1}{2}\Big(\Omega(\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\omega}u)+\Omega(J\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,J\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\omega}u)\Big)dsdt.
We observe that
|Ω⁡(J​∇sσ,ωu,J​∇tσ,ωu)−Ω⁡(∇sσ,ωu,∇tσ,ωu)|=|Ω⁡(J​∇sσ,ωu,J​∇tσ,ωu)−ω⁡(J​∇sσ,ωu,J​∇tσ,ωu)+ω⁡(J​∇sσ,ωu,J​∇tσ,ωu)−Ω⁡(∇sσ,ωu,∇tσ,ωu)|=|Ω⁡(J​∇sσ,ωu,J​∇tσ,ωu)−ω⁡(J​∇sσ,ωu,J​∇tσ,ωu)+ω⁡(∇sσ,ωu,∇tσ,ωu)−Ω⁡(∇sσ,ωu,∇tσ,ωu)|≤‖ω−Ω‖C0​(X)⋅|∇σ,ω(u)|Ω2\begin{split}&\ |\Omega(J\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,J\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\omega}u)-\Omega(\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\omega}u)|\\
=&\ |\Omega(J\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,J\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\omega}u)-\omega(J\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,J\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\omega}u)+\omega(J\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,J\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\omega}u)-\Omega(\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\omega}u)|\\
=&\ |\Omega(J\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,J\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\omega}u)-\omega(J\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,J\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\omega}u)+\omega(\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\omega}u)-\Omega(\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\omega}u)|\\
\leq&\ \|\omega-\Omega\|_{C^{0}(X)}\cdot|\nabla^{\sigma,\omega}(u)|_{\Omega}^{2}\end{split}
(15.2)
Now suppose uu solves (∇σ,ωu)0,1=0(\nabla^{\sigma,\omega}u)^{0,1}=0. Then one has
Ω⁡(∇sσ,ωu,∇tσ,ωu)=Ω⁡(∇sσ,Ωu+Xσsω−Ω​(u),∇tσ,Ωu+Xσtω−Ω​(u))=Ω⁡(∇sσ,Ωu,∇tσ,Ωu)+Ω⁡(∇sσ,Ωu,Xσtω−Ω​(u))+Ω⁡(Xσsω−Ω​(u),∇tσ,Ωu)+Ω⁡(Xσsω−Ω​(u),Xσtω−Ω​(u))=Ω⁡(∇sσ,Ωu,∇tσ,Ωu)+Ω⁡(∇sσ,ωu,Xσtω−Ω​(u))+Ω⁡(Xσsω−Ω​(u),∇tσ,ω(u))+Ω⁡(Xσsω−Ω​(u),XσtΩ−ω​(u))\begin{split}&\ \Omega(\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\omega}u)\\
=&\ \Omega\Big(\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\Omega}u+X_{\sigma_{s}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u),\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\Omega}u+X_{\sigma_{t}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u)\Big)\\
=&\ \Omega(\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\Omega}u,\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\Omega}u)+\Omega(\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\Omega}u,X_{\sigma_{t}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u))+\Omega(X_{\sigma_{s}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u),\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\Omega}u)+\Omega(X_{\sigma_{s}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u),X_{\sigma_{t}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u))\\
=&\ \Omega(\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\Omega}u,\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\Omega}u)+\Omega(\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,X_{\sigma_{t}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u))+\Omega(X_{\sigma_{s}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u),\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\omega}(u))+\Omega(X_{\sigma_{s}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u),X_{\sigma_{t}}^{\Omega-\omega}(u))\end{split}
Notice that if uu converges to capped 1-periodic orbits pip_{i} at the ii-th cylindrical end, then
∫ΣΩ(∇sσ,Ωu,∇tσ,Ωu)dsdt=∑i=1m±𝒜HiΩ(pi)+∫ΣFσ(u)\int_{\Sigma}\Omega(\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\Omega}u,\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\Omega}u)dsdt=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\pm{\mathcal{A}}_{H_{i}}^{\Omega}(p_{i})+\int_{\Sigma}F_{\sigma}(u)
where the first term only depends on the homotopy class of uu and FσF_{\sigma} does not depend on the symplectic form. Then one has
∑i=1m±𝒜HiΩ(pi)=∫ΣΩ(∇sσ,Ωu,∇tσ,Ωu)dsdt−∫ΣFσ(u)−∫Σ(Ω(∇sσ,ωu,Xσtω−Ω(u)+Ω(Xσsω−Ω(u),∇tσ,ωu)−Ω(Xσsω−Ω(u),Xσtω−Ω(u)))dsdt.\sum_{i=1}^{m}\pm{\mathcal{A}}_{H_{i}}^{\Omega}(p_{i})=\int_{\Sigma}\Omega(\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\Omega}u,\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\Omega}u)dsdt-\int_{\Sigma}F_{\sigma}(u)\\
-\int_{\Sigma}\Big(\Omega(\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,X_{\sigma_{t}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u)+\Omega(X_{\sigma_{s}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u),\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\omega}u)-\Omega(X_{\sigma_{s}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u),X_{\sigma_{t}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u))\Big)dsdt.
We would like to estimate the last term. First, on the compact region Σ0\Sigma_{0}, one has
|∫Σ0(Ω(∇sσ,ωu,Xσtω−Ω(u)+Ω(Xσsω−Ω(u),∇tσ,ωu)−Ω(Xσsω−Ω(u),Xσtω−Ω(u)))dsdt|≤C⁡(ϵ)​‖ω−Ω‖C0​(X)2+ϵ​∫Σ0|∇σ,ω(u)|Ω2​dvolΣ\left|\int_{\Sigma_{0}}\Big(\Omega(\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,X_{\sigma_{t}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u)+\Omega(X_{\sigma_{s}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u),\nabla_{t}^{\sigma,\omega}u)-\Omega(X_{\sigma_{s}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u),X_{\sigma_{t}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u))\Big)dsdt\right|\\
\leq C(\epsilon)\|\omega-\Omega\|_{C^{0}(X)}^{2}+\epsilon\int_{\Sigma_{0}}|\nabla^{\sigma,\omega}(u)|_{\Omega}^{2}{\rm dvol}_{\Sigma}
for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and a suitable C⁡(ϵ)>0C(\epsilon)>0. On the other hand, on each half cylinder Ui≅Ii×S1U_{i}\cong I_{i}\times S^{1} where Ii=ℝ±I_{i}={\mathbb{R}}_{\pm}, contained in Σ∖Σ0\Sigma\setminus\Sigma_{0}, we may take (s,t)(s,t) to be the cylindrical coordinate. Then we know that σs=0\sigma_{s}=0. Hence we are left with
∫UiΩ⁡(∇sσ,ωu,XHiω−Ω​(u))​𝑑s​𝑑t.\int_{U_{i}}\Omega(\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,X_{H_{i}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u))dsdt.
(15.3)
Recall the pre-chosen constant ϵ0\epsilon_{0} (see (15.1)). Consider
Ii​(ϵ0):={s∈Ii|∫S1|∇sσ,ω(u)​(s,t)|ω2​𝑑t≥ϵ0}.I_{i}(\epsilon_{0}):=\Big\{s\in I_{i}\ |\ \int_{S^{1}}|\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}(u)(s,t)|_{\omega}^{2}dt\geq\epsilon_{0}\Big\}.
Then |Ii​(ϵ)|≤Eω​(u)/ϵ0|I_{i}(\epsilon)|\leq E^{\omega}(u)/\epsilon_{0}. Since Ω=ω\Omega=\omega near 1-periodic orbits, by our assumption, the integrand of (15.3) vanishes outside Ii​(ϵ0)×S1I_{i}(\epsilon_{0})\times S^{1}. Then by Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, one has
|∫UiΩ⁡(∇sσ,ωu,Xσtω−Ω​(u))​ds​dt|=|∫Ii​(ϵ0)×S1Ω⁡(∇sσ,ωu,Xσtω−Ω​(u))​ds​dt|≤C​‖ω−Ω‖C0​(X)​|Ii​(ϵ0)|​∫Ii​(ϵ0)×S1|∇sσ,ωu|ω2​𝑑s​𝑑t≤C​‖ω−Ω‖C0​(X)​Eω​(u)ϵ0.\left|\int_{U_{i}}\Omega(\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,X_{\sigma_{t}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u))dsdt\right|=\left|\int_{I_{i}(\epsilon_{0})\times S^{1}}\Omega(\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u,X_{\sigma_{t}}^{\omega-\Omega}(u))dsdt\right|\\
\leq C\|\omega-\Omega\|_{C^{0}(X)}\sqrt{|I_{i}(\epsilon_{0})|}\sqrt{\int_{I_{i}(\epsilon_{0})\times S^{1}}|\nabla_{s}^{\sigma,\omega}u|_{\omega}^{2}dsdt}\\
\leq C\|\omega-\Omega\|_{C^{0}(X)}\frac{E^{\omega}(u)}{\sqrt{\epsilon_{0}}}.
On the other hand, when Ω\Omega is close to ω\omega, the norms |⋅|ω|\cdot|_{\omega} and |⋅|Ω|\cdot|_{\Omega} are compatible. Therefore, when Ω\Omega is C0C^{0}-close to ω\omega, one has the estimate
∑i=1m±𝒜HiΩ(pi)≥12EΩ(u)−C\sum_{i=1}^{m}\pm{\mathcal{A}}_{H_{i}}^{\Omega}(p_{i})\geq\frac{1}{2}E^{\Omega}(u)-C
for some constant C>0C>0 by combining the above computations with (15.2) to rearrange the inequalities, provided that ϵ\epsilon is sufficiently small.
Further, to make the symplectic action rational, we define
𝒜𝔽iΩ​(pi):=𝒜HiΩ​(pi)+δpi{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}_{i}}^{\Omega}(p_{i}):={\mathcal{A}}_{H_{i}}^{\Omega}(p_{i})+\delta_{p_{i}}
for a small real number δpi\delta_{p_{i}} making the above rational. Then one still has
∑i=1m±𝒜𝔽iΩ(pi)≥12Eω(u)−C\sum_{i=1}^{m}\pm{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{F}_{i}}^{\Omega}(p_{i})\geq\frac{1}{2}E^{\omega}(u)-C
after changing CC a bit. Then we argue in two cases.
(1)
When Σ\Sigma is an infinite cylinder, σ=H​d​t\sigma=Hdt and JJ only depends on t∈S1t\in S^{1}, one can take C=0C=0 and obtain instead
𝒜𝔽Ω​(p)−𝒜𝔽Ω​(q)≥12​Eω​(u)=12​(𝒜Hω​(p)−𝒜Hω​(q)).{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}}^{\Omega}(p)-{\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}}^{\Omega}(q)\geq\frac{1}{2}E^{\omega}(u)=\frac{1}{2}({\mathcal{A}}_{H}^{\omega}(p)-{\mathcal{A}}_{H}^{\omega}(q)).
This provides an integral action on the associated Floer flow category.
(2)
In other cases, one can add rational constants to 𝒜HiΩ{\mathcal{A}}_{H_{i}}^{\Omega} to make the sum of ±𝒜HiΩ\pm{\mathcal{A}}_{H_{i}}^{\Omega} always positive.
Finally, we choose a common large positive integral multiple of the 𝒜𝔽Ω{\mathcal{A}}^{\Omega}_{\mathbb{F}} constructed above so that the action becomes integral valued and the symplectic form Ω\Omega becomes integral.
∎
15.1.1. Pullback the domain flow category, multimodule, and homotopy
Now choose an integral action 𝒜𝔽Ω:Ob​𝔽→ℤ{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{F}}^{\Omega}:{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}\to{\mathbb{Z}} with associated symplectic form Ω\Omega. For each pair of objects p,q∈Ob​𝔽p,q\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}, abbreviate d=dp​q=𝒜𝔽Ω​(p)−𝒜𝔽Ω​(q)d=d_{pq}={\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{F}}^{\Omega}(p)-{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{F}}^{\Omega}(q). Inside the poset AdA_{d} (of positive partitions of dd), there is an Alexandrov open subset
Ap​qΩ⊆AdA_{pq}^{\Omega}\subseteq A_{d}
whose elements are decompositions
d=d0+⋯+dld=d_{0}+\cdots+d_{l}
such that there exist objects r1,…,rl∈Ob​𝔽r_{1},\ldots,r_{l}\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}} such that
d0=𝒜𝔽Ω(p)−𝒜𝔽Ω(r1),d1=𝒜𝔽Ω(r1)−𝒜𝔽Ω(r2),…,dl=𝒜𝔽Ω(rl)−𝒜𝔽Ω(q).d_{0}={\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{F}}^{\Omega}(p)-{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{F}}^{\Omega}({r_{1}}),\ d_{1}={\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{F}}^{\Omega}(r_{1})-{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{F}}^{\Omega}(r_{2}),\ \ldots,d_{l}={\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{F}}^{\Omega}(r_{l})-{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{F}}^{\Omega}(q).
Now we use these data to “pull back” the monotone flow categories ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom} constructed before. Define a flow category enriched in ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}} whose objects are the same as 𝔽{\mathbb{F}}, and whose morphism from pp to qq is the restriction of ⌊𝒞d{}_{\lfloor}{\mathcal{C}}_{d} to the corresponding open subset
⌊Bp​qΩ⊆⌊Bd.{}_{\lfloor}B_{pq}^{\Omega}\subseteq{}_{\lfloor}B_{d}.
Denote this object by
𝒞p​qΩ=(𝒢p​qΩ,Bp​qΩ,Cp​qΩ).{\mathcal{C}}_{pq}^{\Omega}=({\mathcal{G}}_{pq}^{\Omega},B_{pq}^{\Omega},C_{pq}^{\Omega}).
When Ω\Omega is understood from the context, we often drop it from the notation. Then the restriction of the structural maps of the flow category ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom} gives a flow category
⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞Ω,𝔽{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\Omega,{\mathbb{F}}}
enriched in ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}} whose objects are the same as objects of 𝔽{\mathbb{F}} and whose morphisms are the families ⌊𝒞p​qΩ{}_{\lfloor}{\mathcal{C}}_{pq}^{\Omega}.
Now we summarize the construction as an update of Situation Flow(i).
Situation Flow(ii).
In Siutation Flow(i), one fixes an outercollaring width. ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom} is the monotone flow category enriched in ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}}. Furthermore, let ⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞Ω,𝔽{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\Omega,{\mathbb{F}}} be the flow category enriched in ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}} subject to a chosen integral action on 𝔽{\mathbb{F}}.
Similarly, let 𝕏{\mathbb{X}} be a multimodule associated to a Floer domain Σ\Sigma. Choose an outercollaring width and a compatible set of integral actions on involved flow categories
𝒜𝔽jΩ:Ob​𝔽j→ℤ,\displaystyle\ {\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}_{j}}^{\Omega}:{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}_{j}\to{\mathbb{Z}},\
𝒜𝔽′Ω:Ob​𝔽′→ℤ.\displaystyle\ {\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}^{\Omega}:{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}\to{\mathbb{Z}}.
Then one can choose an integer n𝕏n^{\mathbb{X}} such that for all tuples of objects (p1,…,pm,p′)(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m};p^{\prime}), one has
d:=dp1⋯pm;p′:=∑i=1m𝒜𝔽iΩ(pi)−𝒜𝔽′Ω(p′)+n𝕏>0.d:=d_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}{\mathcal{A}}^{\Omega}_{{\mathbb{F}}_{i}}(p_{i})-{\mathcal{A}}^{\Omega}_{{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}(p^{\prime})+n^{\mathbb{X}}>0.
(15.4)
Let
Ap1⋯pm;p′Ω,𝕏⊆AdA_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\Omega,{\mathbb{X}}}\subseteq A_{d}
be the Alexandrov open subset of partitions of dd corresponding to possible degenerations of Σ\Sigma and let
𝒞p1⋯pm;p′𝕏{\mathcal{C}}_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{X}}
be the restriction to the open subset corresponding to Ap1⋯pm;p′Ω,𝕏A_{p_{1}\cdots p_{m};p^{\prime}}^{\Omega,\mathbb{X}}. Then this provides a multimodule over (𝔻⌊𝕠𝕞Ω,𝔽1,…,𝔻⌊𝕠𝕞Ω,𝔽m;𝔻⌊𝕠𝕞Ω,𝔽′)({}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\Omega,{\mathbb{F}}_{1}},\ldots,{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\Omega,{\mathbb{F}}_{m}};{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\Omega,{\mathbb{F}}^{\prime}}) enriched in ⌊𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞¯rigℂ{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf Curve}}_{\rm rig}^{\mathbb{C}}, denoted by
⌊𝔻𝕠𝕞Ω,𝕏.{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{Dom}^{\Omega,{\mathbb{X}}}.
Remark 15.5.
The constant n𝕏n^{\mathbb{X}} should be thought as shifting the integral action 𝒜𝔽′Ω{\mathcal{A}}^{\Omega}_{\mathbb{F}^{\prime}} by −n𝕏-n^{\mathbb{X}} such that for all (p1,…,pm,p′)(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m};p^{\prime}), we have
