S^ℝ∞={η=(ηl)l∈ℤ|ηl∈ℝ,ηl=0 for ∀|l|≫0,∑l∈ℤηl2=1}.\widehat{S}_{\mathbb{R}}^{\infty}=\Big\{\eta=(\eta_{l})_{l\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\ |\ \eta_{l}\in{\mathbb{R}},\ \eta_{l}=0\text{ for }\forall|l|\gg 0,\ \sum_{l\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\eta_{l}^{2}=1\Big\}.
This is no longer a CW complex; however, all structures should be understood in the sense of limits/colimits. For each pair of nonnegative integers m,nm,n, there is a finite truncation
Sℝm,n:={η∈S^ℝ∞|l<−m​or​l>n⟹ηl=0}.S^{m,n}_{\mathbb{R}}:=\Big\{\eta\in\widehat{S}_{\mathbb{R}}^{\infty}\ |\ l<-m\ {\rm or}\ l>n\Longrightarrow\eta_{l}=0\Big\}.
By abuse of notation, we can extend the Morse function to
f𝔼:S^ℝ∞→ℝ,f𝔼​(η)=∑l=−∞∞l​ηl2.f^{\mathbb{E}}:\widehat{S}_{\mathbb{R}}^{\infty}\to{\mathbb{R}},\ f^{\mathbb{E}}(\eta)=\sum_{l=-\infty}^{\infty}l\eta_{l}^{2}.
Then with respect to the standard Riemannian metric, the pair is Morse–Smale on any such finite truncation.
One can formally write down an equivariant Morse flow category 𝔼{\mathbb{E}} as follows. The set of objects Ob​𝔼{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{E}} is the set of critical points of f𝔼f^{\mathbb{E}} on S^ℝ∞\widehat{S}^{\infty}_{\mathbb{R}}. Between x,y∈Ob​𝔼x,y\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{E}}, one has the morphism space being the compactified moduli space Mx​y𝔼M_{xy}^{\mathbb{E}} of gradient flow lines from xx to yy. Then this is a flow category enriched in 𝐒𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{\bf SMan}}. This flow category satisfies the unobstructedness condition (Definition 7.1) and local finiteness condition (Definition 7.2) with respect to the function f𝔼f^{\mathbb{E}}.
Moreover, the flow category is obviously equivariant with respect to a natural Novikov group ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} action. Here on ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} we define both the energy and the index function by
λ⁡(n)=μ⁡(n)=n.\lambda(n)=\mu(n)=n.
The associated Novikov field is
Λ𝔽2ℤ:=𝔽2​((θ))=𝐊~2.\Lambda_{{\mathbb{F}}_{2}}^{\mathbb{Z}}:={\mathbb{F}}_{2}{(\!(\uptheta)\!)}=\tilde{\bf K}_{2}.
The ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-action on 𝔼{\mathbb{E}} is induced by the ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-action on S^ℝ∞\widehat{S}^{\infty}_{\mathbb{R}}
n⋅(ηl)l∈ℤ:=(ηl−n)l∈ℤn\cdot(\eta_{l})_{l\in{\mathbb{Z}}}:=(\eta_{l-n})_{l\in{\mathbb{Z}}}
which satisfies
f𝔼​(n⋅η)=f𝔼​(η)+λ⁡(n),\displaystyle f^{\mathbb{E}}(n\cdot\eta)=f^{\mathbb{E}}(\eta)+\lambda(n),\
|n⋅η|=|η|+μ⁡(n).\displaystyle\ |n\cdot\eta|=|\eta|+\mu(n).
In characteristic 22, one does not need orientation. Then by the abstract construction of Floer complexes (see Subsection 7.2 and Proposition 7.30), one obtains a differential on
C(𝔼):=CM(f𝔼)={∑i=1∞aiwi|ai∈𝔽2,wi∈critf𝔼,limi→∞f𝔼(wi)=+∞}C({\mathbb{E}}):=CM(f^{{\mathbb{E}}})=\Big\{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}a_{i}w_{i}\ |\ a_{i}\in{\mathbb{F}}_{2},\ w_{i}\in{\rm crit}f^{\mathbb{E}},\ \lim_{i\to\infty}f^{{{\mathbb{E}}}}(w_{i})=+\infty\Big\}
which is a 𝐊~2\widetilde{\bf K}_{2}-module.
One can compute the cohomology easily. For between any two critical points of f𝔼f^{\mathbb{E}} of adjacent indices, there is exactly one gradient trajectory between them. Hence in each degree ll, Cl​(𝔼)C^{l}({\mathbb{E}}) is 2-dimensional while the cohomology is trivial.
However, this trivial cohomology is not what we need. Notice that the function f𝔼f^{\mathbb{E}} (as well as the metric) is invariant under the natural ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}-action on S^ℝ∞\widehat{S}_{\mathbb{R}}^{\infty}. One can consider the ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}-invariant part
C​(𝔼)ℤ2⊆C⁡(𝔼)C({\mathbb{E}})_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}}\subseteq C({\mathbb{E}})
which is 1-dimensional in each degree. The differential is trivial in characteristic 22, hence the cohomology is also 1-dimensional. Therefore, one has
H⁡(C​(𝔼)ℤ2)≅Λ𝔽2ℤ≅𝐊~2H(C({\mathbb{E}})_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}})\cong\Lambda_{{\mathbb{F}}_{2}}^{{\mathbb{Z}}}\cong\widetilde{\bf K}_{2}
as 𝐊~2\widetilde{\bf K}_{2}-modules. Later we will show that the ring structure is also identical to 𝐊~2\widetilde{\bf K}_{2}.
22.1.2. 𝗉>2{\sf p}>2 case
Consider the complex version of the infinite-dimensional sphere. Denote
Sℂ∞={η=(η0,η1,…)|ηl∈ℂ,ηl=0 for ∀l≫0,∑l=0∞|ηl|2=1}.S_{\mathbb{C}}^{\infty}=\Big\{\eta=(\eta_{0},\eta_{1},\ldots)\ |\ \eta_{l}\in{\mathbb{C}},\ \eta_{l}=0\text{ for }\forall l\gg 0,\ \sum_{l=0}^{\infty}|\eta_{l}|^{2}=1\Big\}.
This is a well-defined CW complex and is the universal S1S^{1}-bundle over ℂ​ℙ∞\mathbb{CP}^{\infty}, a model for the classifying space of U⁡(1)U(1). By regarding ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}} as a subgroup of S1S^{1}, Sℂ∞S_{\mathbb{C}}^{\infty} is also the universal ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-bundle over B​ℤ𝗉B{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}.
Now we define the formal negative extension
S^ℂ∞:={η=(ηl)l∈ℤ|ηl∈ℂ,ηl=0 for ∀|l|≫0,∑l∈ℤ|ηl|2=1}.\widehat{S}_{\mathbb{C}}^{\infty}:=\Big\{\eta=(\eta_{l})_{l\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\ |\ \eta_{l}\in{\mathbb{C}},\ \eta_{l}=0\text{ for }\forall|l|\gg 0,\ \sum_{l\in{\mathbb{Z}}}|\eta_{l}|^{2}=1\Big\}.
The ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-action on Sℂ∞S_{\mathbb{C}}^{\infty} extends to S^ℂ∞\widehat{S}_{\mathbb{C}}^{\infty}. Moreover, there is a free ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-action on S^ℂ∞\widehat{S}_{\mathbb{C}}^{\infty} by
n⋅(ηl)↦(ηl−n).n\cdot(\eta_{l})\mapsto(\eta_{l-n}).
(22.1)
Define an ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-invariant function f𝔼:S^ℂ∞→ℝf^{{\mathbb{E}}}:\widehat{S}_{\mathbb{C}}^{\infty}\to{\mathbb{R}} by
f𝔼​(η)=(∑l∈ℤl​|ηl|2)+ϵ​∑l∈ℤRe⁡(ηl𝗉),f^{{\mathbb{E}}}(\eta)=\left(\sum_{l\in{\mathbb{Z}}}l|\eta_{l}|^{2}\right)+\epsilon\sum_{l\in{\mathbb{Z}}}{\rm Re}(\eta_{l}^{{\sf p}}),
(22.2)
where ϵ\epsilon is a sufficiently small positive number. It is a smooth function in the sense that its restriction to each finite truncation is a smooth function. It also respects the ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-action (22.1) in the following way:
f𝔼​(n⋅η)=f𝔼​(η)+n.f^{{\mathbb{E}}}(n\cdot\eta)=f^{{\mathbb{E}}}(\eta)+n.
If we set ϵ=0\epsilon=0, f𝔼f^{{\mathbb{E}}} is a Morse–Bott function with critical submanifolds being the circles
Sl1={η∈S∞||ηl|=1}.S_{l}^{1}=\{\eta\in S^{\infty}\ |\ |\eta_{l}|=1\}.
After turning on ϵ\epsilon, the circle Sl1S_{l}^{1} splits into nondegenerate critical points
w2​l0,…,w2​l𝗉−1,w2​l+10,…,w2​l+1𝗉−1w_{2l}^{0},\ldots,w_{2l}^{{\sf p}-1},\ w_{2l+1}^{0},\ldots,w_{2l+1}^{{\sf p}-1}
where the subindices indicate the number of positive eigenvalues of the Hessian. One can explicitly write down the coordinates of critical points. For the ones with even degrees, we have
w2​l0=(0,…,0,1,0,…),w2​ls=τsw2​l0,s=1,…,𝗉−1,w_{2l}^{0}=(0,\ldots,0,1,0,\ldots),\ w_{2l}^{s}=\tau^{s}w_{2l}^{0},\ s=1,\ldots,{\sf p}-1,
where the only nonzero coordinate of w2​l0w_{2l}^{0} is the ll-th one and τ=e2​π​𝐢𝗉\tau=e^{\frac{2\pi{\bf i}}{{\sf p}}} is the generator of ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}. For the ones with odd degrees, we have
w2​l+10=(0,…,0,eπ​𝐢𝗉,0,…,0),w2​l+1s=τsw2​l+10,s=1,…,𝗉−1.w_{2l+1}^{0}=(0,\ldots,0,e^{\frac{\pi{\bf i}}{{\sf p}}},0,\ldots,0),\ w_{2l+1}^{s}=\tau^{s}w_{2l+1}^{0},\ s=1,\ldots,{\sf p}-1.
If we define the degree of wkmw_{k}^{m} be kk, then the action by n∈ℤn\in{\mathbb{Z}} in (22.1) shifts the grading by 2​n2n.
Lemma 22.1.
There exists a Riemannian metric g𝔼g^{{\mathbb{E}}} on S^ℂ∞\widehat{S}_{\mathbb{C}}^{\infty} satisfying the following conditions.
(1)
g𝔼g^{{\mathbb{E}}} is ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-invariant and invariant under the shift map (22.1).
(2)
(f𝔼,g𝔼)(f^{{\mathbb{E}}},g^{{\mathbb{E}}}) is Morse–Smale (when restricted to any finite truncation of S^ℂ∞\widehat{S}_{\mathbb{C}}^{\infty}).
(3)
If we consider the Morse complex associated to (f𝔼,g𝔼)(f^{{\mathbb{E}}},g^{{\mathbb{E}}}) (restricted to any sufficiently large finite truncation of S^ℂ∞\widehat{S}_{\mathbb{C}}^{\infty}), then the Morse differential, in terms of generators, is
d⁡(w2​li)=w2​l+1i−w2​l+1i+1,\displaystyle\ d(w_{2l}^{i})=w_{2l+1}^{i}-w_{2l+1}^{i+1},\
d⁡(w2​l−1i)=w2​l0+⋯+w2​l𝗉−1.\displaystyle\ d(w_{2l-1}^{i})=w_{2l}^{0}+\cdots+w_{2l}^{{\sf p}-1}.
Proof.
See [62, Section 4] which treated the case on Sℂ∞S_{\mathbb{C}}^{\infty}. One can then use the ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-action to extend the metric to the negative part of S^ℂ∞\widehat{S}_{\mathbb{C}}^{\infty}. The expression of the differential can also be found in [59, Section 2], and we refer the reader to [12, Appendix A] for a comparison between the Morse model and the cellular model used in [59].
∎
Therefore, one can define a flow category 𝔼{{\mathbb{E}}} whose objects are critical points of f𝔼f^{{\mathbb{E}}} and whose morphism spaces are the moduli space of (broken) trajectories between critical points. One can make 𝔼{{\mathbb{E}}} a ℤ⋊ℤ𝗉{\mathbb{Z}}\rtimes{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant Novikov flow category. Indeed, define
λ:ℤ→ℝ,λ⁡(a)=a,\displaystyle\ \lambda:{\mathbb{Z}}\to{\mathbb{R}},\ \lambda(a)=a,\
μ:ℤ→ℤ,μ⁡(a)=2​a.\displaystyle\ \mu:{\mathbb{Z}}\to{\mathbb{Z}},\ \mu(a)=2a.
They are ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-invariant. Hence the triple (ℤ𝗉×ℤ,λ,μ)({{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}\times{\mathbb{Z}},\lambda,\mu) is a Novikov group (Definition 7.21). Next, one can make the Morse flow category 𝔼{{\mathbb{E}}} associated to (f𝔼,g𝔼)(f^{{\mathbb{E}}},g^{{\mathbb{E}}}) a ℤ𝗉×ℤ{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}\times{\mathbb{Z}}-equivariant Novikov flow category. Define the action and grading by
𝒜​(p)=f𝔼​(p),\displaystyle\ {\mathcal{A}}(p)=f^{{\mathbb{E}}}(p),\
|wks|=k.\displaystyle\ |w_{k}^{s}|=k.
Then one can see
𝒜⁡(a​p)=f𝔼​(p)+λ⁡(a),\displaystyle\ {\mathcal{A}}(ap)=f^{{{\mathbb{E}}}}(p)+\lambda(a),\
|a​p|=|p|+μ⁡(a).\displaystyle\ |ap|=|p|+\mu(a).
Then, by the general construction of complexes in Section 7, there is an associated ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-graded complex
C(𝔼):=CM(f𝔼)={∑i=1∞aiwi|ai∈𝐅𝗉,wi∈critf𝔼,limi→∞𝒜(wi)=+∞},C({\mathbb{E}}):=CM(f^{{\mathbb{E}}})=\Big\{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}a_{i}w_{i}\ |\ a_{i}\in{\bf F}_{\sf p},\ w_{i}\in{\rm crit}f^{{\mathbb{E}}},\ \lim_{i\to\infty}{\mathcal{A}}(w_{i})=+\infty\Big\},
which is a graded module over Λ𝐅𝗉ℤ≅𝐊𝗉\Lambda_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}^{\mathbb{Z}}\cong{\bf K}_{\sf p}.
One can compute the chain complex easily from Lemma 22.1. One can see that the total cohomology of C⁡(𝔼)C({\mathbb{E}}) is trivial. If we consider the ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-invariant part, then in degree kk, one has
Ck​(𝔼)ℤ𝗉=𝐅𝗉​⟨wk0+⋯+wk𝗉−1⟩C^{k}({{\mathbb{E}}})_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}={\bf F}_{\sf p}\langle w_{k}^{0}+\cdots+w_{k}^{{\sf p}-1}\rangle
and the differential is trivial in characteristic 𝗉{\sf p}. Hence the cohomology of the ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-fixed part is identified with
H⁡(C​(𝔼)ℤ𝗉)≅𝐊~𝗉H(C({\mathbb{E}})_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}})\cong\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}
as 𝐊𝗉{\bf K}_{\sf p}-modules. We will identify below its multiplicative structure using Morse flow trees.
22.1.3. Equivariant cohomology of free orbits
We consider a simple case of equivariant localization. Let AA be a finite set equipped with a ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-action. Then one has a trivial product A×𝔼A\times{\mathbb{E}} as a flow category whose object set is A×Ob​𝔼A\times{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{E}}. Then one can form the complex
C⁡(A×𝔼):=⨁α∈AC⁡(𝔼)C(A\times{\mathbb{E}}):=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in A}C({\mathbb{E}})
which has a ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-action.
Lemma 22.2.
Let Aℤ𝗉⊆AA_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}\subseteq A be the subset of ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-fixed points. Then
H⁡(C​(A×𝔼)ℤ𝗉)≅𝐊~𝗉Aℤ𝗉.H(C(A\times{\mathbb{E}})_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}})\cong\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}^{A_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}}.
Proof.
One only needs to consider the cases when AA contains a single element and when AA is a ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-torsor. In the former case, the cohomology is 𝐊~𝗉\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}. In the latter case, one can explicitly calculate the differential and show that the cohomology is trivial.
∎
22.2. Ring structure using Morse model
We define the Morse-theoretic multiplicative structure on Hℤ𝗉​(pt)≅𝐊~𝗉H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}({\rm pt})\cong\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}. In both 𝗉=2{\sf p}=2 and 𝗉>2{\sf p}>2 cases, we denote by S∞S^{\infty} the real or complex infinite-dimensional sphere and S^∞\widehat{S}^{\infty} its negative extension.
Let Hℤ𝗉Borel​(pt)H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}^{\rm Borel}({\rm pt}) be the Borel equivariant cohomology in 𝐅𝗉{\bf F}_{\sf p}-coefficients, which can be obtained from the above Morse model by truncating at the nonnegative levels, i.e., via a Morse flow category on S∞⊆S^∞S^{\infty}\subseteq\widehat{S}^{\infty}. We will use Morse flow trees in S∞S^{\infty} to define a ring structure on Hℤ𝗉Borel​(pt)H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}^{\rm Borel}({\rm pt}) and then extend to the Tate version.
Let T2,1T_{2,1} denote the tree which is the disjoint union of two incoming edges T1≅T2≅(−∞,0]T_{1}\cong T_{2}\cong(-\infty,0] and an outgoing edge T∞≅[0,+∞)T_{\infty}\cong[0,+\infty). Let s∈T2,1s\in T_{2,1} denote the coordinate on each edge; when there is no ambiguity, ss corresponds to a real number. To achieve transversality, we choose a ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-invariant family of vector fields YsY_{s} on S∞S^{\infty} parametrized by s∈T2,1s\in T_{2,1}
(1)
Y⁡(s)=0Y(s)=0 when |s|≫0|s|\gg 0.
(2)
For each finite truncation Sn⊆S∞S^{n}\subseteq S^{\infty}, Y|SnY|_{S^{n}} is tangent to Sn⊆S∞S^{n}\subseteq S^{\infty} and ∇Y\nabla Y is sufficiently small in the normal direction of SnS^{n}.
Let YiY_{i} denote the restriction of YY to Ti⊆T2,1T_{i}\subseteq T_{2,1}. A YY-perturbed flow tree is a triple η=(η1,η2,η∞):T2,1→S∞\eta=(\eta_{1},\eta_{2},\eta_{\infty}):T_{2,1}\to S^{\infty} which solves the equation
η′​(s)=∇f𝔼​(η⁡(s))+Ys​(η⁡(s))\eta^{\prime}(s)=\nabla f^{{\mathbb{E}}}(\eta(s))+Y_{s}(\eta(s))
subject to the incidence relation
η1​(0)=η2​(0)=η∞​(0).\eta_{1}(0)=\eta_{2}(0)=\eta_{\infty}(0).
Each flow tree converges to a triple of critical points of gg at ∞\infty of the edges.
Given a triple of critical points w1,w2,w∞∈crit⁡(f𝔼)∩S∞w_{1},w_{2},w_{\infty}\in{\rm crit}(f^{{\mathbb{E}}})\cap S^{\infty}, let Sn⊆S∞S^{n}\subseteq S^{\infty} be the smallest truncation which contains all of them. One can see that a flow tree connecting w1,w2,w∞w_{1},w_{2},w_{\infty} is contained in SnS^{n}. We say that a YY-perturbed flow tree is regular for (w1,w2,w∞)(w_{1},w_{2},w_{\infty}) if it is regular as a flow tree contained in SnS^{n}.2626
26
In fact if it is regular in SnS^{n}, then it is regular in any larger truncation.
For a generic perturbation YY and each triple of critical points w1,w2,w∞w_{1},w_{2},w_{\infty}, one obtains a regular moduli space of solutions, whose mod pp count induces a ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant map
C​M​(f𝔼|S∞)⊗C​M​(f𝔼|S∞)→C​M​(f𝔼|S∞).CM(f^{{\mathbb{E}}}|_{S^{\infty}})\otimes CM(f^{{\mathbb{E}}}|_{S^{\infty}})\to CM(f^{{\mathbb{E}}}|_{S^{\infty}}).
Hence after restriction to the ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-invariant part, one obtains
Hℤ𝗉Borel​(pt)⊗𝐅𝗉Hℤ𝗉Borel​(pt)≅C​M​(f𝔼|S∞)ℤ𝗉⊗𝐅𝗉C​M​(f𝔼|S∞)ℤ𝗉→C​Mℤ𝗉​(f𝔼|S∞)ℤ𝗉≅Hℤ𝗉Borel​(pt).H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}^{\rm Borel}({\rm pt})\otimes_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}^{\rm Borel}({\rm pt})\cong CM(f^{{\mathbb{E}}}|_{S^{\infty}})^{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}\otimes_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}CM(f^{{\mathbb{E}}}|_{S^{\infty}})^{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}\to CM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f^{{\mathbb{E}}}|_{S^{\infty}})^{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}\cong H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}^{\rm Borel}({\rm pt}).
The usual Morse theoretic technique can be used to show that the bilinear map is independent of the choices of YY, and satisfies associativity. Hence Hℤ𝗉Borel​(pt)H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}^{\rm Borel}({\rm pt}) is equipped with a structure of a ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-graded, associative and supercommutative algebra over 𝐅𝗉{\bf F}_{\sf p}.
We know for compact manifolds, the ring structure defined by counting Morse flow trees coincides with the ordinary cohomology ring. Applying this fact to any finite truncation SnS^{n}, one can see the above Morse-theoretic definition of the ring structure coincides with the ordinary one on
Hℤ𝗉Borel​(pt)={𝐅𝗉​[[θ]],𝗉=2,𝐅𝗉​[[𝚄]]​⟨θ⟩,𝗉>2H^{\rm Borel}_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}({\rm pt})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}{\bf F}_{\sf p}{[\![\uptheta]\!]},&\ {\sf p}=2,\\
{\bf F}_{\sf p}{[\![\mathtt{U}]\!]}\langle\uptheta\rangle,&\ {\sf p}>2\end{array}\right.
By inverting θ\uptheta or 𝚄\mathtt{U}, one obtains a ring structure on the Tate equivariant cohomology of a point, which coincides with the standard one on 𝐊~𝗉\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}.
Later we will construct cohomology groups which become modules over 𝐊~𝗉\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}. The module structure is always defined via a certain Morse-theoretic construction first as a module over the positive truncation, then extended by inverting the corresponding variable θ\uptheta or 𝚄\mathtt{U}.
23. Equivariant Morse and Floer Cohomology
The purpose of this section is to discuss both an algebraic and Morse-theoretic approach to equivariant cohomology. The former is used for constructing the quasi-Frobenius map (cf. Equation (23.3)) and the latter uses the Morse flow category discussed in the previous section to define the θ\uptheta-action on equivariant cohomology.
23.1. Tate Equivariant Cohomology
23.1.1. The algebraic construction
Fix a prime 𝗉{\sf p}. The coefficient ring will be 𝐅𝗉{\bf F}_{\sf p} unless otherwise declared. Let DD be a ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant cochain complex with differential dDd_{D}. Let τ:D→D\tau:D\to D be the action of the generator τ∈ℤ𝗉\tau\in{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}. Define cochain complexes of 𝐊𝗉{\bf K}_{\sf p}-modules
Cℤ𝗉​(D):=D⊗𝐊~𝗉≅{D⊗𝐅2​((θ)),𝗉=2,D⊗𝐅𝗉​((𝚄))​⟨θ⟩,𝗉>2.C_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D):=D\otimes\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}\cong\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}D\otimes{\bf F}_{2}{(\!(\uptheta)\!)},&\ {\sf p}=2,\\
D\otimes{\bf F}_{\sf p}{(\!(\mathtt{U})\!)}\langle\uptheta\rangle,&\ {\sf p}>2.\end{array}\right.
where the differential dℤ𝗉d_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}} is defined as follows.
(1)
When 𝗉=2{\sf p}=2, dℤ𝗉d_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}} is θ\uptheta-linear and is determined by
dℤ𝗉​(x⊗θk)=dD​(x)⊗θk+(1−τ)​(x)⊗θk+1.d_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(x\otimes\uptheta^{k})=d_{D}(x)\otimes\uptheta^{k}+(1-\tau)(x)\otimes\uptheta^{k+1}.
(23.1)
(2)
When 𝗉>2{\sf p}>2, dℤ𝗉d_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}} is 𝚄\mathtt{U}-linear and is determined by
dℤ𝗉​(x⊗1)=dD​(x)⊗1+(−1)|x|​(1−τ)​(x)⊗θ,dℤ𝗉​(x⊗θ)=dD​(x)⊗θ+(−1)|x|​(1+τ+⋯+τp−1)​(x)⊗𝚄.\begin{split}d_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}(x\otimes 1)&\ =d_{D}(x)\otimes 1+(-1)^{|x|}(1-\tau)(x)\otimes\uptheta,\\
d_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}(x\otimes\uptheta)&\ =d_{D}(x)\otimes\uptheta+(-1)^{|x|}(1+\tau+\cdots+\tau^{p-1})(x)\otimes\mathtt{U}.\end{split}
(23.2)
Here |x||x| is the cohomological grading of xx.
The resulting cohomology, called the (Tate) equivariant cohomology of DD, is denoted by
Hℤ𝗉​(D)H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D)
which is naturally a 𝐊𝗉{\bf K}_{\sf p}-module.
In fact the equivariant cohomology Hℤ𝗉​(D)H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D) can be made a module over 𝐊~𝗉\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p} in a non-obvious way (unless 𝗉=2{\sf p}=2). We choose to construct the module structure in the Morse-theoretic approach. We will not use the above algebraic definition formally, but only provide it for algebraic intuition.
Remark 23.1.
If we work with D⊗𝐊𝗉D\otimes{\bf K}_{\sf p} equipped with the same differentials (23.1) and (23.2), then we obtain the Borel-equivariant cohomology. We mostly stick with the Tate setting because of intended applications.
The equivariant complex is functorial. Namely, if f:D→D′f:D\to D^{\prime} is a ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant chain map, then it induces a chain map
fℤ𝗉:Cℤ𝗉​(D)→Cℤ𝗉​(D′).f_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}:C_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D)\to C_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D^{\prime}).
If f0f_{0} and f1f_{1} are ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariantly chain homotopic, then there is a corresponding 𝐊𝗉{\bf K}_{\sf p}-linear chain homotopy from f0,ℤ𝗉f_{0,{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}} to f1,ℤ𝗉f_{1,{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}.
There are two special cases of the above construction which will appear in this paper soon. The first special case is when the ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-action on the complex DD is trivial. In this case
Hℤ𝗉​(D)≅H⁡(D)⊗𝐊~𝗉.H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D)\cong H(D)\otimes\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}.
Notice that this is a priori only an isomorphism of 𝐊𝗉{\bf K}_{\sf p}-modules but not 𝐊~𝗉\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}-modules.
The second special case is the 𝗉{\sf p}-fold tensor power. Let DD be a non-equivariant cochain complex of 𝐅𝗉{\bf F}_{\sf p}-vector spaces. The tensor power
(D⊗𝗉,dD⊗𝗉)(D^{\otimes{\sf p}},d_{D}^{\otimes{\sf p}})
has the ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-action by permuting the factors as follows: let τ∈ℤ𝗉\tau\in{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}} be the generator, then τ\tau acts on the 𝗉{\sf p}-fold tensor product by
τ(x1⊗⋯⊗x𝗉)=(−1)|x1|​(|x2|+⋯+|x𝗉|)x2⊗⋯⊗x𝗉⊗x1.\tau(x_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{\sf p})=(-1)^{|x_{1}|(|x_{2}|+\cdots+|x_{\sf p}|)}x_{2}\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{\sf p}\otimes x_{1}.
Then one has the chain complex
Cℤ𝗉​(D⊗𝗉).C_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D^{\otimes{\sf p}}).
One can calculate the Tate equivariant cohomology by the so-called quasi-Frobenius map. This map is not induced from any chain-level construction. We first define the quasi-Frobenius map
q​F:H⁡(D)→Hℤ𝗉​(D⊗𝗉)qF:H(D)\to H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D^{\otimes{\sf p}})
(23.3)
in the case when the differential of DD is trivial. In this case, Hℤ𝗉​(D)≅H⁡(D)⊗𝐊~𝗉H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D)\cong H(D)\otimes\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}. Define
q​F​(x)=x⊗⋯⊗x⏟𝗉∈Cℤ𝗉​(D⊗𝗉)​∀x∈H⁡(D)⊆Hℤ𝗉​(D).qF(x)=\underbrace{x\otimes\cdots\otimes x}_{{\sf p}}\in C_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D^{\otimes{\sf p}})\ \forall x\in H(D)\subseteq H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D).
The image is contained in the kernel of dℤ𝗉d_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}} hence induces a map to Hℤ𝗉​(D⊗𝗉)H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D^{\otimes{\sf p}}). Moreover, we can see that the cohomological map is linear over 𝐅𝗉{\bf F}_{\sf p}.
In general, when the differential of DD is nontrivial, there exists a ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant chain homotopy equivalence
(H⁡(D),0)∼(D,dD).(H(D),0)\sim(D,d_{D}).
Then we define q​FqF as the composition
H⁡(D)\textstyle{H(D)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}Hℤ𝗉​(H​(D)⊗𝗉)\textstyle{H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(H(D)^{\otimes{\sf p}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}Hℤ𝗉​(D⊗𝗉)\textstyle{H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D^{\otimes{\sf p}})}
Moreover, any two ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant chain homotopy equivalences between H⁡(D)H(D) and DD are equivariantly homotopic. Hence the resulting map
q​F:H⁡(D)→Hℤ𝗉​(D⊗𝗉)qF:H(D)\to H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D^{\otimes{\sf p}})
is well-defined. Furthermore, the following functoriality property of q​FqF holds.
Lemma 23.2.
The quasi-Frobenius map is functorial. Namely, if f:D1→D2f:D_{1}\to D_{2} is a cochain map, then there is a commutative diagram
H⁡(D1)\textstyle{H(D_{1})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}q​F\scriptstyle{qF}f\scriptstyle{f}Hℤ𝗉​(D1⊗𝗉)\textstyle{H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D_{1}^{\otimes{\sf p}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}fℤ𝗉\scriptstyle{f_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}H⁡(D2)\textstyle{H(D_{2})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}q​F\scriptstyle{qF}Hℤ𝗉​(D2⊗𝗉)\textstyle{H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D_{2}^{\otimes{\sf p}})}
(23.4)
This functoriality implies that the quasi-Frobenius map is an isomorphism with field coefficients.
Proposition 23.3.
There is a 𝐊𝗉{\bf K}_{\sf p}-linear extension of q​FqF which is an isomorphism
H⁡(D)⊗𝐊~𝗉→Hℤ𝗉​(D⊗𝗉).H(D)\otimes\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}\to H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D^{\otimes{\sf p}}).
Proof.
By the definition of q​FqF and the above lemma, one only needs to verify this for the case when the differential of DD is trivial. The fact that q​FqF induces an isomorphism follows from [62, Lemma 3.1].
∎
23.1.2. Novikov coefficients
Now we extend the above algebraic constructions to complex of modules over Novikov fields. First recall that when Π1,Π2\Pi_{1},\Pi_{2} are Novikov groups, then one has a completed tensor product
ΛΠ1​⊗^​ΛΠ2≅ΛΠ1⊕Π2.\Lambda^{\Pi_{1}}\widehat{\otimes}\Lambda^{\Pi_{2}}\cong\Lambda^{\Pi_{1}\oplus\Pi_{2}}.
Then if D1D_{1} resp. D2D_{2} are non-Archimedean normed over ΛΠ1\Lambda^{\Pi_{1}} resp. ΛΠ2\Lambda^{\Pi_{2}}, then one has a completed tensor product
D1​⊗^​D2D_{1}\widehat{\otimes}D_{2}
which is a non-Archimedean normed vector space over ΛΠ1⊕Π2\Lambda^{\Pi_{1}\oplus\Pi_{2}}.
The above equivariant construction requires the following specialization. Let (Π,λ,μ)(\Pi,\lambda,\mu) be a Novikov group, which is typically the one defined by (1.1). In the equivariant setting we consider another standard one which is
(ℤ,λ𝗉,μ𝗉)({\mathbb{Z}},\lambda_{\sf p},\mu_{\sf p})
where λ𝗉:ℤ→ℝ\lambda_{\sf p}:{\mathbb{Z}}\to{\mathbb{R}} is the canonical inclusion while
μ𝗉​(a)={a,𝗉=2,2​a,𝗉>2\mu_{\sf p}(a)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}a,&\ {\sf p}=2,\\
2a,&\ {\sf p}>2\end{array}\right.
Now let DD be a complex of Λ𝐅𝗉Π\Lambda_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}-vector spaces. Then the completed tensor product D​⊗^​𝐊~𝗉D\widehat{\otimes}\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p} is a vector space over the Novikov field
ΛΠ⊕ℤ:=Λ𝐅𝗉Π⊕ℤ={∑i=1∞ciTai+bi|ci∈𝐅𝗉,ai∈Π,bi∈ℤ,infiω⁡(ai)>−∞,infibi>−∞,limi+∞ω⁡(ai)+bi=+∞}\Lambda^{\Pi\oplus{\mathbb{Z}}}:=\Lambda^{\Pi\oplus{\mathbb{Z}}}_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}c_{i}T^{a_{i}+b_{i}}\ \left|\ \begin{array}[]{l}c_{i}\in{\bf F}_{\sf p},\ a_{i}\in\Pi,\ b_{i}\in{\mathbb{Z}},\\
\displaystyle\inf_{i}\omega(a_{i})>-\infty,\ \inf_{i}b_{i}>-\infty,\ \lim_{i+\infty}\omega(a_{i})+b_{i}=+\infty\end{array}\right.\right\}
We typically write TbiT^{b_{i}} as θbi\uptheta^{b_{i}} (when 𝗉=2{\sf p}=2) or 𝚄bi\mathtt{U}^{b_{i}} (when 𝗉>2{\sf p}>2). Then this Novikov field consists of formal infinite 𝐅𝗉{\bf F}_{\sf p}-linear combinations of monomials Tai​Pi​(θ)T^{a_{i}}P_{i}(\uptheta) or Tai​Pi​(𝚄)T^{a_{i}}P_{i}(\mathtt{U}) where PiP_{i} is a Laurent series with bounded pole orders while ω⁡(ai)→+∞\omega(a_{i})\to+\infty.
We can define the equivariant differential on the tensor product D​⊗^​𝐊~𝗉D\widehat{\otimes}\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p} using the same formula as before. However, most of the time, we will enlarge the Novikov field via
Λ𝐅𝗉Π⊕ℤ↪Λ𝐊𝗉Π\Lambda_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi\oplus{\mathbb{Z}}}\hookrightarrow\Lambda_{{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}
where the latter does not require bounded pole orders for the coefficient of TaiT^{a_{i}}. Then define
(Cℤ𝗉​(D):=D​⊗^​𝐊~𝗉,dℤ𝗉)\left(C_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D):=D\widehat{\otimes}\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p},d_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}\right)
where the differential is still defined in the same way.
One often needs to take a more convenient field extension. Consider
Λ𝐊𝗉Π\Lambda_{{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}
where 𝐊𝗉{\bf K}_{\sf p} is the field of Laurent series in θ\uptheta (for 𝗉=2{\sf p}=2) or 𝚄\mathtt{U} (for 𝗉>2{\sf p}>2). Elements in Λ𝐊𝗉Π\Lambda_{{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi} are formal infinite 𝐅𝗉{\bf F}_{\sf p}-linear combinations of monomials Tai​PiT^{a_{i}}P_{i} where PiP_{i} is a Laurent series without bound on pole orders, or equivalently, formal infinite 𝐊𝗉{\bf K}_{\sf p}-linear combinations of TaiT^{a_{i}} with ω⁡(ai)→+∞\omega(a_{i})\to+\infty. Then one often needs to use
Cℤ𝗉​(D)​⊗ΛΠ⊕ℤ​Λ𝐊𝗉Π.C_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D)\underset{\Lambda^{\Pi\oplus{\mathbb{Z}}}}{\otimes}\Lambda_{{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}.
We can also consider Cℤ𝗉​(D⊗𝗉)C_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D^{\otimes{\sf p}}) when DD is a non-equivariant cochain complex of ΛΠ\Lambda^{\Pi}-modules. We consider the completed tensor power (over 𝐅𝗉{\bf F}_{\sf p})
D⊗𝐅𝗉^⋯⊗𝐅𝗉^D⏞𝗉\overbrace{D\widehat{\underset{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}{\otimes}}\cdots\widehat{\underset{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}{\otimes}}D}^{{\sf p}}
which is a module over
ΛΠ𝗉:=ΛΠ⊗𝐅𝗉^⋯⊗𝐅𝗉^ΛΠ.\Lambda^{\Pi^{\sf p}}:=\Lambda^{\Pi}\widehat{\underset{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}{\otimes}}\cdots\widehat{\underset{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}{\otimes}}\Lambda^{\Pi}.
Consider the natural morphism of Novikov monoids (see Definition 7.21)
Π⊕⋯⊕Π\textstyle{\Pi\oplus\cdots\oplus\Pi\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}ℝk⊕⋯⊕ℝk\textstyle{{\mathbb{R}}^{k}\oplus\cdots\oplus{\mathbb{R}}^{k}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}Π\textstyle{\Pi\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}ℝk\textstyle{{\mathbb{R}}^{k}}
where the vertical arrows are (a1,…,a𝗉)↦a1+⋯+a𝗉(a_{1},\ldots,a_{\sf p})\mapsto a_{1}+\cdots+a_{\sf p}. Then there is an induced ring morphism
ΛRΠ𝗉→ΛRΠ.\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi^{{\sf p}}}\to\Lambda_{R}^{\Pi}.
Denote
D⊗^​𝗉:=(D⊗𝐅𝗉^⋯⊗𝐅𝗉^D⏞𝗉)​⊗ΛΠ𝗉​ΛΠD^{\widehat{\otimes}{\sf p}}:=\left(\overbrace{D\widehat{\underset{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}{\otimes}}\cdots\widehat{\underset{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}{\otimes}}D}^{{\sf p}}\right)\underset{\Lambda^{\Pi^{{\sf p}}}}{\otimes}\Lambda^{\Pi}
which is a module over ΛRΠ\Lambda_{R}^{\mathbb{\Pi}}. Then we have the chain complex
Cℤ𝗉​(D⊗^​𝗉),C_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D^{\widehat{\otimes}{\sf p}}),
whose differential is defined similarly using (23.1) and (23.2). In this situation, we still have the quasi-Frobenius map well-defined on the cohomology level
q​F:H∗​(D)→Hℤ𝗉∗​(D⊗^​𝗉).qF:H^{*}(D)\to H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}^{*}(D^{\widehat{\otimes}{\sf p}}).
However it is only linear over 𝐅𝗉{\bf F}_{\sf p} but not the Novikov field Λ𝐅𝗉Π\Lambda_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}. Instead, one has Frobenius linearity in the Novikov variable
q​F​(Ta​x)=T𝗉​a​q​F​(x).qF(T^{a}x)=T^{{\sf p}a}qF(x).
23.1.3. Quantitative results
One considers a key quantitative property of the quasi-Frobenius map. Let DD be a Floer-type complex over Λ𝐅𝗉Π\Lambda_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi} (Definition 7.34). Then the tensor product
D⊗^​𝗉D^{\widehat{\otimes}{\sf p}}
is also a Floer-type complex over Λ𝐅𝗉Π\Lambda_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}. The equivariant complex, after tensoring with Λ𝐊𝗉Π\Lambda_{{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}, becomes a Floer-type complex over this larger Novikov field
Cℤ𝗉​(D⊗^​𝗉)⊗Λ𝐊𝗉Π.C_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D^{\widehat{\otimes}{\sf p}})\otimes\Lambda_{{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}.
Then for each τ∈ℝ\tau\in{\mathbb{R}}, define the filtered cohomology
Hℤ𝗉≤τ:=H⁡((Cℤ𝗉​(D⊗^​𝗉)⊗Λ𝐊𝗉Π)≤τ).H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}^{\leq\tau}:=H((C_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D^{\widehat{\otimes}{\sf p}})\otimes\Lambda_{{\bf K}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi})^{\leq\tau}).
Via localization, one can prove the following result.
Lemma 23.4.
For each τ\tau, there exists a quasi-Frobenius map
q​F:H≤τ​(D)→Hℤ𝗉≤𝗉​τ​(D⊗𝗉)qF:H^{\leq\tau}(D)\to H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}^{\leq{\sf p}\tau}(D^{\otimes{\sf p}})
satisfying
(1)
For τ<σ\tau<\sigma, the following diagram commutes
H≤τ​(D)\textstyle{H^{\leq\tau}(D)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}q​F\scriptstyle{qF}Hℤ𝗉≤𝗉​τ​(D⊗𝗉)\textstyle{H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}^{\leq{\sf p}\tau}(D^{\otimes{\sf p}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}H≤σ​(D)\textstyle{H^{\leq\sigma}(D)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}q​F\scriptstyle{qF}Hℤ𝗉≤𝗉​σ​(D⊗𝗉)\textstyle{H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}^{\leq{\sf p}\sigma}(D^{\otimes{\sf p}})}
(2)
After tensoring with 𝐊~𝗉\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}, for each τ\tau, q​FqF induces an isomorphism of Λ𝐊𝗉,0Π\Lambda_{{\bf K}_{\sf p},0}^{\Pi}-modules
q​F:H≤τ​(D)⊗𝐊~𝗉→Hℤ𝗉≤𝗉​τ​(D⊗𝗉).qF:H^{\leq\tau}(D)\otimes\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}\to H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}^{\leq{\sf p}\tau}(D^{\otimes{\sf p}}).
Proof.
See [62].
∎
23.2. ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant Morse complexes
23.2.1. Equivariant Morse cohomology for ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-manifolds
Let MM be a compact oriented manifold equipped with a ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-action. Let f:M→ℝf:M\to{\mathbb{R}} be a ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-invariant Morse function. One would like to define a ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant Morse cochain complex C​Mℤ𝗉​(f)CM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f).
First we assume that there exists a ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-invariant Riemannian metric gg on MM making (f,g)(f,g) Morse–Smale. Namely, one can achieve equivariant transversality. Then one obtains a cochain complex C​M​(f,g)CM(f,g) which has a ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-action. Hence the previous algebraic construction provides a way to obtain an equivariant Morse complex
C​Mℤ𝗉​(f):=Cℤ𝗉​(C​M∗​(f,g)).CM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f):=C_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(CM^{*}(f,g)).
In fact the equivariant complex can also be obtained via Morse model. Consider the product function
F:M×S^∞→ℝ,F⁡(x,w)=f⁡(x)+f𝔼​(w)F:M\times\widehat{S}^{\infty}\to{\mathbb{R}},\ F(x,w)=f(x)+f^{\mathbb{E}}(w)
and the product metric, which provides a Morse flow category 𝕄​#​𝔼{\mathbb{M}}\#{{\mathbb{E}}}. Consider the associated Morse cochain complex
C​M​(F)CM(F)
which coincides with the tensor product C​M​(f)⊗𝔼CM(f)\otimes{\mathbb{E}}. This complex has a ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-action given by the ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-action on C​M​(f)CM(f) and the ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-action on 𝔼{\mathbb{E}}. Then define
C​Mℤ𝗉​(f):=(C​M​(f)⊗𝔼)ℤ𝗉CM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f):=(CM(f)\otimes{\mathbb{E}})_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}
i.e., the ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-fixed part.
Lemma 23.5.
The complex C​Mℤ𝗉​(f)CM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f) coincides with the algebraically defined complex Cℤ𝗉​(D)C_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(D).
Proof.
Define a linear map
C​M​(f)⊗𝐊~𝗉→C​M​(F)ℤ𝗉CM(f)\otimes\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}\to CM(F)_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}
as follows.
(1)
When 𝗉=2{\sf p}=2, define
x⊗θk↦x⊗qk++τ⁡(x)⊗qk−x\otimes\uptheta^{k}\mapsto x\otimes q_{k}^{+}+\tau(x)\otimes q_{k}^{-}
where qk±q_{k}^{\pm} are the two critical points of f𝔼f^{{\mathbb{E}}} and τ\tau is the action on C​M​(f)CM(f).
(2)
When 𝗉>2{\sf p}>2, define
x⊗𝚄k↦∑l=1p(τl​x)⊗w2​kl,x⊗𝚄k​θ↦∑l=1p(τl​x)⊗w2​k+1l\begin{split}x\otimes\mathtt{U}^{k}&\mapsto\sum_{l=1}^{p}(\tau^{l}x)\otimes w_{2k}^{l},\\
x\otimes\mathtt{U}^{k}\uptheta&\mapsto\sum_{l=1}^{p}(\tau^{l}x)\otimes w_{2k+1}^{l}\end{split}
where wilw_{i}^{l} are the critical points of f𝔼f^{{\mathbb{E}}}.
One can check that this linear map is a bijective cochain map.
∎
The two special cases mentioned above also arises in the Morse-theoretic context. First, suppose ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}} acts trivially on MM. Then a Morse–Smale pair (f,g)(f,g) is equivariantly transverse, resulting in the identification
H​Mℤ𝗉​(f,g)≅H​M​(f,g)⊗𝐊~𝗉.HM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f,g)\cong HM(f,g)\otimes\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}.
On the other hand, if (f,g)(f,g) is Morse–Smale on MM, then the 𝗉{\sf p}-fold power
(f𝗉,g⊕𝗉)(f^{{\sf p}},g^{\oplus{\sf p}})
is Morse–Smale on M𝗉M^{{\sf p}}. One obtains the cochain complex
C​M​(f𝗉)⊗C⁡(𝔼)CM(f^{\sf p})\otimes C({\mathbb{E}})
whose ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-invariant has cohomology H​Mℤ𝗉​(f𝗉,g⊗𝗉)HM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f^{\sf p},g^{\otimes{\sf p}}). When MM is compact, Morse-theoretic technique proves that the resulting cohomology is independent of the choice of (f,g)(f,g) and coincides with Hℤ𝗉​(M𝗉)H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(M^{\sf p}).
Now assume that one does not have equivariant transversality. Let MM be equipped with a ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-action, f:M→ℝf:M\to{\mathbb{R}} is a ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-invariant Morse function. Still consider the product
F:M×S^∞→ℝ.F:M\times\widehat{S}^{\infty}\to{\mathbb{R}}.
Now the ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-action on M×S^∞M\times\widehat{S}^{\infty} is free, allowing us to achieve equivariant transversality. There are many concrete choices of perturbations. For example, one can perturb the function ff to allow it to depend on w∈S^∞w\in\widehat{S}^{\infty}, i.e., a ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-invariant function (w,x)↦fv​(x)(w,x)\mapsto f_{v}(x) on S^∞×M\widehat{S}^{\infty}\times M such that fv​(x)=f​(x)f_{v}(x)=f(x) when (v,x)(v,x) is close to a critical point of g×fg\times f. One can further ensure that the set of critical points is unchanged under the perturbation provided that the perturbation is sufficiently small in C1C^{1}-norm. Then one can consider the coupled flow line equation for (ξ,η):ℝ→M×S^∞(\xi,\eta):{\mathbb{R}}\to M\times\widehat{S}^{\infty}:
η′​(s)=∇fζ⁡(s)​(η⁡(s)),\displaystyle\ \eta^{\prime}(s)=\nabla f_{\zeta(s)}(\eta(s)),\
ζ′​(s)=∇g​(ζ⁡(s)),\displaystyle\ \zeta^{\prime}(s)=\nabla g(\zeta(s)),
which has again an obvious translation symmetry. Define the Morse cochain complex as the (completed) tensor product
C​M​(f)⊗C​M​(g)CM(f)\otimes CM(g)
whose differential counts rigid perturbed flow lines. Define
C​Mℤ𝗉​(f):=(C​M​(f)⊗C​M​(g))ℤ𝗉CM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f):=(CM(f)\otimes CM(g))^{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}
as a subcomplex, whose chain homotopy type is independent of the perturbation.
By using perturbed flow trees in S^∞\widehat{S}^{\infty}, one can also define a module structure of H​Mℤ𝗉​(f)HM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f) over 𝐊~𝗉≅Hℤ𝗉​(pt)\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}\cong H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}({\rm pt}) induced by a chain-level bilinear map
C​Mℤ𝗉​(f)⊗𝐅𝗉C​Mℤ𝗉​(g)→C​Mℤ𝗉​(f).CM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f)\otimes_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}CM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(g)\to CM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f).
More precisely, choose a perturbation YY over the tree T2,1T_{2,1} which can be used to define the ring structure on S^∞\widehat{S}^{\infty}. Choose another generic family of functions
fs,v:M→ℝf_{s,v}:M\to{\mathbb{R}}
parametrized by s∈ℝs\in{\mathbb{R}} and v∈S∞v\in S^{\infty} such that 1) fs,v=ff_{s,v}=f near s=0s=0 and 2) fs,v=fvf_{s,v}=f_{v} for |s|≫0|s|\gg 0 and 3) fs,γ​v​(γ​x)=fs,v​(x)f_{s,\gamma v}(\gamma x)=f_{s,v}(x) for all γ∈ℤ𝗉\gamma\in{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}. Consider pairs (ξ,η)(\xi,\eta) where η=(ζ1,ζ2,ζ∞):T2,1→S∞\eta=(\zeta_{1},\zeta_{2},\zeta_{\infty}):T_{2,1}\to S^{\infty} is a YY-perturbed flow tree and ξ:ℝ→M\xi:{\mathbb{R}}\to M solves the equation
ξ′​(s)={∇fs,ζ1​(s)​(ξ​(s)),s≤0,∇fs,ζ∞​(s)​(ξ​(s)),s≥0\xi^{\prime}(s)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}\nabla f_{s,\zeta_{1}(s)}(\xi(s)),&\ s\leq 0,\\
\nabla f_{s,\zeta_{\infty}(s)}(\xi(s)),&\ s\geq 0\end{array}\right.
The coefficients of the equation on ξ\xi is smooth. We then impose critical point asymptotics ξ⁡(±∞)∈crit⁡(f)\xi(\pm\infty)\in{\rm crit}(f). By choosing a generic fs,vf_{s,v}, one obtains equivariant transversality and hence defines a chain map
(C​M​(f)⊗C​M​(g))⊗C​M​(g)→C​M​(f)⊗C​M​(g).\big(CM(f)\otimes CM(g)\big)\otimes CM(g)\to CM(f)\otimes CM(g).
Its restriction to the ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-invariant part gives
C​Mℤ𝗉​(f)⊗C​Mℤ𝗉​(g)↪(C​M​(f)⊗C​M​(g)⊗C​M​(g))ℤ𝗉→C​Mℤ𝗉​(f)CM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f)\otimes CM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(g)\hookrightarrow(CM(f)\otimes CM(g)\otimes CM(g))^{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}\to CM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f)
hence a bilinear map
H​Mℤ𝗉​(f)⊗𝐅𝗉𝐊~𝗉→H​Mℤ𝗉​(f).HM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f)\otimes_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}\to HM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f).
One can further show that this map defines a 𝐊~𝗉\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}-module structure on H​Mℤ𝗉​(f)HM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f) using a standard TQFT argument.
One can further define a multiplicative structure on H​Mℤ𝗉​(f)HM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f) via the cochain-level map
C​Mℤ𝗉​(f)⊗𝐅𝗉C​Mℤ𝗉​(f)→C​Mℤ𝗉​(f)CM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f)\otimes_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}CM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f)\to CM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f)
via gradient flow trees in M×S^∞M\times\widehat{S}^{\infty}, whose associativity can be verified in the standard way. Lastly, because the multiplicative structure respects the 𝐊~𝗉\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}-module structure, hence it descends to a map
H​Mℤ𝗉​(f)​⊗𝐊~𝗉​H​Mℤ𝗉​(f)→H​Mℤ𝗉​(f).HM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f)\underset{\widetilde{\bf K}_{\sf p}}{\otimes}HM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f)\to HM_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(f).
24. Quantum Steenrod Operations—Proof of Theorem H
The classical Steenrod operation can be viewed as a ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant extension of the map x↦x𝗉x\mapsto x^{\sf p} in cohomology in characteristic 𝗉{\sf p}. Proposed by Fukaya [31], the quantum Steenrod operation deforms the classical one in analogy to the case that the quantum cup product deforms the classical cup product. Under topological restrictions such as monotonicity, the quantum Steenrod operation has been constructed by Seidel [61], Wilkins [72], and Seidel–Wilkins [59] (see also the recent survey by Wilkins [73]).
The use of the FOP transverse perturbations allows us to define integer, hence 𝐅𝗉{\bf F}_{\sf p}-counts of pseudoholomorphic curves, leading to a definition of the quantum Steenrod operation on all compact symplectic manifolds. In this section we go over the construction using the Morse model.
24.1. Geometric setup
24.1.1. The flow categories and bimodules associated to quantum Steenrod operation
Fix a prime 𝗉{\sf p}. Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a compact symplectic manifold and JJ be a compatible almost complex structure. We abbreviate the data (X,ω,J)(X,\omega,J) by XX. We can reduce the consideration to a fixed JJ using argument such as continuation maps. Therefore we will not address the dependence on JJ. Recall
Π=π2​(X)ker​ω∩ker​c1.\Pi=\frac{\pi_{2}(X)}{{\rm ker}\omega\cap{\rm ker}c_{1}}.
Let (f,g)(f,g) be a Morse–Smale pair on XX which defines a Morse flow category 𝕄¯\underline{\smash{\mathbb{M}}}. Let 𝕄{\mathbb{M}} be the trivial product 𝕄¯×Π\underline{\smash{\mathbb{M}}}\times\Pi, which is naturally a Π\Pi-equivariant flow category. Its objects are denoted by
x=(x¯,ax)∈Ob​𝕄¯×Π.x=(\underline{\smash{x}},a_{x})\in{\rm Ob}\underline{\smash{\mathbb{M}}}\times\Pi.
Let 𝔼\mathbb{E} be the ℤ×ℤ𝗉{\mathbb{Z}}\times{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant flow category associated to the Morse–Smale pair on S^∞\widehat{S}^{\infty}. Let 𝕄¯​#​𝔼\underline{\smash{\mathbb{M}}}\#{\mathbb{E}} be the “coupling” of 𝕄¯\underline{\smash{\mathbb{M}}} and 𝔼{\mathbb{E}}, which is a flow category with object set
Ob⁡(𝕄¯​#​𝔼)=Ob​𝕄¯×𝔼.{\rm Ob}(\underline{\smash{\mathbb{M}}}\#{\mathbb{E}})={\rm Ob}\underline{\smash{\mathbb{M}}}\times{\mathbb{E}}.
The morphism space between two objects is the moduli space of flow lines in X×S^∞X\times\widehat{S}^{\infty}. Denote
𝕄​#​𝔼=(𝕄¯​#​𝔼)×Π.\mathbb{M}\#{\mathbb{E}}=(\underline{\smash{\mathbb{M}}}\#{\mathbb{E}})\times\Pi.
This flow category is equivariant with respect to the free action by
Π𝗉=Π×ℤ×ℤ𝗉=:Π×ℤ𝗉.\mathbb{\Pi}_{\sf p}=\Pi\times{\mathbb{Z}}\times{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}=:{\mathbb{\Pi}}\times{\mathbb{Z}}_{{\sf p}}.
We describe a multimodule 𝕏ℚ​𝕊​𝕥{\mathbb{X}}^{\mathbb{QSt}} over
(𝕄,…,𝕄⏟𝗉,𝔼,𝕄​#​𝔼)(\underbrace{\mathbb{M},\ldots,\mathbb{M}}_{{\sf p}},{\mathbb{E}};{\mathbb{M}}\#{\mathbb{E}})
as follows. Consider the Riemann surface Σℚ​𝕊​𝕥\Sigma^{\mathbb{QSt}} which is identified with ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{CP}^{1} with 𝗉+1{\sf p}+1 marked points, where the 𝗉{\sf p} negative markings are at all 𝗉{\sf p}-th roots of unity
z1,…,z𝗉∈ℂ⊆ℂ∪{∞}=ℂ​ℙ1z_{1},\ldots,z_{\sf p}\in{\mathbb{C}}\subseteq{\mathbb{C}}\cup\{\infty\}=\mathbb{CP}^{1}
and the positive marking is z∞=∞z_{\infty}=\infty.
Consider pairs
(u,v)(u,v)
where u:Σℚ​𝕊​𝕥→Xu:\Sigma^{\mathbb{QSt}}\to X is a JJ-holomorphic sphere in XX with these 𝗉+1{\sf p}+1 special markings and v:ℝ→S∞v:{\mathbb{R}}\to S^{\infty} is a Morse trajectory of 𝔼{{\mathbb{E}}} in S∞S^{\infty}. For each tuple of objects
(x1,…,x𝗉,w)∈Ob𝕄×⋯×Ob𝕄×Ob𝔼,p′=(x′,w′)∈Ob𝕄#𝔼(x_{1},\ldots,x_{\sf p},w)\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{M}}\times\cdots\times{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{M}}\times{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{E}},\ p^{\prime}=(x^{\prime},w^{\prime})\in{\rm Ob}{\mathbb{M}}\#{\mathbb{E}}
let
M̊x1⋯x𝗉w;p′ℚ​𝕊​𝕥\mathring{M}_{x_{1}\cdots x_{\sf p}w;p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{QSt}}
be the space of such pairs (u,v)(u,v) such that
∫S2u∗​ω=ax1+⋯+ax𝗉−ax′\int_{S^{2}}u^{*}\omega=a_{x_{1}}+\cdots+a_{x_{\sf p}}-a_{x^{\prime}}
satisfying the constraints
u(zi)∈Wx¯ius,i=1,…,𝗉,u(z∞)∈Wx¯′st,andlims→−∞v(s)=w,lims→+∞v(s)=w′.u(z_{i})\in W^{\rm us}_{\underline{\smash{x}}_{i}},\ i=1,\ldots,{\sf p},\ u(z_{\infty})\in W^{\rm st}_{{\underline{\smash{x}}}^{\prime}},\ {\rm and}\ \lim_{s\to-\infty}v(s)=w,\ \lim_{s\to+\infty}v(s)=w^{\prime}.
Let Mx1⋯x𝗉w;p′ℚ​𝕊​𝕥M_{x_{1}\cdots x_{\sf p}w;p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{QSt}} be the compactification of M̊x1⋯x𝗉w;p′ℚ​𝕊​𝕥\mathring{M}_{x_{1}\cdots x_{\sf p}w;p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{QSt}} compactified in the following way: at markings, one takes the ordinary Gromov compactification; the Morse breakings at negative ends are allowed independently at different edges while the breakings on the positive ends are required to be “synchronized.”
Proposition 24.1.
The spaces Mx1⋯x𝗉w;p′ℚ​𝕊​𝕥M_{x_{1}\cdots x_{\sf p}w;p^{\prime}}^{\mathbb{QSt}} define a Novikov multimodule, denoted by 𝕏ℚ​𝕊​𝕥{\mathbb{X}}^{\mathbb{QSt}}, over (𝕄,…,𝕄,𝔼,𝕄ℤ𝗉)({\mathbb{M}},\ldots,{\mathbb{M}},{{\mathbb{E}}};{\mathbb{M}}^{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}), which is equivariant with respect to the morphism of Novikov groups
Π×⋯×Π⏞𝗉×ℤ{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overbrace{\Pi\times\cdots\times\Pi}^{{\sf p}}\times{\mathbb{Z}}}ℝ𝗉×ℝ{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbb{R}}^{{\sf p}}\times{\mathbb{R}}}Π×ℤ{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Pi\times{\mathbb{Z}}}ℝ×ℝ{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbb{R}}\times{\mathbb{R}}}(A1,…,A𝗉,a)↦(A1+⋯+A𝗉,a)\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A_{1},\ldots,A_{{\sf p}},a)\mapsto(A_{1}+\cdots+A_{{\sf p}},a)}(t1,…,t𝗉,s)↦(t1+⋯+t𝗉,s)\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(t_{1},\ldots,t_{{\sf p}},s)\mapsto(t_{1}+\cdots+t_{{\sf p}},s)}
(24.1)
Moreover, as a weak bimodule over (𝕄×⋯×𝕄×𝔼;𝕄ℤ𝗉)({\mathbb{M}}\times\cdots\times{\mathbb{M}}\times{{\mathbb{E}}};\mathbb{M}^{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}), it is ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant.
Proof.
This follows from the usual description of compactifications of moduli spaces of broken Morse trajectories and our choice of Novikov group actions. Note that the sphere bubbles in the Gromov compactification do not introduce new strata.
∎
Now we state the technical theorem leading to the definition of the quantum Steenrod operation. Notice that the involved flow categories are already enriched in the category of stratified smooth manifolds, in particular, the category 𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm NC}. Fix an outercollaring width.
Theorem 24.2 (The AMS construction for quantum Steenrod operation).
Fix an outercollaring width.
(1)
For any integral symplectic form Ω\Omega tamed by JJ, there exists a class of lifts (called AMS lifts) of the outercollaring ⌊𝕏ℚ​𝕊​𝕥{}_{\lfloor}{\mathbb{X}}^{\mathbb{QSt}} to ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm NC}, as a multimodule over (𝕄⌊,⋯,𝕄⌊,𝔼⌊;𝕄𝔼⌊)({}_{\lfloor}{\mathbb{M}},\cdots,{}_{\lfloor}{\mathbb{M}},{}_{\lfloor}{{\mathbb{E}}};{}_{\lfloor}{\mathbb{M}}^{{\mathbb{E}}}), which is equivariant with respect to the morphism (24.1) and which is ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant as a weak bimodule.
(2)
Any two AMS lifts of 𝕏ℚ​𝕊​𝕥\mathbb{X}^{\mathbb{QSt}} are equivariantly homotopic. Namely, if 𝕏~0ℚ​𝕊​𝕥\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{0}^{\mathbb{QSt}} and 𝕏~1ℚ​𝕊​𝕥\tilde{\mathbb{X}}_{1}^{\mathbb{QSt}} are both AMS lifts of ⌊𝕏ℚ​𝕊​𝕥{}_{\lfloor}\mathbb{X}^{\mathbb{QSt}}, then there exists a Π𝗉\mathbb{\Pi}_{\sf p}-equivariant lift of the trivial homotopy from ⌊𝕏ℚ​𝕊​𝕥{}_{\lfloor}{\mathbb{X}}^{\mathbb{QSt}} to ⌊𝐝𝐎𝐫𝐛¯rigNC{}_{\lfloor}\underline{\smash{\bf dOrb}}_{\rm rig}^{\rm NC}.
The proof of this theorem is postponed to the end of this section. We first derive the consequence, i.e., the definition of the quantum Steenrod operation.
Remark 24.3.
One can also prove the corresponding result for the comparison of using different JJ’s. We omit the detailed statement.
24.2. Steenrod operations
As the flow categories involved are already transverse, they themselves can be regarded as their FOP transverse perturbations. Then by Theorem N, one can find a (Π×ℤ)⋊ℤ𝗉(\Pi\times{\mathbb{Z}})\rtimes{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-equivariant FOP transverse perturbation of 𝕏~ℚ​𝕊​𝕥\tilde{\mathbb{X}}^{\mathbb{QSt}}, whose isotropy free locus 𝕏̊ℚ​𝕊​𝕥\mathring{\mathbb{X}}^{\mathbb{QSt}} is a multimodule enriched in 𝚿​𝐌𝐚𝐧¯\underline{\smash{{\bf\Psi}{\bf Man}}}. Notice that equivariant feature of Theorem N guarantees that all existing symmetries can be respected by the FOP transverse perturbation.
Then by Proposition 7.18 and Proposition 7.32, one obtains a chain map
Φ~ℚ​𝕊​𝕥:=((C(𝕄)⊗𝐅𝗉^⋯⊗𝐅𝗉^C(𝕄)⏞𝗉)​⊗𝐅𝗉^​C​(𝔼))​⊗ΛΠ𝗉×ℤ​ΛΠ→C⁡(𝕄​#​𝔼).\widetilde{\Phi}^{\mathbb{QSt}}:=\left(\left(\overbrace{C({\mathbb{M}})\widehat{\underset{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}{\otimes}}\cdots\widehat{\underset{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}{\otimes}}C({\mathbb{M}})}^{{\sf p}}\right)\widehat{\underset{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}{\otimes}}C({{\mathbb{E}}})\right)\underset{\Lambda^{\Pi^{{\sf p}}\times{\mathbb{Z}}}}{\otimes}\Lambda^{\mathbb{\Pi}}\to C({\mathbb{M}}\#{{\mathbb{E}}}).
The restriction to the ℤ𝗉{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}-invariant part is denoted by Φℚ​𝕊​𝕥\Phi^{\mathbb{QSt}}.
Proposition 24.4.
Up to chain homotopy, the map Φ~ℚ​𝕊​𝕥\widetilde{\Phi}^{\mathbb{QSt}} does not depend on choices.
Proof.
This follows from Part (2) of Theorem 24.2 and the homotopy case of Theorem N.
∎
It reduces to a linear map between homology, which, in 𝐅𝗉{\bf F}_{\sf p}-coefficients, reads
Φℚ​𝕊​𝕥:Hℤ𝗉​(C​(𝕄)⊗𝗉)→H⁡(𝕄ℤ𝗉).\Phi^{\mathbb{QSt}}:H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(C(\mathbb{M})^{\otimes{\sf p}})\to H(\mathbb{M}^{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}).
One can see that
Hℤ𝗉​(C∗​(𝕄)⊗𝗉)≅Hℤ𝗉​(C​M​(f,g)⊗𝗉)⊗Λ𝐅𝗉Π.H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(C^{*}(\mathbb{M})^{\otimes{\sf p}})\cong H_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{\sf p}}}(CM(f,g)^{\otimes{\sf p}})\otimes\Lambda_{{\bf F}_{\sf p}}^{\Pi}.
Then by pre-composing with the quasi-Frobenius map (23.3) one obtains a map in homology
